title: French C1
description: The fifth step in French, from B2 to CEFR level C1, the level of the DALF C1. Lessons cover choosing a register for every reader, the grammar of spoken French, the formal sentence with inversion and ne used alone, precise verbs and a clean style, the subjunctive in independent clauses and alternatives, the sequence of tenses in every mood, the stylistic values of the tenses, degrees of certainty and distance, fine distinctions in cause, consequence and concession, cohesion in long texts, presupposition, implication and irony, idioms, collocations and support verbs, academic French with quotation and paraphrase, learned word formation, participial clauses and the long sentence, the summary and the compte rendu, the synthèse de documents, the essai argumenté, the exposé, diplomatic debate, following a lecture and taking notes, and the DALF C1. About 620 new words build on the roughly 2,500 core words of French A1 to B2 for about 3,100 in all. Conjugation drills carry every form of A1 to B2, optional honors lessons explore French in Belgium, Switzerland and Québec, slang, professional writing, wordplay, rhetoric, Montaigne, Zola and the Dreyfus affair, Proust and a capstone dossier on spelling reform, and a reading list suggests DALF books, podcasts and free classics for this level. The standard is the French of France; Belgian, Swiss and Québec usage is noted where it differs. Unlocks when French B2 is complete.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Bouquin, livre, ouvrage: choosing a register
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 you met the three levels of French: *familier* (*le boulot, bosser, la bagnole*), *courant*
(*le travail, travailler, la voiture*) and *soutenu* (*l'emploi, exercer, le véhicule*). At B2 you
wrote formal letters. C1 asks for something harder: choosing the level for *this* reader, keeping
it from the first line to the last, and noticing when someone else gets it wrong.

This lesson treats the **[[register]]** (*le niveau de langue*, or *le registre* in linguistics) as a
choice. You'll meet informal and formal words in groups of three, the grammar that marks a register
as clearly as the words do, the rules of *tu* and *vous* at work, and how to repair a message that
slips out of its register. The theme is the world of work: a job interview, a team chat, an email to
HR and an office party. Spoken syntax comes in lesson 02, the formal sentence in 03, precise verbs in
04.

## One request, four readers

Being able to adjust the way you speak and write to the person and the situation is called
**[[sociolinguistic appropriateness]]**. It is one of the things the CEFR expects at C1: not "speaking
formally", but speaking right for the listener.

Here is the same request (Can you send me the report?) to four readers:

- To a colleague you know well, in the team chat: *Tu peux m'envoyer le rapport ? Merci !*
- To your manager, by email: *Pourriez-vous m'envoyer le rapport avant jeudi ? Merci d'avance.*
- To a stranger in another department: *Bonjour, je me permets de vous écrire au sujet du rapport
  annuel. Pourriez-vous me le faire parvenir ?*
- To an administration: *Je vous serais reconnaissant(e) de bien vouloir me transmettre le rapport
  mentionné dans votre courrier du 3 mars.*

Notice what changes: *tu* becomes *vous*; the present (*tu peux*) becomes the conditional (*pourriez-
vous*), then a fixed formula (*je vous serais reconnaissant de bien vouloir*); *envoyer* becomes
*faire parvenir*, then *transmettre*; the sentence gets longer and the context more explicit. None
of these versions is "better". Each one fits one reader, and would sound strange to the others: the
chat line is rude to an administration, and the administration formula sounds cold, even ironic,
to a friend.

![A ladder with three rungs. The bottom rung, labelled familier, holds the message "T'as pigé le truc ? Je suis crevé." The middle rung, courant, holds "Tu as compris l'idée ? Je suis fatigué." The top rung, soutenu, holds "Avez-vous saisi l'enjeu ? Je suis exténué." The register markers are in bold and underlined: t'as, pigé, truc and crevé; tu as, compris and fatigué; avez-vous, saisi, enjeu and exténué. An arrow at the side reads "plus formel", pointing up.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Triplets: three words, three registers

Many everyday ideas have a word at each level. A few you know already; the lesson's new words are
in the left and right columns.

| familier | courant | soutenu |
|---|---|---|
| *un bouquin* | *un livre* | *un ouvrage* |
| *crevé* | *fatigué* | *épuisé, exténué* |
| *bosser* | *travailler* | *exercer (un métier)* |
| *piger* | *comprendre* | *saisir* |
| *se planter* | *se tromper* | *commettre une erreur* |
| *se grouiller* | *se dépêcher* | *se hâter* |
| *chiper* (02) | *voler* | *dérober* |
| *se fringuer* | *s'habiller* | *se vêtir* |
| *rigoler* (02) | *rire* | *s'esclaffer* (burst out laughing) |
| *chez moi* | *chez moi, à la maison* | *à mon domicile* |
| — | *demander, se renseigner* | *s'enquérir de* |

Other informal words of the lesson, each with its neutral partner: *le flic* (*le policier*), *les
fringues* (*les vêtements*), *le gosse* (*l'enfant*), *le toubib* (*le médecin*), *la clope* (*la
cigarette*), *râler* (*se plaindre*). Dictionaries mark them *fam.* (*familier*); words that can
shock are marked *vulg.* (*vulgaire*).

### Why a register word is not a synonym

The three words of a triplet don't always mean the same thing, and they don't combine with the
same words:

- *Un ouvrage* is a substantial or technical book (*un ouvrage de référence*); you wouldn't call a
  holiday thriller *un ouvrage*. *Un bouquin* is any book you read, said casually.
- *Exercer* goes with a profession (*exercer le métier d'avocate*), not with a day at the office:
  ~~j'ai exercé toute la journée~~ → *j'ai travaillé* (or, informally, *j'ai bossé*) *toute la
  journée*.
- *Épuisé* is stronger than *fatigué*: completely drained. *Crevé* covers both, but only in speech.
- *Dérober* suggests stealth: documents or jewels *dérobés*. *Chiper* is for small things, often
  as a joke.

So when you move a text up or down a register, check each word in a dictionary example, not just
in a thesaurus.

## Grammar marks register too

A message can contain no informal word and still sound informal. These features carry the
register:

| feature | familier | courant | soutenu |
|---|---|---|---|
| "we" | *on* | *on* or *nous* | *nous* |
| negation | *je sais pas* | *je ne sais pas* | *je ne sais* (with *savoir, pouvoir, oser, cesser*: lesson 03) |
| question | *Tu viens ?* | *Est-ce que tu viens ?* | *Viens-tu ? Venez-vous ?* |
| "that" | *ça* | *ça, cela* | *cela* |
| sentences | short, unfinished, with *ben, bon, quoi* | complete | longer, with subordinate clauses and nouns |
| reference | *le truc, le machin* | the right noun | the precise noun (*le dispositif*) |

Two of these need care. *On* for "we" is normal in everyday speech and in many emails; in a report or
a formal letter, write *nous*. And the dropped *ne* is so common in speech that keeping it can sound
stiff among friends; in writing, outside a chat message, keep it.

## Tu and vous at work

The choice between *tu* and *vous* is a register choice with social consequences. Using *tu* is
**[[tutoiement]]** (*le tutoiement*, verb *tutoyer*); using *vous* is **[[vouvoiement]]** (*le vouvoiement*,
verb *vouvoyer*).

![A diagram of a workplace seen from "moi", a young employee in the centre, with four figures around: above, on a raised platform and holding a folder, le supérieur hiérarchique; on the right, at a desk, la collègue; on the left, next to a ball, le coéquipier; below, behind a shop counter, la cliente. Arrows marked vous go up to the manager and down to the customer; arrows marked tu go to the colleague and the teammate. A note says that the older or more senior person proposes tu.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In France, as a rule of thumb:

- *Vous* with clients, with people you don't know, with older people and with most managers (*le
  supérieur hiérarchique*), at least at first.
- *Tu* between colleagues of the same level who know each other, in many start-ups and creative
  jobs, in sports clubs, and among students.
- The person of higher status or the older person usually proposes the switch: *On peut se tutoyer,
  si vous voulez.* Proposing it yourself to your manager can be seen as familiarity (*la
  familiarité*), even rudeness.
- Once you have switched, going back to *vous* is cold and signals a conflict.
- Some companies use *tu* from the first day (*le tutoiement est de rigueur*); others keep the
  *vouvoiement* even between people who have worked together for years. Follow the house custom.

In Québec, *tu* is far more widespread, including at work and with strangers of your own age; in
Belgium and Switzerland, usage is close to France's. Honors lesson 04h1 looks at these varieties.

## Register clashes

A **[[register clash]]** is a word or a structure out of line with the rest of the text. It is the
commonest register mistake at C1, because learners know many words but not always their level.

- An informal word in a formal email: *Je vous remercie de votre réponse, mais je n'ai pas pigé la
  deuxième partie.* → *… mais je n'ai pas bien saisi la deuxième partie.*
- An overformal word in a text message to a friend: *Je m'enquiers de ta santé.* → *Ça va mieux ?*
  Used on purpose, the clash is a joke; used by accident, it sounds odd.
- A mixed structure: *Pourriez-vous me dire c'est quand, la réunion ?* → *Pourriez-vous me dire
  quand a lieu la réunion ?*

To repair a clash, change the whole sentence, not one word: a formal verb in an informal sentence
creates a new clash. And keep in mind that a neutral word fits almost everywhere: when in doubt,
choose the *courant* word.

## Swearing: recognise, don't produce

French has many swear words (*les jurons*) and rude words (*les grossièretés*, *les gros
mots*). Recognise the commonest: *merde* (vulgar, about as strong as English "shit", very common)
and *putain* (vulgar, used as an all-purpose exclamation in speech). Words that insult a person are
stronger still. In a foreign language you rarely judge their force correctly, so keep them for
recognition. For your own exclamations, use the mild substitutes everyone accepts: *Mince !*, *Zut
!*, *Punaise !*

Calling a remark *vulgaire* is a strong judgement; *grossier* (rude) and *déplacé* or *inapproprié*
(inappropriate) are the usual words at work. In formal French, *la bienséance* is the set of
unwritten rules of propriety.

## Dialogue: the job interview

Malik Benali applies for a job in an engineering firm. The interviewer, Mme Lefort, moves between
formal and slightly warmer French; Malik keeps to *vous* throughout, as he should.

```dialogue
# L'entretien d'embauche
Mme Lefort: Bonjour, monsieur Benali. Asseyez-vous, je vous en prie. Vous avez trouvé facilement ?
= Good morning, Mr Benali. Do sit down. Did you find us easily?
Malik: Oui, merci. Je suis venu en avance, je craignais les bouchons.
= Yes, thank you. I came early: I was worried about the traffic.
Mme Lefort: Vous avez bien fait. Alors, pourquoi notre entreprise ?
= You were right to. So, why our company?
Malik: J'ai lu votre rapport sur le recyclage des batteries. C'est un domaine où je souhaiterais exercer mes compétences.
= I read your report on battery recycling. It's a field where I would like to use my skills.
Mme Lefort: Et dans votre poste actuel, qu'est-ce qui vous a le plus appris ?
= And in your current job, what has taught you the most?
Malik: Une erreur, honnêtement. La première année, je me suis trompé dans un calcul de coûts. J'ai appris à tout vérifier deux fois.
= A mistake, honestly. In my first year I got a cost calculation wrong. I learned to check everything twice.
Mme Lefort: C'est une réponse que j'apprécie. Dernière question : le tutoiement est la règle chez nous, cela vous gêne ?
= That's an answer I appreciate. Last question: tu is the rule here; does that bother you?
Malik: Pas du tout. Je m'y ferai très vite.
= Not at all. I'll get used to it very quickly.
```

Malik says *je me suis trompé*, not *je me suis planté*: the informal verb would make the same
admission sound careless. He waits for the interviewer to raise the *tutoiement*.

## Reading: a message to the team, and a message to HR

The same news, told twice by Camille, an engineer, after the office party went wrong. Read both and
look for every difference in register.

> Message 1 (team chat)
>
> Salut tout le monde ! Bon, hier soir, au pot de départ de Jacques, ça a un peu dérapé. Vers 22 h,
> quelqu'un a chipé la caisse avec l'argent du cadeau, et on a dû appeler les flics. Ils sont venus,
> ils ont pris nos noms, et ils ont dit qu'ils rappelleraient. Personne a été blessé, heureusement. Pour être honnête, j'ai rien pigé à
> leurs questions, j'étais crevée. Jacques a râlé toute la soirée, le pauvre. Bref, si quelqu'un a vu
> un truc bizarre, dites-le-moi, je fais le lien avec les RH. Et grouillez-vous, ils veulent les
> infos avant vendredi ! Autre chose : la salle était pas fermée à clé, n'importe qui pouvait
> entrer. Je vais proposer qu'on mette quelqu'un à l'entrée la prochaine fois, parce que là, franchement,
> c'était la loose. Ah, et Nadia, t'as oublié ta veste et un bouquin sur la table, je te les garde.
> Merci, la team.
>
> Message 2 (email to the human resources department)
>
> *Objet : incident lors du pot de départ de M. Jacques Morel*
>
> Madame, Monsieur,
>
> Je me permets de vous signaler un incident survenu hier soir, 14 novembre, lors du pot de départ
> de M. Jacques Morel, organisé dans la salle de réunion du deuxième étage.
>
> Vers 22 heures, la caisse contenant la somme collectée pour le cadeau de M. Morel a été dérobée.
> Nous avons immédiatement prévenu la police, qui s'est rendue sur place, a relevé l'identité des
> personnes présentes et nous a indiqué qu'elle reprendrait contact avec nous. Fort heureusement,
> personne n'a été blessé. M. Morel, très
> affecté, a exprimé à plusieurs reprises son mécontentement.
>
> Je vous informe que j'ai invité mes collègues à me transmettre tout élément utile. Je centraliserai
> ces informations et vous les ferai parvenir avant vendredi, conformément à la demande de la police.
>
> Par ailleurs, je souhaiterais attirer votre attention sur un point. La salle n'était pas fermée à
> clé et l'accès à l'étage n'était pas contrôlé. Afin d'éviter qu'un tel incident se reproduise, il me
> semblerait utile qu'une personne soit chargée de l'accueil lors des prochains événements internes.
>
> Je reste à votre disposition pour tout renseignement complémentaire et vous prie d'agréer, Madame,
> Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
>
> Camille Durand, ingénieure, service Batteries

Message 1, to colleagues: last night, at Jacques's leaving drinks, things got out of hand; someone
pinched the cash box with the gift money and the team had to call the police, who took names and
will call back. Camille admits she understood nothing of their questions because she was exhausted;
Jacques grumbled all evening. She asks anyone who saw anything odd to tell her before Friday,
points out that the room wasn't locked, and suggests someone watch the door next time (*c'était la
loose*, slang: it was a mess). She has kept the jacket and book Nadia forgot.

Message 2, to HR: the same facts, in order, with the date, place and time; *dérobée* replaces
*chipé*, *la police* replaces *les flics*, *a exprimé son mécontentement* replaces *a râlé*. The
email leaves out Camille's tiredness (irrelevant to HR), Nadia's jacket and the call to hurry,
and turns the suggestion into a formal proposal (*il me semblerait utile que* + subjunctive). (*Le pot de départ*:
leaving drinks. *Déraper*: to get out of hand. *Survenir*: to happen, formal. *Relever l'identité*:
to take down names. *Le mécontentement*: displeasure.)

### What changed, point by point

1. Greeting and closing: *Salut tout le monde / Merci, la team* → *Madame, Monsieur / je vous prie
   d'agréer …*
2. Words: *chipé → dérobée, les flics → la police, pigé → (left out), râlé → exprimé son
   mécontentement, les infos → ces informations*.
3. Grammar: *on a dû → nous avons*; *j'ai rien pigé* (no *ne*) disappears; the passive *a été
   dérobée* puts the event first and the unknown thief out of sight.
4. Content: the email adds facts (date, place, Mr Morel's surname) and drops feelings and jokes.

## Your turn: shift the register

The assignment below asks you to do what Camille did, with a new message. Work in three passes:
first list the facts, then choose the reader's register for every word and structure, and finally
reread the whole text for one last clash (a *on*, a *ça*, a missing *ne*). Open the assignment to
save your work and use the rubric; you can also draft on paper first.

```assignment
writing: fr5-m1-registre
```

## Common mistakes

- Treating a triplet as three synonyms: ~~exercer au bureau~~, ~~un ouvrage de plage~~. Check what
  the formal word combines with.
- One informal word in a formal text (*pigé, les infos, OK*) or one stiff formula in a chat message.
- Proposing *tu* to a manager or a client yourself. Wait for it to be offered.
- Writing *on* for "we" in a report or a formal letter: use *nous*.
- Repairing a clash with a single word and leaving the informal structure (*c'est quand, la
  réunion ?*).
- Using a swear word you heard in a film: its force is hard to judge from outside.

## Key points

- At C1, register is a choice for a reader: the same request changes for a colleague, a manager, a
  stranger and an administration.
- Triplets (*bouquin / livre / ouvrage, piger / comprendre / saisir*) differ in register and often
  in meaning and collocation.
- Grammar marks register: *on / nous*, *ne*, the form of the question, *ça / cela*, sentence length.
- *Tu* and *vous*: *vous* by default with clients, strangers and most managers; the senior person
  proposes *tu*; follow the house custom. Québec uses *tu* far more.
- A register clash is a word or structure out of line with the text; repair the whole sentence.
- Recognise swear words; for your own use, *mince, zut, punaise*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Ben, genre, du coup: the grammar of spoken French
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Native speakers chatting among themselves are the hardest French a learner hears. The words are
often simple; what changes is the grammar: missing *ne*, sentences built back to front, syllables
swallowed, and little words (*ben, quoi, genre*) that seem to mean nothing. At C1 you need to follow
all of it, and to use some of it yourself with friends without sounding like a textbook or a
caricature.

This lesson describes spoken French as a system with its own rules, first for understanding, then
for careful use in informal settings. The theme is friends and social life: a voice message, a
podcast conversation and a group chat read aloud. Choosing a register is lesson 01; verlan and slang
are honors lesson 04h3.

## The spoken sentence

Five features turn up in almost every informal conversation in France. None of them is a mistake in
speech; all of them are out of place in an essay.

1. No *ne*: *Je sais pas. C'est pas grave. Il y a personne.* The *pas*, *personne* or *jamais*
   carries the negation alone.
2. *Ça* for *cela*, *on* for *nous*: *Ça me plaît. On y va ?* In speech, *nous* as a subject is
   much less common than *on*; it is often a stressed pronoun: *Nous, on reste.*
3. Questions by intonation, with the question word at the end: *Tu pars quand ? Elle habite où ?
   Tu fais quoi ce soir ?* The voice rises; there is no inversion and often no *est-ce que*.
4. *C'est qui qui …, c'est quoi que …* (informal): *C'est qui qui a pris mes clés ?* Careful
   French says *Qui a pris mes clés ?* Recognise it; don't write it.
5. Presentatives that open a sentence: *Y a Paul qui a appelé* (Paul called), *C'est ma sœur qui
   organise*, *Voilà, c'est tout.* They put the new information in its own frame.

## Dislocation: the normal order of speech

At B2 you used **[[dislocation]]** for emphasis: a noun is moved to the front or the end of the sentence
and a pronoun takes its place (*Ce film, je l'ai adoré. Je l'ai adoré, ce film.*). In conversation it
is not emphasis at all: it is the ordinary way to say what you're talking about before saying
something about it.

- *Moi, mon frère, sa voiture, elle est en panne.* — My brother's car has broken down. (Three topics
  stacked, then the sentence.)
- *Les soirées chez Karim, j'y vais plus.* — I don't go to Karim's parties any more.
- *Il est sympa, ton coloc.* — Your flatmate's nice.
- *Le resto, on l'a réservé pour huit heures ?* — Did we book the restaurant for eight?

To understand a dislocated sentence, find the pronoun (*elle, y, il, l'*) and put the fronted noun
back in its place. To write it formally, do the same: *La voiture de mon frère est en panne.*

## Reduced forms: hearing what isn't said

In rapid speech, unstressed syllables drop and words fuse. These **[[reduced forms]]** are what you
actually hear:

| you hear | in full | | you hear | in full |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *chuis* | *je suis* | | *y a* | *il y a* |
| *t'as, t'es* | *tu as, tu es* | | *faut que* | *il faut que* |
| *ch'ais pas* | *je ne sais pas* | | *p't-être* | *peut-être* |
| *i(l) va* ("y va") | *il va* | | *m'sieur* | *monsieur* |
| *j'te dis* | *je te dis* | | *qu'est-ce tu fais ?* | *qu'est-ce que tu fais ?* |

The unstressed *e* (*le, je, de, que*) is the first sound to go: *j'te l'dis*. *Tu* before a vowel
becomes *t'* (*t'as vu ?*), which writing allows only in a chat or when quoting speech. Don't write
these forms in an email or an essay; in a novel they mark a character's voice.

![A sound wave of a voice message, drawn as a band of vertical bars, with the words underneath: "Salut, chuis devant le resto, t'as vu l'heure ? Y a plus de place, faut qu'on se grouille." Four stretches of the wave are shaded and labelled with the reduced form heard there: chuis, t'as, y a and faut que.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A voice message

Inès leaves a message for her friend Léa. Listen line by line, then read the translation.

```dialogue
# Message vocal d'Inès
Inès: Coucou, c'est moi. Bon, ben, chuis devant le resto, là, et t'es pas là.
= Hi, it's me. Right, well, I'm outside the restaurant, and you're not here.
Inès: Y a déjà un monde fou, genre une queue jusqu'au coin de la rue.
= It's already packed, like a queue to the corner of the street.
Inès: Du coup, faut qu'on se grouille, sinon on aura jamais de table.
= So we need to hurry, or we'll never get a table.
Inès: Et il tombe de la flotte, évidemment. J'ai pas de parapluie, j'te dis pas la galère.
= And it's raining, of course. I haven't got an umbrella, you can't imagine the hassle.
Inès: Bref, tu te pointes quand ? Rappelle-moi, quoi. Bisous !
= Anyway, when are you turning up? Call me back, OK? Love!
```

Count the features: no *ne* four times (*t'es pas, on aura jamais, j'ai pas, j'te dis pas*), five
reduced forms (*chuis, t'es, y a, faut que, j'te*), a question word at the end (*tu te pointes quand ?*), and the
markers *bon, ben, genre, du coup, bref, quoi*. *J'te dis pas la galère* (literally "I'm not telling
you the hassle") means "you can't imagine".

## Discourse markers: small words, real jobs

A **[[discourse marker]]** is a word that organises the conversation rather than adding content. Take it
out and the information is the same; the speaker's attitude and the turn-taking are lost.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: What discourse markers do
  accDescr: Four jobs of spoken discourse markers, each with its markers. Hesitating or starting: ben, bah, bon, euh. Agreeing or answering: ouais, carrément, grave, c'est clair. Approximating or quoting: genre, en mode. Closing a turn or summing up: quoi, hein, bref, du coup.
  M[Discourse markers] --> H["Hesitating, starting: ben, bah, bon, euh"]
  M --> A["Agreeing, answering: ouais, carrément, grave, c'est clair"]
  M --> P["Approximating, quoting: genre, en mode"]
  M --> C["Closing a turn, summing up: quoi, hein, bref, du coup"]
```

- *Ben* (also *bah*): hesitation, or "well, obviously": *Ben, je sais pas. Ben oui !*
- *Bon*: opens or closes a topic: *Bon, on y va ? Bon, bref.*
- *Quoi* at the end of a statement: sums up, "you know": *Il est gentil, mais lent, quoi.*
- *Hein*: asks for agreement or attention: *C'est loin, hein ?* (right?) On its own, *Hein ?* is
  a blunt "what?".
- *Genre*: approximation (*genre vingt personnes*, about twenty people), or introducing a
  quotation or an attitude (*Et lui, genre, il s'en fiche*). Very common among young people.
- *En mode* + noun or clause: in a certain mood or manner (*Je suis en mode vacances*; *Il est
  arrivé en mode "c'est moi le chef"*). A recent use, mostly among younger speakers.
- *Du coup* (A2): "so, as a result", now often a simple link or filler. Some speakers find it
  overused.
- *Carrément, grave, c'est clair*: strong agreement: *On y va ? – Carrément ! – Grave !*

Two more you'll hear at once: *bof* (meh, unconvinced) and *t'inquiète* (no worries, from *ne
t'inquiète pas*). *Ça roule* means "all good" or "OK, it's a deal".

## Intensifiers and informal vocabulary

Speech has its own intensifiers: *vachement* (all ages: *vachement bien*), *trop* meaning "very"
among younger speakers (*c'est trop bien*: it's really good, not "too good"), *super, hyper*, and
*grave* after the verb (*j'ai grave faim*). In writing, use *très, vraiment, particulièrement*.

The lesson's informal words, with the neutral word you'd write:

| informal | neutral | | informal | neutral |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *marrant* | *drôle* | | *le resto* | *le restaurant* |
| *se marrer, rigoler* | *rire, s'amuser* | | *le bahut* | *le lycée, le collège* |
| *galérer, la galère* | *avoir du mal, la difficulté* | | *le pif* | *le nez* |
| *le machin* | *le truc, la chose* | | *chiper* | *voler* |
| *se pointer* | *arriver* | | *la flotte* | *l'eau, la pluie* |
| *filer* (give) | *donner* | | *nickel* | *impeccable, parfait* |
| *ouais* | *oui* | | *la tchatche* | *l'aisance à parler* |

*Au pif* means "at a guess": *J'ai répondu au pif.* *Avoir de la tchatche* is to have the gift of the
gab. *Nickel* is invariable: *des chaussures nickel*.

## Reading: a podcast conversation

Two hosts of an invented podcast, *Entre potes*, talk about how friendships change after thirty. The
transcript keeps the features of speech; read it aloud if you can.

> Sami : Bon, aujourd'hui, on parle d'un truc qui nous concerne tous, je pense : les amis après
> trente ans. Toi, Clara, tes potes du bahut, tu les vois encore ?
>
> Clara : Ben… franchement, de moins en moins. Y en a deux que je vois genre une fois par an, à
> Noël, et encore. Les autres, ils ont des gosses, un boulot à l'autre bout de la France… C'est pas
> qu'on s'aime plus, hein, c'est juste que ça s'organise plus, quoi.
>
> Sami : C'est clair. Moi, ce qui m'a frappé, c'est le groupe WhatsApp. Au début, on s'envoyait
> cinquante messages par jour, on se marrait grave. Maintenant, c'est trois photos d'anniversaire et
> un « on se fait un resto bientôt ? » auquel personne répond.
>
> Clara : Le fameux « on se fait un resto » ! C'est marrant, parce que tout le monde dit oui et
> personne propose de date. Du coup, j'ai pris l'habitude de filer directement une date et un lieu.
> Genre : « Samedi 14, chez Mario, 20 h. » Et là, bizarrement, les gens se pointent.
>
> Sami : Ouais, c'est malin. Mais t'as pas peur de passer pour la cheffe ?
>
> Clara : Bof. Je préfère passer pour la cheffe que galérer six mois. Et puis, faut dire, y a
> une chose qu'on oublie : les nouvelles amitiés. Au boulot, au club de foot de mon fils, j'ai
> rencontré des gens vachement bien.
>
> Sami : Ça, c'est vrai. Les amis d'enfance, c'est précieux, mais les amis qu'on choisit à
> quarante ans, ils sont souvent plus proches de ce qu'on est devenu.
>
> Clara : Exactement. Bon, une dernière chose, et après on passe aux messages des auditeurs : la
> règle d'or, pour moi, c'est de pas attendre que l'autre appelle. Si t'as envie de voir quelqu'un,
> appelle. Point.
>
> Sami : T'inquiète, je vais t'appeler. Pour un resto.
>
> Clara : Tu rigoles, mais je vais te prendre au mot !
>
> Sami : Promis. Allez, premier message, celui de Théo, un auditeur de Rennes. Je lis : « Salut !
> Mon meilleur pote, il est parti bosser à Montréal y a trois ans. Depuis, on s'appelle tous les
> dimanches, et franchement, on se parle plus qu'avant. » Ben voilà, Théo, t'as tout compris.
>
> Clara : Comme quoi, la distance, c'est pas forcément le problème. C'est l'habitude qui compte.

Summary, paragraph by paragraph. Sami introduces the subject: friends after thirty. Clara sees her
school friends less and less: two of them once a year; the others have children and jobs far away;
it's not lack of affection but of organisation. Sami notes how the group chat has shrunk to birthday
photos and an unanswered "let's do a restaurant soon". Clara's trick is to send a date and a place
straight away, and then people turn up; she'd rather look bossy than struggle for six months, and
she values new friends from work and her son's football club. Sami agrees that friends chosen later
often fit who we've become; Clara's golden rule is not to wait for the other person to call. Sami
jokes he'll call her for a restaurant, and she says she'll hold him to it. A listener, Théo, writes
that since his best friend left to work in Montréal three years ago they phone every Sunday and
talk more than before; Clara concludes that distance isn't necessarily the problem, habit is.

(*Et encore*: and even that's not certain. *Comme quoi*: which goes to show. *Malin*: clever. *Passer pour*: to come across as. *Faut
dire*: it has to be said. *Prendre quelqu'un au mot*: to take someone at their word.) Notice the
written-language features the speakers keep: *auquel personne répond* is a careful relative, even if
the *ne* is gone; *ce qui m'a frappé, c'est …* is a cleft sentence.

## Worked example: from speech to writing

Clara writes a paragraph for the podcast's website. She keeps the content and changes the grammar.

- Spoken: *Les autres, ils ont des gosses, un boulot à l'autre bout de la France… C'est pas qu'on
  s'aime plus, hein, c'est juste que ça s'organise plus, quoi.*
- Written: *Les autres ont des enfants et un emploi à l'autre bout de la France. Ce n'est pas que
  nous ne nous aimions plus : c'est simplement que les rencontres sont devenues difficiles à
  organiser.*

Five steps: undo the dislocation (*Les autres, ils ont → Les autres ont*); restore *ne* (*ce n'est
pas, ne … plus*); replace informal words (*gosses → enfants, boulot → emploi*); drop the markers
(*hein, quoi*); and turn *on* into *nous* where the text is formal. (*Ce n'est pas que* takes the
subjunctive in careful writing, *que nous ne nous aimions plus*; in speech the indicative is common.)

## Using it yourself

With friends, a few features make you sound natural: dropping *ne* in quick replies (*Je sais pas*),
*on* for "we", questions by intonation, and *ben, bon, quoi* now and then. Don't overdo the markers:
three *genre* in a sentence sounds like an imitation. Keep reduced forms for listening; they come by
themselves when you speak fast. And never carry spoken features into a formal email or an exam text.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *trop* as "too much": *c'est trop bien* = it's really good.
- Taking *quoi* or *hein* at the end as a question word: *C'est fini, quoi* is not "What is finished?"
- Missing the negation when *ne* is gone: *J'ai pas faim* is negative. Listen for *pas, plus,
  jamais, personne, rien*.
- Writing reduced forms (*chuis, t'as, y a*) outside a chat message or a quotation.
- Turning a dislocated sentence into nonsense when you rewrite it: put the noun back where the
  pronoun was.
- Using every marker at once, or using *genre* and *en mode* with people who don't.

## Key points

- Spoken French drops *ne*, uses *ça* and *on*, asks questions by intonation (*Tu pars quand ?*) and
  opens with presentatives (*y a, c'est, voilà*).
- Dislocation (*Moi, mon frère, sa voiture, elle est en panne*) is the ordinary order of speech.
- Reduced forms (*chuis, t'as, y a, faut que, p't-être*) are for hearing, not writing.
- Discourse markers hesitate (*ben, bon*), agree (*carrément, grave, c'est clair*), approximate or
  quote (*genre, en mode*) and close a turn (*quoi, hein, bref*).
- Informal intensifiers: *vachement, trop, grave*; in writing, *très, vraiment*.
- To write it, undo the dislocation, restore *ne*, swap the informal words and drop the markers.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Sans doute a-t-il raison: the formal sentence
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 02 took French apart as people speak it. This lesson goes to the other end of the scale: the
sentence of speeches, official statements, editorials and careful essays. Its words are formal, but
what really marks it is grammar: the subject placed after the verb, *ne* used without *pas*, negations
such as *nullement*, and long sentences that open with an adverbial or an apposition.

You already know some of it: inversion after *ainsi* and *aussi* (B2 17), after *peut-être*, *sans
doute* and *à peine* (B2 20), and *ne … guère* (B1). Here you'll put it together, add the rest of the
formal toolbox, and learn when each device is required and when it is a choice. The theme is
diplomacy and official occasions: a state visit, a treaty signing and an ambassador's address. The
countries and people are invented. The formal letter was B2 22; rhetoric is honors lesson 12h2.

## Stylistic inversion

In a formal sentence the subject can follow the verb after certain words. This is **stylistic
inversion**: the meaning doesn't change, but the sentence belongs to careful writing and formal
speech.

There are two kinds:

- Simple inversion: the verb, then the subject: *Reste la question du financement.*
- Complex inversion (with a noun subject): the noun stays in front, and a pronoun repeating it
  follows the verb with a hyphen: *Sans doute le ministre a-t-il raison.* With a pronoun subject,
  the pronoun simply moves: *Sans doute a-t-il raison.* The *-t-* goes between two vowels, as in
  questions (*a-t-il, signera-t-elle*).

### After adverbs at the head of the clause

| word at the head | meaning | inversion |
|---|---|---|
| *aussi* | therefore | the rule in careful writing: *Aussi la délégation a-t-elle quitté la salle.* (Without inversion, *aussi* at the head reads as "also".) |
| *ainsi* | thus, so | optional: *Ainsi le traité entre-t-il en vigueur* or *Ainsi, le traité entre en vigueur.* |
| *peut-être, sans doute* | perhaps, probably | inversion in writing (*Peut-être viendra-t-il*); in everyday French, *peut-être qu'il viendra*, or the adverb after the verb (*Il viendra peut-être*) |
| *à peine … que* | hardly … when | inversion in writing: *À peine l'avion s'était-il posé que la foule a applaudi.* |
| *du moins* | at least (correcting) | usual in writing: *Du moins le croit-on.* |
| *tout au plus* | at the most | optional: *Tout au plus peut-on espérer un compromis.* |
| *encore* | even so, still | usual when *encore* means "but then": *Encore faut-il que le texte soit ratifié.* (still, it has to be ratified) |

Careful with *sans doute*: in modern French it means "probably", not "without a doubt" (that is *sans aucun
doute*). *Sans doute a-t-il raison* is a polite way of saying he's probably right.

### Rares sont, tel est, reste

Three openings put an adjective or a verb before a noun subject (simple inversion, no pronoun):

- *Rares sont les traités ratifiés aussi vite.* — Few treaties are ratified so quickly.
- *Telle est la position de notre gouvernement.* — Such is our government's position. (*Tel*
  agrees with the subject: *tels sont les faits*.)
- *Reste à savoir si le Parlement suivra.* — It remains to be seen whether Parliament will follow.
  *Restent deux questions.* (*Reste* usually agrees with a plural noun that follows, though the
  invariable *Reste deux questions* is also found.)

### In relative and comparative clauses

After *que, où, comme*, formal French often puts a noun subject after the verb, with simple
inversion and no hyphen:

- *la salle où se tiendra la cérémonie* — the room where the ceremony will be held
- *le traité que signeront les deux chefs d'État* — the treaty the two heads of state will sign
- *comme le rappelait l'ambassadrice* — as the ambassador pointed out

This works only with a noun subject (*comme elle le rappelait*, never ~~comme le rappelait-elle~~),
and best when the verb has no object of its own. Normal order is always correct too: *la salle où la
cérémonie se tiendra*. Inversion here is a matter of rhythm: it puts the heavy noun at the end.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a formal inversion
  accDescr: Start with the word at the head of the clause. If it is aussi meaning therefore, invert. If it is peut-être, sans doute, à peine, du moins or encore, invert in writing. If it is rares sont, tel est or reste, put the adjective or verb before the noun. If the clause starts with que, où or comme and the subject is a noun, inversion is optional. Otherwise keep normal order.
  S[Word at the head of the clause] --> A{"aussi = therefore?"}
  A -- yes --> I1[Invert: aussi a-t-il]
  A -- no --> B{"peut-être, sans doute, à peine, du moins, encore?"}
  B -- yes --> I2[Invert in writing]
  B -- no --> C{"rares sont, tel est, reste?"}
  C -- yes --> I3[Adjective or verb, then noun]
  C -- no --> D{"que, où, comme + noun subject?"}
  D -- yes --> I4[Inversion optional]
  D -- no --> N[Normal order]
```

## Ne alone

In formal French, four verbs can be negated with ***ne* alone**, without *pas*, when they are followed
by an infinitive (or, for *savoir*, by a clause): *cesser, oser, pouvoir, savoir*.

- *Il ne cesse de pleuvoir depuis l'arrivée de la délégation.* — It hasn't stopped raining since …
- *Je n'ose y croire.* — I hardly dare believe it.
- *Je ne peux accepter ces conditions.* (Literary: *je ne puis*.)
- *Je ne sais si le traité sera ratifié.* — I don't know whether …

With these verbs *pas* is still correct and more usual (*il ne cesse pas de pleuvoir*); *ne* alone is
the formal choice. With other verbs, *ne* alone survives only in a few fixed phrases and in older
literature; in your own French, use *pas*: ~~je ne veux accepter~~ → *je ne veux pas accepter*.

A few fixed phrases keep *ne* alone in any register that uses them:

- *si je ne m'abuse* — if I'm not mistaken
- *Il y a longtemps que je ne l'ai vu.* — I haven't seen him for a long time. (Also *que je ne l'ai
  pas vu*.)
- *Que ne l'avez-vous dit plus tôt !* — Why didn't you say so earlier! (literary: *que* = why)

### Je ne saurais: the polite refusal

The conditional of *savoir* with *ne* alone means "I could not possibly". It is the diplomat's way of
saying no firmly and politely:

- *Je ne saurais accepter une telle proposition.* — I could not possibly accept such a proposal.
- *Je ne saurais vous dire à quelle heure il arrivera.* — I really couldn't tell you …

## Formal negation

| formal | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *ne … nullement* | not at all, in no way | *Cette visite ne signifie nullement un changement de politique.* |
| *ne … aucunement* | in no way, not in the least | *Nous n'avons aucunement l'intention de nous retirer.* |
| *ne … guère* (B1) | hardly, scarcely | *Il ne reste guère de temps.* |
| *ne … point* | not (literary) | *Je ne le crois point.* (recognition: classical texts, some speeches) |

*Nullement* and *aucunement* replace *pas*: never ~~ne … pas nullement~~. Both can stand alone as a
reply: *Vous opposez-vous à ce texte ? – Nullement.* This is **[[formal negation]]**: stronger than *pas
du tout*, and colder.

## The vocabulary of ceremonies

At a state visit (*une visite officielle*, or *une visite d'État* for the most formal kind), *le chef
d'État* (*la cheffe d'État* for a woman) is received by his or her counterpart. *Le protocole*
decides who enters first, where everyone sits and who speaks: the order of precedence is *la
préséance*. An ambassador (*l'ambassadeur, l'ambassadrice*) leads the embassy; *la délégation* is the
group sent to negotiate; *les dignitaires* are the senior guests. The two countries sign *un traité*,
which each parliament must then *ratifier*.

The adjectives of the occasion: *solennel* (solemn: *une cérémonie solennelle*), *diplomatique*,
*courtois*. Pronunciation: in *solennel* and *la solennité*, the first *e* sounds like *a*: so-la-nel,
so-la-ni-té. A speaker may *faire l'éloge de* someone (praise them), show *déférence* (deference) to
a senior guest, or treat the hosts with *courtoisie*. Some verbs: *cesser* (formal for *arrêter*),
*daigner* (to deign, often ironic: *Il n'a pas daigné répondre*), *s'abstenir* (to abstain, to refrain
from: *trois pays se sont abstenus*).

![A state-visit scene. In the centre, two heads of state shake hands behind a table on which lies an open document between two pens. On the left, a woman with a sash and a folder stands in front of a group of three people in dark suits. On the right, a man with an earpiece and a clipboard. In the background, a row of seated guests between two flags. Labels: les chefs d'État, le traité, l'ambassadrice, la délégation, le chef du protocole, les dignitaires.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The rhythm of the formal sentence

Formal sentences are longer, but not heavier. Two devices give them shape:

- A fronted adverbial, which sets the scene before the main clause: *Au terme de deux jours
  d'entretiens, les deux délégations sont parvenues à un accord.*
- An apposition, a noun or participle group placed beside the subject: *Arrivée dans la
  matinée, la présidente a été accueillie par le chef du protocole. Fidèle à sa tradition, notre pays
  …*

Both let you put the background first and keep the main clause short. In careful writing a participle
in apposition refers to the subject: ~~Arrivée dans la matinée, le chef du protocole l'a accueillie~~
attaches *arrivée* to *le chef du protocole*, as if he had arrived (and the feminine participle
doesn't even agree with him).

## Dialogue: preparing the ceremony

The chef du protocole briefs a young diplomat (*une jeune diplomate*) the evening before the signing.

```dialogue
# La veille de la signature
Le chef du protocole: Demain, la présidente entrera la première, suivie du chef de la délégation varonienne.
= Tomorrow the president will enter first, followed by the head of the Varonian delegation.
La diplomate: Et l'ambassadrice ? Elle souhaitait prononcer une allocution.
= And the ambassador? She wanted to give an address.
Le chef du protocole: Elle parlera après les deux chefs d'État. Tel est l'ordre de préséance, et je ne saurais le modifier.
= She'll speak after the two heads of state. That is the order of precedence, and I couldn't possibly change it.
La diplomate: Les journalistes demandent si le traité sera ratifié avant l'été.
= The journalists are asking whether the treaty will be ratified before the summer.
Le chef du protocole: Sans doute le sera-t-il. Encore faut-il que le Parlement varonien se réunisse à temps.
= It probably will be. Still, the Varonian parliament has to meet in time.
La diplomate: Le chef de l'opposition varonienne a annoncé que son groupe s'abstiendrait.
= The leader of the Varonian opposition has announced that his group would abstain.
Le chef du protocole: Il n'a pas daigné nous en informer. Cela ne change nullement notre programme.
= He didn't deign to tell us. That in no way changes our programme.
```

## Reading: an ambassador's address

The ambassador of Norvalie, an invented country, speaks at the signing of a treaty with the
Republic of Varonie, another one.

> Monsieur le Président de la République, Madame la Présidente, Mesdames et Messieurs les
> ambassadeurs, Mesdames et Messieurs,
>
> C'est un honneur, et je dirais même une émotion, de prendre la parole en ce jour où s'achèvent
> trois années de négociations. Rares sont les accords qui auront demandé autant de patience ; plus
> rares encore sont ceux qui auront été conduits dans un tel climat de courtoisie. Que les deux
> délégations en soient ici remerciées.
>
> Permettez-moi tout d'abord de faire l'éloge de celui sans qui ce traité n'existerait pas. Arrivé en
> Varonie au cœur d'une crise diplomatique, mon prédécesseur, M. Anton Lisek, n'a jamais cessé de
> croire au dialogue. Il ne lui a pas été donné de voir ce jour ; du moins sa méthode lui
> survivra-t-elle.
>
> Ce traité, Mesdames et Messieurs, ne règle pas tout. Il ne prétend nullement effacer un siècle de
> méfiance. Tout au plus pose-t-il les bases d'une coopération : l'ouverture de nos frontières aux
> étudiants, un fonds commun pour la recherche, une commission chargée de veiller à son application.
> Encore faudra-t-il que nos deux parlements le ratifient, et je n'ose imaginer qu'ils puissent s'y
> refuser.
>
> À la jeunesse de nos deux pays, je voudrais adresser un mot particulier. C'est pour elle, avant
> tout, que ce texte a été écrit. Dès la rentrée prochaine, quelque deux mille étudiants pourront
> suivre une partie de leur cursus de l'autre côté de la frontière. Peut-être certains d'entre eux
> deviendront-ils, à leur tour, diplomates ; du moins auront-ils appris à se connaître avant d'avoir
> à négocier. Il n'est guère de meilleure garantie de paix.
>
> Certains, de part et d'autre, auraient préféré que nous attendions. Je respecte leur prudence, mais
> je ne saurais la partager. Attendre, c'eût été laisser à d'autres le soin de décider à notre place.
> Aussi nos gouvernements ont-ils choisi d'agir.
>
> Comme le rappelait ce matin Madame la Présidente, la diplomatie n'est pas l'art d'éviter les
> désaccords, mais celui de les rendre utiles. Telle est, je crois, la leçon de ces trois années.
>
> Je tiens enfin à remercier nos hôtes varoniens pour la qualité de leur accueil. Le protocole a
> été, comme toujours, d'une précision remarquable, et la solennité de cette cérémonie dit assez
> l'importance que nos deux peuples attachent à ce jour.
>
> Je vous remercie.

Summary, paragraph by paragraph. The ambassador opens with the formal list of address. She calls the
day an honour and an emotion, ending three years of negotiations: few agreements needed so much
patience, fewer still were conducted with such courtesy, and she thanks both delegations. She praises
her predecessor, who arrived in a diplomatic crisis and never stopped believing in dialogue; he did
not live to see the day, but at least his method will outlive him. The treaty doesn't solve
everything or erase a century of mistrust; at most it lays the foundations of cooperation (open
borders for students, a joint research fund, a commission to oversee it), and both parliaments still
have to ratify it. She addresses the young: from next autumn about two thousand students will study
part of their course across the border; perhaps some will become diplomats, and at least they will
know each other before they have to negotiate, the best guarantee of peace. Some wanted to wait; she respects their caution but cannot share it, since waiting
would have let others decide; so the governments chose to act. As the president said that morning,
diplomacy makes disagreements useful rather than avoiding them. She thanks the hosts: the protocol was
precise and the solemnity of the ceremony shows how much the day matters.

(*De part et d'autre*: on both sides. *C'eût été*: it would have been, the conditionnel passé
deuxième forme: recognition only; everyday French says *ç'aurait été*. *Veiller à*: to see to.)
Count the formal devices: inversions after adverbs (*du moins* twice, *tout au plus, encore,
peut-être, aussi*),
*rares sont, telle est*, an inversion after *comme*, an inversion in a relative (*où s'achèvent*),
*ne … nullement*, *ne … guère*, *n'ose imaginer* and *je ne saurais*. (*Il n'est guère de* … =
there is hardly any …, formal.)

## Common mistakes

- *Aussi* at the head without inversion: *Aussi nous avons décidé* reads as "Also, we decided".
  Write *Aussi avons-nous décidé* for "therefore".
- Forgetting the pronoun in complex inversion: *Sans doute le ministre a raison* is found, but careful
  writing prefers *Sans doute le ministre a-t-il raison*; *Le ministre a sans doute raison* is always
  safe. Never ~~Sans doute a le ministre raison~~.
- Reading *sans doute* as "without a doubt". It means "probably".
- Inverting a pronoun after *comme* or *que*: ~~comme le disait-il~~ → *comme il le disait*.
- *Ne* alone with any verb: only *cesser, oser, pouvoir, savoir* (and the fixed phrases).
- Adding *pas* to *nullement* or *aucunement*.
- Saying *so-lèn-nel*: it is so-la-nel.

## Key points

- Stylistic inversion follows *aussi* (therefore: the rule), *peut-être, sans doute, à peine, du
  moins, encore* (in writing) and is optional after *ainsi* and *tout au plus*.
- With a noun subject use complex inversion: *Sans doute le ministre a-t-il raison.*
- *Rares sont …, Tel est …, Reste …* put the noun subject last.
- After *que, où, comme*, a noun subject may follow the verb: *comme le rappelait l'ambassadrice*.
- *Ne* alone with *cesser, oser, pouvoir, savoir*: *Il ne cesse de pleuvoir. Je ne saurais accepter.*
- *Ne … nullement, ne … aucunement*: in no way; *ne … point* is literary.
- Fronted adverbials and appositions give the formal sentence its rhythm; a participle in apposition
  refers to the subject.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Effectuer, élaborer, recenser: precision and variety in writing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A B2 text is correct and clear. A C1 text is also precise: each verb says exactly what happens, the
same word doesn't come back three times in a paragraph, nothing is said twice, and the sentences vary
in length and shape. Markers at the DALF C1 look at the range and precision of your vocabulary as
well as its accuracy.

This lesson gives you the tools: precise verbs to replace the all-purpose ones, ways to avoid
repetition, the redundancies to cut, ways to lighten a heavy sentence, and the editor's final pass on
a draft. The theme is writing and publishing: a manuscript, an editor's feedback and a publishing
house. Cohesion devices such as *ce dernier* are lesson 11; collocations with support verbs (*prendre
une décision, porter plainte*) are lesson 14.

## Replacing the all-purpose verbs

*Faire, dire, mettre, avoir, être, il y a* and *donner* fit almost any sentence; that is their
weakness. An **[[all-purpose verb]]** (*un verbe passe-partout*) tells the reader little, and three in a
paragraph make a text sound like a first draft. Replace them with a verb that names the action:

| all-purpose | precise | example |
|---|---|---|
| *faire un paiement* | *effectuer* | *Le virement a été effectué le 3 mars.* |
| *faire une vérification* | *procéder à* | *L'éditrice a procédé à une dernière vérification.* |
| *faire un plan* | *élaborer, dresser* | *élaborer une stratégie, dresser une liste* |
| *faire une tâche* | *accomplir, mener à bien* | *accomplir une mission* |
| *commencer à faire* | *entreprendre* | *Il a entrepris une biographie de mille pages.* |
| *dire une règle* | *énoncer, formuler* (B1) | *La préface énonce les principes de la collection.* |
| *donner son avis* | *émettre* (B2), *exprimer* | *émettre un avis, des réserves* |
| *avoir trois parties* | *comporter, compter* | *Le roman comporte trois parties.* |
| *avoir un record, des droits* | *détenir* | *La maison détient les droits de traduction.* |
| *faire un métier* | *exercer* | *Elle exerce le métier de correctrice.* |
| *être* (= form, amount to) | *constituer, représenter* | *Ce texte constitue la première version du roman.* |
| *faire la liste de* | *recenser* | *recenser les erreurs, les besoins* |
| *mettre plus de détails* | *étoffer* | *Il faudrait étoffer votre conclusion.* |

Three cautions. First, precise verbs are often formal: *effectuer* and *procéder à* belong to reports
and administrative letters, not to a friendly email (lesson 01). Second, they are not all
interchangeable: *dresser* goes with *une liste*, *élaborer* with *un plan*, and *accomplir* with *une
tâche* but not with a payment (~~accomplir un paiement~~). Check the dictionary examples. Third, *faire* is not banned: *faire une
erreur, faire attention, faire partie de* are perfectly good French.

## Avoiding repetition

French style dislikes repeating a noun in neighbouring sentences more than English does. There are
four ways round it:

1. A synonym (*un synonyme*): *le manuscrit … le texte*; *l'éditrice … la responsable de la collection*. Beware of
   false synonyms that shift the meaning (a *bouquin* is not an *ouvrage*: lesson 01).
2. A **[[hyperonym]]**, a more general word that covers the first: *le roman → l'ouvrage, le livre*;
   *la tulipe → la fleur*. The general word usually comes after the specific one, once the reader knows what it refers to.
3. A pronoun: *le manuscrit … il …*; *le, la, en, y*; *celui-ci*.
4. Nominalisation (B2 14): *L'auteur a corrigé son texte. Cette correction a pris trois mois.*

Here is a paragraph that repeats itself, then a version that doesn't:

- *L'auteur a envoyé son manuscrit à une maison d'édition. La maison d'édition a lu le manuscrit et a
  trouvé que le manuscrit était trop long. La maison d'édition a demandé à l'auteur de couper cent
  pages.*
- *L'auteur a envoyé son manuscrit à une maison d'édition. Le comité de lecture, qui l'a trouvé trop
  long, lui a demandé de couper cent pages.*

The second version uses a more precise subject (*le comité de lecture*), a relative clause and two
pronouns (*l', lui*): thirty-six words become twenty-five.

## Redundancy and pleonasm

**[[Redundancy]]** (*la redondance*) is saying again what the text has already said: a second sentence
that repeats the first in other words, or *en conclusion, pour conclure* one after the other. A
**[[pleonasm]]** (*le pléonasme*) is redundancy inside one phrase: two words that mean the same thing.

| pleonasm | why | correct |
|---|---|---|
| *monter en haut, descendre en bas* | *monter* already means going up | *monter, descendre* |
| *prévoir à l'avance* | *prévoir* is "to foresee" | *prévoir* |
| *un hasard imprévu* | chance is unforeseen | *un hasard* |
| *collaborer ensemble* | *collaborer* includes "together" | *collaborer* |
| *voire même* | *voire* already means "or even" (common, but criticised) | *voire* or *et même* |
| *car en effet* | two connectors for one cause | *car* or *en effet* |
| *au jour d'aujourd'hui* | *aujourd'hui* already contains *jour* | *aujourd'hui, à l'heure actuelle* |

The last one needs a word of nuance: *au jour d'aujourd'hui* is common in speech, often for emphasis
or as a joke, and usage guides criticise it. Avoid it in writing; don't correct a speaker for it.
Some pleonasms are accepted as emphasis: *Je l'ai vu de mes propres yeux.* In writing, a pleonasm
looks like carelessness; a redundant paragraph (*un paragraphe redondant*) looks like padding.

## Lightening a heavy sentence

Heaviness (*la lourdeur*) usually comes from piling up the same structure: three relative clauses,
four *de* in a row, or a string of *que*.

- Heavy: *Le livre que l'auteur qui a reçu le prix que la critique attendait a publié est déjà
  épuisé.*
- Lighter: *Lauréat du prix tant attendu par la critique, l'auteur voit déjà son livre épuisé.*

To lighten (*alléger*) a sentence, try in this order:

1. Split it in two.
2. Replace a relative clause with an adjective, a participle or an apposition: *l'auteur, lauréat du
   prix, …*
3. Replace *que* + clause with an infinitive when the subject is the same: *Il pense qu'il finira →
   Il pense finir.*
4. Turn a chain of *de* into a verb: *la date de remise de la version définitive du manuscrit → la
   date à laquelle l'auteur remettra son manuscrit définitif.*

## Concision, clarity and rhythm

Concision (*la concision*) is saying a lot in few words; it is a quality, not just shortness. A
concise text (*un texte concis*) has no empty phrases (*il est important de noter que, dans le cadre
de, au niveau de*) and no redundancy. But concision isn't density: a paragraph of noun groups with
no verbs is short and hard to read. Aim for *la clarté* first.

Vary the rhythm. A long sentence followed by a short one gives weight to the short one. Vary the
openings, too: not every sentence should start with its subject. Begin some with a time phrase, a
connector, a participle or a complement: *Trois mois plus tard, … Sans attendre la réponse, … Ce
roman, elle l'a réécrit quatre fois.* A text that flows (*un style fluide*) has no jolts; a title
or a final sentence that strikes (*percutant*) uses few, concrete words.

## The editor's pass

Before sending a text, reread it as an editor would, in several passes, each looking for one thing:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The editor's pass on a draft
  accDescr: Five passes in order. First, content and plan, checking that each paragraph has one idea. Second, register, checking every word and structure suits the reader. Third, repetition and redundancy, replacing repeated nouns and cutting pleonasms. Fourth, heavy sentences, splitting or lightening them. Fifth, typos and agreement, reading slowly for misprints, accents and agreements.
  P1[1. Content and plan: one idea per paragraph] --> P2[2. Register: right for the reader]
  P2 --> P3[3. Repetition and redundancy]
  P3 --> P4[4. Heavy sentences: split or lighten]
  P4 --> P5[5. Typos, accents and agreement]
```

The last pass is slow reading for *les coquilles*, the misprints: a missing accent, a doubled word,
*ces* for *ses*, a participle that doesn't agree. In publishing, *la coquille* is the classic word for
a typo.

![A typed manuscript page, "Chapitre 3", with an editor's marks in red. The misspelt word "mmer" is circled and linked to a margin box reading la coquille; the sentence "Le temps était froid ce matin-là", which repeats the one before it, is circled and linked to la redondance; "monter en haut" is circled and linked to le pléonasme; a long sentence with three relative clauses is underlined with a wavy line and linked to la lourdeur.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: an editor's letter

Hélène Marchal, an editor at an invented publishing house, writes to a first-time author about her
manuscript.

> Chère Madame Roussel,
>
> Le comité de lecture des Éditions du Phare a examiné avec attention votre manuscrit, *Les Saisons
> de Kerlan*, et je suis heureuse de vous annoncer qu'il souhaite le publier dans notre collection
> « Premiers romans ». Avant de procéder à la mise en page, je voudrais toutefois vous soumettre
> quelques remarques.
>
> Votre roman comporte trois parties d'inégale longueur. La première constitue, de l'avis général,
> la plus réussie : le style y est fluide, les dialogues sont vifs et le personnage de la grand-mère
> s'impose dès les premières pages. La deuxième partie, en revanche, souffre de certaines lourdeurs.
> J'ai recensé une quinzaine de phrases qui dépassent cinq lignes et qui enchaînent les relatives ;
> je vous propose de les alléger, en les coupant ou en remplaçant une relative par une apposition.
>
> Vous trouverez également, en marge, les redondances que nous avons relevées. Plusieurs
> paragraphes redisent ce que le lecteur sait déjà, et deux ou trois pléonasmes se sont glissés dans
> le texte (« prévoir à l'avance », « collaborer ensemble »). Rien de grave, mais un texte plus concis
> gagnera en force. À l'inverse, la conclusion me paraît un peu mince : il faudrait l'étoffer, car
> le lecteur quitte Kerlan trop vite.
>
> J'ai aussi remarqué que certains mots reviennent très souvent : « maison » apparaît onze fois dans
> le premier chapitre. Un synonyme, un pronom ou une tournure différente suffiront le plus souvent ;
> mais ne sacrifiez pas la précision à la variété : la maison de Kerlan est un lieu, pas un simple
> « bâtiment ».
>
> Le titre, enfin, fait débat au sein de l'équipe. Certains le trouvent poétique ; d'autres
> aimeraient une formule plus percutante pour la couverture. Je ne vous impose rien, mais je vous
> invite à réfléchir à deux ou trois propositions.
>
> Pour la suite, nous avons élaboré le calendrier suivant : vous nous remettrez la version révisée
> d'ici au 15 mars ; notre correctrice, qui exerce ce métier depuis vingt ans, effectuera ensuite une
> relecture complète, et vous recevrez les épreuves début avril. Elle traquera les dernières
> coquilles, mais je compte sur vous pour vérifier les noms propres et les dates, que nous ne
> connaissons pas aussi bien que vous.
>
> Je mesure le travail que je vous demande. Vous avez accompli l'essentiel : il reste à donner à
> votre texte toute la clarté qu'il mérite. Je reste à votre disposition pour en parler de vive voix.
>
> Bien cordialement,
>
> Hélène Marchal, éditrice

Summary, paragraph by paragraph. The reading committee wants to publish the manuscript in its "first
novels" series; before layout, the editor has some remarks. The novel has three unequal parts: the
first is the best (flowing style, lively dialogue, a strong grandmother), the second is heavy, with
about fifteen sentences of more than five lines strung together with relatives, to be cut or
lightened. The margins show redundancies and a few pleonasms; a more concise text will be stronger,
but the ending is thin and should be fleshed out. Some words come back too often (*maison* eleven
times in chapter one): a synonym, a pronoun or a new turn of phrase will do, but precision matters
more than variety. The team is divided over the title, and the editor
asks for two or three punchier alternatives. Timetable: revised version by 15 March, then a full
proofread by a proofreader with twenty years' experience, proofs in early April; the author should
check names and dates. The author has done the essential work; what remains is clarity.

(*La mise en page*: layout. *Les épreuves*: proofs. *Traquer*: to hunt down. *De vive voix*: in
person. *Bien cordialement*: a warm but professional closing, usual in emails and letters between
professionals who know each other.)

## Dialogue: on the phone with the editor

```dialogue
# Au téléphone
Mme Roussel: J'ai bien reçu votre lettre. Pour le titre, je comprends, mais j'y tiens beaucoup.
= I got your letter. About the title, I understand, but I'm very attached to it.
Mme Marchal: Je ne vous demande pas d'y renoncer. Il faudrait seulement un sous-titre plus percutant.
= I'm not asking you to give it up. We just need a punchier subtitle.
Mme Roussel: Et la traduction ? Une agence italienne m'a contactée.
= And the translation? An Italian agency has contacted me.
Mme Marchal: Selon votre contrat, c'est nous qui détenons les droits de traduction. Transmettez-moi leur message, je m'en occupe.
= Under your contract, we hold the translation rights. Forward me their message, I'll deal with it.
Mme Roussel: Entendu. Je vous envoie la version révisée avant le 15 mars.
= Understood. I'll send you the revised version before 15 March.
```

## Worked example: an editor's pass on one paragraph

The draft:

> *Au jour d'aujourd'hui, il y a beaucoup de gens qui font des livres. Il y a des gens qui font des
> livres pour gagner de l'argent et il y a des gens qui font des livres parce qu'ils aiment écrire.
> Les maisons d'édition reçoivent beaucoup de manuscrits et elles ne peuvent pas publier tous les
> manuscrits qu'elles reçoivent.*

1. Cut the pleonasm: *Au jour d'aujourd'hui → Aujourd'hui*.
2. Replace the all-purpose verbs: *font des livres → écrivent*; *il y a des gens qui → certains …
   d'autres*.
3. Remove the repetition: the second *manuscrits* becomes *tous*.
4. Vary the rhythm and the openings.

> *Aujourd'hui, on n'a jamais autant écrit. Certains auteurs cherchent un revenu ; d'autres
> écrivent par plaisir. Submergées de manuscrits, les maisons d'édition ne peuvent pas tous les
> publier.*

The result is half as long and keeps the content. The participle *Submergées* in apposition refers
to *les maisons d'édition*, the subject.

## Common mistakes

- Swapping *faire* for a precise verb that doesn't fit: ~~accomplir un paiement~~ → *effectuer un
  paiement*.
- Using formal verbs (*effectuer, procéder à*) in a friendly message.
- Using a hyperonym before the specific word: usually *le roman* first, *l'ouvrage* after.
- Pleonasms: *monter en haut, prévoir à l'avance, voire même, car en effet*.
- Mistaking concision for density: a sentence of five noun groups and no verb.
- Rereading once for everything. Reread in passes, the last one slowly, for *coquilles*.

## Key points

- Replace all-purpose verbs with precise ones: *effectuer, procéder à, élaborer, accomplir,
  entreprendre, énoncer, comporter, détenir, exercer, constituer, recenser, étoffer*. Check what each
  combines with.
- Avoid repetition with a synonym, a hyperonym, a pronoun or a nominalisation.
- Cut redundancy and pleonasms; *au jour d'aujourd'hui* is common in speech but criticised.
- Lighten a heavy sentence: split it, use an apposition, a participle or an infinitive, turn a chain
  of *de* into a verb.
- Concise is not dense: aim for clarity, vary sentence length and openings.
- Reread in passes: content, register, repetition, heaviness, then typos and agreement.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Septante, la tuque, la votation: French in Belgium, Switzerland and Québec
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 was about register: the same speaker choosing *bouquin*, *livre* or *ouvrage* for different
readers. This lesson is about a different kind of variation: the French of different places. A
Belgian civil servant, a Swiss teacher and a Québec journalist all write standard French, and all of
them also use words that a reader in Paris may not know. A **[[regionalism]]** (*un régionalisme*) is a
word, sense or construction used in one French-speaking area and not in the others.

At B1 you met *septante, nonante, le souper, le dépanneur, magasiner, le chum, le kot, la drache* and
*le natel*. Here you'll go further: what really differs between France, Belgium, Switzerland and
Québec, what doesn't, the bodies that advise on French in each, and how to read a message from each
place. None of these varieties is better or worse than another: each is the standard of its own
speakers. Slang is a separate subject (honors 04h3).

## Three kinds of regionalism

Linguists name regionalisms after their area: a **[[Belgicism]]** (*un belgicisme*), a **[[helvetism]]**
(*un helvétisme*, from *Helvetia*, the Latin name of Switzerland) and a **[[Québécism]]** (*un
québécisme*). They come in three kinds:

- A word that doesn't exist in France: *la panosse* (Switzerland: floorcloth), *la tuque* (Québec:
  woolly hat).
- A French word with another sense: *la tirette* is a zip in Belgium (also heard in Switzerland and
  Alsace) but only a pull tab, a pull cord or a pull-out shelf in most of France; *le char* is a car in informal Québec French, a chariot or a tank in France; *tantôt*
  means "later today" in Belgium and Québec.
- A different word for an institution: *le bourgmestre* (Belgium: mayor), *la votation*
  (Switzerland: a vote by the people on a question).

```map
base: world
title: A word from each place
view: fit
point: Paris (le portable, la serpillière) | 48.86, 2.35 | France
point: Bruxelles (le GSM, le bourgmestre) | 50.85, 4.35 | Belgique
point: Liège (la tirette, à tantôt) | 50.63, 5.57 | Belgique
point: Genève (le natel, la votation) | 46.20, 6.14 | Suisse romande
point: Lausanne (la panosse, huitante) | 46.52, 6.63 | Suisse romande
point: Montréal (le cellulaire, le char) | 45.50, -73.57 | Québec
point: Québec (la tuque, magasiner) | 46.81, -71.21 | Québec
caption: Simplified: each word is used in the whole area of its group, not only in the city shown, and several are understood elsewhere.
```

## Vocabulary: one thing, four words

| France | Belgium | Switzerland | Québec |
|---|---|---|---|
| *le portable* | *le GSM* | *le natel* | *le cellulaire, le cell* |
| *le maire* | *le bourgmestre* | *le syndic* (some cantons), *le maire* | *le maire* |
| *la fermeture éclair* | *la tirette* | *la fermeture éclair*, also *la tirette* | *la fermeture éclair* |
| *la serpillière* | *la serpillière*, regional *la loque* | *la panosse* | *la serpillière* |
| *le bonnet* | *le bonnet* | *le bonnet* | *la tuque* |
| *la voiture* | *la voiture* | *la voiture* | *l'auto*, informal *le char* |
| *à tout à l'heure* | *à tantôt* | *à tout à l'heure* | *à tantôt*, *à tout à l'heure* |
| *soixante-dix, quatre-vingt-dix* | *septante, nonante* | *septante, huitante* (some cantons), *nonante* | *soixante-dix, quatre-vingt-dix* |
| *le petit-déjeuner, le déjeuner, le dîner* | *le déjeuner, le dîner, le souper* | *le déjeuner, le dîner, le souper* | *le déjeuner, le dîner, le souper* |

Three notes on the table. *Le GSM* (pronounced gé-èsse-èm) comes from the name of the mobile network
standard. *Huitante* is heard in some Swiss cantons (Vaud, Valais, Fribourg); Geneva and the rest
say *quatre-vingts*. And the meal names are a trap for visitors: in Belgium, Switzerland and Québec,
*le dîner* is lunch and *le souper* is dinner, as they once were everywhere in France.

## Grammar and usage: a few differences

The grammar of the written standard is the same everywhere. A few spoken features differ:

- Belgium: *savoir* is used where France says *pouvoir* for ability or possibility: *Je ne sais
  pas venir demain* (= *je ne peux pas venir*); *Ma voiture ne sait pas démarrer.* In France, *savoir*
  + infinitive is mostly a learned skill (*Elle sait nager*), apart from the formal *je ne saurais*
  (lesson 03); *savoir* for a one-off possibility is Belgian. Belgians also say *s'il vous plaît* when
  handing something over, where people in France say *voilà* or *tenez*.
- Québec: *tu* is far more widespread than in France, with strangers of your age, in shops and at
  work. In speech, questions often take the particle *-tu*: *Tu viens-tu ?* (are you coming?), *C'est-
  tu loin ?* (is it far?). Recognise it; it is informal and you don't need to use it. And *bienvenue*
  answers *merci* (you're welcome), where France says *de rien* or *je vous en prie*.
- Everywhere: regional French uses *tantôt, septante* or *le souper* in every register: they are
  not informal words. *Le char*, on the other hand, is informal in Québec itself.

### Pronunciation, in general terms

Accents differ more than words. Québec French has strong vowels and, before *i* and *u*, turns *t*
and *d* into *ts* and *dz* (*tu* sounds close to "tsu", *dire* close to "dzire"). Many Belgian and
Swiss speakers keep distinctions that most speakers in France have lost, such as a longer vowel at
the end of a feminine word (*aimée* vs *aimé*) and the vowels of *brin* and *brun*. This course's voice is from France, so you won't hear
these accents here: radio from Brussels, Geneva and Montréal is the best practice.

## What doesn't differ

The written standard is shared. A report from Brussels, an article in a Geneva daily and a Québec
government page follow the same spelling, grammar and conventions as a text from Paris, with a few
local words. The DALF C1 is the same exam in every country. For you, this means: write the French of
France (this course's standard), recognise the main regionalisms, and never correct a Belgian, Swiss
or Québec speaker for using their own.

## Who advises on French

Each area has public bodies that watch over the language. They advise and publish; none of them
tells private people how to speak (the OQLF's legal powers concern businesses, public signs and the
workplace).

- Québec: the *Office québécois de la langue française* (OQLF), created in 1961 as the *Office de
  la langue française*, applies the *Charte de la langue française*, the law of 1977 that makes French
  the official language of Québec. It publishes the *Banque de dépannage linguistique* and the *Grand
  dictionnaire terminologique*, which proposes French terms for new things (*le courriel* for email).
  Terminology is lesson 16h1.
- Belgium (Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles): the *Conseil de la langue française et de la politique
  linguistique* advises the government on language policy and on how French is changing; the
  Fédération's administration also publishes usage guides, for example on feminine job titles.
- Switzerland: the *Délégation à la langue française* (DLF), created in 1992 under the
  intercantonal conference of public education of French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino (CIIP),
  represents Swiss French in international discussions, works with its counterparts in France,
  Québec and Belgium, and watches how French is used.

In France, the equivalent government body is the *Délégation générale à la langue française et aux
langues de France*, alongside the Académie française.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: a message from Liège

> Salut Thomas ! Je ne sais pas venir ce midi, j'ai un dîner avec la bourgmestre. Par contre, je
> passe chez toi tantôt, vers cinq heures. Tu peux me rendre ma veste ? La tirette est cassée, je
> vais la faire réparer. Appelle-moi sur mon GSM si besoin. À tantôt !

Six Belgicisms: *je ne sais pas venir* (I can't come), *le dîner* (lunch, so *ce midi* fits), *la
bourgmestre* (the mayor), *tantôt* (later today: this afternoon), *la tirette* (the zip) and *le GSM*
(mobile), with *À tantôt !* as the goodbye. Regional words come in clusters. In France: *Je ne peux
pas venir ce midi, je déjeune avec la maire. Par contre, je passe chez toi tout à l'heure …*

### Example 2: a message from Montréal

> Allô ! T'es-tu arrivée ? Il fait moins vingt, mets ta tuque. Mon char est au garage, on va prendre
> le métro. On soupe chez ma sœur à six heures. Merci pour le cadeau ! – Bienvenue !

The question particle (*T'es-tu arrivée ?* = are you here yet?), *la tuque* (hat), *le char* (car,
informal), *souper* (to have dinner, the evening meal at six) and the final *Bienvenue* (you're
welcome). *Allô* is used in Québec as an everyday greeting, not only on the phone.

### Example 3: Switzerland or France?

> La votation sur les pistes cyclables aura lieu le 9 juin. Pour le stand, on a besoin de nonante
> chaises et d'une panosse pour la cuisine.

*La votation, nonante* and *la panosse* place the writer in French-speaking Switzerland: France would
say *le référendum local* (or *la consultation*), *quatre-vingt-dix* and *la serpillière*. *Nonante*
alone could also be Belgian; *la votation* settles it.

## Common mistakes

- Treating regional words as informal or incorrect: *septante* and *le souper* are standard in their
  areas.
- Reading Québec's *Tu viens-tu ?* as a mistake or a repetition: *-tu* is a question particle.
- Accepting a lunch invitation for *le dîner* in Brussels and turning up in the evening.
- Using *le char* or *la tuque* in France and expecting to be understood.
- Overcorrecting Belgian *savoir*: in France *Il sait nager* is right; it's only *savoir* for
  possibility that is Belgian.
- Ranking the varieties: they are all French.

## Key points

- A regionalism is a word, sense or construction of one area: a Belgicism, a helvetism or a
  Québécism.
- Some are new words (*la panosse, la tuque*), some new senses (*la tirette, le char, tantôt*), some
  institutions (*le bourgmestre, la votation*).
- Belgium: *savoir* for *pouvoir*, *septante, nonante*, *le GSM, à tantôt*. Switzerland: *le natel,
  la votation, la panosse, huitante* in some cantons. Québec: *tu* far more widely, the particle *-tu*,
  *bienvenue*, *la tuque, le char*.
- *Le dîner* is lunch and *le souper* dinner in all three.
- The written standard is shared; accents differ more than words.
- Advisory bodies: the OQLF and the 1977 *Charte* in Québec, the *Conseil de la langue française et de
  la politique linguistique* in the Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles, the DLF (1992) in Switzerland.
