lessons.title: Le courriel, la note et le procès-verbal: professional writing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B2 you wrote formal letters: a complaint, a request, a cover letter. Most professional writing
today is shorter and more frequent: emails, internal memos, meeting agendas and minutes. Each has
conventions a French colleague expects, and getting them wrong looks careless even when the French
is correct. This lesson applies lesson 01's register choices to these documents: the **professional
email** (*le courriel professionnel*), the reminder, the tone for bad news and for a request, the
memo, the agenda and the minutes. Every document here is invented. The report and the *note de
synthèse* are honors lesson 24h2.

## The professional email

![An email window. The header has a From line, a To line, a Cc line with one address and the subject line "Réunion de travail du 12 mai : ordre du jour". The body starts with the greeting "Bonjour Madame Diallo,", followed by grey bars standing for three short paragraphs, the closing "Bien cordialement," and a signature with a name and a job title. At the bottom, a paper clip and the file name ordre-du-jour.pdf. Labels on the right point to the parts: en copie, l'objet, la formule d'appel, la formule de politesse, la pièce jointe.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The subject line (*l'objet*) says what the message is about, in a few words, usually as a noun
group: *Objet : réunion de travail du 12 mai, ordre du jour*. Not *Question* or *Urgent !!!*. If the
email asks for an action, say so: *Demande de validation : budget 2027*.

The greeting, *la formule d'appel*, depends on how well you know the reader:

| reader | greeting |
|---|---|
| someone you don't know, or an institution | *Madame, Monsieur,* |
| a named person you don't know well | *Madame,* or *Bonjour Madame Diallo,* |
| a colleague you call *vous* | *Bonjour Madame Diallo,* or *Bonjour Aïssata,* (if you use first names) |
| a colleague you call *tu* | *Bonjour Paul,* or *Salut Paul,* (informal) |

*Cher Monsieur, Chère Madame* (without the name) are warm but formal; *Cher Monsieur Martin* is
heard but some find it too familiar from a stranger. A comma follows the greeting, and the message
starts on the next line with a capital letter.

The body starts with the purpose, not with pleasantries: *Je vous écris pour vous transmettre
l'ordre du jour de la réunion de jeudi.* One email, one subject; short paragraphs; the request in
its own sentence, with a date if you need one.

Copies: *mettre quelqu'un en copie* (Cc) when they need to know but not to act; *en copie
cachée* (Cci, bcc) to hide addresses, for example in a mailing to many people. Use *Répondre à tous*
only if everyone needs your answer.

The attachment (*la pièce jointe*, A1): *Vous trouverez ci-joint le compte rendu.* Name the file
clearly.

The closing: in emails, the long letter formula (*Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, l'expression de
mes salutations distinguées*) is used only for formal letters sent as email, such as a complaint or a
job application. Between professionals, a short formula is the norm:

- *Cordialement* — neutral, the commonest.
- *Bien cordialement* — a little warmer.
- *Bien à vous* — courteous, a little more personal.
- *Belle journée*, *Bonne fin de semaine* — friendly, among colleagues.

Then your name, job title and phone number in a signature.

### The reminder

When an email gets no answer, a reminder (*la relance*) recalls the first message without
accusing anyone:

- *Je me permets de revenir vers vous au sujet de mon message du 3 mai.* (*Revenir vers vous* is very
  common in business French, though some usage guides criticise it as a calque of English "get
  back to you"; *je reprends contact avec vous* is an alternative.)
- *Sauf erreur de ma part, je n'ai pas encore reçu votre réponse.* (Unless I'm mistaken: it leaves
  room for a lost message.)
- *Pourriez-vous me faire savoir d'ici vendredi si …*

Wait a reasonable time (often a week), keep it shorter than the first message, and attach or quote
the original.

### Tone for bad news and for a request

Bad news: say it early, give the reason briefly, offer what you can.

- *J'ai le regret de vous informer que votre demande n'a pas pu être retenue.* (I regret to inform
  you …)
- *Malheureusement, nous ne serons pas en mesure de livrer avant le 20.* (We won't be able to …)
- *En revanche, nous pouvons vous proposer …* (On the other hand …)

A request: use the conditional or a polite formula, and make it easy to say yes.

- *Pourriez-vous me transmettre le fichier avant jeudi ?*
- *Je vous serais reconnaissante de bien vouloir valider ce document.*
- *Seriez-vous disponible pour un appel mardi ou mercredi ?*

## The internal memo

*La note de service* is a short internal document from management to staff, giving information or
instructions. It has a header and no greeting or closing formula:

> Note de service n° 14
>
> De : Direction des ressources humaines — À : tout le personnel — Date : 2 juin
>
> Objet : horaires d'été
>
> Du 1er juillet au 31 août, les bureaux seront ouverts de 8 h à 17 h. Les salariés qui souhaitent
> adapter leurs horaires sont invités à en informer leur responsable avant le 20 juin. La présente
> note fait l'objet d'une diffusion par courriel et d'un affichage dans le hall.

Its style: impersonal (*les salariés sont invités à*), present and future tenses, no feelings, one
subject. *La diffusion* is the circulation of a document: *la liste de diffusion* is the mailing
list.

## The agenda and the minutes

Before a meeting, *l'ordre du jour* lists the items to discuss, each with a short heading (*un
intitulé*), usually a noun group:

> Réunion de travail du 12 mai — ordre du jour
>
> 1. Approbation du procès-verbal de la réunion du 14 avril
> 2. Point sur le budget du second semestre
> 3. Choix du prestataire pour le site web
> 4. Questions diverses

*Questions diverses* (any other business) usually comes last. *Point sur …* means "update on …".

After the meeting, someone writes the **[[minutes]]**. *Le procès-verbal* (*le PV*) is the official,
formal record, kept by boards, councils and associations' general meetings; *le compte rendu* is the less formal
summary of an ordinary meeting. Both usually have the same parts: date, place, people present and
apologies (*présents, excusés*), the agenda, what was said and decided under each item, the actions
(who does what by when) and the date of the next meeting.

Two style rules. Tenses: the present (*La directrice rappelle que …*) or the passé composé (*La
directrice a rappelé que …*); choose one and keep it. And the style is impersonal and factual: *Il
est décidé que …, Le comité approuve …, La question est reportée à la prochaine réunion.* Minutes
report decisions, not every remark. Once approved, they are circulated (*diffusés*) to the
participants, and the actions are tracked: *le suivi* (the follow-up) of each decision.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: a request to someone you don't know

> Objet : demande de devis, traduction d'un rapport (40 pages)
>
> Madame, Monsieur,
>
> Notre bureau d'études prépare un rapport de quarante pages sur la maintenance des voies ferrées,
> que nous devons remettre en anglais à un client britannique. Pourriez-vous nous adresser un devis
> pour sa traduction, ainsi que le délai que vous jugez nécessaire ?
>
> Vous trouverez ci-joint un extrait de dix pages. Le texte définitif sera disponible le 3 juin.
>
> Je reste à votre disposition pour toute précision.
>
> Cordialement,
>
> Julien Faure, chef de projet

The subject says what is asked. The first paragraph gives the context and the request in one
sentence; the second the practical details; the closing is the short professional formula, since
this is an email, not a formal letter.

### Example 2: the reminder

> Objet : relance, demande de devis du 20 mai
>
> Madame, Monsieur,
>
> Je me permets de revenir vers vous au sujet de ma demande de devis du 20 mai, que je joins de
> nouveau à ce message. Sauf erreur de ma part, je n'ai pas reçu de réponse. Pourriez-vous me faire
> savoir d'ici au 30 mai si vous êtes en mesure de traiter ce dossier ?
>
> Cordialement,
>
> Julien Faure

Shorter than the first, no reproach, a date for the answer, and the first message attached.

### Example 3: from notes to minutes

The secretary's notes: *Budget : Marc dit qu'on dépasse de 10 %. Décidé : on coupe les
déplacements. Marc fait un tableau pour le 1er juin.* In the minutes:

> 2. Point sur le budget du second semestre
>
> M. Marc Lenoir indique que les dépenses dépassent de 10 % le budget prévu. Il est décidé de
> réduire les frais de déplacement. Action : M. Lenoir présentera un tableau révisé le 1er juin.

The informal *on coupe* becomes an impersonal decision (*il est décidé de réduire*), the speaker is
named with his title, and the action states who, what and when. The present (*indique*) is used
throughout.

## Common mistakes

- An empty subject line (*Question, Info*) or none at all.
- *Salut* or a first name to someone you haven't met; the long letter formula at the end of a quick
  internal email.
- Several subjects in one email: one gets answered, the others are lost.
- Copying everyone, then *Répondre à tous* to say *Merci*.
- A reminder that accuses (*Vous n'avez toujours pas répondu*). Use *sauf erreur de ma part*.
- Minutes that mix tenses or report every remark; actions with no name or no date.

## Key points

- A professional email: an informative subject line, a greeting fitted to the reader, the purpose in
  the first sentence, one subject, a short closing (*Cordialement, Bien cordialement, Bien à vous*).
- *Mettre en copie* for those who need to know; *Cci* to hide addresses.
- A reminder (*la relance*) is short, polite and dated: *Je me permets de revenir vers vous … Sauf
  erreur de ma part …*
- Bad news early, with a reason and an alternative; requests in the conditional.
- *La note de service*: internal, impersonal, a header and no greeting.
- *L'ordre du jour* lists items as headings, ending with *questions diverses*; *le procès-verbal* (or
  *compte rendu*) records decisions and actions in one tense, impersonally, and is followed up.

lessons.title: Argot et verlan (recognition)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 02 covered informal French: *ben, genre, vachement, la galère*, words every French speaker
uses. Slang goes one step further. It belongs to groups (teenagers, a city's suburbs, a profession,
a generation) and it changes fast. At C1 you will meet it in films, series, songs, social media and
overheard conversations, and you need to understand it. You don't need to use it, and in most
situations you shouldn't.

At B1 you met verlan (*le verlan*) and the words *ouf* and *relou*, and saw *chelou* and *meuf* in
passing. This
lesson explains where French slang comes from, how verlan really works, why slang ages so quickly,
and when to keep it to yourself. Everything here is for recognition: in the questions and the vocabulary
reviews you only ever have to understand slang, never type it.

## Where slang comes from

**[[Argot]]** (*l'argot*, with a silent *t*) first meant the secret language of thieves and beggars. In
the Middle Ages, gangs had their own jargon so that outsiders couldn't follow them; in the 1450s
the poet François Villon wrote a few ballads in the jargon of one such gang, the *Coquillards*. In
the 19th century, Paris argot filled novels and songs, and many of its words passed into everyday
informal French: *le fric* (money), *le flic* (cop) and *la thune*, which was a five-franc coin before
it meant money in general (its origin is uncertain). Today *l'argot* means any slang: *l'argot des
jeunes, l'argot militaire*.

Slang takes words from everywhere:

- Old argot, revived: *le daron* (dad; *la daronne*, mum; *les darons*, parents) is a centuries-old
  word for the master of the house, now back in fashion with teenagers.
- Arabic, through North African French and the army in the 19th century, then through the
  suburbs: *le toubib* (doctor, from North African Arabic *ṭbīb*; lesson 01), *kiffer* (to love, B1), *le seum* (frustration: *avoir le
  seum*, to be gutted; usually traced to an Arabic word for poison).
- Romani, the language of the Roma: *chouraver* (to steal) is the classic example.
- English, mostly through music and the internet: *chiller* (to chill out), *le crush*.
- Regional French, and French itself, cut short or turned inside out: *le resto, le prof*, and
  verlan.

Dictionaries give these origins with more or less certainty; many popular etymologies (stories about
where a word "really" comes from) are invented after the fact. When a source says "origin unknown",
believe it.

## How verlan works

Verlan is made by reversing a word's syllables. It works on sounds, not spelling, and the name shows
it: *l'envers* (the reverse) → *vers-l'en* → *verlan*.

![A diagram of how verlan words are built, in three rows. Row one, two syllables: bizarre, split into the syllables bi and zar, swapped to zar and bi, then joined again, giving zarbi. Row two: femme, a one-syllable word, given an extra syllable fa and meu, swapped to meu and fa, giving meuf. Row three: reverlanisation, where beur, already verlan of arabe, is reversed again into rebeu, and meuf into feumeu.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two syllables: swap them. *Bizarre* (bi-zarre) → *zarbi*; *louche* (lou-che) → *chelou*; *méchant*
(mé-chant) → *chanmé*; *énervé* loses its first vowel (*(é)-ner-vé* → *vé-ner*) and becomes *vénère*.

One syllable: add a vowel, then swap. A one-syllable word is said with a final "eu" sound to get
two syllables: *femme* (fa-meu) → *meu-fa*, and the last vowel drops: *meuf*. *Fête* (fê-teu) →
*teu-fê* → *teuf*. *Fou* simply reverses its sounds: *ouf*.

Dropping and trimming: after the swap, the final vowel often disappears, as in *meuf* and *teuf*.
Spelling follows the sound and isn't fixed (*vénère* or *vener*), and nor is agreement (*des types
chelou* or *chelous*).

Reversing again: when a verlan word becomes too common, speakers reverse it again: this is
**[[reverlanisation]]**. *Meuf* becomes *feumeu*. *Beur*, the verlan of *arabe* that spread in the 1980s
as a name for young people of North African descent, became so widespread that it was reversed again into *rebeu*.
Both are ethnic labels: they can sound outdated or offensive depending on who says them, so recognise
them only.

## The words of this lesson

| slang | how | neutral | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| *chelou* | verlan of *louche* | *louche, bizarre* | shady, weird |
| *zarbi* | verlan of *bizarre* | *bizarre* | weird |
| *vénère* | verlan of *énervé* | *énervé, en colère* | wound up, angry |
| *la meuf* | verlan of *femme* | *la femme* | also girlfriend; can sound disrespectful |
| *la teuf* | verlan of *fête* | *la fête* | *faire la teuf*: to party |
| *chanmé* | verlan of *méchant* | *génial, super* | in slang *méchant* can mean "terrific" |
| *le daron* | old argot | *le père* | *la daronne, les darons* |
| *la thune* | old argot | *l'argent* | *de la thune, pas une thune* |
| *le seum* | from Arabic | *la frustration, la déception* | *avoir le seum* |

*La meuf* needs care. It is everyday among young people (*ma meuf*, my girlfriend; *une meuf*, a
woman), and it is in general dictionaries, but said of a woman you don't know, or to her, it can be
heard as disrespectful. *Chanmé* shows how slang reverses meaning: *méchant* (nasty) is used for
"amazingly good", and its verlan carries the same praise.

## Slang in music, film and social media

Rap, from the 1990s on, spread verlan and suburban slang across France, and new words still often
reach the general public through songs. Films did the same: *La Haine* (Mathieu Kassovitz, 1995),
set in a housing estate near Paris, made the slang of its three young heroes familiar to a whole
generation of cinema-goers. Today social media and series spread a word in weeks, and kill it almost
as fast. You'll understand them better if you watch with French subtitles, which often write slang as
it is said.

## Why slang ages fast

Slang marks belonging. Once a word is used by everyone (by parents, advertisers, politicians, or
learners), it stops marking the group, and the group replaces it. *Chébran* (verlan of *branché*,
trendy) was fashionable in the 1980s; today it sounds like a parody of that decade. This is why
dictionaries always lag behind slang, why a slang word from a ten-year-old textbook can make
teenagers laugh, and why *ouf* and *relou*, which have lasted, are the exception.

## When not to use slang

- In an exam, a job interview, a formal email, anything written for someone you don't know.
- With people older than you, or anyone who doesn't use it themselves.
- When you're not sure of the meaning or the force: a slang word in a foreign accent often sounds
  like an imitation, and a few can offend.

Among friends who use it, a word or two (*c'est chelou, j'ai le seum*) will be understood and
accepted. Even then, a learner who speaks clear informal French (lesson 02) sounds more natural than
one who collects slang.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: decoding a group chat

> Hier c'était la teuf chez Yanis, trop chanmé. Mais sa meuf était vénère parce que ses darons sont
> rentrés plus tôt. Moi j'avais plus une thune pour le taxi, j'ai le seum.

Neutral version: *Hier, il y avait une fête chez Yanis, c'était génial. Mais sa copine était en
colère parce que ses parents sont rentrés plus tôt. Moi, je n'avais plus d'argent pour le taxi, je
suis dégoûté.* Translation: There was a party at Yanis's yesterday, it was brilliant. But his
girlfriend was angry because his parents came home early. I had no money left for a taxi, I'm gutted.
(*Ses darons* are Yanis's parents, not the girlfriend's: the context says whose house it was.)

### Example 2: building verlan

Take *pourri* (rotten). Two syllables, *pou-rri*, swapped: *ripou*, which is real slang for a corrupt
cop (and a 1984 film comedy, *Les Ripoux*). Take *mère*: one syllable, said *mè-reu*, swapped:
*reu-mè* → *la reum*. The method is regular; which words actually exist is not. You can't invent
verlan and expect to be understood, only recognise it.

### Example 3: what would you say instead?

A friend writes *C'est zarbi, ce mail du boss.* In a reply to your manager you would say: *Ce message
me paraît étrange.* Slang (*zarbi*), informal (*le boss*) and anglicism (*le mail*) all go; *étrange*
and *ce message* fit a professional reply.

## Common mistakes

- Reversing the spelling instead of the sounds: *femme* is *meuf*, not ~~emmef~~.
- Taking *chanmé* or *méchant* in slang as negative: here they praise.
- Using *la meuf* with a stranger, or about a colleague.
- Trusting a colourful origin story over a dictionary's "origin uncertain".
- Learning slang from old lists: check the date before you trust the word.
- Using slang to sound fluent. Clear informal French does that better.

## Key points

- *L'argot* began as the secret language of thieves; today it means any group's slang.
- Slang comes from old argot (*le daron, la thune*), Arabic (*le toubib, le seum*), Romani
  (*chouraver*), English (*chiller*) and French turned around (verlan).
- Verlan reverses sounds: two syllables are swapped (*zarbi, chelou, chanmé, vénère*); one-syllable
  words gain a vowel first (*meuf, teuf*), or simply reverse their sounds (*ouf*). Reverlanisation reverses again (*feumeu, rebeu*).
- *La meuf* is common but can sound disrespectful; ethnic labels are for recognition only.
- Slang ages fast: what everyone uses, the group drops.
- Recognise slang; in exams, at work and with strangers, use the neutral word.

lessons.title: Advienne que pourra: the subjunctive at C1
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

B1 and B2 taught the subjunctive after a trigger: a verb (*il faut que*), a conjunction (*bien
que*), a superlative. This lesson is about the subjunctive where the trigger is hidden: in a
clause that stands alone, in two alternatives set side by side, and in a second clause that
repeats a conjunction with plain *que*. You meet these in editorials, legal texts and debates.
The theme is bioethics: consent, clinical trials, organ donation and genetic research. The texts
present several positions and take none.

## The subjunctive with no main verb

An **[[independent subjunctive]]** is a subjunctive in a clause with no main verb in front of it.
Think of it as the second half of a sentence whose first half (*je veux que, je souhaite que,
j'ordonne que*) has been left out. That is why it expresses what the speaker wants, orders or
imagines, never a plain fact.

![A chart of the subjunctive without a main verb, in four boxes. Order or wish: Qu'il patiente ! Que personne ne sorte ! Set phrase: Advienne que pourra. Qu'à cela ne tienne. Hypothesis: Qu'un seul donneur se retire, et l'essai s'arrête. Literary wish, for recognition: Puisse-t-il guérir !](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Orders and wishes for a third person

The imperative has no form for *il, elle, ils*. French uses *que* + subjunctive instead:

- *Qu'il patiente !* — Let him wait! / He'll have to wait.
- *Que personne ne sorte avant la fin de la séance.* — Nobody is to leave before the end of the
  session.
- *Que les volontaires se présentent à 8 heures, à jeun.* — Volunteers should come at 8 am,
  without eating.

In a notice or a rule, the tone is firm and impersonal. Said about a particular person, it can
sound cold or exasperated (*Qu'il se débrouille !* — He can sort it out himself!).

### Set phrases

B1 taught *Vive …, Soit !, Ainsi soit-il, coûte que coûte, sauve qui peut*. C1 adds:

- *Advienne que pourra.* — Come what may. (*advenir*, to happen: "let happen what can happen")
- *Qu'à cela ne tienne.* — Never mind, that's no obstacle. (*tenir à*, to depend on: "let it not
  depend on that")
- *Que je sache* — as far as I know; *pas que je sache* — not that I know of. It goes with a
  statement, very often a negative one: *Le comité n'a rien décidé, que je sache.*
- *Grand bien vous fasse !* — Much good may it do you! Polite in a toast, but usually ironic:
  the speaker disapproves.
- *Dieu vous entende !* — Let's hope you're right! (literally "may God hear you")

Each one is frozen: you can't change the tense or the words, only the pronoun of *grand bien vous
fasse* and *Dieu vous entende* (*grand bien lui fasse, Dieu t'entende*). *Pour autant que je
sache* (as far as I know) is lesson 10's.

### Que + subjunctive as a hypothesis

In formal French a *que*-clause can open a two-part sentence as a condition, with *et* before
the consequence:

- *Qu'un seul donneur se retire, et l'essai s'arrête.* — If even one donor withdraws, the trial
  stops.
- *Que la loi change, et tout le dossier est à revoir.* — If the law changes, the whole file has
  to be reviewed.

The meaning is the same as *si* + indicative, but the sentence is shorter and more emphatic.

### Literary wishes (recognition only)

Literature and solemn speeches put the wish in an inversion with *pouvoir*, with no *que*:
*Puisse-t-il guérir !* (may he recover!), *Puissent ces recherches aboutir !* (may this research
succeed!). *Plût au ciel qu'il fût là !* (if only he were here!) uses the imperfect subjunctive
of *plaire* and of *être*. Recognise these; in your own writing, write *Pourvu qu'il guérisse !*

## Alternatives: que … ou que, soit que … soit que

An **[[alternative clause]]** sets two possibilities side by side and says that the main clause
holds either way. Both halves take the subjunctive, because neither is asserted:

- *Qu'on l'approuve ou qu'on le rejette, ce texte fera date.* — Whether you approve of it or
  reject it, this text will be a landmark.
- *Que le patient soit majeur ou mineur, son avis doit être recherché.* — Whether the patient is
  an adult or a minor, his or her view must be sought.
- *Qu'il le veuille ou non, il devra signer.* — Whether he likes it or not, he'll have to sign.

*Que … ou non* is the short version, and the most common one in speech. Careful writing usually
repeats the *que* (*ou qu'on le rejette*); with two short verbs it is sometimes left out (*qu'on
l'aime ou le déteste*).

**[[Soit que … soit que]]** + subjunctive is formal and gives two possible causes or explanations
(whether because … or because …):

- *Certains volontaires abandonnent, soit qu'ils craignent les effets secondaires, soit qu'ils
  ne voient aucun bénéfice.* — Some volunteers drop out, either because they fear the side
  effects or because they see no benefit.

Don't confuse it with plain *soit … soit* (either … or) before nouns, which takes no
subjunctive: *soit le patient, soit sa famille*.

## Que standing for a repeated conjunction

When two clauses depend on the same conjunction, French doesn't repeat it: the second clause
starts with *que*. This **[[substitute que]]** keeps the mood of the conjunction it replaces:

- *Comme le comité était divisé et qu'il manquait des données, la décision a été reportée.* —
  As the committee was divided and data were missing, the decision was postponed. (*comme* +
  indicative, so *que* + indicative)
- *Quand la loi aura été votée et que les décrets seront parus, …* — When the law has been
  passed and the decrees have been published, … (*quand* + indicative)
- *Bien que l'essai soit prometteur et qu'il ait reçu des fonds, il reste fragile.* — Although
  the trial is promising and has received funding, it remains fragile. (*bien que* +
  subjunctive)

**Si is the exception.** After *si* + indicative, the *que* of the second clause traditionally
takes the subjunctive, and careful writing still prefers it. The indicative is also accepted and
very common:

- *Si le comité donne son accord et que les fonds soient disponibles, l'essai commencera en
  mars.*
- *Si le comité donne son accord et que les fonds sont disponibles, l'essai commencera en mars.*

Both are correct; the subjunctive sounds more formal. This course won't mark either one wrong.
In your own formal writing, choose the subjunctive and stay consistent.

## De ce que after verbs of feeling

Some verbs of feeling are built with *de* (*se plaindre de, s'étonner de, se féliciter de*).
Before a clause, *de* becomes *de ce que*. Both moods occur after it: the indicative presents
the cause as a fact, the subjunctive treats it as the object of the feeling. *De ce que* is
heavier and more formal than plain *que*.

- *Les associations se plaignent de ce que les familles ne sont pas consultées.* — The
  associations complain that families are not consulted. (fact: indicative, the usual choice
  here)
- *Le rapporteur s'étonne de ce qu'aucune étude n'ait été publiée.* — The rapporteur is
  surprised that no study has been published. (subjunctive, as after *s'étonner que*)

## Reading: a debate on a clinical trial

> **Essai génétique : le comité d'éthique ne tranche pas**
>
> Faut-il autoriser l'essai clinique que propose l'équipe du professeur Morel ? Réuni jeudi, le
> comité d'éthique de l'hôpital Saint-Aubin n'a pas rendu d'avis définitif. L'essai porte sur une
> maladie génétique rare de l'enfant : il s'agirait de corriger une erreur du génome dans les
> cellules des jeunes patients, et non dans l'embryon, ce qui écarte, selon l'équipe, tout soupçon
> d'eugénisme. La question éthique n'en reste pas moins entière.
>
> Pour les partisans de l'essai, le temps presse. « Qu'on attende encore deux ans, et une
> vingtaine d'enfants auront perdu la vue », plaide une généticienne. Les familles, elles, se
> plaignent de ce que la recherche biomédicale avance plus vite à l'étranger. Que l'essai
> réussisse ou qu'il échoue, ajoutent-elles, il apportera des connaissances précieuses. Un père,
> dont la fille est atteinte, résume : « Qu'on nous laisse au moins le choix. »
>
> Les opposants ne contestent pas l'urgence. Ils s'inquiètent de la façon dont le consentement
> sera recueilli. Les patients ont entre six et douze ans : leurs parents signeront, mais l'enfant
> doit lui aussi être informé et son avis recherché. « Un consentement éclairé suppose qu'on ait
> compris les risques. Que l'on m'explique comment un enfant de six ans le pourrait. Où est son
> libre arbitre ? », objecte un juriste. D'autres craignent que les enfants ne deviennent des
> cobayes, soit que les familles, désespérées, acceptent n'importe quel traitement, soit que
> l'équipe, pressée de publier, minimise les risques.
>
> Entre ces positions, une troisième voie se dessine. Si l'équipe réduit le nombre de patients et
> qu'un médecin indépendant suive chaque famille, plusieurs membres du comité se disent prêts à
> voter pour. Le respect de la dignité et de l'intégrité du corps humain n'interdit pas la
> recherche, rappelle la présidente : il oblige à l'encadrer. « Nous ne voulons ni bloquer la
> science ni laisser s'installer une dérive. » Reste la question du coût : s'il fonctionne, le
> traitement sera l'un des plus chers jamais mis sur le marché. Qu'il soit remboursé ou non,
> préviennent les associations, il risque de creuser les inégalités entre les familles.
>
> La loi française, rappelons-le, encadre ces questions depuis les premières lois de bioéthique
> de 1994, révisées en 2004, en 2011 et en 2021 : la révision de 2004 a interdit le clonage
> humain, celle de 2021 a ouvert la procréation médicalement assistée aux couples de femmes et
> aux femmes seules. Le comité se réunira de nouveau en mai. D'ici là, une seule consigne : que
> chacun lise le dossier complet. Advienne que pourra, disait-on autrefois ; en bioéthique, on
> préfère mesurer chaque pas.

Summary, paragraph by paragraph:

1. A hospital ethics committee hasn't decided whether to allow a trial for a rare genetic disease
   in children. The correction would be made in the children's cells, not in an embryo, which
   rules out eugenics, the team says; the ethical question remains. *Ne tranche pas*: doesn't
   decide; *rendre un avis*: to give an opinion.
2. Supporters say two more years of waiting would cost some twenty children their sight; families
   complain that research moves faster abroad, and a father asks for the right to choose.
   *Plaider*: to argue; *atteinte*: affected (by the disease).
3. Opponents worry about consent: the patients are six to twelve, and a lawyer asks how a
   six-year-old could understand the risks, or choose freely. Others fear the children will become
   guinea pigs. *Recueillir*: to collect; *minimiser*: to play down.
4. A middle way: with fewer patients and an independent doctor for each family, several members
   would vote yes. Respect for dignity doesn't forbid research, the chair says, but requires
   regulating it. The cost may widen inequalities between families, whether or not it is
   reimbursed. *Une troisième voie se dessine*: a third way is emerging.
5. French law has regulated these questions since the bioethics laws of 1994, revised in 2004
   (which banned human cloning), 2011 and 2021 (which opened medically assisted reproduction to
   couples of women and single women). The committee meets again in May.

Notice the lesson's constructions: *Qu'on attende …, et …* (hypothesis), *se plaignent de ce
que* + indicative, *Que l'essai réussisse ou qu'il échoue* (alternative), *Que l'on m'explique*
(an order), *soit que … soit que* (two possible causes), *Si … et qu'un médecin … suive*
(substitute *que*, careful style), *que chacun lise* (an instruction).

## Dialogue: two views on organ donation

```dialogue
# Don d'organes : faut-il demander aux familles ?
Inès: Que je sache, la loi présume que tout adulte accepte le don d'organes, sauf s'il l'a refusé de son vivant.
= As far as I know, the law presumes every adult agrees to organ donation, unless they refused it while alive.
Bastien: Oui, mais en pratique, les médecins parlent toujours aux proches. Qu'ils s'y opposent, et on renonce souvent au prélèvement.
= Yes, but in practice doctors always talk to the family. If they object, the removal is often given up.
Inès: Grand bien leur fasse ! Pendant ce temps, des patients attendent une greffe.
= Much good may it do them! Meanwhile, patients are waiting for a transplant.
Bastien: Tu es dure. Les proches sont en deuil. Qu'on prenne le temps de les écouter, c'est la moindre des choses.
= You're being harsh. The family are grieving. Taking the time to listen to them is the least we can do.
Inès: Je ne dis pas le contraire. Mais qu'on les écoute ou non, la volonté du défunt devrait compter d'abord.
= I'm not saying otherwise. But whether we listen to them or not, the wishes of the deceased should come first.
Bastien: Et s'il n'a jamais rien dit ? Qu'à cela ne tienne, me diras-tu : la loi tranche. Moi, je trouve que c'est plus compliqué.
= And if he never said anything? Never mind, you'll tell me: the law decides. I think it's more complicated.
```

*Le défunt* (the deceased) is lesson 07's word. *Les proches*: close family; *le prélèvement*:
removal (of an organ); *être en deuil*: to be in mourning. In France, an adult's consent to organ
donation after death is presumed unless they refused while alive (for example on the national
register of refusals); if they aren't on it, the medical team talks to the relatives to find out
whether the person had refused.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The stages of a clinical trial
  accDescr: A clinical trial goes from information to informed consent, then inclusion of the volunteer, then the trial itself, then follow-up. At any stage the volunteer may withdraw.
  A["Information"] --> B["Informed consent"]
  B --> C["Inclusion"]
  C --> D["Trial"]
  D --> E["Follow-up"]
  B -. "withdrawal possible" .-> X["Volunteer leaves"]
  C -.-> X
  D -.-> X
```

Consent can be withdrawn at any time.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: what does the hidden main verb say?

*Que personne ne touche au dossier.* What is missing in front? *Je veux / J'ordonne*. So it's an
order, and the subjunctive *touche* is required. Compare *Personne ne touche au dossier*: a
statement in the indicative (nobody touches the file). The *que* is the signal.

### Example 2: choose the mood in a second clause

*Puisque le donneur était compatible et qu'il ___ (être) volontaire, la greffe a eu lieu.*
*Que* stands for *puisque*, which takes the indicative: *qu'il était volontaire*.

*Si la greffe réussit et que le patient ___ (aller) bien, il rentrera chez lui.* *Que* stands
for *si*: *qu'il aille bien* in careful style, *qu'il va bien* in common use. Both are correct.

## Common mistakes

- **Indicative in an independent order:** ~~*Qu'il attend !*~~ → *Qu'il attende !* Without a
  main verb, the *que* itself calls for the subjunctive.
- **Changing a set phrase:** ~~*Advienne ce qui pourra*~~, ~~*que je savais*~~. They are frozen.
- **Reading *que je sache* as a wish.** It means "as far as I know", usually after a negative.
- **Indicative after *que … ou que*:** ~~*Qu'il vient ou qu'il ne vient pas*~~ → *Qu'il vienne ou
  non*.
- **Changing the mood of a substitute *que*** after *comme, quand, puisque, parce que*:
  ~~*Comme il pleuvait et qu'il fasse froid*~~ → *et qu'il faisait froid*. Only *si* allows the
  switch.

## Key points

- Without a main verb, *que* + subjunctive gives an order or wish for a third person (*Qu'il
  patiente !*) or a formal hypothesis (*Qu'un seul donneur se retire, et l'essai s'arrête*).
- C1 set phrases: *advienne que pourra, qu'à cela ne tienne, que je sache, grand bien vous fasse,
  Dieu vous entende*. *Puisse-t-il …* and *Plût au ciel …* are for recognition.
- Alternatives: *que … ou que* + subjunctive, *que … ou non*, formal *soit que … soit que*.
- A substitute *que* keeps the mood of the conjunction it replaces, except after *si*: then the
  subjunctive (careful) or the indicative (common) are both correct.
- *Se plaindre de ce que, s'étonner de ce que*: both moods occur; formal.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Il croyait qu'elle viendrait: tense agreement in every mood
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

When a sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause, the tense of the subordinate depends
on two things: the tense of the main verb, and whether the subordinate action comes before, at
the same time as, or after it. B1 taught this for the indicative and reported speech, and B2
added the subjonctif passé and the conditionnel passé. This lesson puts it all in one system and
adds the cases where the rule bends: general truths, mixed hypotheses, and the long report
written in the past, where a single wrong tense breaks the timeline. The theme is archaeology and
heritage: a rescue dig on a building site, dating a find, and looting.

## One system

The **[[concordance des temps]]** (sequence of tenses) is the set of rules that match the tense of a
subordinate clause to the tense of the main verb. Ask two questions: is the main verb present,
past or future? Is the subordinate action earlier, simultaneous or later?

![A chart with three rows for the main verb (present: pense / doute; past: pensait / doutait; future: pensera / doutera) and three columns for the mood of the subordinate: indicative (after elle pense que), subjunctive (after elle doute que) and infinitive (after elle pense). Present: il est parti / il part / il partira; qu'il soit parti / qu'il parte; être partie / partir. Past: il était parti / il partait / il partirait; qu'il soit parti / qu'il parte; être partie / partir. Future: as present.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### In the indicative

After a main verb in the present or the future, the subordinate takes the tense it would
have on its own:

- *L'archéologue pense que la nécropole date de l'Antiquité.* (same time)
- *Elle pense qu'on a trouvé le site par hasard.* (earlier)
- *Elle pense qu'on trouvera d'autres tombes.* (later)
- *Demain, elle annoncera qu'on a trouvé une amphore.* (future main verb: same tenses)

After a main verb in the past (passé composé, imparfait, plus-que-parfait, passé simple),
everything shifts back one step:

| relation | present main verb | past main verb |
|---|---|---|
| same time | *Il dit que la strate est intacte.* | *Il a dit que la strate était intacte.* |
| earlier | *Il dit qu'on a pillé le site.* | *Il a dit qu'on avait pillé le site.* |
| later | *Il dit qu'on fouillera en mai.* | *Il a dit qu'on fouillerait en mai.* |
| done before a later point | *Il dit qu'on aura fini en mai.* | *Il a dit qu'on aurait fini en mai.* |

In the past, the conditionnel présent is the future of the past (*Il croyait qu'elle
viendrait*: he thought she would come), and the conditionnel passé is its futur antérieur
(*Il croyait qu'elle serait partie avant midi*: he thought she would have left by noon).

### In the subjunctive

Everyday modern French uses only two subjunctive tenses, whatever the tense of the main verb. Choose by
the time relation alone:

- same time or later: present subjunctive. *Je veux / Je voulais / Je voudrai qu'on protège
  le site.*
- earlier: subjonctif passé. *Je suis / J'étais ravie qu'on ait retrouvé le sarcophage.*

So *Le préfet a exigé qu'on suspende les travaux* is the normal modern sentence. In classical
prose (and in some formal writing today) a past main verb takes the imperfect subjunctive
(*qu'on suspendît les travaux*) and, for an earlier action, the pluperfect subjunctive (*qu'on
eût suspendu*). Recognise these forms in literature; write the present and past subjunctive.
After a past main verb, natives and grammars accept both systems: this course asks you to
produce the modern one and never marks the classical one wrong when you read it.

### Infinitive and participle

The infinitive has two tenses, measured from the main verb in the same way:

- present infinitive, same time or later: *Elle espérait trouver des vestiges.* — She hoped to
  find remains.
- past infinitive (*avoir* or *être* + participle), earlier: *Il affirme avoir vu les pilleurs.*
  — He claims to have seen the looters. *Après avoir exhumé le squelette, ils l'ont photographié.*

The participle works the same way: *Fouillant le site, elle a trouvé une pièce* (while she was
digging) / *Ayant fouillé le site pendant dix ans, elle connaissait chaque strate* (after ten
years of digging).

## When the rule bends

### General truths and facts still true

A **[[general truth]]** (*présent de vérité générale*) can keep the present after a past main verb,
because it is still true when you speak:

- *Le guide a rappelé que la céramique se conserve mieux que le bois.* — The guide pointed out
  that pottery keeps better than wood.
- *Elle nous a expliqué que la préhistoire s'achève avec l'invention de l'écriture.* — She
  explained to us that prehistory ends with the invention of writing.

With a fact that is still true, both tenses are correct, with a nuance:

- *Il a rappelé que le site datait du Néolithique.* — reports what he said, in the past.
- *Il a rappelé que le site date du Néolithique.* — the speaker also vouches that it is still
  true now.

Both are good French; the present adds the speaker's own commitment. The same goes for this
sentence about a real cave: *La conférencière a rappelé que la grotte Chauvet, découverte en
décembre 1994, abrite (abritait) certaines des plus anciennes peintures rupestres connues.* With
something that is no longer true, only the shifted tense works: *Elle m'a dit que le chantier était fermé* (it may
have reopened since).

### Mixed hypotheticals

A **[[mixed hypothetical]]** is a *si*-sentence whose condition and result belong to different times.
The two classic patterns:

- past condition, present result: *si* + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel présent.
  *Si on avait fouillé plus tôt, on saurait aujourd'hui qui était enterré là.* — If they had
  dug earlier, we would know today who was buried there.
- permanent condition, past result: *si* + imparfait → conditionnel passé.
  *S'il était prudent, il n'aurait pas creusé là.* — If he were a careful man, he wouldn't have
  dug there. (He isn't careful, in general; the digging is over.)

Check each half separately: *avait fouillé* is over and done; *saurait* is now. *Était prudent*
is a permanent trait; *n'aurait pas creusé* is a single past act.

## A rescue dig on a building site

```dialogue
# Sur le chantier de fouilles
Le chef de chantier: On nous avait dit que le terrain était vierge. Personne ne pensait qu'il y aurait des tombes !
= We'd been told the ground was untouched. Nobody thought there would be graves!
L'archéologue: Le diagnostic avait pourtant montré qu'une nécropole s'étendait sous la parcelle. Il fallait bien qu'on fouille avant que vous ne construisiez.
= Yet the survey had shown that a necropolis lay under the plot. We had to dig before you built.
Le chef de chantier: Et combien de temps cela va prendre ? Mon client espérait avoir terminé le gros œuvre en juin.
= And how long will it take? My client hoped to have finished the main structure by June.
L'archéologue: Si on avait été prévenus en janvier, on aurait déjà fini. Là, il faudra encore six semaines.
= If we had been told in January, we would have finished already. As it is, it'll take another six weeks.
Le chef de chantier: Six semaines… Si mon client était patient, je vous dirais que ce n'est rien.
= Six weeks… If my client were a patient man, I'd tell you it's nothing.
L'archéologue: Dites-lui que la loi impose les fouilles, et qu'on ne dégage pas un sarcophage intact à la hâte.
= Tell him the law requires the dig, and that you don't uncover an intact sarcophagus in a hurry.
```

Notice *pensait qu'il y aurait* (future of the past), *avait montré qu'une nécropole
s'étendait* (same time in the past), *Il fallait qu'on fouille* (modern subjunctive after a
past verb), *espérait avoir terminé* (past infinitive: done before a later point), *Si on avait
été prévenus …, on aurait déjà fini* (unreal past). *Le diagnostic* is the survey that tests the
ground before building; *la parcelle*: the plot; *le gros œuvre*: the shell of a building.

In France, preventive archaeology (*l'archéologie préventive*) works this way: the State can
require a survey before building work and, if remains are found, a dig, carried out by
archaeologists such as those of the Inrap, the public institute created by a law of 2001 (it began work in 2002).

## Reading: a dig report written in the past

![A cross-section of the ground at a dig: a modern layer at the top, then a medieval layer with pottery, then a Gallo-Roman layer with an amphora and a stone sarcophagus, then the natural subsoil.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> **Rapport de fouille préventive, parcelle 14, Vaurenne (extrait)**
>
> Tout est parti d'une découverte fortuite. En creusant les fondations d'un parking, un ouvrier avait
> mis au jour le col d'une amphore. Le chantier a été suspendu le jour même, et le service
> régional de l'archéologie a prescrit un diagnostic. Celui-ci a confirmé que des vestiges
> étaient enfouis sous près de deux mètres de remblais.
>
> Les fouilles, ouvertes en mai, ont d'abord permis de distinguer deux strates sous les remblais. La plus récente contenait des tessons de
> céramique médiévale, qui attestent une occupation du Moyen Âge ; dans la plus ancienne, qui
> reposait sur le sol naturel, nous avons dégagé une nécropole antique : quarante-deux
> sépultures, dont celles de plusieurs enfants, et un sarcophage de pierre resté intact. Nous pensions au départ que le cimetière
> se limiterait à la moitié nord de la parcelle ; en réalité, il la couvrait presque
> entièrement.
>
> La datation repose sur deux indices. Les amphores appartiennent à un type que l'on connaît bien
> et qui circulait aux Ier et IIe siècles. Les analyses au carbone 14, reçues en octobre, ont
> confirmé que les ossements dataient de la même période. Il fallait toutefois que nous
> vérifiions que le sarcophage n'avait pas été déplacé : rien ne l'indiquait. Seul un fragment de
> verre, plus tardif, reste à expliquer.
>
> Malheureusement, le site n'a pas échappé au pillage. Une nuit de juillet, des pilleurs munis de
> détecteurs de métaux ont creusé une dizaine de trous. Si le terrain avait été gardé dès le
> départ, nous n'aurions sans doute rien perdu ; s'il était surveillé aujourd'hui comme il le
> mérite, nous serions plus sereins pour la suite. Les objets volés, sans doute des monnaies,
> n'ont pas été retrouvés ; nous craignons qu'ils n'aient déjà été vendus en ligne. La gendarmerie
> a été prévenue, et l'enquête se poursuit.
>
> Pendant l'été, le chantier de fouilles a été ouvert au public deux samedis : plus de huit cents
> visiteurs sont venus voir les archéologues au travail. Beaucoup ignoraient qu'une nécropole
> dormait sous leur futur parking.
>
> Nous avons exhumé les quarante-deux squelettes, qui seront étudiés au laboratoire. Le promoteur
> espérait que les travaux reprendraient en septembre ; nous lui avons indiqué qu'ils ne
> pourraient reprendre qu'après la fin de nos relevés. Rappelons que l'archéologie préventive ne
> s'oppose pas à la construction : elle permet de connaître l'histoire d'un lieu avant que ses
> vestiges ne soient ensevelis sous le béton. Le rapport définitif sera remis à l'État au
> printemps.

Summary, paragraph by paragraph:

1. A worker digging the foundations of a car park found the neck of an amphora by chance. Work
   stopped, and a survey confirmed that remains lay under about two metres of fill. *Le col*:
   neck; *les remblais*: fill, backfill; *prescrire*: to order.
2. The dig, opened in May, found two layers under the fill: medieval pottery in the upper one and,
   in the lower one, resting on the natural ground, an ancient necropolis of forty-two graves, with an intact stone sarcophagus. It
   turned out to cover almost the whole plot. *Les tessons*: shards; *la sépulture*: grave.
3. The amphorae are of a well-known type of the 1st and 2nd centuries, and carbon-14 tests
   confirmed the same period for the bones; the sarcophagus hadn't been moved. Only a later piece
   of glass remains unexplained. *Les ossements*: bones.
4. Looters with metal detectors dug a dozen holes one night in July. Had the site been guarded,
   probably nothing would have been lost; if it were watched now, the team would feel calmer. The stolen
   objects, probably coins, may already have been sold online.
5. Over 800 visitors came on two open Saturdays; many didn't know a necropolis lay under their
   future car park.
6. The skeletons have been exhumed for study. The developer hoped work would resume in September;
   it can resume only after the recording is over. Preventive archaeology lets us know a place's
   history before its remains are buried under concrete. *Les relevés*: survey records, plans.

Every tense in the report follows the main verb: *avait mis au jour* (before the suspension),
*a confirmé que des vestiges étaient enfouis* (same time, in the past), *pensions que le
cimetière se limiterait* (future of the past), *ont confirmé que les ossements dataient*
(shifted; *datent* would add the writer's own commitment), *Il fallait que nous vérifiions*
(modern subjunctive), *espérait que les travaux reprendraient* (future of the past), and two
mixed or unreal hypotheses in paragraph 4, then *nous craignons qu'ils n'aient déjà été vendus*
(subjonctif passé: done before the fear). In *un type que l'on connaît bien et qui circulait aux Ier et IIe siècles*, *circulait* stays in
the past because it describes the past, and *connaît* is in the present because it is true now.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: shift a statement into the past

*Le guide explique que la grotte de Lascaux a été découverte en septembre 1940 par des
adolescents, que ses peintures préhistoriques sont fragiles et qu'on n'ouvrira jamais plus la
grotte au public.* → *Le guide a expliqué que la grotte avait été découverte en 1940, que ses
peintures étaient fragiles et qu'on n'ouvrirait jamais plus la grotte au public.* (The cave has
been closed to visitors since 1963; visitors see a replica. *Sont fragiles* could also stay in
the present: it is still true.) A shorter one:

*L'archéologue affirme que le sarcophage est intact, qu'on l'a déplacé au XIXe siècle et qu'on
l'ouvrira demain.* → *L'archéologue a affirmé que le sarcophage était intact, qu'on l'avait
déplacé au XIXe siècle et qu'on l'ouvrirait le lendemain.* Notice *demain* → *le lendemain*:
time words shift too.

### Example 2: which subjunctive?

*Le maire exigeait que les pilleurs ___ (être) poursuivis.* Same time or later, so the present
subjunctive: *soient*. *Le maire regrettait que les pilleurs ___ (ne pas être) arrêtés plus
tôt.* Earlier: *n'aient pas été arrêtés*. In a novel of 1900 you might read *fussent* and
*n'eussent pas été*: same meaning, classical concordance.

### Example 3: build a mixed hypothetical

Fact 1: the site wasn't protected last year. Fact 2: today, half the coins are missing. → *Si le
site avait été protégé l'an dernier, il ne manquerait pas aujourd'hui la moitié des pièces.*
(plus-que-parfait → conditionnel présent)

## Common mistakes

- **Future instead of conditional after a past verb:** ~~*Il a dit qu'il viendra*~~ in a past
  narrative → *qu'il viendrait*. (*Il a dit qu'il viendra* is possible in speech when the coming
  is still ahead of the moment of speaking.)
- **Writing the imperfect subjunctive in a modern text:** *qu'il vînt* in an essay sounds
  affected. Write *qu'il vienne*.
- **Present infinitive for an earlier action:** ~~*Il affirme voir les pilleurs hier*~~ → *Il
  affirme avoir vu les pilleurs hier.*
- **Conditionnel after *si*:** ~~*Si on aurait fouillé*~~ → *Si on avait fouillé*. Common in
  casual speech, never in careful French.
- **Forgetting time words:** *hier, demain, la semaine prochaine* become *la veille, le
  lendemain, la semaine suivante* in a past narrative.

## Key points

- Main verb present or future: the subordinate takes its own tense. Main verb past: imparfait
  (same time), plus-que-parfait (earlier), conditionnel (later), conditionnel passé (done before
  a later point).
- Subjunctive in modern French: present (same time or later) or past (earlier), whatever the main
  tense. The imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive are for recognition.
- Infinitive and participle: present for the same time or later, past for earlier.
- A general truth can stay in the present; a fact still true can too, which adds the speaker's
  commitment.
- Mixed hypotheticals: *si* + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel présent; *si* + imparfait →
  conditionnel passé.
