the lesson.

lessons.title: Dans la mesure où, en ce sens que: cause and consequence at C1
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 3 is about the links between ideas and about what a text says without saying it. This
first lesson goes back to cause and consequence, which you met at B1 and B2.

You already have a large set of tools. You met *parce que* at A1, *comme* and *car* at A2, and
*puisque, étant donné que, vu que, à force de, sous prétexte que* at B1; B2 added *d'autant que, non que, du moment que, de
là, il en résulte que* and the verbs *entraîner, susciter, découler de, résulter de*. At C1 the
question is no longer "how do I say *because*?" but "which *because* tells my reader the right
thing?" Each **[[cause connector]]** presents the cause in its own way: as news, as something the
reader already accepts, as background, as an afterthought, or as someone else's claim. This
lesson sorts them by that, then adds the formal connectors that C1 texts use: *dans la mesure
où, en ce sens que, il s'ensuit que, tant et si bien que*, the **[[explanatory c'est que]]**, and four
verbs of cause and effect.

The theme is the economy and work: the slowdown of industry, offshoring, job insecurity and
public debt. The figures are the Insee's, with their year, and the lesson sets out the arguments
without recommending a policy.

## Choosing among the connectors you know

Those that introduce a clause take the indicative. What changes is how the cause is presented.

- *Parce que* gives the cause as new information: it answers the question "why?". It is the
  only one that can answer *Pourquoi ?* on its own: *Pourquoi l'usine ferme-t-elle ? — Parce que
  les commandes ont chuté.* (*Puisque …* or *Car …* would not answer the question.)
- *Puisque* gives a cause the reader already knows or accepts: *Puisque les commandes ont
  chuté, l'usine ferme* (we all know orders fell). That is why it can sound pointed in an
  argument: *Puisque je vous le dis !* (because I'm telling you, so stop arguing).
- *Comme* puts the cause first, as background, before the main clause: *Comme la demande
  baissait, l'entreprise a réduit sa production.* In this sense it normally comes before the main
  clause.
- *Car* adds a justification after the statement, often for the speaker's right to say it:
  *L'usine va fermer, car les commandes ne cessent de baisser.* It is mostly written; careful
  writers avoid starting a sentence with *Car*.
- *Sous prétexte que* reports a cause someone gives and the writer doubts: *La direction a
  supprimé la prime sous prétexte que les ventes stagnaient.*
- *À force de* + noun or infinitive presents a cause by repetition or accumulation: *À force de
  reporter les investissements, l'entreprise a perdu des clients.*

![A chart titled "Which connector of cause?" with six boxes, each pairing a connector with how it presents the cause: puisque, the reader already knows or accepts it; parce que, new information, the answer to "why?"; comme, it comes first, as background; car, a justification added afterwards; sous prétexte que, someone's claim that the writer doubts; à force de, repeated again and again.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dans la mesure où: a cause, or an extent

*Dans la mesure où* + indicative (or conditionnel) has two readings, and a careful writer makes
sure only one fits.

- Cause ("since, given that"): *Dans la mesure où les salaires ont stagné, la consommation a
  ralenti.* Here you could say *puisque* or *étant donné que*.
- Extent ("insofar as, to the extent that"): *Les aides sont utiles dans la mesure où elles
  créent des emplois durables.* Here the meaning is "only as far as": the aid is useful when, and
  as much as, it creates lasting jobs.

To check which reading you have, replace it. If *puisque* works, it's a cause; if *si et seulement
si* or *pour autant que* (lesson 10) works, it's an extent. Some sentences allow both: *Le
projet est rentable dans la mesure où les coûts baissent* can mean "because costs are falling"
or "as long as costs fall". If your reader could hesitate, choose another connector. *Dans la
mesure du possible* (as far as possible) is a fixed phrase.

## En ce sens que: explaining a claim

*En ce sens que* + indicative explains in what way a statement is true: "in that". It follows an
evaluation, often an adjective:

- *La réforme est risquée, en ce sens qu'elle fragilise les plus précaires.* — The reform is
  risky in that it weakens the people in the most insecure situations.
- *Cette crise est inédite en ce sens qu'elle touche tous les secteurs à la fois.* — This crisis
  is unprecedented in that it affects every sector at once.

You'll often hear *dans le sens où*, especially in speech. Some style guides prefer *en ce sens
que* in careful writing, so use that one in an essay.

## Attendu que: a legal ground (recognition)

*Attendu que* + indicative ("whereas, given that") introduces the grounds of a legal or
administrative decision. Court rulings were long written as one sentence made of a chain of
*attendus*: *Attendu que le contrat n'a pas été signé par les deux parties, …* The highest civil
and criminal court, the Cour de cassation, has used a more direct style since October 2019, but you'll
still meet *attendu que* in older rulings, in contracts and in by-laws, next to *considérant que*.
Recognise it; don't use it in an essay. Don't confuse it with *alors que* and *tandis que* (B1),
which set two facts against each other: *attendu que* gives a reason.

## C'est que and c'est parce que

The **[[explanatory c'est que]]** goes from an observed fact to its explanation:

- *S'il hésite, c'est qu'il doute.* — If he is hesitating, it's because he has doubts.
- *Les prix montent : c'est que la demande dépasse l'offre.* — Prices are rising: that's because
  demand is outstripping supply.

The speaker infers the explanation from what can be seen. *Si … c'est parce que* instead puts a
known cause in focus, often to correct a wrong one: *Si l'usine ferme, ce n'est pas à cause des
salaires, c'est parce que les commandes se sont effondrées.* With *ce n'est pas que* +
subjunctive (B2), the two make a neat pair: *Ce n'est pas qu'il soit paresseux, c'est qu'il est
épuisé.*

## Tenir à: to be due to

B1 taught *tenir à* as "to be keen on" (*Je tiens à venir*). With a thing as its subject, *tenir
à* means "to be due to, to come from":

- *La baisse du chômage tient surtout à la démographie.* — The fall in unemployment is mainly due
  to demographics.
- *Le succès de cette région tient à ce qu'elle a su attirer des entreprises.* — This region's
  success comes from its having managed to attract companies (*tenir à ce que* + indicative).

## Consequence at C1

- *Il s'ensuit que* + indicative (it follows that) draws a logical conclusion, in formal writing:
  *Les recettes fiscales reculent ; il s'ensuit que le déficit se creuse.* The verb is
  *s'ensuivre* and is used only in the third person. In the negative, *il ne s'ensuit pas que*
  usually takes the subjunctive.
- *Tant et si bien que* + indicative (so much so that, with the result that) tells a result that
  built up over time, in a slightly literary narrative tone: *Les commandes ont baissé d'année en
  année, tant et si bien que l'usine a fermé.*
- *Partant* (hence, therefore) is literary: recognise it, don't use it. *Plus d'usine, partant
  plus d'emplois* = no more factory, and therefore no more jobs. The formal written equivalent
  is *de là* (B2).

## Verbs of cause and effect

Verbs carry cause and effect more compactly than connectors, which suits the nominal style of
C1 writing.

- *imputer qqch à qqn / à qqch*: to attribute (usually something bad): *On impute la hausse du
  chômage à la crise.* The adjective is *imputable à*.
- *induire*: to cause, to lead to (formal): *La hausse des taux induit un ralentissement de
  l'investissement.* *Induire en erreur* means "to mislead".
- *aboutir à*: to end in, to lead to: *Les négociations ont abouti à un accord.* *Aboutir* alone
  means "to succeed": *Le projet a abouti.*
- *se traduire par*: to show up as, to result in: *La crise s'est traduite par une vague de
  licenciements.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A chain of causes and effects in offshoring
  accDescr: Lower labour costs abroad lead firms to offshore production. Offshoring results in factory closures and redundancies. Redundancies show up as job insecurity in the region, which leads to lower consumption and a slowdown of the local economy. A side branch says that the closures are also attributed to automation.
  A["Coût du travail plus faible ailleurs"] -- induit --> B["Délocalisation de la production"]
  B -- se traduit par --> C["Fermetures et licenciements"]
  D["Automatisation"] -- on impute aussi à --> C
  C -- aboutit à --> E["Précarité dans le bassin d'emploi"]
  E -- il s'ensuit --> F["Consommation en baisse, ralentissement local"]
```

## Reading: deindustrialisation

> *Désindustrialisation : comprendre avant de juger*
>
> En quarante ans, la France a perdu une large part de ses emplois industriels. On aurait tort,
> pourtant, d'imputer ce recul à un seul facteur. Si tant de villes moyennes ont vu fermer leurs
> usines, c'est que plusieurs mouvements se sont conjugués.
>
> La part la plus visible du recul tient aux délocalisations. Dans les années 1990 et 2000, nombre d'entreprises
> ont délocalisé tout ou partie de leur production vers des pays où le coût du travail était plus
> faible. Présentée au nom de la compétitivité, cette stratégie s'est traduite par des vagues de
> licenciements dans les anciens bassins industriels. Encore faut-il nuancer : les économistes
> rappellent qu'une part importante du recul ne relève pas des délocalisations. À cela s'ajoute
> la concurrence des pays émergents, dont la montée en gamme a induit une pression constante sur
> les prix : incapables d'innover, bien des entreprises ont vu fondre leurs marges, puis ont
> fermé, faute de repreneur.
>
> Les gains de productivité y ont aussi contribué, en ce sens qu'une usine moderne produit
> davantage avec moins de salariés. Par ailleurs, les entreprises ont confié à des prestataires
> extérieurs le nettoyage, la restauration ou la logistique, tant et si bien que des emplois
> autrefois comptés dans l'industrie le sont aujourd'hui dans les services. Une partie de la
> désindustrialisation est donc statistique.
>
> Ses effets sociaux, eux, sont bien réels. Dans la mesure où les nouveaux emplois de services
> sont souvent moins qualifiés et plus instables, le marché du travail s'est polarisé : d'un côté
> des postes très qualifiés, de l'autre la précarité des contrats courts et de l'intérim, dont les
> jeunes peu diplômés et les salariés licenciés en fin de carrière sont les premiers à souffrir. Il
> s'ensuit que la question industrielle est devenue une question politique, celle des territoires
> qui se sentent oubliés.
>
> Reste à savoir que faire. Depuis la crise sanitaire, les plans de relance économique ont
> multiplié les aides à la réindustrialisation. Mais ces aides ont un coût, alors même que la
> situation des finances publiques est tendue : selon l'Insee, le déficit public a atteint 5,1 % du PIB en
> 2025, et la dette publique 115,6 % du PIB à la fin de la même année. Les uns plaident pour une
> baisse de la fiscalité des entreprises, seule capable selon eux de restaurer leur compétitivité ;
> les autres jugent qu'elle reporterait la charge sur les autres contribuables, et qu'un simple
> ralentissement de l'activité, a fortiori une récession, aboutirait à creuser encore le déficit.
> Le débat, on le voit, ne fait que commencer.

*Summary by paragraph.*

1. France has lost a large share of its industrial jobs in forty years; the decline shouldn't be
   blamed on one factor (*imputer à*): several trends combined (*se conjuguer*).
2. Offshoring is the most visible cause: production moved to low-wage countries in the 1990s and
   2000s, which showed up as (*s'est traduite par*) waves of redundancies. But much of the decline
   isn't due to (*ne relève pas de*) offshoring. Competition from emerging countries also caused
   (*a induit*) constant pressure on prices; firms that couldn't innovate closed.
3. Productivity gains played a part, in that (*en ce sens que*) a modern factory needs fewer
   workers; and cleaning, catering and logistics were outsourced, so much so that (*tant et si
   bien que*) those jobs now count as services. Part of the decline is a statistical effect.
4. The social effects are real: since (*dans la mesure où*: here a cause) new service jobs are
   often less skilled and less stable, the job market has polarised (young people with few
   qualifications and older workers made redundant suffer most); it follows that (*il
   s'ensuit que*) industry has become a political question for regions that feel forgotten.
5. Recovery plans have funded reindustrialisation, but public finances are stretched (the 2025
   deficit and end-2025 debt from the Insee). One side wants lower business taxes; the other says
   other taxpayers would pay, and that a slowdown, let alone (*a fortiori*) a recession, would
   lead to (*aboutirait à*) an even deeper deficit.

## Dialogue: two economists on the radio

```dialogue
# Deux économistes, une même usine
Journaliste: Pourquoi l'usine de Montcel ferme-t-elle ?
= Why is the Montcel factory closing?
Claire Morin: Parce que ses commandes ont baissé de moitié en trois ans.
= Because its orders have halved in three years.
Hugo Lenoir: Et si elles ont baissé, c'est que le groupe a délocalisé la production de ses pièces.
= And if they've fallen, it's because the group has offshored the production of its parts.
Claire Morin: Je ne dirais pas cela. La baisse tient d'abord à la conjoncture : tout le secteur ralentit.
= I wouldn't say that. The fall is due first of all to the economic situation: the whole sector is slowing down.
Hugo Lenoir: Puisque tout le secteur ralentit, pourquoi ses concurrents embauchent-ils ?
= If the whole sector is slowing down, why are its competitors hiring?
Claire Morin: Dans la mesure où ils ont investi plus tôt, ils sont plus compétitifs. Cela dit, la direction ne peut pas tout imputer à la crise.
= Since they invested earlier, they're more competitive. That said, the management can't blame everything on the crisis.
Hugo Lenoir: Nous sommes donc d'accord sur un point : les licenciements se traduiront par une précarité accrue dans la vallée.
= So we agree on one point: the redundancies will result in greater job insecurity in the valley.
```

Notice *parce que* answering the question, *c'est que* inferring an explanation, *tenir à* for
"to be due to", and Hugo's *puisque*, which takes up Claire's own claim in order to turn it
against her.

## Common mistakes

- *Puisque* or *car* in answer to *Pourquoi ?*: only *parce que* answers the question.
- *Comme* after the main clause in the causal sense: *L'entreprise a réduit sa production, comme
  la demande baissait* reads oddly, or as "while". Put *comme* first, or use *parce que* or *car*.
- A *dans la mesure où* that can be read two ways. Reread it and ask: cause or extent?
- *Il s'ensuit que* with the subjunctive: it states a fact, so it takes the indicative (*il
  s'ensuit que le déficit se creuse*).
- *Attendu que* or *partant* in an essay: they are legal and literary, for recognition.
- Reading *tenir à* as "to be keen on" when its subject is a thing: *La crise tient à …* means "is
  due to".

## Key points

- *Parce que* = new information (answers "why?"); *puisque* = known or accepted (can sound
  pointed); *comme* = first, as background; *car* = a justification afterwards; *sous prétexte
  que* = a cause the writer doubts; *à force de* = by repetition.
- *Dans la mesure où* + indicative = cause (since) or extent (insofar as): make sure one reading
  fits. *En ce sens que* + indicative = in that.
- *Attendu que* (legal) and *partant* (literary) are for recognition.
- *C'est que* infers an explanation from a fact; *si … c'est parce que* puts a cause in focus.
- *Tenir à* = to be due to; *il s'ensuit que* = it follows that; *tant et si bien que* = so much
  so that.
- *Imputer à, induire, aboutir à, se traduire par* carry cause and effect in a formal style.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Tant s'en faut, il reste que: concession and opposition at C1
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

An argument at C1 rarely says "yes" or "no". It grants part of the other side's case and then
holds its ground, or it refuses a claim politely but firmly. This is **[[concession]]**: admitting a
fact or an argument that seems to go against your conclusion, without giving up the conclusion.

You already know the main tools. A2 gave you *pourtant* and *par contre*; B1 *certes, cependant,
néanmoins, en revanche* and *tout en* + gérondif; B2 added *quel que soit, si … que,
quand bien même, encore que, il n'empêche que, toujours est-il que, il n'en reste pas moins que,
pour autant, loin de, quitte à*. This lesson adds the formal connectors that refuse a claim
(*tant s'en faut, loin s'en faut*), the ones that keep a point standing after a concession (*il
reste que, il n'en demeure pas moins que*), two adverbs (*au demeurant, cela dit*), a
**[[concessive inversion]]** (*si grand soit-il*), and a **[[restrictive clause]]** with *pour autant
que*. It ends with the paragraph that concedes and then counters, the backbone of the DALF essay.

The theme is ecology: degrowth, sobriety, the ecological transition and greenwashing. The lesson
gives each side its best arguments and takes neither.

## Refusing a claim: tant s'en faut, loin s'en faut

*Tant s'en faut* and *loin s'en faut* ("far from it", "not by a long way") come after a statement
that something is *not* so, and make the denial stronger. They are formal and usually close the
sentence, after a comma:

- *La transition écologique n'est pas achevée, tant s'en faut.* — The ecological transition is not
  complete, far from it.
- *Tous les pays n'ont pas réduit leurs émissions, loin s'en faut.* — Not all countries have cut
  their emissions, not by a long way.

Both come from the old impersonal verb *s'en falloir* (to be lacking), which you'll also meet in
*il s'en faut de beaucoup* (far from it) and *peu s'en est fallu* (it very nearly happened). In
everyday speech, *loin de là* says the same thing. *Tant s'en faut* is the older form; some purists
object to *loin s'en faut* as a blend of *loin de là* and *tant s'en faut*, so in an exam *tant
s'en faut* is the safe choice.

## The point still stands: il reste que, il n'en demeure pas moins que

After a concession, these phrases bring back the point you are defending. They take the
indicative, since they state a fact:

- *Certes, la taxe carbone pèse sur les ménages modestes ; il reste qu'elle incite à moins
  consommer d'énergie fossile.* — Admittedly, the carbon tax weighs on low-income households; the
  fact remains that it encourages people to use less fossil energy.
- *La décroissance a des partisans sincères. Il n'en demeure pas moins qu'aucun pays ne l'a
  appliquée à grande échelle.* — Degrowth has sincere supporters. It is still true that no country
  has applied it on a large scale.

They belong to one family with B2's *il n'en reste pas moins que*, *toujours est-il que* and *il
n'empêche que*. From the most formal to the most everyday: *il n'en demeure pas moins que* →
*il n'en reste pas moins que* → *il reste que, toujours est-il que* → *il n'empêche que* → *n'empêche*
(informal, on its own: *N'empêche, il a raison*).

## Two adverbs: au demeurant, cela dit

- *Au demeurant* (formal) adds a point "for that matter", often one that strengthens what you've
  said or slightly qualifies it: *Cette mesure, au demeurant peu coûteuse, a été bien accueillie.*
  — This measure, which for that matter costs little, was well received.
- *Cela dit* (that said, having said that) turns from what you've just granted to a
  reservation, in speech and in writing: *Le projet est séduisant. Cela dit, son financement reste
  flou.* You'll hear *ceci dit* just as often. Some style guides prefer *cela dit*, since *cela*
  points back to what has been said and *ceci* normally points forward; in an exam, *cela dit* is
  the safe choice.

## Si grand soit-il: the concessive inversion

B2 taught *si* + adjective + *que* + subjunctive (*si ambitieux qu'il soit*: however ambitious it
may be). Formal French can drop *que* and invert the subject pronoun: *si* + adjective + *soit* +
pronoun.

- *Si ambitieux soit-il, ce plan reste flou.* — However ambitious it may be, this plan remains
  vague.
- *Si coûteuse soit-elle, la transition est inévitable.* — However costly it may be, the transition
  is unavoidable.
- *Si nombreux soient-ils, les militants ne représentent pas toute l'opinion.* — However many of
  them there are, activists don't represent all opinion.

The adjective agrees with the subject, and the pronoun after *soit* anticipates the noun that
follows: *coûteuse … elle … la transition*. The verb is nearly always *être*, in the subjunctive.

The same concession can be written *tout* + adjective + *qu'il est* or *qu'il soit* (*tout
ambitieux qu'il est*). Grammars accept both moods here, so neither is wrong; the indicative
presents the fact as real. *Tout* agrees before a feminine adjective starting with a consonant:
*toute coûteuse qu'elle soit*.

## Pour autant que: as far as, provided that

*Pour autant que* + subjunctive sets a limit on what you claim: it is a **[[restrictive clause]]**.

- *Pour autant que je sache, aucune étude ne le prouve.* — As far as I know, no study proves it.
  (Lesson 05's *que je sache* says the same, shorter.)
- *La taxe sera acceptée, pour autant que les recettes soient redistribuées.* — The tax will be
  accepted, provided that the revenue is redistributed.

Don't confuse it with B2's *pour autant* (for all that), an adverb with no clause: *Il a perdu ;
il ne renonce pas pour autant* (he lost; he isn't giving up for all that).

## Tout en + gérondif: while, although

B1 taught *tout en* + gérondif for two things done at once (*Il travaille tout en écoutant de la
musique*). When the two actions don't sit well together, the same structure becomes a
concession: *Tout en reconnaissant l'urgence climatique, elle refuse toute taxe nouvelle.* —
While she acknowledges the climate emergency, she rejects any new tax. The subject of the
gérondif is the subject of the main verb.

## En revanche or par contre?

Both mean "on the other hand", and both are used by good writers. In the nineteenth century
Littré condemned *par contre*, following a remark by Voltaire, and the objection lasted. André
Gide defended the phrase: *en revanche* adds an idea of compensation that is not always wanted,
and nobody would announce a bereavement as a "revanche". Today the Académie française says *par
contre* cannot be called a mistake, since excellent authors have used it, but notes that usage
advises against it wherever another adverb fits. In practice: both are current, *par contre* is more
frequent in speech, and *en revanche* is the safe choice in a formal essay.

![A chart titled "Conceding at C1, by grammar and register" in three columns. Clause in the indicative: il n'en demeure pas moins que (formal), il reste que (neutral), il n'empêche que (neutral). Subjunctive or inversion: si ambitieux soit-il (formal), pour autant que + subjunctive (formal), si ambitieux qu'il soit (written). Adverb or phrase: tant s'en faut and loin s'en faut (formal), au demeurant (formal), cela dit (neutral), par contre (neutral).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Concede, then counter

The C1 argument paragraph usually moves in three steps: grant (*certes, il est vrai que, on ne
saurait nier que*), counter (*il n'en demeure pas moins que, il reste que, cela dit*), and support
the counter with a fact or an example.

> *Certes, les défenseurs de la croissance verte n'ont pas tort de rappeler que l'innovation a
> déjà permis de réduire les émissions de certains secteurs. Il n'en demeure pas moins que ces
> gains sont souvent annulés par la hausse de la consommation : des voitures moins gourmandes,
> mais plus nombreuses et plus lourdes, émettent au total à peine moins. Si prometteuse soit-elle,
> la technologie ne suffira donc pas à elle seule à tenir les objectifs fixés, pour autant que l'on
> puisse en juger aujourd'hui.*

Admittedly, the defenders of green growth are right to point out that innovation has already cut
the emissions of some sectors. It is still true that these gains are often cancelled out by rising
consumption: cars that use less fuel, but are more numerous and heavier, emit barely less in
total. However promising it may be, technology alone will therefore not be enough to meet the targets
that have been set, as far as one can judge today.

## Reading: sobriety or green growth?

> *Sobriété ou croissance verte : le débat qui divise les écologistes*
>
> Rares sont les sujets qui suscitent autant de passion. D'un côté, les partisans de la
> décroissance estiment que l'on ne peut produire toujours plus sur une planète aux ressources
> limitées. De l'autre, ceux de la croissance verte jugent que l'innovation permettra de concilier
> prospérité et neutralité carbone, objectif que la France s'est fixé pour 2050.
>
> Le constat de départ, lui, fait consensus. Selon le rapport de synthèse du GIEC publié
> en 2023, la température moyenne à la surface du globe a dépassé de 1,1 °C, sur la période
> 2011-2020, celle de la période 1850-1900. L'atténuation du changement climatique n'a donc rien
> de facultatif. Reste à savoir comment l'obtenir.
>
> Pour le collectif Sobriété maintenant, la réponse passe par la frugalité. « Nous ne demandons
> pas aux gens de revenir à la bougie, explique l'une de ses militantes. Nous demandons de
> consommer moins, et mieux. » Le mouvement dénonce la surexploitation des ressources et
> l'artificialisation des sols, qui fait disparaître chaque année des terres agricoles. Il dénonce
> aussi l'écoblanchiment des grandes marques, qui vantent un produit « responsable » tout en
> augmentant leurs ventes. Ses propositions se veulent concrètes : réparer plutôt que remplacer,
> limiter la publicité pour les produits les plus polluants, abaisser la vitesse sur les
> autoroutes. « La frugalité n'est pas un sacrifice, assure la militante, c'est une liberté
> retrouvée. »
>
> L'économiste Paul Ternier, que ses adversaires disent productiviste, n'est pas convaincu, tant
> s'en faut. « La décroissance, si séduisante soit-elle sur le papier, signifierait moins de
> recettes publiques, donc moins d'hôpitaux et d'écoles. » Selon lui, l'innovation a déjà fait
> chuter le coût des énergies renouvelables, et rien n'indique que ce mouvement doive s'arrêter. Il
> plaide pour une taxe carbone plus élevée, pour autant que ses recettes soient reversées aux
> ménages modestes. Au demeurant, ajoute-t-il, les pays qui investissent le plus dans les énergies
> propres sont souvent les plus riches.
>
> Cela dit, les deux camps se rejoignent sur un point : la sensibilisation ne suffit plus. Les
> jeunes, chez qui l'écoanxiété progresse, attendent des actes. Quant aux climatosceptiques, ils
> se font plus discrets qu'il y a vingt ans, sans avoir disparu, loin s'en faut. Il reste que
> l'activisme, des manifestations aux recours en justice, a changé de visage : on ne cherche plus
> seulement à sensibiliser l'opinion, mais à contraindre les décideurs. Encore faudra-t-il
> convaincre une opinion inquiète pour son pouvoir d'achat, qui soupçonne souvent l'effort de
> peser d'abord sur les plus modestes.

*Summary by paragraph.*

1. Degrowth supporters say you can't keep producing more on a finite planet; green-growth
   supporters think innovation will reconcile prosperity and carbon neutrality, France's target
   for 2050.
2. The starting point is agreed: in the IPCC's synthesis report of 2023, global surface
   temperature in 2011–2020 was 1.1 °C above that of 1850–1900. Mitigation is
   not optional; the question is how.
3. An invented group, *Sobriété maintenant*, calls for frugality ("consume less, and better"),
   and denounces overexploitation, land take (*l'artificialisation des sols*) and the greenwashing
   of brands that praise a "responsible" product while selling more (*tout en*: concession). It
   proposes repairing rather than replacing, limiting advertising for the most polluting products
   and lower motorway speeds.
4. An invented economist, called growth-first (*productiviste*) by his opponents, rejects degrowth
   (*tant s'en faut*): however attractive (*si séduisante soit-elle*), it would mean less public
   money; innovation has already made renewables cheaper. He wants a higher carbon tax, provided that (*pour autant que* + subjunctive) its revenue
   goes back to low-income households; for that matter (*au demeurant*), the countries investing
   most in clean energy are often the richest.
5. Both camps agree that awareness-raising is no longer enough; the young, among whom
   eco-anxiety is growing, want action; climate sceptics are quieter but far from gone (*loin
   s'en faut*); activism now aims to constrain decision-makers, not just to make the public aware.
   A public worried about its purchasing power still has to be convinced.

## Dialogue: a radio debate

```dialogue
# Deux invités, un même constat
Animatrice: Inès Royer, la décroissance, n'est-ce pas un retour en arrière ?
= Inès Royer, isn't degrowth a step backwards?
Inès Royer: Pas du tout. Nous défendons une vie frugale, pas la pauvreté. Cela dit, je reconnais que le mot fait peur.
= Not at all. We stand for a frugal life, not poverty. That said, I admit the word frightens people.
Marc Dalbin: Il fait peur parce qu'il annonce moins d'emplois. Tout en partageant vos inquiétudes, je crois à l'innovation.
= It frightens them because it means fewer jobs. While I share your concerns, I believe in innovation.
Inès Royer: L'innovation n'a pas fait baisser la consommation d'énergie mondiale, loin s'en faut.
= Innovation hasn't brought world energy consumption down, far from it.
Marc Dalbin: Certes. Il n'en demeure pas moins qu'elle a rendu l'énergie solaire bon marché.
= Admittedly. It is still true that it has made solar energy cheap.
Inès Royer: Si bon marché soit-elle, elle ne compense pas la hausse de la demande.
= However cheap it may be, it doesn't make up for the rise in demand.
Animatrice: Vous êtes donc d'accord sur un point : il faut agir vite.
= So you agree on one point: we must act fast.
```

## Common mistakes

- *Tant s'en faut* after a plain positive statement: *La transition est réussie, tant s'en faut*
  contradicts itself. The phrase reinforces a denial: *La transition n'est pas réussie, tant s'en
  faut.*
- *Il reste que* or *il n'en demeure pas moins que* + subjunctive: they take the indicative.
- Mixing the two concessive forms (*si ambitieux qu'il soit-il*). Choose one: *si ambitieux qu'il
  soit* or *si ambitieux soit-il*.
- *Pour autant que* + indicative: in standard French it takes the subjunctive (*pour autant que je
  sache*).
- Confusing *pour autant* (for all that, no clause) with *pour autant que* (as far as, + clause).
- Using *par contre* in a formal exam essay when you're unsure: it isn't wrong, but *en revanche* is
  safer.

## Key points

- **[[Concession]]** grants a point without giving up the conclusion: grant (*certes*), counter (*il
  n'en demeure pas moins que, il reste que, cela dit*), support.
- *Tant s'en faut, loin s'en faut* reinforce a denial (far from it), formally.
- *Il reste que, il n'en demeure pas moins que* + indicative: the point still stands.
- *Au demeurant* = for that matter (formal); *cela dit* (or *ceci dit*) = that said.
- *Si* + adjective + *soit-il* = however … it may be (formal inversion); the adjective agrees.
- *Pour autant que* + subjunctive = as far as, provided that.
- *Tout en* + gérondif can concede: while, although.
- *En revanche* and *par contre* are both current; *en revanche* is the safe exam choice.

lessons.title: Ce dernier, à savoir, somme toute: cohesion in long texts
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 09 and 10 linked one idea to the next: cause, consequence, concession. A long text needs
more than that. The reader must always know who or what each sentence is about, how one
paragraph leads to the next, and where the argument is going. Two words name this:

- **[[Cohesion]]** is the set of visible links between sentences: pronouns and other words that
  refer back, connectors, repeated or related words, punctuation.
- **[[Coherence]]** is the logic underneath: the ideas follow, nothing contradicts, and the reader
  can see the plan. A text can be cohesive and still incoherent (every sentence linked, but the
  argument going nowhere).

The DALF C1 synthesis and essay are marked partly on both, and the reading paper uses long texts
that rely on them. The theme is towns and urban planning: urban sprawl, the fifteen-minute city,
gentrification and the regeneration of old industrial sites. The towns in the examples are
invented; the concepts are real.

## Referring back: anaphora

**[[Anaphora]]** is any word that points back to something already named, so that you don't repeat
it. You know the pronouns (*il, le, lui, en, y*, B1 *lequel*). C1 texts add three families.

### Ce dernier, celui-ci, le premier … le second

*Ce dernier* (*cette dernière, ces derniers, ces dernières*) refers to the last-named noun
that matches its gender and number:

- *Le maire a reçu l'urbaniste. Ce dernier a présenté son projet de piétonnisation.* — The mayor
  met the town planner. The latter presented his pedestrianisation plan.

Here *il* could mean either man; *ce dernier* chooses the planner. *Celui-ci* does the same job
(in the pair *celui-ci … celui-là*, "the latter … the former", *celui-là* is now literary). For exactly two items, *le
premier … le second* (or *la première … la seconde*) means "the former … the latter":

- *Deux options s'offrent à la ville : le tramway et le bus à haut niveau de service. Le premier
  coûte plus cher, le second transporte moins de voyageurs.* — The town has two options: the tram
  and the rapid bus. The former costs more, the latter carries fewer passengers.

*Ce dernier* can still be unclear. In *Le maire a transmis le rapport de l'urbaniste à son
adjoint ; ce dernier l'a jugé trop optimiste*, the last-named man is the deputy, but a reader may
hesitate between the deputy and the planner. When two antecedents fit, don't rely on the rule:
repeat the noun (*l'adjoint*). Where the candidates differ in gender or number, a relative *lequel,
laquelle* (B1) can also pick one out, since it marks both.

![A diagram titled "Who is ce dernier?" with four examples. In each, an arrow goes from the word that points back to what it refers to, and the full sentence is written underneath: "ce dernier" points to "l'urbaniste"; "cette décision" points to "le conseil a voté la piétonnisation"; "le premier … le second" points to "le tramway … le bus"; "ledit terrain" points to "le terrain des anciennes forges".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Lexical anaphora

You can also refer back with a noun. Three ways:

- a **[[hyperonym]]**, a more general word: *la rue piétonnière … cet aménagement; le tramway … ce
  mode de transport*;
- a nominalisation of a verb in the previous sentence: *Le conseil a voté la végétalisation
  des cours d'école. Cette décision a été saluée.* (*voter* → *cette décision*; *annoncer* → *cette
  annonce*);
- a demonstrative + a noun that sums up and judges: *ce choix, cette mesure, ce paradoxe, ce
  recul*.

The judging noun is a quiet way of taking a stand: *cette réforme* is neutral, *cette
improvisation* is not.

### Ledit, ladite (recognition)

Legal and administrative French refers back with *ledit, ladite, lesdits, lesdites* (the
aforesaid), written as one word, which also contracts: *audit, auxdits, dudit, desdites*. *La
commune a acquis le terrain des anciennes forges ; ledit terrain sera aménagé en parc.* Recognise
it in a contract or a council decision; in an essay, write *ce terrain*.

## Thematic progression

Every sentence has a theme (what it's about, usually at the start) and something new it says
about it. **[[Thematic progression]]** is the way themes follow each other through a paragraph.
There are three common patterns:

- Constant theme: the same theme each time. *La ville nouvelle a été créée en 1970. Elle
  compte aujourd'hui 80 000 habitants. Elle souffre pourtant d'un manque de commerces.*
- Linear: the new element of one sentence becomes the theme of the next. *La commune a
  racheté une friche industrielle. Cette friche accueillera un quartier mixte. Ce quartier
  associera logements, bureaux et commerces.*
- Split theme: a general theme is divided into parts, each taken in turn. *L'agglomération
  regroupe trois types d'espaces. Le centre est dense et ancien. La première couronne est faite de
  grands ensembles. La périphérie, enfin, est pavillonnaire.*

A good paragraph often mixes them. A paragraph where the themes jump with no link is the
commonest cause of a text that "doesn't flow".

## The paragraph

At C1 each paragraph develops one idea. It usually opens with a **[[topic sentence]]** that states
the idea, then explains, illustrates and limits it, and ends with a sentence that concludes or
leads to the next paragraph. In the DALF synthesis, the reader should be able to rebuild your plan
from your topic sentences alone.

## Connectors for organising a long text

B1 gave you *d'une part … d'autre part, en premier lieu, par ailleurs, en outre, en définitive*;
B2 *de surcroît, qui plus est, en d'autres termes*. Two C1 additions:

- *À savoir* (namely) introduces the precise content of what you've just announced, often a list:
  *Le plan vise trois objectifs, à savoir réduire la place de la voiture, densifier le centre et créer des
  espaces verts.* Unlike *c'est-à-dire*, it doesn't reformulate: it spells out.
- To conclude: *somme toute* (all in all, all things considered: it sums up, often with a
  slightly concessive tone), *au bout du compte* (when all is said and done, in the end: the final
  result of a process), *en fin de compte* (at the end of the day, ultimately; very common in
  speech and writing). Their meanings overlap a lot; in most sentences any of them, or *en
  définitive*, fits.

## Punctuation for long sentences

- The semicolon joins two independent clauses that are closely linked, or separates the
  items of a list when they contain commas: *Le centre se vide ; la périphérie s'étend.*
- The colon announces an explanation, a consequence, a list or a quotation: *Le constat est
  simple : la ville s'étale.*
- Dashes (*tirets*) and parentheses set off an aside; dashes make it more visible.
- In France a space comes before *; : ? !* and inside *« »*. On a computer it should be a non-breaking
  space, so the sign never starts a line.

## Reading: a town that stopped sprawling

> *Saint-Aurèle : quand une ville cesse de s'étaler*
>
> Pendant quarante ans, Saint-Aurèle a grandi par sa périphérie. Lotissements pavillonnaires,
> zones commerciales, ronds-points : l'étalement urbain y a suivi le modèle de tant d'autres
> agglomérations françaises. Ce modèle, pratique pour qui possède une voiture, a eu un coût, à
> savoir des terres agricoles bétonnées, des trajets toujours plus longs et un centre-ville qui se
> vidait. En vingt ans, la surface bâtie de la commune avait progressé bien plus vite que sa
> population.
>
> En 2021, la loi Climat et résilience a fixé un objectif national de « zéro artificialisation nette »
> des sols à l'horizon 2050. Pour Saint-Aurèle, ce cap a tout changé. Puisqu'il devenait difficile
> de s'étendre, il fallait construire la ville sur la ville. La municipalité s'est donc tournée vers
> une friche industrielle de douze hectares, les anciennes forges, abandonnées depuis les années
> 1990.
>
> L'urbaniste chargée du projet, Nadia Ferhat, a défendu deux principes. Le premier est la densité :
> des immeubles de quatre à six étages plutôt que des pavillons. Le second est la mixité fonctionnelle
> : logements, bureaux, commerces et équipements dans un même quartier. Cette dernière s'inspire de
> la « ville du quart d'heure », concept popularisé par le chercheur Carlos Moreno, selon lequel chaque
> habitant devrait trouver l'essentiel à moins de quinze minutes à pied ou à vélo.
>
> La requalification des forges ne s'est pas faite sans débats. Lors de la concertation, des habitants
> du quartier prioritaire voisin ont dit craindre la gentrification : la hausse des loyers qu'amènerait
> le nouveau quartier ne risquait-elle pas de les repousser plus loin ? La ville a répondu en réservant un
> tiers des logements au parc social. D'autres ont regretté la piétonnisation de la rue principale,
> redoutée par les commerçants. Ces derniers reconnaissent aujourd'hui que la rue piétonnière attire
> davantage de clients qu'avant.
>
> Reste la question du climat. Les étés plus chauds font du centre un îlot de chaleur. La végétalisation
> des places et des cours d'école, ainsi que la plantation de mille arbres, devrait abaisser la
> température ressentie de quelques degrés, selon les services de la ville. Les urbanistes
> rappellent toutefois qu'un arbre met des années à donner de l'ombre : c'est sur une décennie
> que l'on pourra juger le résultat.
>
> Somme toute, Saint-Aurèle n'a rien inventé. Elle n'est ni une ville nouvelle sortie de terre, ni un
> modèle pour toutes les communes. Mais en fin de compte, elle montre qu'un aménagement plus sobre de
> l'espace reste possible, pour peu qu'on accepte d'en débattre.

*Summary by paragraph.* (Saint-Aurèle and its people are invented; the 2021 law and the
fifteen-minute city are real.)

1. For forty years the town grew through its outskirts, following the urban-sprawl model; the
   cost, namely (*à savoir*), lost farmland, longer journeys and an emptying centre. Built-up land
   grew much faster than the population.
2. The 2021 Climate and Resilience Act set a national goal of "zero net land take" by 2050, so the
   town had to build within itself, on a twelve-hectare brownfield site, the old forges.
3. The planner defended two principles: the former (*le premier*), density; the latter (*le
   second*), mixed use, inspired by the "fifteen-minute city" popularised by Carlos Moreno.
4. During public consultation, residents of the nearby deprived neighbourhood feared
   gentrification; a third of the homes were set aside as social housing. Shopkeepers opposed
   pedestrianisation; the latter (*ces derniers*) now admit it brings more customers.
5. Hotter summers make the centre a heat island; greening and a thousand trees should lower the
   felt temperature by a few degrees, though trees take years to give shade.
6. All in all (*somme toute*), the town invented nothing, and is neither a new town nor a model
   for all; but ultimately (*en fin de compte*) it shows that more sparing planning is possible.

Notice the anaphora: *ce modèle* (lexical), *ce cap* (a summing-up noun for the national goal), *le premier … le
second*, *cette dernière* (the last-named principle, mixed use), *ces derniers* (the shopkeepers).

## Dialogue: a public consultation

```dialogue
# Réunion de concertation
Urbaniste: Le projet a trois volets, à savoir le logement, les commerces et les espaces verts.
= The project has three parts, namely housing, shops and green spaces.
Habitante: Et la rue des Forges ? Vous allez la fermer aux voitures ?
= And the rue des Forges? Are you going to close it to cars?
Urbaniste: Oui, sa piétonnisation est prévue pour l'an prochain. Cette mesure a été votée en juin.
= Yes, its pedestrianisation is planned for next year. That measure was voted in June.
Habitante: Ma voisine et sa fille tiennent la boulangerie. Cette dernière craint de perdre des clients.
= My neighbour and her daughter run the bakery. The daughter is afraid of losing customers.
Urbaniste: Je comprends. Au bout du compte, les rues piétonnières attirent souvent plus de monde.
= I understand. In the end, pedestrian streets often attract more people.
Habitante: Souvent, oui. Mais pas toujours.
= Often, yes. But not always.
```

*Cette dernière* is clear here: it points to *sa fille*, the last-named woman. The translation
says "the daughter", because English "the latter" would sound stiff in speech.

![A simplified town plan with labels. In the middle, le centre ancien, a dense oval of buildings crossed by la rue piétonnière. Around it, le quartier pavillonnaire, a wide ring of small detached houses. Near the river at the bottom right, la friche, three empty industrial sheds and a chimney. Dashed arrows labelled l'étalement urbain point from the ring out into the fields, towards a few new houses and a shopping zone.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Common mistakes

- *Ce dernier* for a noun that isn't the last one named of its gender and number. Check what comes
  just before it.
- *Le premier … le second* for more than two items: use *l'un … l'autre … le troisième*, or
  repeat the nouns.
- *À savoir* used to reformulate (*Il est parti, à savoir il a démissionné*): use *c'est-à-dire*
  or *autrement dit*.
- *Ledit* in an essay: it belongs to legal and administrative texts.
- No space before *; : ? !* when typing French in France: the space is expected there.
- A paragraph without a topic sentence: the reader can't see your plan.

## Key points

- **[[Cohesion]]** = visible links; **[[coherence]]** = logic. A C1 text needs both.
- *Ce dernier* = the last-named noun of its gender and number; *le premier … le second* = the
  former … the latter (two items). If two antecedents fit, repeat the noun.
- Lexical anaphora: a hyperonym, a nominalisation (*cette décision*), a summing-up noun.
- Thematic progression: constant, linear, split.
- One idea per paragraph, announced by a topic sentence.
- *À savoir* = namely; *somme toute, au bout du compte, en fin de compte* conclude.
- *Ledit, ladite* (aforesaid) are legal: recognition only.

lessons.title: Ce n'est pas faux: presupposition, implication and irony
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A C1 reader, in the Council of Europe's description, understands not only what a text says but
what it implies. Lesson 08 showed how a writer signals how sure they are. This lesson looks at
what lies under the words: what a sentence takes for granted, what a speaker leaves you to work
out, and what an ironic writer says while meaning the opposite.

B2 gave you the vocabulary of hidden meaning: *le sous-entendu, sous-entendre, insinuer,
l'allusion, faire allusion à, la langue de bois*. Here you'll learn to tell three layers apart,
**[[presupposition]]**, **[[implication]]** and **[[irony]]**, to spot **[[connotation]]**, and to report all of
this neutrally, which the DALF synthesis requires.

The theme is political and media communication: a press conference, a satirical column, a
headline that can be read two ways. Every politician, party and newspaper in the lesson is
invented.

## Presupposition: what is taken for granted

A **[[presupposition]]** (*le présupposé*) is information a sentence takes as already true. Its test
is simple: it survives when you turn the sentence into a negative or a question.

- *Le ministre a cessé de contredire son Premier ministre.* — The minister has stopped
  contradicting his Prime Minister.
- *Le ministre n'a pas cessé de contredire …* / *A-t-il cessé de contredire … ?*

All three sentences presuppose that he used to contradict him. That is what *cesser de*
presupposes. Words that trigger a presupposition include:

- *cesser de, arrêter de, continuer à, recommencer à, de nouveau, encore, ne … plus*: *Il ne ment
  plus* presupposes he lied;
- *aussi, même*: *Même la porte-parole l'admet* presupposes that others admit it, and that she was
  among the least likely to;
- factive verbs, which present their clause as true: *regretter que, savoir que, s'apercevoir
  que, reconnaître que*: *Elle reconnaît que le chiffre était faux*;
- definite descriptions: *le nouveau scandale* presupposes there was an old one;
- *enfin*: *Le gouvernement a enfin réagi* presupposes that it was late.

A question built on a presupposition traps the person who answers: *Depuis quand votre parti
trompe-t-il les électeurs ?* Answering with a date accepts the accusation. Journalists and
debaters use this; a careful listener refuses the frame: *Votre question présuppose ce qu'elle
devrait démontrer.*

![An iceberg in the sea. Above the water, the sentence "Le ministre a enfin reconnu son erreur." Just below the surface, what the sentence takes for granted: he made a mistake, and he was slow to admit it. Deep below, what the speaker may want the listener to infer: he can't be trusted.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Implication: what the speaker leaves you to infer

An **[[implication]]** (*l'implicite* in the wide sense, and *le sous-entendu*, B2) is what the
speaker wants you to infer from the words *and the situation*. Unlike a presupposition, it
depends on context, and the speaker can deny it.

- *Il est déjà minuit …* (said by a host) — implies "it's time for you to go". The host can
  always say, "I was only giving the time."
- *Mon adversaire, lui, n'a jamais été condamné … pour l'instant.* — The last words insinuate
  that he will be.

An insinuation is a hostile implication made on purpose. To speak *à demi-mot* is to say
something without spelling it out, and a listener who understands *à demi-mot* gets it at once.
*Le non-dit* is what everyone knows and nobody says; *lire entre les lignes* means finding it.
*Une mauvaise langue* is a person who gossips and insinuates.

## Irony, antiphrasis and the second degré

**[[Irony]]** says something while meaning something else, usually the opposite, and lets the
listener see the gap. Its simplest form is **[[antiphrasis]]** (*l'antiphrase*), saying the exact
opposite: *Bravo, quelle organisation !* after a fiasco.

How do you spot it in writing? Look for a clash between the words and the facts (praise for a
failure), exaggeration (*un succès historique* for a minor event), a register that doesn't fit
(solemn words for something trivial), quotation marks around a word the writer doesn't accept
(*sa « réforme »*), and words of false surprise (*Quelle surprise !*).

Related words: *le second degré* is the opposite of literal meaning (*c'est du second degré* = it's
not meant literally); a *pince-sans-rire* person jokes with a straight face; *le persiflage* is
mocking banter that seems polite; *railler* and *la raillerie* are open mockery; a *narquois*
smile or tone is sardonic; *une pique* is a barbed remark aimed at one person.

## Saying less: litotes and polite indirectness

**Litotes** (B2) says less in order to mean more. Some are fixed in everyday speech:

- *Ce n'est pas faux.* — literally "it isn't false". It usually signals a **reserved
  agreement**: you have a point, but I'm not fully with you. In some contexts it is simply warm
  agreement, so listen to the tone.
- *Ce n'est pas mal du tout* (it's very good); *il n'est pas idiot* (he's clever).

Politeness often works by indirectness, and the C1 speaker reads it: *Vous auriez l'heure ?* (=
what time is it?); *Je ne suis pas sûr de vous suivre* (often = I disagree); *Il serait peut-être
bon de revoir ce point* (= this needs redoing). A rhetorical question is a statement in
question form: *Qui pourrait s'y opposer ?* means "nobody could".

To sort what you read or hear, ask these questions in order:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Said, presupposed, implied or ironic?
  accDescr: A decision chart. Is it stated in the words? If yes, it is explicit. If not, does it survive when the sentence is negated? If yes, it is a presupposition. If not, does it depend on the situation, so that the speaker could deny it? If yes, it is an implication. If the words seem to mean the opposite of what the speaker thinks, it is irony.
  A["Is it stated in the words?"] -- yes --> B["Explicit"]
  A -- no --> C["Does it survive negation?"]
  C -- yes --> D["Presupposition"]
  C -- no --> E["Does it depend on the situation? Could the speaker deny it?"]
  E -- yes --> F["Implication"]
  B --> G["Do the words mean the opposite of what the speaker thinks?"]
  G -- yes --> H["Irony"]
```

## Connotation and double meaning

**[[Connotation]]** is what a word suggests beyond what it denotes. Two words can name the same
thing and connote opposite judgments:

| neutral or positive | negative connotation |
|---|---|
| *le gouvernement* | *le régime* |
| *une personne* | *un individu* |
| *un rassemblement* | *un attroupement* |
| *une contribution* | *une taxe* (in some contexts) |
| *un plan social* | *des licenciements* |

*Un plan social* (officially now *un plan de sauvegarde de l'emploi*) is the softer term; *des licenciements* says what happens. Writers
choose between them to connote a stance: *Ce mot connote le mépris. Dans ce contexte, « régime »
a une connotation péjorative.*

A double meaning (*le double sens*) is a phrase that can be read two ways, and its
ambiguity (*l'ambiguïté*) may be deliberate or accidental. An equivocal statement (*un
propos équivoque*) is ambiguous in a way that leaves doubt, often suspicious; *l'équivoque* is that
ambiguity, and a speaker who wants to be clear says *pour lever toute équivoque*. A *non-sens*, by
contrast, has no logical meaning at all.

### One headline, two readings

> *Le ministre attaque les journalistes sans preuve.*

Reading 1: the minister has no proof (*sans preuve* goes with *attaque*). Reading 2: he attacks
the journalists who have no proof. The ambiguity may be an accident of word order, or it may be
the editor's way of saying something without being sued for it. Rewritten unambiguously: *Sans
apporter de preuve, le ministre attaque les journalistes.*

### Example: three layers in one sentence

> *« Contrairement à d'autres, je n'ai jamais changé d'avis sur l'Europe. »*

- Explicit: the speaker says he has always held the same view on Europe. That is *explicite*.
- Presupposed: *contrairement à d'autres* takes for granted that other people did change their
  minds.
- Implied: in a debate against a rival who once changed position, the listener infers "my
  rival is inconsistent". That is the *insinuation*, and it stays deniable: *Je ne visais
  personne.*

A journalist reporting it neutrally would write: *Le candidat a affirmé n'avoir jamais changé
d'avis sur l'Europe, une formule que beaucoup ont comprise comme une pique adressée à son
adversaire.* Note *une formule*: a neutral word. *Une insinuation* would already be a judgment,
and *une attaque* a stronger one. The connotation of the reporting noun is part of the report.
When a sentence is ambiguous (*un propos ambigu*), say so rather than choosing a reading for the
reader: *Le propos reste ambigu : il peut viser …, ou …*

## Reporting the implicit neutrally

In a synthesis or a summary, you must report what a document implies without adding your own
opinion. Useful verbs: *laisser entendre que, suggérer que, insinuer que* (hostile),
*sous-entendre que*. Useful frames: *Sans le dire explicitement, l'auteur présente la réforme comme un
échec. — Le ton ironique de la chronique montre que son auteur désapprouve la mesure.* Keep the
difference between what is explicit (stated) and what is implicit (implied) visible: *Le
texte affirme que …; il laisse entendre que …*

## Reading: a satirical column

> *Chronique : la transparence, quelle belle idée*
>
> Il faut saluer le courage de Gérard Vallon. Hier matin, le ministre de la Simplification a enfin
> reconnu que son plan de « choc administratif » n'avait pas tout à fait atteint ses objectifs.
> Certes, le nombre de formulaires a doublé ; certes, les délais se sont allongés. Mais qui
> pourrait reprocher à un ministre d'avoir trop simplifié ? Saluons aussi sa constance : depuis
> deux ans, il annonce chaque trimestre que le plus dur est derrière nous.
>
> La conférence de presse, elle, fut un modèle du genre. Interrogé sur les sommes engagées, le
> ministre a répondu, avec ce sourire narquois que ses collaborateurs disent « bienveillant », que
> la question était « intéressante » et qu'il y reviendrait « en temps utile ». Pour lever toute
> équivoque, il a ajouté que le gouvernement n'avait « rien à cacher ». On ne l'avait pas accusé
> de cacher quoi que ce soit, mais il est toujours rassurant de le savoir. La salle a apprécié la
> performance. Les journalistes, eux, sont repartis avec leurs questions intactes : ce sera
> toujours cela de moins à préparer pour la prochaine fois.
>
> Les mauvaises langues, qui ne manquent jamais dans les couloirs des ministères, murmurent que
> le plan a surtout servi à occuper un ministre dont personne ne savait que faire. Nous n'en croyons rien, évidemment. Nous
> constatons seulement que, lorsqu'une journaliste lui a demandé s'il comptait rester à son poste,
> M. Vallon a répondu qu'il était « au service des Français ». Qui en doutait ?
>
> Interrogé sur le rapport parlementaire qui juge son plan « coûteux et mal évalué », le ministre a
> salué « un travail sérieux », dont il « partage l'esprit ». Traduisons : il ne l'a pas lu. Puis,
> avec ce sens de la nuance qui fait sa réputation, il a regretté que « certains » préfèrent « le
> dénigrement systématique à l'action ». Ces « certains », chacun l'aura compris, n'ont pas de nom :
> c'est tout l'art de l'insinuation. Quant à savoir si le plan serait prolongé, la réponse fut d'une
> clarté exemplaire : « Rien n'est exclu. » Un conseiller a précisé ensuite que le rapport « ne
> disait rien de nouveau », ce qui, venant du cabinet, ressemble fort à un aveu.
>
> Saluons enfin l'élégance de sa pique finale à l'opposition, dont « les propositions tiennent sur
> un timbre-poste ». Le persiflage est un art ; encore faut-il que le timbre ne soit pas plus épais
> que le plan. Le ministre, dit-on, est reparti satisfait. Il avait de bonnes raisons de l'être :
> une heure durant, il a parlé de transparence sans que personne ait appris où était passé
> l'argent.

*Summary by paragraph.* (Vallon and his ministry are invented.)

1. The columnist "salutes" the minister's courage: he has at last admitted (*enfin*: he was late)
   that his plan didn't quite work; forms have doubled and delays grown, "but who could blame a
   minister for simplifying too much?" (antiphrasis and a rhetorical question). For two years he
   has announced every quarter that the worst is over.
2. At the press conference he dodged the question on costs with a sardonic smile, promised to
   come back to it "in due course", and said the government had "nothing to hide", which nobody
   had suggested (an implication the columnist turns against him). The journalists left with
   their questions unanswered, "that much less to prepare next time".
3. Gossips say the plan mainly served to keep him busy; the columnist "doesn't believe a word of
   it" (irony), then reports his empty answer about staying in office.
4. Asked about a parliamentary report calling the plan costly and badly assessed, he praised it
   ("translation: he hasn't read it"), blamed unnamed "certain people" (an insinuation), and
   answered with an empty "nothing is ruled out", which the columnist calls exemplary clarity. An
   adviser said the report "said nothing new", which sounds like an admission.
5. He mocked the opposition's proposals as fitting on a postage stamp; banter is an art, "provided
   the stamp isn't thicker than the plan" (a final dig, *la pique*). He left satisfied: for an hour
   he spoke of transparency without anyone learning where the money went.

The irony is never stated: it comes from the gap between the praise (*courage, modèle,
élégance*) and the facts, from the quotation marks of distance, and from the false naivety of
*Qui en doutait ?*

## Dialogue: at the press conference

```dialogue
# Questions au porte-parole
Journaliste: Le gouvernement a-t-il renoncé à la réforme ?
= Has the government given up the reform?
Porte-parole: Le gouvernement n'a jamais renoncé à réformer. Il prend le temps de la concertation.
= The government has never given up on reforming. It is taking the time to consult.
Journaliste: Donc la réforme est reportée.
= So the reform is postponed.
Porte-parole: Ce n'est pas faux. Disons qu'elle n'est pas pour demain.
= That's not untrue. Let's say it won't happen tomorrow.
Journaliste: Le ministre de l'Économie la juge pourtant urgente.
= Yet the economy minister considers it urgent.
Porte-parole: Le ministre a ses convictions. Je n'ai pas d'autre commentaire.
= The minister has his convictions. I have no further comment.
```

Read between the lines: *prendre le temps de la concertation* implies a delay; *Ce n'est pas
faux* is a reserved admission; *Le ministre a ses convictions* implies disagreement inside the
government, without saying it.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing presupposition and implication: a presupposition survives negation (*Il n'a pas
  cessé de mentir* still presupposes lying); an implication depends on context and can be denied.
- Taking *Ce n'est pas faux* as plain "yes": it is often a reserved agreement.
- Reading irony literally, or seeing it everywhere. Look for a clash with the facts.
- Reporting an implication as a statement in a synthesis: write *l'auteur laisse entendre que*,
  not *l'auteur dit que*.
- *Équivoque* as "equivalent": it means ambiguous, often suspiciously so.

## Key points

- **[[Presupposition]]** = what a sentence takes for granted; it survives negation and questions.
  Triggers: *cesser de, encore, ne … plus, aussi, même, enfin, regretter que, savoir que*.
- **[[Implication]]** = what the speaker leaves you to infer from words and context; it can be denied.
- **[[Irony]]** says one thing and means another; **[[antiphrasis]]** says the opposite. Spot it by a clash
  with the facts, exaggeration, register, quotation marks.
- *Ce n'est pas faux* is usually a reserved agreement (litotes).
- **[[Connotation]]**: *gouvernement / régime*, *personne / individu*.
- Report the implicit neutrally: *laisse entendre que, suggère que, sans le dire explicitement*.

lessons.title: Calembours et contrepèteries: French wordplay
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 12 showed how French says things without saying them: presupposition, implication,
irony. Humour uses the same machinery for fun. Understanding a French joke is a real C1 skill:
the Council of Europe's C1 descriptors include humour among the things a proficient user follows,
and French humour leans heavily on the language itself. This lesson looks at the **[[pun]]**
(*le calembour*), the **[[spoonerism]]** (*la contrepèterie*), the punchline, absurd humour and
self-mockery, the press cartoon, and how to explain a joke in French without killing it.

Every joke here is invented for the lesson. The comedians named are described, never quoted.

## Why French is rich in puns

French has many homophones, words that sound the same and are spelled differently, because
its spelling keeps letters that are no longer pronounced. Four of them name the picture below:

- *le ver* (worm), *le verre* (glass), *vert* (green), *le vers* (line of poetry), and the
  preposition *vers* (towards).

![Four pictures in a row under the title "[vɛʁ] one sound, four words", each with its French word and English meaning below: a worm coming out of an apple (le ver, worm), a glass of water (le verre, glass), a green leaf (vert, green), and a page with four lines of a poem (le vers, line of poetry).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Other families: *la mer, la mère, le maire*; *sans, cent, le sang, il sent*; *le cou, le coup, le
coût*; *la fin, la faim*; *le vin, vingt, vain*. Elision and the linking of words add more: *l'ami*
and *la mie* sound alike. A **[[pun]]** that plays on such a sound is a *calembour*. *Le jeu de mots*
is the wider term: any play on words, including a word with two meanings or a phrase slightly
distorted.

### Example 1: building and explaining a calembour

> *Pourquoi le poète ne croque-t-il jamais de pommes ? — Parce qu'il préfère les vers.*

Why doesn't the poet bite into apples? Because he prefers *les vers*: the worms you find in
apples, or the lines of poetry he writes. In French you'd explain it like this:

> *Le calembour repose sur l'homophonie entre « les vers » (les animaux) et « les vers » (de la
> poésie). La question fait attendre une raison liée aux pommes ; la réponse en donne une liée au
> métier du poète. Les deux sens se rencontrent dans le même mot.*

The pun rests on the homophony between the two words. The question makes you expect a reason
about apples; the answer gives one about the poet's job. Both meanings meet in one word.

Notice the vocabulary of explanation: *reposer sur* (to rest on), *jouer sur le double sens de*
(to play on the double meaning of), *faire attendre* (to make you expect), *la chute* (the
punchline).

## Puns in the press

French headlines love the *jeu de mots*, often on a fixed expression taken literally:

- *Inondations : le maire se jette à l'eau.* — *Se jeter à l'eau* means "to take the plunge"
  (decide to act); in a flood story it is also literal.
- *Prix du carburant : les automobilistes font le plein … de colère.* — *Faire le plein* is "to
  fill up the tank"; the ending turns it into "they're filled with anger".

The pause, written *…*, marks the moment the reader's expectation is turned. That moment is *la
chute*. A good headline pun stays clear and quick; a strained one makes readers groan.

## La contrepèterie: swapping sounds

A **[[spoonerism]]** swaps sounds (usually the first consonants, sometimes vowels) between two words,
so that a new phrase appears. In French, *la contrepèterie* is an old game: Rabelais already
played it in the sixteenth century, and *Le Canard enchaîné* has run a weekly column of them for
decades. The rule of the game is that the author never gives the solution: the reader must find
the hidden phrase.

There is a catch. Most classic French contrepèteries are bawdy: the innocent sentence hides a rude
one, and that's the joke. The examples here are invented and clean, so they are milder than the
real thing:

- *Il a mangé le bout du pain.* → swap *b* and *p*: *Il a mangé le pou du bain.* (He ate the
  bathtub louse.)
- *Elle a renversé le pot de lait.* → swap *p* and *l*: *le lot de paix* (a share of peace).
- *Il a coupé la pomme de terre.* → swap *p* and *t*: *Il a coupé la tomme de père.* (He cut the
  "father's tomme", an absurd cheese on the model of *la tomme de chèvre*.)

Spoonerisms work on sounds, not spelling: *lait* becomes *paix* because both end in the
same vowel, whatever their letters.

## The punchline, the quip, absurd humour

- *La chute* is the punchline: the last turn that changes the meaning of everything before it.
- *La boutade* is a quick witty remark, often a joke that hides a serious point: *Il a répondu par
  une boutade.*
- *L'absurde* is humour that follows a logic to an impossible conclusion. A sentence like *Pour ne plus
  perdre mes clés, je les ai cachées. Je ne sais plus où* is absurd in a small way: each step is
  logical, and the result is nonsense.
- *La dérision* is mockery that makes something look ridiculous (*tourner en dérision*);
  *l'autodérision* is turning it on yourself, a much-valued trait in French public life.

## Two humorists, described

- Raymond Devos (1922–2006) was born in Mouscron, in Belgium, to French parents, and made his
  career in France. *Humoriste* is the usual French label for a solo comedian like him. His stage
  monologues typically start from an ordinary situation, take a word or an expression literally,
  and follow its logic further and further into the absurd. Critics call him a magician of words.
- Pierre Desproges (1939–1988), born in Pantin near Paris, was known for a learned, black and
  often provocative humour. On France Inter radio he played the prosecutor of a mock court, in *Le
  Tribunal des flagrants délires*, and on television he made *La Minute nécessaire de monsieur
  Cyclopède*, short parodies of educational films. He died of cancer in April 1988.

Neither can be understood without hearing them; both are widely available in recordings. When
you listen, notice how much of the effect comes from rhythm and from the gap between a serious
tone and an absurd content.

## The press cartoon

*Le dessin de presse* (the press cartoon) and *la caricature* (a drawing that exaggerates a
person's features) have a long tradition in France. *Le Canard enchaîné*, a satirical weekly,
published its first issue on 10 September 1915, in the middle of the First World War, against
the official propaganda of the time; it stopped after five issues and came back on 5 July 1916.
It still appears every Wednesday, without advertising.

### Example 2: explaining a cartoon

The cartoon (invented): a minister stands on the deck of a small boat that is half under water,
holding a steering wheel, and says to the passengers: *Tout va bien, nous gardons le cap.*

> *Le dessinateur tourne en dérision l'optimisme du gouvernement. La caricature joue sur le
> contraste entre l'image, un bateau qui coule, et le discours rassurant du ministre. « Garder le
> cap », expression habituelle des responsables politiques, est pris au pied de la lettre : le
> ministre tient bien la barre, mais le bateau sombre. L'humour naît de cet écart.*

The cartoonist mocks the government's optimism. The cartoon plays on the contrast between the
image, a sinking boat, and the minister's reassuring words. *Garder le cap* (to stay on course), a
politicians' stock phrase, is taken literally: the minister is indeed at the helm, but the boat
is going down. The humour comes from that gap.

## How to explain a joke in French

Explaining a joke is a fair C1 task (in a discussion of a cartoon, for example). Useful frames:

- *Le jeu de mots repose sur …* / *joue sur le double sens de …*
- *L'humour naît du décalage entre … et …*
- *La chute renverse …* / *On s'attend à …, or …*
- *L'auteur tourne en dérision …* / *pratique l'autodérision*
- *C'est du second degré.*

Say what is expected, what comes instead, and which word carries both meanings.

## Common mistakes

- Explaining a pun by spelling: say which two meanings share the sound.
- Thinking a *contrepèterie* works on letters: it swaps sounds.
- Confusing *la caricature* (an exaggerating drawing) with *le dessin animé* (a cartoon film).
- Using *l'humoriste* for any funny person: it names someone whose profession is humour.
- Quoting a comedian's line in an exam to show culture: describe the style instead, in your own
  words.

## Key points

- French homophones (*ver, verre, vert, vers*) make the **[[pun]]** (*calembour*) easy; *jeu de mots*
  is the wider term.
- The **[[spoonerism]]** (*contrepèterie*) swaps sounds between two words; the reader finds the
  hidden phrase; classic ones are often bawdy.
- *La chute* = punchline; *la boutade* = quip; *l'absurde, la dérision, l'autodérision*.
- Raymond Devos (1922–2006): wordplay and the absurd; Pierre Desproges (1939–1988): black,
  learned humour; *Le Canard enchaîné*: first issue 10 September 1915.
- To explain a joke: what you expect, what comes, which word holds both meanings.
