lessons.title: Ethos, pathos, logos: rhetoric and great speeches
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 12 taught you to read what a text does to its reader without saying so. Rhetoric is the
old name for that art, practised on purpose: *la rhétorique* is the art of persuading by speech.
French schools and universities still teach its classical tools, French political life still
values *l'éloquence*, and a few speeches belong to the country's shared memory.

This lesson gives you the three means of persuasion described by Aristotle, the five parts of a
classical speech, and four French speeches, described and analysed, never quoted. It is strictly
neutral on the questions those speeches addressed: it looks at what each speech did, how it was
built and what followed. Lesson 21 will turn this into method for your own exposé.

## The three proofs: ethos, pathos, logos

In his *Rhetoric* (fourth century BC), Aristotle distinguished three kinds of proof that a speaker
can use. French uses the Greek words.

- **[[Ethos]]** is the speaker's character as the audience perceives it: competence, honesty,
  goodwill. An *orateur* (or *oratrice*) who is believed has already half won.
- **[[Pathos]]** is the emotion the speaker stirs in the audience: pity, indignation, pride, fear.
  *Émouvoir* (to move) is its verb: *Elle a ému l'Assemblée.*
- **[[Logos]]** is the reasoning itself: facts, figures, arguments, refutation.

Every good speech mixes the three. A speech of pure logos convinces without moving; pure pathos
moves but doesn't last; without ethos, neither is believed. *Haranguer* (to harangue) is to
address a crowd forcefully, usually with pathos and little logos. Note its aspirated *h*: *je
harangue, il a harangué la foule, que je harangue*, never *j'harangue*.

## The five parts of a classical speech

Latin rhetoric divided a speech into parts; French teaching usually keeps these five, still used
to analyse speeches.

![A timeline of a classical speech from left to right in five segments: exorde (opening), narration (the facts), confirmation (the arguments for), réfutation (answering the arguments against) and péroraison (the closing appeal). A curve above the timeline shows the emotional intensity rising slightly in the narration, staying low in the confirmation and réfutation, and peaking in the péroraison.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

1. *L'exorde* (the **[[exordium]]**, masculine: *un exorde*) opens the speech. It wins attention and
   goodwill, and often builds the speaker's ethos.
2. *La narration* sets out the facts: what the situation is, how it came about.
3. *La confirmation* gives the arguments for the speaker's position: logos above all.
4. *La réfutation* answers the opponents' arguments, one by one.
5. *La péroraison* (the **[[peroration]]**) closes the speech. It sums up and appeals to the
   audience, and it is usually where pathos is strongest.

Speakers also use figures of speech (B2 lesson 20h2): **l'anaphore** (a word repeated at the
start of successive clauses), **la gradation**, **l'antithèse**, **la question rhétorique**. In a
speech, repetition and rhythm do the work that paragraphs do on the page: the ear needs them.

Two more words for what speeches are. *Un plaidoyer* is a speech in defence of someone or of a
cause (*un plaidoyer pour l'école publique*); *un réquisitoire* is a prosecutor's speech, and by
extension a scathing attack (*un réquisitoire contre la politique du gouvernement*). *La tribune*
is the rostrum from which deputies speak (*monter à la tribune*), and also an opinion piece in a
newspaper.

## Four French speeches

### Victor Hugo on poverty (9 July 1849)

Hugo, already a famous poet, was then a deputy in the Assemblée nationale législative of the
Second Republic. During a debate on public assistance and provident schemes, he argued that
poverty could not only be relieved but destroyed, and that this was the duty of legislators.
The speech is famous for its narration: concrete, precise descriptions of how the poorest
families of Paris lived, which give the pathos its force. Its logos is a duty argument: if such
poverty exists, society as a whole is answerable for it. Much of the conservative majority
did not share his view, and no great law came out of it at once, but it is often studied in French schools as an example of eloquence put at the service of a social cause.

### André Malraux and Jean Moulin (19 December 1964)

Jean Moulin had been sent by General de Gaulle to unite the movements of the Resistance; he
created the Conseil national de la Résistance in May 1943, was arrested near Lyon in June and
died in July 1943 after torture. On 19 December 1964 his presumed ashes were carried into the
Panthéon, in the presence of de Gaulle, then President, and André Malraux, minister of cultural
affairs, gave the speech. Malraux, himself a former Resistance fighter, brought strong ethos. The
speech is almost entirely pathos: a solemn rhythm, repetitions, the evocation of the dead and of
the suffering of those who resisted, and a péroraison addressed directly to the young people of
France. It is often cited as a model of funeral eloquence, *l'éloge funèbre*, and as a key moment
in the national memory of the Resistance.

### Simone Veil and the abortion bill (26 November 1974)

Simone Veil, minister of health under President Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, presented to the
Assemblée nationale the bill on the voluntary termination of pregnancy (*interruption volontaire
de grossesse*, IVG). Her opening built her ethos from her own situation: a woman minister addressing a chamber in
which women were very few. The speech relies mainly on logos and ethos: a measured, factual tone, a
description of the legal and social situation, and the argument that the law should address a
reality rather than ignore it; pathos is used sparingly. The debate lasted more than twenty-five
hours over three days and two nights, and its opponents' speeches were often very hard. The
Assemblée voted for the bill in the night of 29 November 1974, by 284 votes to 189, mainly
thanks to the left and the centrists; about two thirds of the government's own majority voted
against. The law of 17 January 1975 was passed for five years, and a law of 31 December 1979
made it permanent.

### Robert Badinter and the death penalty (17 September 1981)

Robert Badinter, garde des Sceaux (minister of justice) under President François Mitterrand,
presented the bill to abolish the death penalty. A lawyer who had
defended people facing execution, he spoke with the ethos of experience. The speech is built on a
long narration of earlier attempts at abolition in France, a confirmation that presents
abolition as a question of principle, and an extended réfutation of the main argument of its
opponents, deterrence. Its opponents argued that the death penalty deterred crime and answered a
demand for justice, and polls at the time suggested that a majority of French people still
supported it. The Assemblée voted for the bill the next day by a large majority, and the law of 9
October 1981 abolished the death penalty. In 2007, a constitutional amendment wrote the abolition
into the Constitution.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: finding the parts of a speech

An invented speech by a mayor opening a library (in summary, then two sentences in French):

> *Mesdames et Messieurs, je ne serai pas long : vous êtes venus pour les livres, pas pour moi.*
> (exorde: humour and modesty build ethos)
>
> Then: the old library closed ten years ago; the building was empty; three hundred people signed
> a petition (narration). The new library will be open on Sundays, free for under-eighteens, and
> it cost less than a roundabout (confirmation, logos). Some say libraries are useless in the age of
> screens; yet the town's waiting lists are full (réfutation).
>
> *Alors, poussez la porte : ce lieu est le vôtre.* (péroraison: a direct appeal)

### Example 2: three ways to close

The same péroraison for a speech asking a town council to keep a night bus, written three ways:

- Logos: *Ce bus coûte 40 000 euros par an ; le supprimer obligerait trois cents salariés de nuit
  à prendre leur voiture.*
- Ethos: *J'ai pris ce bus pendant dix ans pour aller travailler ; je sais ce qu'il représente.*
- Pathos: *Pensez à l'infirmière qui sort de l'hôpital à deux heures du matin et attend, seule,
  sous la pluie.*

The strongest closing combines them: a figure, a person, and the speaker's own experience. Ask
of any speech you analyse: who is speaking (ethos), what feelings are called on (pathos), what
is the argument (logos)?

## Describing a speech in French

- *L'orateur s'appuie sur l'ethos / le pathos / le logos.*
- *Dès l'exorde, elle établit sa légitimité.*
- *La péroraison cherche à émouvoir l'auditoire.*
- *Ce plaidoyer réfute un à un les arguments adverses.*
- *Un discours éloquent* (eloquent), *d'une grande éloquence*.

## Common mistakes

- *Le exorde* or *une exorde*: it's *l'exorde*, masculine (*un exorde*).
- *J'harangue*: *haranguer* has an aspirated *h* (*je harangue, le harangueur*).
- *Émouvoir* for "to move house" or "to move an object": that's *déménager* and *bouger* or
  *déplacer*. *Émouvoir* is to move emotionally.
- Analysing a speech with your own view of its cause: describe the means and the effects.
- Quoting a famous line from memory in an exam: describe it; a misquotation does more harm than
  none.

## Key points

- **[[Ethos]]** (the speaker's credibility), **[[pathos]]** (the audience's emotions), **[[logos]]** (the
  reasoning).
- Five parts: **[[exordium]]** (*l'exorde*), narration, confirmation, réfutation, **[[peroration]]** (*la
  péroraison*).
- *Un plaidoyer* defends, *un réquisitoire* attacks; *monter à la tribune*.
- Hugo on poverty (9 July 1849), Malraux for Jean Moulin (19 December 1964), Veil on the IVG bill
  (26 November 1974), Badinter on the death penalty (17 September 1981).
- *Haranguer* has an aspirated *h*; *émouvoir* is irregular (*émeut, ému*).

lessons.title: Tourner autour du pot: idioms at C1
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B1 you met a dozen idioms (*avoir le cafard, poser un lapin, tomber dans les pommes* …), and
at B2 *se serrer la ceinture*. At C1 the question is no longer "what does it mean?" but "how does
it behave, and where can I use it?".

An **[[idiom]]** (*une expression idiomatique*) is a group of words whose meaning isn't the sum of its
parts: *tourner autour du pot* has nothing to do with pots; it means to beat about the bush. This
lesson adds twenty-six everyday idioms and four skills: which parts of an idiom can change, its
register, the wordplay of headlines, and where French and English idioms match or mislead. The
theme is everyday life and work: a meeting that goes wrong, a family quarrel that ends well.

## Literal and figurative

Every idiom has a literal reading (the picture its words make) and a **[[figurative meaning]]** (what
speakers actually mean by it). *Jeter l'éponge* is literally "to throw the sponge"; figuratively it
means to give up, like a boxer's corner throwing in the towel. Learners see the picture, which
natives no longer do: use it as a memory hook, but translate meanings, not words:

- *Arrête de tourner autour du pot : tu démissionnes ou pas ?* — Stop beating about the bush: are
  you resigning or not?
- *Dix minutes de retard, tu ne vas pas en faire tout un fromage !* — Ten minutes late: don't make
  a mountain out of a molehill! (informal)
- *Ton message tombe à pic : je cherchais justement une traductrice.* — Your message comes at just
  the right time: I was looking for a translator.

![Six picture cards, each showing the literal image behind an idiom, with the idiom written underneath: a sponge flying into a boxing ring (jeter l'éponge), a pear cut into two halves with a knife (couper la poire en deux), a full vase with one drop falling and water running over the rim (la goutte d'eau qui fait déborder le vase), a sailing boat pushed by wind arrows from behind (avoir le vent en poupe), a goat next to a cabbage (ménager la chèvre et le chou), and a cyclist bent low with his head over the handlebars (avoir la tête dans le guidon).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## What changes and what doesn't

An idiom is a **[[frozen expression]]** (*une expression figée*): its words and its determiners are
fixed. Swap in a synonym or change *le* to *un* and the idiom is gone, or people smile:

- *jeter l'éponge*, not ~~jeter une éponge~~ or ~~lancer l'éponge~~;
- *prendre la mouche*, not ~~prendre une mouche~~;
- *avoir d'autres chats à fouetter*, not ~~avoir des autres chats~~ (*d'* is the *de* that replaces
  *des* before an adjective).

But an idiom isn't a block of stone. Its verb is an ordinary verb, and the grammar around it
moves:

| what moves | example |
|---|---|
| tense and person | *Hier, la directrice lui a passé un savon.* |
| object pronouns | *tirer les vers du nez à quelqu'un* → *Elle lui a tiré les vers du nez.* |
| negation | *Ne mettons pas la charrue avant les bœufs.* |
| adverbs, some adjectives | *Il s'est complètement mis le doigt dans l'œil. Elle lui a passé un sacré savon.* |
| possessives | *mettre son grain de sel* → *Je mets toujours mon grain de sel.* |

One detail trips up even advanced learners: in *se mettre le doigt dans l'œil* the *se* is
indirect (the finger is put "to oneself") and the direct object, *le doigt*, comes after
the verb, so the participle doesn't agree: *elle s'est mis le doigt dans l'œil*, like *elle s'est
lavé les mains*.

## Twenty-six idioms by situation

Informal idioms are marked (inf.); the rest are neutral.

### At work: meetings and decisions

| idiom | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *tourner autour du pot* | to beat about the bush | *Arrête de tourner autour du pot.* |
| *appeler un chat un chat* | to call a spade a spade | *Appelons un chat un chat : le projet a six mois de retard.* |
| *mettre la charrue avant les bœufs* | to put the cart before the horse | *Choisir le logo avant d'avoir un produit, c'est mettre la charrue avant les bœufs.* |
| *avoir la tête dans le guidon* (inf.) | to be too busy to see the bigger picture | *En fin d'année, toute l'équipe a la tête dans le guidon.* |
| *avoir d'autres chats à fouetter* | to have other fish to fry | *Désolé, j'ai d'autres chats à fouetter.* |
| *mettre son grain de sel* (inf.) | to put your two cents in (unasked) | *Il faut toujours qu'elle mette son grain de sel.* |
| *couper la poire en deux* | to split the difference | *Tu proposes 400 euros, il en demande 600 : coupez la poire en deux.* |
| *ménager la chèvre et le chou* | to try to please both sides, to sit on the fence | *À force de ménager la chèvre et le chou, le maire n'a satisfait personne.* |
| *être sur la même longueur d'onde* | to be on the same wavelength | *Avec ma nouvelle cheffe, on est sur la même longueur d'onde.* |
| *avoir le bras long* | to have friends in high places | *Son oncle a le bras long : il lui a trouvé un stage au ministère.* |

### Conflict and tempers

| idiom | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *prendre la mouche* | to take offence, to fly off the handle | *Il prend la mouche dès qu'on critique son travail.* |
| *passer un savon à quelqu'un* (inf.) | to give someone a telling-off | *Le chef lui a passé un savon.* |
| *casser du sucre sur le dos de quelqu'un* (inf.) | to badmouth someone behind their back | *Ils cassent du sucre sur le dos du directeur.* |
| *la goutte d'eau qui fait déborder le vase* | the last straw | *Ce retard, c'est la goutte d'eau qui fait déborder le vase.* |
| *en faire tout un fromage* (inf.) | to make a mountain out of a molehill | *Il en a fait tout un fromage.* |
| *se mettre le doigt dans l'œil* (inf.) | to be completely wrong | *Si tu crois qu'il va s'excuser, tu te mets le doigt dans l'œil.* |

### Secrets and suspicion

| idiom | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *tirer les vers du nez à quelqu'un* | to worm information out of someone | *Elle lui a tiré les vers du nez.* |
| *vendre la mèche* | to let the cat out of the bag | *Qui a vendu la mèche ?* |
| *mettre la puce à l'oreille* | to make someone suspicious | *Son silence m'a mis la puce à l'oreille.* |

### Success, failure and moods

| idiom | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *avoir le vent en poupe* | to be on a roll | *Cette start-up a le vent en poupe.* |
| *faire chou blanc* | to draw a blank, to get no result | *La police a fouillé la maison et a fait chou blanc.* |
| *jeter l'éponge* | to throw in the towel | *Après trois échecs, il a jeté l'éponge.* |
| *tomber à pic* | to come at just the right time | *Ton aide tombe à pic.* |
| *être aux anges* | to be over the moon | *Elle a eu le poste : elle est aux anges.* |
| *broyer du noir* | to be down in the dumps | *Depuis son départ, il broie du noir.* |
| *avoir le cœur sur la main* | to be very generous | *Ma voisine a le cœur sur la main.* |

A few notes. *La poupe* is the stern of a ship, so *avoir le vent en poupe* is literally to have
the wind behind you. *Broyer du noir* is darker and lasts longer than *avoir le cafard* (B1),
which can be a passing low mood. In a past narrative you'll hear both *la goutte d'eau qui fait
déborder le vase* (kept as a fixed noun group) and *la goutte d'eau qui a fait déborder le vase*.

## Register: which idioms go where

Most idioms are neutral or informal; very few are formal. This lesson labels six as informal:
*se mettre le doigt dans l'œil, en faire tout un fromage, avoir la tête dans le guidon, casser
du sucre sur le dos de quelqu'un, passer un savon* and *mettre son grain de sel*. They're perfect
among friends and colleagues, risky in a formal letter, and out of place in an essay.

The others are neutral: you'll read them in the press and hear them in radio interviews, and a
well-chosen one can liven up an essay, for example *avoir le vent en poupe, jeter l'éponge,
mettre la charrue avant les bœufs, ménager la chèvre et le chou* or *couper la poire en deux*.
Judgements differ at the edges (a teacher might cross out *faire chou blanc* in an essay; a
journalist wouldn't), so ask who will read you, and when in doubt use a plain word (*se tromper,
critiquer, réprimander, échouer*).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Can I use this idiom here?
  accDescr: A decision chart. If the reader is a friend or a close colleague, an informal or neutral idiom is fine. If not, an idiom labelled informal is replaced by a plain word such as se tromper or critiquer. A neutral idiom is used if it is the only one in the paragraph, perhaps introduced by comme on dit; if the paragraph already has one, keep the best and cut the rest.
  A["An idiom comes to mind"] --> B{"Reader: a friend or close colleague?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Informal or neutral idiom: fine"]
  B -- no --> D{"Is the idiom informal?"}
  D -- yes --> E["Use a plain word: se tromper, critiquer"]
  D -- no --> F{"First idiom in this paragraph?"}
  F -- yes --> G["Use it, perhaps after comme on dit"]
  F -- no --> H["Keep the best one, cut the rest"]
```

## Idioms in headlines

The press loves idioms, above all when the literal meaning comes back to life. Read a headline
twice: once figuratively, then asking whether the subject makes the picture literally true. These
headlines are invented:

- *Réforme des retraites : le gouvernement jette l'éponge* — plain figurative use: the government
  gives up.
- *Salon du fromage : les producteurs en font tout un fromage* — the cheesemakers are making a fuss
  about something, and *fromage* is literal too.
- *Tour de France : le maillot jaune garde la tête dans le guidon* — the race leader is literally
  bent over his handlebars and figuratively focused on the next stage only.
- *Voile : les skippeurs bretons ont le vent en poupe* — Breton sailors are on a roll, and the
  wind is literally behind them.

## English equivalents and false friends

Many idioms have an English partner with a different picture: *appeler un chat un chat* / call a
spade a spade, *avoir d'autres chats à fouetter* / have other fish to fry, *vendre la mèche* / let
the cat out of the bag, *mettre la charrue avant les bœufs* / put the cart before the horse.
Meaning and register match; the English picture translated word for word gives nonsense:
~~appeler une bêche une bêche~~, ~~laisser le chat sortir du sac~~.

Some pairs mislead:

- *faire chou blanc* is getting no result. English "I drew a blank" can also mean "I couldn't
  remember"; for that, French says *j'ai eu un trou de mémoire*.
- *avoir le bras long* is about connections, not about the long arm of the law.
- *tomber à pic* also has a literal meaning: *la falaise tombe à pic dans la mer* — the cliff
  drops sheer into the sea.
- *être aux anges* is pure joy; it has nothing to do with death.

Where do idioms come from? Dictionaries often tell a story: *faire chou blanc* would come from a
regional pronunciation of *coup blanc* in skittles (a throw that knocks nothing down), and
*ménager la chèvre et le chou* is often linked to the old puzzle of a farmer who must ferry a
wolf, a goat and a cabbage across a river. Such stories are traditional explanations, sometimes
disputed. Use them as memory hooks, and don't present them as facts in an essay.

## Two idioms well, not ten badly

In a DALF essay, one or two idioms in a neutral register, placed where they add precision or
colour, show control. Ten in a row show a list learned by heart. Compare:

- Overloaded: *Le gouvernement tourne autour du pot, ménage la chèvre et le chou et met la charrue
  avant les bœufs : bref, il se met le doigt dans l'œil.*
- Controlled: *En annonçant des sanctions avant d'avoir fixé des règles claires, le gouvernement
  met la charrue avant les bœufs. Il cherche à rassurer à la fois les entreprises et les
  associations ; mais à force de ménager la chèvre et le chou, il risque de ne convaincre
  personne.*

The second version keeps two neutral idioms, each tied to a fact (penalties announced before
the rules; trying to reassure both businesses and charities), and drops the informal one.

## Reading: La réunion du lundi

An employee tells the story of a Monday meeting on her blog.

> Un lundi de juin, notre réunion d'équipe devait durer une demi-heure. Elle en a duré deux, et je
> crois qu'aucun d'entre nous ne l'oubliera de sitôt.
>
> Tout a commencé par un détail. Notre directrice, Mme Ferrand, d'ordinaire si directe, a passé dix
> minutes à nous parler de « réorganisation » et de « nouvelles synergies » sans jamais dire de quoi
> il s'agissait. Quand quelqu'un tourne autour du pot à ce point, c'est rarement bon signe. Ce flou
> m'a mis la puce à l'oreille ; mon voisin, Karim, avait l'air de penser la même chose.
>
> C'est Sophie, notre stagiaire, qui a fini par vendre la mèche, bien malgré elle. Elle a demandé,
> très innocemment, si le déménagement à Lyon était toujours prévu pour mars. Silence de mort.
> Personne, à part la direction, n'était censé être au courant. On a appris plus tard que le
> responsable informatique, qui a le bras long mais la langue un peu trop déliée, lui avait tout
> raconté à la cafétéria.
>
> Mme Ferrand a pris la mouche. Au lieu d'appeler un chat un chat et de reconnaître que la décision
> était prise, elle a reproché à Sophie de colporter des rumeurs, puis elle a annoncé qu'elle
> passerait un savon au responsable informatique, absent ce jour-là. Karim, qui a le cœur sur la
> main, a pris la défense de la stagiaire : on ne pouvait pas lui en vouloir d'avoir posé la
> question que tout le monde se posait.
>
> C'est alors que Bertrand, qui ne rate jamais une occasion de mettre son grain de sel, a déclaré
> que ce déménagement était « une chance ». Il se mettait le doigt dans l'œil : la moitié de
> l'équipe a des enfants scolarisés ici, et personne n'a envie de partir. Pour certains, sa remarque
> a été la goutte d'eau qui fait déborder le vase. Deux collègues ont quitté la salle.
>
> Il faut dire que nous avions tous la tête dans le guidon depuis des mois. La direction, de son
> côté, avait mis la charrue avant les bœufs : elle avait signé le bail des nouveaux locaux avant
> même de consulter le personnel.
>
> La suite ? Après une semaine de négociations, la direction a coupé la poire en deux : le
> déménagement aura lieu, mais un an plus tard que prévu, et ceux qui le souhaitent pourront
> télétravailler. Bertrand, lui, ne parle plus de « chance ». Quant à Sophie, elle a été embauchée
> en septembre. Comme quoi, une question naïve tombe parfois à pic.

Glosses: *de sitôt* — any time soon; *d'ordinaire* — usually; *le flou* — the vagueness; *bien
malgré elle* — quite unintentionally; *censé* — supposed to; *la langue déliée* — a loose tongue;
*colporter des rumeurs* — to spread rumours; *le bail* — the lease; *comme quoi* — which goes to
show.

In short: the director talked vaguely about "reorganisation" until the intern innocently gave
away the secret move to Lyon, leaked by a well-connected IT manager. The director took offence, a
colleague's remark that the move was "an opportunity" was the last straw, and two people walked
out. Management, which had signed the lease before consulting anyone, finally split the
difference, and the intern was hired. Notice how the idioms built on a verb change tense like any
verb.

## Dialogue: la fête des parents

Claire and her brother Julien are organising their parents' fortieth wedding anniversary, and
they've fallen out.

```dialogue
# La fête des parents
Claire: Julien, il faut qu'on parle de la fête de papa et maman. Tu boudes depuis dimanche.
= Julien, we need to talk about Mum and Dad's party. You've been sulking since Sunday.
Julien: Je ne boude pas. Je trouve juste que tu as cassé du sucre sur mon dos devant tante Lise.
= I'm not sulking. I just think you badmouthed me behind my back in front of Aunt Lise.
Claire: Qui t'a raconté ça ? Lise ? Elle adore tirer les vers du nez aux gens, puis tout déformer.
= Who told you that? Lise? She loves worming things out of people and then twisting it all.
Julien: Peut-être. Mais tu as dit que je n'avais rien organisé.
= Maybe. But you said I hadn't organised anything.
Claire: J'ai dit que j'avais cherché une salle pendant un mois et que j'avais fait chou blanc. C'est tout. Tu ne vas pas en faire tout un fromage.
= I said I'd looked for a hall for a month and drawn a blank. That's all. Don't make a mountain out of a molehill.
Julien: D'accord. De toute façon, j'ai d'autres chats à fouetter. Et j'ai peut-être une solution : le restaurant de Malik a le vent en poupe, il est plein tous les soirs, mais il veut bien nous prêter sa terrasse le 14 juin.
= All right. Anyway, I've got other fish to fry. And I may have a solution: Malik's restaurant is doing really well, it's full every evening, but he's happy to lend us his terrace on 14 June.
Claire: Sérieusement ? Maman broyait du noir à l'idée qu'on ne fasse rien. Elle va être aux anges.
= Seriously? Mum was down in the dumps at the idea that we wouldn't do anything. She'll be over the moon.
Julien: Et pour le budget, on partage moitié-moitié ?
= And for the budget, shall we go halves?
Claire: Moitié-moitié. Tu vois, quand on veut, on est sur la même longueur d'onde.
= Halves. You see, when we want to, we're on the same wavelength.
```

## Common mistakes

- Changing a determiner: ~~jeter une éponge~~ → *jeter l'éponge*; ~~prendre une mouche~~ →
  *prendre la mouche*.
- Swapping in a synonym: ~~lancer l'éponge~~, ~~couper la pomme en deux~~.
- Agreeing the participle in *se mettre le doigt dans l'œil*: *elle s'est mis le doigt dans
  l'œil* (the direct object, *le doigt*, comes after the verb).
- Keeping *son* with every person: *je mets mon grain de sel*.
- Translating the English picture: ~~laisser le chat sortir du sac~~ → *vendre la mèche*.
- Using *faire chou blanc* for a memory blank → *avoir un trou de mémoire*.
- Piling up idioms in an essay, or using an informal one there.

## Key points

- An idiom has a figurative meaning that its words don't give; translate the meaning.
- It is frozen: no synonyms, no change of determiner. Tense, person, pronouns, negation and
  adverbs move normally.
- Six idioms here are informal (*se mettre le doigt dans l'œil, en faire tout un fromage, avoir
  la tête dans le guidon, casser du sucre sur le dos de quelqu'un, passer un savon, mettre son
  grain de sel*); the others are neutral and can appear in the press.
- Headlines revive the literal meaning for a pun: read them twice.
- Matching English idioms usually have a different picture; a few look alike and mislead.
- Origin stories are memory hooks, often uncertain.
- In an essay, one or two neutral idioms, tied to a fact, are worth more than ten.
- Proverbs are lesson 16h2; collocations such as *prendre une décision* are lesson 14.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Faire preuve de, mettre en œuvre: collocations and support verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can know every word in a sentence and still sound foreign, because words have partners. In
French you *prendre* a decision, *poser* a question and *émettre* reservations; rain is *battante*,
not "strong", and an interest is *vif*, not "lively". These habitual partnerships are
**[[collocations]]**: combinations that aren't idioms (their meaning is clear) but that a native
chooses without thinking, while the other options sound wrong or foreign.

At C1, collocations are what make a report, a synthesis or an essay sound written by a French
speaker. This lesson covers:

- **[[support verbs]]** (*verbes supports*: *faire preuve de, mettre en œuvre, donner lieu à* …),
  their nouns and their prepositions;
- adjectives and adverbs that intensify (*un vif intérêt, hautement improbable*);
- verb + noun pairs (*soulever une question, combler une lacune*);
- calques from English to avoid;
- the vocabulary of public projects.

The theme is a public project: an invented town, Montvalon, builds a tram line, from the
specifications to the final review. B2 lesson 14 taught nominalisation (*l'augmentation des
prix*); support verbs are how French puts those nouns to work.

## Support verbs

A **[[support verb]]** (*verbe support*) carries the tense and the person while the noun carries the
meaning: *faire preuve de patience* means roughly "to be patient", *porter atteinte à la
réputation de quelqu'un* means "to harm someone's reputation". The verb is almost empty; that's
why you can't change it: *on fait preuve de courage*, never ~~on montre preuve de courage~~; *on
met en œuvre un plan*, never ~~on fait en œuvre~~.

Learn each one with its preposition, which is part of the expression:

| support verb | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *faire preuve de* | to show (a quality) | *Les riverains ont fait preuve de patience.* |
| *mettre en œuvre* | to implement | *La ville mettra en œuvre le plan dès janvier.* |
| *faire l'objet de* | to be the subject of | *Le projet fait l'objet d'une enquête publique.* |
| *donner lieu à* | to give rise to | *Le tracé a donné lieu à de vifs débats.* |
| *porter atteinte à* | to harm, to infringe | *Le chantier porte atteinte au patrimoine.* |
| *tirer parti de* | to make the most of | *La ville a su tirer parti des aides de l'État.* |
| *avoir trait à* | to relate to | *Les questions avaient trait au stationnement.* |
| *mettre l'accent sur* | to stress | *La maire a mis l'accent sur la sécurité.* |
| *prêter à confusion* | to be confusing | *Le terme « zone apaisée » prête à confusion.* |
| *prendre en charge* | to take charge of, to cover (costs) | *La région prend en charge 30 % du coût.* |
| *mettre en place* | to set up | *Un comité de suivi a été mis en place.* |
| *faire face à* | to face, to cope with | *Les commerçants font face à une baisse de leur chiffre d'affaires.* |
| *prendre acte de* | to take formal note of | *Le conseil a pris acte du retard.* |
| *donner suite à* | to follow up, to act on | *La mairie n'a pas donné suite à la pétition.* |
| *mettre fin à* | to put an end to | *Ce vote met fin à la polémique.* |
| *faire état de* | to mention, to report | *Le rapport fait état d'un surcoût.* |

Four more verbs work like this, each with its own preposition: *se heurter à* (to come up against:
*le projet se heurte à l'opposition des riverains*), *se solder par* (to end in a result: *la
réunion s'est soldée par un échec*), *remédier à* (to remedy: *remédier aux retards*, never
~~remédier les retards~~), and *passer outre* (to disregard, to override). Careful writing keeps *à*
after *passer outre*: *passer outre aux objections*; the direct construction (*passer outre les
objections*) is very common in the press. Used alone, *passer outre* means "to go ahead
regardless": *malgré l'avis négatif, le maire a décidé de passer outre*. In compound tenses you'll
meet both *il a passé outre* and *il est passé outre*; with a direct object, only *avoir* (*il
a passé outre les objections*).

Several support verbs have more than one sense. *Prendre en charge* is to take charge of a task,
to cover costs (*la Sécurité sociale prend en charge une partie des frais*) and to look after a
person (*un patient pris en charge aux urgences*); a taxi also *prend en charge* a passenger. *Faire
face à* is to cope with a problem, but also, literally, to face a place: *la mairie fait face à la
gare*. The context decides.

Two nouns come from these verbs: *la mise en œuvre* (implementation) and *la mise en place*
(setting up). *La mise en œuvre* is putting a decision into practice; *la mise en place* is
setting up a structure or a system: *la mise en place d'une navette gratuite*.

## Why support verbs matter: the nominal style

Support verbs let a sentence put a noun at its centre, which is the style of reports and the
press (B2 14). Compare:

- *On a beaucoup critiqué le projet.* → *Le projet a fait l'objet de nombreuses critiques.*
- *Les habitants ont été patients.* → *Les habitants ont fait preuve de patience.*
- *La mairie n'a pas répondu à la demande.* → *La mairie n'a pas donné suite à la demande.*

The nominal version is more formal and more impersonal: it says less about who did what. In
conversation the verbal version is usually better.

![A wheel with "verbe support" at the centre and six spokes. Faire: preuve de, l'objet de, face à, état de. Mettre: en œuvre, en place, fin à, l'accent sur. Prendre: en charge, acte de. Porter: atteinte à. Donner: lieu à, suite à. Tirer: parti de.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Adjectives and adverbs that intensify

An **[[intensifier]]** is a word that strengthens another, and French chooses them by habit. English
"strong" or "big" become many different words:

| noun | usual intensifier | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *l'intérêt* | *un vif intérêt* | keen interest |
| *le désaccord* | *un profond désaccord* | deep disagreement |
| *la hausse, la baisse* | *une hausse sensible* | a noticeable rise |
| *le refus* | *un refus catégorique* | a flat refusal |
| *la pluie* | *une pluie battante* | driving rain |
| *l'échec* | *un échec cuisant* | a bitter failure |
| *la majorité* | *une large majorité* | a large majority |

*Sensible* is a false friend here: *une hausse sensible* is noticeable, not sensible (*raisonnable*).

Adverbs pair with adjectives in the same way: *hautement improbable* (highly unlikely), *vivement
recommandé* (strongly recommended), *nettement supérieur* (clearly better), *largement
majoritaire*, *parfaitement conscient*. *Très improbable* is correct, but *hautement improbable*
sounds like a report.

## Verbs and their nouns

Some verbs and nouns go together in written French; learn them in pairs:

- *soulever une question* — to raise a question; *soulever des objections*.
- *lever un doute* — to remove a doubt; *lever une ambiguïté*.
- *émettre des réserves* — to express reservations; *émettre un avis*.
- *nourrir des craintes* — to have fears (*nourrir des doutes, des espoirs*).
- *combler une lacune* — to fill a gap (B2); *combler un retard*.
- *respecter un délai* — to meet a deadline; *tenir une promesse* — to keep a promise.
- *remplir une condition* — to meet a condition.

How do you learn them? Not word by word. When you read an article, note each key noun with the
verb and the adjective that come with it (*soulever une vive inquiétude, prendre une décision
difficile, émettre de sérieuses réserves*) and reuse the whole group in your next piece of
writing. A good learner's dictionary gives these partners in its examples: read them, not only
the translation.

## Calques to avoid

A **[[calque]]** is a word-for-word copy of a foreign expression. Some English calques are plain
mistakes; others are spreading and disputed:

- ~~faire une décision~~ → *prendre une décision*; ~~demander une question~~ → *poser une
  question*.
- ~~prendre place~~ for "to take place" → *avoir lieu* (*prendre place* means to take a seat).
- ~~adresser un problème~~ → *traiter un problème, s'attaquer à un problème, remédier à un
  problème*. *Adresser* in French is to address a letter, a criticism or a question *à quelqu'un*.
- *faire sens* (from "make sense") is now common in speech and in the press, but many style guides
  and teachers still prefer *avoir du sens* or *avoir un sens* in careful writing. Use those in
  an exam.

## The language of projects

A public project has its own words, which you'll meet in any report:

- *le cahier des charges* — the specifications, the document that says what must be built and
  to what standard;
- *l'échéancier* (masculine) — the schedule of deadlines, the timeline;
- *la feuille de route* — the roadmap, the plan of action (also used in politics);
- *le levier* — a lever, and figuratively a means of action: *la fiscalité est un levier de la
  transition écologique*;
- then *la mise en œuvre*, and at the end *le bilan* (A2), the review.

![A timeline of a tram project in four stages from left to right: a document with a list (le cahier des charges), a calendar with coloured bars (l'échéancier), a red tram on rails beside a crane (la mise en œuvre), and a bar chart with a tick mark (le bilan), each above a dot on an arrow pointing right.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: le tramway de Montvalon

An article from a regional newspaper (invented).

> *Tramway de Montvalon : un chantier sous tension*
>
> Annoncée en 2021, la première ligne de tramway de Montvalon devait mettre fin aux embouteillages
> du centre-ville. Le cahier des charges, adopté par le conseil municipal à une large majorité,
> prévoyait neuf kilomètres de voies, quatorze stations et une mise en service à l'automne 2026.
> Trois ans plus tard, l'échéancier a pris un sérieux retard.
>
> La mise en œuvre s'est en effet heurtée à des obstacles imprévus. En creusant près de la place du
> Marché, les ouvriers ont découvert des vestiges médiévaux, ce qui a donné lieu à six mois de
> fouilles. Le projet a également fait l'objet de deux recours d'habitants, selon lesquels le tracé
> portait atteinte à leur qualité de vie. Le tribunal administratif les a rejetés, mais le chantier
> n'a pas pu avancer pendant la procédure.
>
> Face aux critiques, la maire, Hélène Brunet, a mis l'accent sur le dialogue. Un comité de suivi
> a été mis en place, et la mairie affirme avoir donné suite à la plupart des demandes des
> riverains. L'opposition, qui fait état d'un surcoût de quarante millions d'euros, nourrit
> toutefois de vives craintes. Elle reproche à la ville de passer outre aux réserves émises par
> ses propres experts et juge « hautement improbable » une ouverture avant 2028.
>
> Les commerçants, eux, font face à une baisse sensible de leur chiffre d'affaires. Pour y remédier,
> la ville prend en charge une partie de leurs pertes et a lancé une navette gratuite. Elle a
> surtout su tirer parti des aides de l'État et de la région, un levier sans lequel le budget
> n'aurait jamais été bouclé.
>
> Reste la question du stationnement, qui a trait à toute la politique de la ville : la notion de
> « zone apaisée », qui figure dans la nouvelle feuille de route, prête à confusion, car personne
> ne sait si les voitures y seront interdites ou seulement ralenties. Lors du dernier conseil, les
> élus ont pris acte du retard et voté un nouveau calendrier : mise en service en 2028. Le projet
> se soldera-t-il par un succès ? Les habitants, qui ont jusqu'ici fait preuve d'une grande
> patience, attendent de voir.

Glosses: *les embouteillages* — traffic jams; *la mise en service* — the start of service; *les
vestiges* — remains; *les fouilles* — excavations; *le recours* — legal challenge; *le tracé* — the
route; *les riverains* — local residents; *le surcoût* — extra cost; *boucler un budget* — to
balance a budget; *attendre de voir* — to wait and see.

In short: the tram line announced in 2021 is two years late, because of medieval remains and two
legal challenges. The mayor has set up a monitoring committee, while the opposition reports a
large extra cost and accuses the town of ignoring its experts. The town partly compensates shopkeepers,
has made the most of state and regional grants, and has approved a new timetable, but the parking
plan remains unclear.

Count the support verbs: there are more than fifteen, and each one replaces a plainer verb
(*mettre fin aux embouteillages* = *supprimer les embouteillages*).

## Dialogue: au conseil municipal

A councillor from the opposition questions the deputy mayor in charge of transport.

```dialogue
# Au conseil municipal
Conseiller: Monsieur l'adjoint, votre feuille de route prévoyait une ouverture en 2026. Pourquoi ne l'avez-vous pas respectée ?
= Deputy mayor, your roadmap planned an opening in 2026. Why haven't you kept to it?
Adjoint: Nous avons dû faire face à des imprévus : les fouilles archéologiques n'étaient pas dans le cahier des charges.
= We had to cope with unforeseen events: the archaeological digs weren't in the specifications.
Conseiller: Vos experts avaient émis des réserves dès 2022. Vous avez choisi de passer outre.
= Your experts had expressed reservations as early as 2022. You chose to disregard them.
Adjoint: Nous en avons pris acte, et nous avons modifié l'échéancier. Mais je refuse qu'on dise que nous avons agi sans concertation.
= We took note of them, and we changed the schedule. But I won't have it said that we acted without consultation.
Conseiller: Alors, levez un doute : qui prendra en charge le surcoût ?
= Then clear up one doubt: who will cover the extra cost?
Adjoint: L'État et la région, à hauteur de 60 %. Le reste sera financé sans hausse d'impôts.
= The State and the region, up to 60 %. The rest will be funded without a tax rise.
```

## Common mistakes

- Changing the support verb: ~~montrer preuve de~~ → *faire preuve de*; ~~faire en œuvre~~ →
  *mettre en œuvre*.
- Dropping or changing the preposition: ~~remédier les retards~~ → *remédier aux retards*; *faire
  face à*, *donner lieu à*, *avoir trait à*.
- Adding an article where there is none: ~~faire la preuve de patience~~ in this sense → *faire
  preuve de patience* (*faire la preuve de* means to prove).
- Calques: ~~faire une décision~~, ~~demander une question~~, ~~prendre place~~ for "take place".
- Translating "big" or "strong" word for word: *un grand intérêt* is correct but plainer than *un
  vif intérêt*; for a refusal, *catégorique* is the usual partner.
- *Sensible* = noticeable in *une hausse sensible*, not "sensible".

## Key points

- A collocation is a habitual partnership of words; the alternatives aren't wrong in grammar, but
  they don't sound French.
- A support verb carries tense and person; the noun carries the meaning. Learn verb, noun and
  preposition together.
- *La mise en œuvre* puts a decision into practice; *la mise en place* sets up a structure.
- Intensifiers are chosen by habit: *un vif intérêt, un profond désaccord, une hausse sensible,
  hautement improbable*.
- Avoid calques: *prendre une décision, poser une question, avoir lieu*.
- Project words: *le cahier des charges, l'échéancier, la feuille de route, le levier, le bilan*.
- Idioms are lesson 13; academic formulas are lesson 15.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Comme le souligne l'auteur: academic French
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

If you study or work in research in France, or read French scholarship, you'll meet a style with
its own rules: a *nous* that means "I", quotations framed by « guillemets », Latin phrases, and
formulas such as *il convient de* that hardly occur anywhere else. This is the **academic
register**: the formal, impersonal and carefully sourced French of theses, articles and
conference papers. Its conventions also help in the DALF, whose essay rewards precise sourcing
and hedged claims.

This lesson covers:

- the academic voice: *nous*, *on*, impersonal formulas;
- introducing sources, quoting them and paraphrasing them, and why **[[plagiarism]]** is a serious
  matter;
- defining and classifying;
- Latin phrases used in French;
- the words of the university and of research.

The theme is the university: a master's dissertation, a conference, and a plagiarism case
(all invented).

## The academic voice

### *Nous* of modesty

French academic writers avoid *je*. A single author writes *nous*: this is the **nous de
modestie**, the "we" of modesty. The verb is plural, but adjectives and participles agree with
the real author, so they stay singular:

- *Nous sommes convaincu que …* — I am convinced that … (a man writing)
- *Nous sommes convaincue que …* — the same, written by a woman
- *Dans ce chapitre, nous nous sommes efforcée de …* — In this chapter I have tried to …

### *On* and impersonal formulas

*On* is the other way out of *je* (*on observe que, on peut supposer que*). Impersonal formulas
put the claim, not the writer, in front:

- *il convient de* + infinitive — it is advisable to, one should: *Il convient de distinguer
  deux cas.* (*Il convient que* takes the subjunctive: *il convient que le lecteur soit prévenu*.)
- *il importe de* + infinitive — it is important to: *Il importe de préciser la méthode.* (*Il
  importe que* + subjunctive: *il importe que les données soient vérifiées*.)
- *force est de constater que* (B1) — one has to admit that.

Both *il convient de* and *il importe de* are formal; in speech you'd say *il faut* or *c'est
important de*.

## Introducing and citing a source

French introduces an author's view with a small set of phrases:

- *Selon Dupont, …* / *D'après Dupont, …* — according to Dupont (neutral);
- *Pour Dupont, …* — in Dupont's view; *Aux yeux de Dupont, …* — in Dupont's eyes;
- *Comme le souligne / le rappelle / le montre Dupont, …* — as Dupont stresses / recalls / shows.

*Comme le montre Dupont* adopts the author's claim as true; *selon Dupont* keeps a distance. The
verbs that judge an author's claim (*prétendre, admettre, reconnaître* …) are B2 lesson 19:
choose them deliberately.

## Quoting

A **[[citation]]** in academic French is a quotation (in academic English "citation" usually means
the reference: careful). French conventions:

- French quotation marks, « like this », with a non-breaking space inside each one.
- *[…]* (three dots in square brackets) marks a cut in the quoted text.
- *[sic]* after a word means "thus in the original": the error isn't yours. *Sic* is Latin for
  "thus".
- The reference goes in a footnote, *la note de bas de page*, called by a small raised
  number, or in brackets after the quotation: *(Dupont, 2019, p. 42)*.
- In footnotes you'll meet *ibid.* (the same source as the previous note) and *op. cit.* (the
  work already cited). Recognise them; many style guides now prefer short author–date references.

![A page of a dissertation headed 2. Méthodologie. In the main text, a quotation opens and closes with French quotation marks; inside it, a cut is marked with three dots in square brackets and a misspelled word, trés, is followed by [sic]. A small raised number 1 follows the closing quotation mark. Below a short separator line at the bottom of the page, footnote 1 gives the author, the title, the city, the year and the page. Five red numbered markers point to these parts, and a key names them: les guillemets, une coupure, sic, l'appel de note, la note de bas de page.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Paraphrase and plagiarism

A **[[paraphrase]]** (*la paraphrase*; the verb is *paraphraser*) restates a source's idea in your
own words and your own sentence structure, and it still names the source. **[[Plagiarism]]** (*le
plagiat*; the verb is *plagier*) is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, whether
you copy a sentence or rework it lightly without saying where it comes from.

Here is an invented source and three ways of using it:

- Source: *L'étalement urbain allonge les trajets quotidiens et rend la voiture indispensable aux
  ménages modestes.* (Martin, 2018) — Urban sprawl lengthens daily journeys and makes the car
  indispensable for low-income households.
- Plagiarism: *L'étalement des villes allonge les déplacements quotidiens et rend l'automobile
  indispensable aux familles modestes.* A few synonyms, the same sentence, no source.
- Paraphrase: *Comme le montre Martin (2018), plus une ville s'étend, plus les ménages aux revenus
  faibles dépendent de leur voiture.* New structure, new words, the source named.
- Quotation: *Pour Martin, l'étalement urbain « rend la voiture indispensable aux ménages
  modestes » (2018, p. 12).*

Changing a few words doesn't make a paraphrase; naming the source is what keeps it honest.

## Defining and classifying

Academic texts define their terms before using them:

- *on entend par* — by … we mean: *On entend par « ville moyenne » une commune de 20 000 à
  100 000 habitants.*
- *se définir comme* — to be defined as: *Le concept se définit comme …*
- *relever de* — to come under, to be a matter of: *Cette question relève de la sociologie
  plutôt que de l'économie. Cela relève de l'exploit.*
- *se répartir en* — to be divided into: *Les réponses se répartissent en trois groupes.*
- *on distingue* — one distinguishes: *On distingue trois types de sources.*

*Le concept* and *la notion* are close: *le concept* is a defined, theoretical idea (*le concept de
classe sociale*); *la notion* is often a more basic or looser idea (*la notion de temps*, *avoir
des notions d'anglais* = a basic knowledge). *Conceptualiser* is to turn an observation into a
concept.

## Latin phrases

French uses a few Latin phrases, usually written without accents and often in italics:

- *a priori* — at first sight, in principle: *A priori, rien ne s'y oppose.* It is also a
  noun: *un a priori* is a preconception (*avoir des a priori sur quelqu'un*). The 1990
  recommendations also give *à priori*; *a priori* remains the usual spelling.
- *a posteriori* — with hindsight, after the facts: *On ne peut juger ce choix qu'a
  posteriori.* (1990: *à postériori*.)
- *a fortiori* — all the more so: *Si les adultes s'y perdent, a fortiori les enfants.* You'll
  also see *à fortiori*, an older spelling that the 1990 recommendations also give.
- *stricto sensu* — in the strict sense; *lato sensu* — in the broad sense.

## The university and research

- A master's student writes *le mémoire* (masculine; *la mémoire*, A2, is memory) and defends
  it at *la soutenance*, the viva. A doctoral student, *le doctorant* or *la doctorante*,
  writes *la thèse* (B1) and *soutient sa thèse* (defends it).
- Every piece of work ends with *la bibliographie*, the list of works cited; a teacher's
  reading list is also *une bibliographie*.
- Research is published in *la revue scientifique* (an academic journal) after *l'évaluation
  par les pairs* (peer review), and presented at *le colloque*, an academic conference.
- *La méthodologie* says how the research was done; *empirique* research rests on data
  and observation rather than theory alone.
- *La source primaire* is a document from the time studied (an archive, an interview, a
  register); a book about it is a secondary source.

Hypotheses in research often take the conditionnel (B2 10): *ces résultats suggéreraient un lien*
(these results would suggest a link) signals a claim the author doesn't yet fully commit to.

## Reading: un mémoire sous le soupçon

A news item from the website of an invented university.

> *Intégrité scientifique : un mémoire sous le soupçon*
>
> Deux jours avant sa soutenance, prévue le 12 juin, une étudiante de master en sociologie a appris
> que son mémoire présentait 30 % de similitudes avec d'autres textes, selon le logiciel utilisé
> par l'université. A priori, le chiffre était alarmant. A posteriori, il était trompeur : la
> plupart des passages signalés étaient des citations placées entre guillemets, avec leur note de
> bas de page, ou des titres de la bibliographie.
>
> Restaient deux pages du chapitre consacré à la méthodologie. Elles reproduisaient, à quelques
> synonymes près et sans aucune référence, un article paru dans une revue scientifique en 2021.
> L'étudiante a expliqué qu'elle avait voulu paraphraser l'article et qu'elle avait « oublié »
> d'en indiquer la source. Pour sa directrice de mémoire, l'argument ne tient pas : une
> paraphrase doit toujours nommer sa source, et remplacer quelques mots ne suffit pas à en faire
> une.
>
> La commission compétente a estimé que l'affaire relevait du plagiat, mais d'un plagiat limité.
> La soutenance a été reportée à septembre ; l'étudiante a réécrit le chapitre et a finalement
> obtenu son diplôme. « Il convient de distinguer la fraude délibérée de la maladresse », a
> rappelé le doyen, qui a toutefois souligné qu'un mémoire engageait la responsabilité de son
> auteur.
>
> L'affaire a relancé le débat lors du colloque annuel des doctorants, en octobre. Plusieurs
> intervenants ont rappelé que l'évaluation par les pairs, censée garantir la qualité des
> publications, détecte mal les emprunts non signalés, a fortiori lorsqu'ils sont traduits d'une
> autre langue. On entend par plagiat, a précisé une juriste, « toute reprise d'un texte ou d'une
> idée sans mention de son origine », ce qui inclut les idées et pas seulement les mots. Une
> doctorante a présenté une étude empirique menée dans trois universités : la moitié des
> étudiants interrogés ne savaient pas conceptualiser la différence entre paraphrase et plagiat,
> et beaucoup confondaient la notion de « source primaire » avec celle de source fiable.
>
> Il importe, ont conclu les organisateurs, de former les étudiants dès la licence : apprendre à
> citer, c'est aussi apprendre à penser par soi-même.

Glosses: *les similitudes* — similarities; *trompeur* — misleading; *à quelques synonymes près* —
apart from a few synonyms; *la directrice de mémoire* — the dissertation supervisor; *ne pas tenir* — not to
hold up; *la maladresse* — clumsiness; *le doyen* — the dean; *l'intervenant* — the speaker; *la
licence* — the bachelor's degree.

In short: plagiarism software flagged a master's dissertation, but most matches were properly
quoted. Two pages, however, copied an article without a source; the committee called it limited
plagiarism, the viva was postponed and the student graduated after rewriting. At a doctoral
conference, speakers noted that peer review misses unacknowledged borrowing and that many
students can't tell paraphrase from plagiarism.

## A model introduction

The opening of an invented master's dissertation, with its translation.

> Le présent mémoire porte sur les usages du vélo dans les villes moyennes françaises. On entend
> ici par « ville moyenne » une commune de 20 000 à 100 000 habitants. Cette notion, qui relève à
> la fois de la géographie et de l'aménagement, reste floue : comme le souligne Martin (2018), elle
> n'a pas de définition unique. Nous adopterons une démarche empirique, fondée sur une enquête
> menée auprès de 300 cyclistes et sur l'analyse de sources primaires (délibérations municipales,
> plans de circulation). Nous sommes consciente des limites de cet échantillon : il convient donc
> de lire nos résultats comme des pistes plutôt que comme des conclusions. Nous présenterons
> d'abord le cadre théorique, puis la méthodologie, avant d'analyser les résultats.

This dissertation deals with how bicycles are used in France's medium-sized towns. By "medium-sized
town" we mean here a municipality of 20,000 to 100,000 inhabitants. This notion, which belongs to
both geography and planning, remains vague: as Martin (2018) stresses, it has no single
definition. We will take an empirical approach, based on a survey of 300 cyclists and on the
analysis of primary sources (council decisions, traffic plans). We are aware of the limits of this
sample: our results should therefore be read as leads rather than conclusions. We will first
present the theoretical framework, then the methodology, before analysing the results.

Notice *consciente*: one woman wrote it, so the *nous* of modesty takes a feminine singular
adjective.

## Common mistakes

- Plural agreement with the *nous* of modesty: one author writes *nous sommes convaincu(e)*, not
  ~~convaincus~~.
- English quotation marks in French text: use « … » with spaces inside.
- Thinking that changing a few words makes a paraphrase: change the structure and name the source.
- *Le mémoire* or *la mémoire*: the dissertation is masculine.
- Confusing *citation* (a quotation in French) with the English "citation" (a reference).
- *Il convient de* + noun: it takes an infinitive (*il convient de préciser*); *il convient que*
  takes the subjunctive.

## Key points

- The **[[nous de modestie]]** has a plural verb and a singular adjective that agrees with the author.
- *Il convient de, il importe de* (+ infinitive) and *il importe que, il convient que* (+
  subjunctive) are formal.
- *Selon, d'après, pour, aux yeux de* report a view; *comme le montre* adopts it.
- « … », […] for a cut, [sic] for an error in the original, a footnote for the reference.
- A paraphrase uses your words and still names the source; plagiarism hides the source.
- *On entend par, se définir comme, relever de, se répartir en* define and classify.
- *A priori, a posteriori, a fortiori* are usually written without accents.
- The synthesis is lesson 19; the school *dissertation* is honors lesson 20h1.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Chronophage, énergivore: learned word formation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

*Chronophage* (time-consuming), *énergivore* (energy-guzzling), *hyperconnecté* (always online):
the French press coins words like these every week, and a C1 reader understands them on sight,
because they are built from a few dozen Greek and Latin pieces. This lesson teaches those pieces
and the rules for putting them together:

- **[[learned words]]** (*mots savants*) and their Greek and Latin elements;
- **[[derivation]]** (prefixes and suffixes) and **[[compounding]]** (joining two elements or words);
- compound nouns and their plurals, traditional and 1990;
- sigles and acronyms: gender, plural, pronunciation;
- how to guess the meaning of a word you've never seen.

The theme is technology and society: the energy cost of data centres, biometrics, and being
always online.

## Learned words and popular words

Most French words come from Latin by a long road: centuries of sound change wore them down.
*Fragilis* became *frêle*, *hospitale* became *hôtel*, *potionem* became *poison*. Later, scholars
borrowed the same Latin words again, almost unchanged: *fragile, hôpital, potion*. Words borrowed
straight from written Latin or Greek are **[[learned words]]** (*mots savants*: *un mot savant*); the worn-down ones
are popular words. Pairs like *frêle / fragile* or *chose / cause* are called doublets.

Learned words are long, transparent and international, which makes them easy for English
speakers: *la biométrie* is biometrics, *la misogynie* is misogyny, *la xénophobie* is xenophobia.
They are also the material of new coinages.

## Stem, root, prefix, suffix

Take *illisible* (illegible). It has three parts:

- *il-*, a **[[prefix]]** (*le préfixe*): a piece added before;
- *-lis-*, the **[[stem]]** (*le radical*): the part that carries the meaning, here from *lire*;
- *-ible*, a **[[suffix]]** (*le suffixe*): a piece added after, here making an adjective.

*La racine* (the root) is the historical source shared by a family of words, often a Latin or Greek
form (*leg-*, "read", is behind *lire, lisible, légende, lecture*). In everyday grammar talk,
*le radical* is the form you can see in the word, and *la racine* is the older form behind it.

![A word broken into three coloured boxes: il, lis and ible, forming illisible. Below it, a second word, chronophage, is shown as two boxes, chrono and phage, joined by a plus sign.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Building words with prefixes and suffixes is **[[derivation]]** (*la dérivation*): *lire → lisible →
illisible*. Joining two elements that can each carry meaning is **[[compounding]]** (*la
composition*): *chrono* + *phage* → *chronophage*, *porte* + *monnaie* → *porte-monnaie*.

## Greek and Latin elements

| element | meaning | examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-logie* | study, science | *la biologie, la méthodologie* |
| *-graphe, -graphie* | writing | *le biographe, la bibliographie* |
| *-phile / -phobe* | who loves / who fears or hates | *francophile, xénophobe* |
| *-cratie, -crate* | power | *la technocratie, le technocrate* |
| *-cide* | that kills | *l'insecticide, le génocide* |
| *-vore, -phage* | that eats | *énergivore, budgétivore, chronophage* |
| *chrono-* | time | *la chronologie, chronophage* |
| *bio-* | life | *la biométrie, biodégradable* |
| *géo-* | earth | *la géographie, la géothermie* |
| *auto-* | self | *l'autoportrait, l'autodérision* |
| *télé-* | far | *le télétravail, la télécommande* |
| *poly-, multi-* | many | *polyvalent, multitâche* |
| *hyper- / hypo-* | over / under | *hyperconnecté, l'hypothermie* |
| *micro- / méga-* | small / very big | *le micro-ordinateur, la mégapole* |
| *miso-* | hatred | *la misogynie* |
| *xéno-* | foreign | *la xénophobie* |

Some of these deserve a closer look:

- *-vore* (Latin, "eat") and *-phage* (Greek, "eat") make the most productive press words of the
  moment. *Énergivore* is a device or building that eats energy, *budgétivore* a project that eats
  budgets, *chronophage* a task that eats time: *Les réunions sont chronophages.* All three are
  neutral and common in reports.
- *Poly-* gives *polyvalent* (versatile, multipurpose: *une salle polyvalente*, a multipurpose
  hall; *une employée polyvalente*) and the noun *la polyvalence*.
- *La mégapole* is a very large city; *la mégalopole* is also used, often for a chain of cities
  that have grown together.
- *Misogyne* and *xénophobe* are adjectives and nouns: *un discours misogyne, un misogyne*.
- *Francophile* (who loves France and French things) is the opposite of *francophobe*.

### Word families

Once you know an element, a whole family opens. Take *-cratie* (power) and *-crate* (the person
who holds it): *la démocratie* (power of the people) and *le démocrate*, *la bureaucratie* (power
of offices) and *le bureaucrate*, *la technocratie* (power of technical experts) and *le
technocrate*. The adjectives end in *-cratique*: *démocratique, technocratique*. *Technocrate* is
often critical: it suggests an official who decides from figures and far from people's lives
(*une décision de technocrates*).

*-Phobie* has two families too. In medicine it is an irrational fear: *la claustrophobie* (of
closed spaces), *l'arachnophobie* (of spiders). In social and political vocabulary it is hostility:
*la xénophobie* (towards foreigners), *l'homophobie*. *Xénophobe* and *misogyne* (hostile to
women; noun *la misogynie*) are neutral, precise words for a serious accusation: in an essay they
are more precise than *raciste* or *sexiste*, which mean something else, so use them with care
and with evidence.

## Prefixes that change the meaning

| prefix | meaning | examples |
|---|---|---|
| *in-* (*im-, il-, ir-*) | not | *inutile, impossible, illisible, irréversible* |
| *dé-* (*dés-*) | undo, remove | *déconnecter, désactiver* |
| *mé-, mal-* | badly | *méconnaître, malhonnête* |
| *a-* (*an-*) | without | *apolitique, analphabète* |
| *anti- / contre-* | against | *antivirus, contre-productif* |
| *sur- / sous-* | over / under | *surcharger, sous-estimer* |

*In-* usually changes its form before certain letters: *im-* before *b, m, p* (*imbuvable,
impossible*), *il-* before *l* (*illisible*), *ir-* before *r* (*irréel*). There are a few
exceptions (*inlassable*), so check a new word in the dictionary. A prefix often makes an antonym
(*l'antonyme*, a word of opposite meaning): *connecté / déconnecté, lisible / illisible*. Not
every antonym is built this way: *chaud / froid*.

## Suffixes that make adjectives

| suffix | meaning | examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-able, -ible* | that can be … | *biodégradable, lisible* |
| *-if (-ive)* | that does … | *intensif, addictif* |
| *-el (-elle)* | relating to | *virtuel, professionnel* |
| *-ien (-ienne)* | relating to, from | *quotidien, parisien* |
| *-ique* | relating to | *numérique, biométrique* |

*Biodégradable* combines a learned element, a stem and a suffix: *bio-* (life), *dégrad-* (break
down) and *-able*: that living organisms can break down.

## Compound nouns and their plurals

A **[[compound word]]** (*le mot composé*) joins two or more words: *le porte-monnaie, l'arc-en-ciel,
le chef-d'œuvre*. Their plurals follow two systems, both correct today in France:

- Traditionally, each part takes *s* only if the meaning allows it: *des chefs-d'œuvre* (several
  masterpieces, each one "of work"), *des porte-monnaie* (things that carry money: *monnaie* stays
  singular), *des après-midi*.
- The 1990 recommendations simplify verb + noun and preposition + noun compounds: the last word
  takes *s* in the plural, and only in the plural: *des porte-monnaies, des après-midis, des
  gratte-ciels*. Other compounds keep their traditional plural: *des chefs-d'œuvre, des
  arcs-en-ciel*.

Neither spelling is a mistake. Choose one system and keep to it in a text.

![A table of compound plurals in three columns: singular, traditional plural and 1990 plural. Un porte-monnaie: des porte-monnaie, des porte-monnaies. Un après-midi: des après-midi, des après-midis. Un gratte-ciel: des gratte-ciel, des gratte-ciels. Un chef-d'œuvre: des chefs-d'œuvre in both columns. Un arc-en-ciel: des arcs-en-ciel in both columns. These last two rows are grey, with a note that their plural is the same in both systems.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Sigles, acronyms and abbreviations

A *sigle* (A2) is made of initials. When you read it letter by letter, it stays a sigle: *la SNCF*
[ɛs ɛn se ɛf], *le PDG*. When you read it as a word, it is an **[[acronym]]** (*l'acronyme*):
*l'ONU* [ɔny], *l'Unesco*, *le Smic*. Three rules:

- Gender is usually the gender of the first noun of the full name: *la SNCF* (*la Société nationale
  …*), *l'ONU* is feminine (*l'Organisation des Nations unies*), *le Smic* (*le salaire minimum
  …*).
- Plural: sigles normally don't change in writing: *des ONG*, *des PDG*. Acronyms that have
  become ordinary words take *s* and lower case: *un ovni, des ovnis; un laser, des lasers*.
- Writing: sigles in capitals without full stops (*la SNCF*; *S.N.C.F.* with dots is
  old-fashioned); long acronyms often with one capital (*l'Unesco, le Smic*).

*L'abréviation* (feminine) is a shortened word: *M.* (monsieur), *Mme* (madame), *p.* (page),
*cf.* (compare), *etc.* French writes no full stop when the abbreviation ends with the word's last
letter: *Mme, Dr*, but *M.* and *p.*

## Guessing new words

Faced with a new coinage, split it and ask what each element means:

- *une application addictive et chronophage* — *chrono-* (time) + *-phage* (eats): it eats your
  time.
- *un adolescent hyperconnecté* — *hyper-* (over) + *connecté*: online too much, always online.
- *la biométrie* — *bio-* (life) + *-métrie* (measurement): measuring the body (fingerprints, face,
  iris) to identify someone.
- *un dispositif budgétivore* — a scheme that eats the budget.

Journalists also invent playful words for one article (*smartphonophile, réunionite*). Label them
as such if you reuse them, and keep them out of formal essays unless you put them in quotation
marks.

## Reading: la face cachée du nuage

An article from a technology magazine (invented, with figures from ADEME, France's public
environment and energy agency, and Arcep, the telecoms regulator).

> *Numérique : la face cachée du nuage*
>
> Nous l'oublions volontiers : chaque photo stockée « dans le nuage » dort en réalité sur un disque
> dur, quelque part dans un centre de données. Ces bâtiments, refroidis jour et nuit, sont
> notoirement énergivores. Selon l'ADEME, le numérique représentait 2,5 % de l'empreinte carbone
> de la France en 2020 ; une nouvelle évaluation, publiée en janvier 2025, chiffre cette part à
> 4,4 % pour l'année 2022, les centres de données en représentant près de la moitié (46 %). Une
> partie de la hausse tient, il est vrai, à la méthode : la seconde étude a pris en compte, en
> plus, les centres de données situés à l'étranger qui servent les usages français.
>
> La tendance n'en inquiète pas moins les experts. Une étude prospective de l'ADEME et de l'Arcep,
> remise au gouvernement en 2023, estimait que l'empreinte carbone du numérique pourrait
> augmenter d'environ 45 % d'ici à 2030 si rien ne change. Des leviers existent pourtant : garder
> ses appareils plus longtemps, car leur fabrication pèse lourd, ou renoncer à certains usages
> superflus.
>
> Car nos usages, eux, explosent. La biométrie, longtemps réservée aux aéroports, est entrée dans
> nos poches : on déverrouille son téléphone d'un regard. Les adolescents, souvent décrits comme
> hyperconnectés, passent des heures sur des applications que leurs parents jugent chronophages.
> Les adultes ne font guère mieux : qui n'a jamais consulté ses courriels professionnels à minuit ?
>
> Faut-il pour autant céder à la technophobie ? Les ingénieurs que nous avons interrogés refusent
> ce débat de technocrates. Ils misent sur des machines plus sobres, sur des serveurs polyvalents
> qui récupèrent leur chaleur pour chauffer des logements, voire sur des composants biodégradables,
> encore au stade expérimental. La polyvalence, disent-ils, est la clé : un même appareil doit
> pouvoir servir longtemps et à plusieurs usages.
>
> Reste une question de vocabulaire. Le mot « nuage » donne une image légère et immatérielle d'une
> industrie bien réelle. Les spécialistes, eux, parlent d'infrastructures, de mégawatts et de
> mètres cubes d'eau : les termes savants sont moins poétiques, mais plus honnêtes.

Glosses: *volontiers* — readily; *notoirement* — notoriously; *chiffrer* — to put a figure on;
*tenir à* — to be due to (B1: to be keen on); *n'en … pas moins* — nonetheless; *peser lourd* — to
weigh heavily; *déverrouiller* — to unlock; *miser sur* — to bet on; *sobre* — frugal, efficient.

In short: the "cloud" is made of energy-hungry data centres. According to ADEME, digital
technology accounted for 2.5 % of France's carbon footprint in 2020, and a new assessment
published in January 2025 put it at 4.4 % in 2022, with data centres responsible for 46 %; part of
the rise comes from also counting data centres abroad that serve French users. ADEME and Arcep's 2023 forecast warned of a rise
of about 45 % by 2030 if nothing changes. Engineers bet on frugal, versatile machines rather than
rejecting technology, and the writer notes that the poetic word "cloud" hides a heavy industry.

Count the learned words: *énergivore, biométrie, hyperconnectés, chronophages, technophobie,
technocrates, polyvalents, biodégradables, polyvalence, mégawatts*. You can unpack every one of
them with the tables above, including *technophobie*, which isn't in your word list.

## Dialogue: un mot de trop ?

Two colleagues at a digital agency read a client's brief.

```dialogue
# Un mot de trop ?
Nadia: Écoute ça : « Nous voulons une application moins énergivore, moins chronophage et plus polyvalente. »
= Listen to this: "We want an app that uses less energy, takes up less time and is more versatile."
Thomas: Trois mots savants dans une phrase. Ils ont dû lire un rapport de l'ADEME.
= Three learned words in one sentence. They must have read an ADEME report.
Nadia: Attends, ce n'est pas fini : « Le public visé, des jeunes hyperconnectés, se méfie de la biométrie. »
= Wait, there's more: "The target audience, young people who are always online, is wary of biometrics."
Thomas: Bon, ça, au moins, c'est clair : pas de reconnaissance faciale. Et le budget ?
= Well, that at least is clear: no facial recognition. And the budget?
Nadia: Ils écrivent « cf. annexe », mais il n'y a pas d'annexe.
= They write "see appendix", but there's no appendix.
Thomas: Alors je propose un nouveau mot pour notre réunion de demain : la « briefophobie ».
= Then I'm proposing a new word for our meeting tomorrow: "brief-o-phobia".
```

*Briefophobie* is a joke coinage, built like *xénophobie* on an English loan: you understand it
at once, and you'd never write it in a report.

## Common mistakes

- Wrong prefix form: ~~inlisible~~ → *illisible*; ~~inpossible~~ → *impossible*.
- *L'ONU* as masculine: the full name starts with *l'Organisation*, so it is feminine: *l'ONU est
  intervenue*.
- An *s* on a sigle: ~~des ONGs~~ → *des ONG*.
- Mixing the two plural systems in one text (*des porte-monnaies* and *des après-midi*).
- Using a playful coinage (*réunionite*) in a formal essay without quotation marks.
- Trusting the look of a learned word too far: in everyday French *polyvalent* is versatile, and
  *la polyvalence* versatility; the chemistry sense (several valencies) belongs to science.

## Key points

- Learned words (*mots savants*) come almost unchanged from written Latin or Greek; popular words
  were worn down by sound change.
- Derivation adds prefixes and suffixes to a stem; compounding joins two meaningful elements.
- *-vore, -phage* (eats), *-cratie* (power), *-phile / -phobe* (loves / fears), *chrono-* (time),
  *bio-* (life), *poly-* (many), *hyper-* (over) build most new press words.
- *In-* usually becomes *im-, il-, ir-* before *b, m, p, l, r*.
- Compound plurals: traditional (*des porte-monnaie*) or 1990 (*des porte-monnaies*); both are
  correct.
- Sigles are read letter by letter, acronyms as words; the gender is that of the first noun; sigles
  don't take *s*.
- Anglicisms and official terms are honors lesson 16h1.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Courriel, mot-dièse, infox: official terminology and anglicisms
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 16 showed how French builds words from Greek and Latin. This honors lesson looks at the
other great source of new words, English, and at the people whose job is to propose French
replacements. You'll learn:

- how an **[[official term]]** (*un terme recommandé*) is made and published in France, and who must
  use it;
- what the 1994 language law requires, and what it doesn't;
- how Québec does the same work, sometimes with different answers;
- which official terms caught on and which didn't;
- how **[[portmanteau words]]** (*mots-valises*) such as *courriel* and *infox* are built.

At B1 you met *l'anglicisme*, *le néologisme* and *l'emprunt* (lesson 92 there). The debate about
them is old and lively; this lesson presents it, and takes no side.

## Franglais: an old debate

*Le franglais* (from *français* + *anglais*) is French full of English words: *Je t'envoie le
deck avant le call, on fait un point ASAP.* The word became widely known through René Étiemble's
polemical book *Parlez-vous franglais ?* (1964). Since then two views have faced each other:

- for some, borrowing is how languages have always grown (French gave English thousands of words,
  and took *le budget, le tunnel, le sport* in return), and speakers will choose;
- for others, a flood of unadapted English words in work, advertising and science pushes French
  out of whole domains, and the State should offer an equivalent (*un équivalent*) for each
  new notion.

French public policy follows the second line for official use, while leaving everyday speech
free. That is the job of terminology.

## How a term becomes official in France

*La terminologie* is the study and the set of terms of a specialised field; *le
terminologue* (*un* or *une terminologue*) is the specialist who studies and proposes them. In
France the system works like this (as the Ministry of Culture describes it):

- About twenty groups of experts, spread over the ministries, watch for new terms in their fields
  (health, digital technology, finance, sport …) and propose French equivalents with a
  definition.
- Their proposals go to the *Commission d'enrichissement de la langue française*, created in
  1996 under another name (*Commission générale de terminologie et de néologie*), which took its
  present name in 2015.
- The Académie française gives its opinion on each term (usage, form, grammar).
- With the minister's agreement, the term is published in the *Journal officiel*, then entered in
  *FranceTerme*, the free online database of official terms (nearly 8,000 terms according to
  the Ministry in 2019).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How an official term is made in France
  accDescr: An English term appears in a field. An expert group in a ministry proposes a French equivalent and a definition. The Commission d'enrichissement de la langue française examines it. The Académie française gives its opinion. The minister agrees, and the term is published in the Journal officiel. It is then entered in the FranceTerme database. It binds the State's services; for everyone else it is a recommendation.
  A["A new English term appears"] --> B["Expert group: French equivalent + definition"]
  B --> C["Commission d'enrichissement de la langue française"]
  C --> D["Académie française: opinion"]
  D --> E["Minister agrees"]
  E --> F["Published in the Journal officiel"]
  F --> G["Entered in FranceTerme"]
  G --> H["Binding for the State; a recommendation for everyone else"]
```

Publication binds the State's services: a ministry's documents must use the official term where
one exists. For everyone else, it is only a recommendation.

## What the law requires

The *loi Toubon* (the law of 4 August 1994 on the use of the French language, named after the
culture minister of the time) makes French compulsory in many situations, without banning other
languages alongside it:

- for consumers: product descriptions, instructions, guarantees and invoices;
- in advertising, written or spoken;
- at work: employment contracts, internal rules, documents an employee needs to do the job;
- in public services, and in teaching, exams and theses, with exceptions (international schools,
  some courses in foreign languages);
- in public signs and announcements; translations are allowed next to the French.

What the law does not do is force private people, companies or the media to use the official
terms. In July 1994 the Conseil constitutionnel struck out that part of the bill in the name of
freedom of expression. You may say *hashtag*; a ministry, in its official documents, writes
*mot-dièse*.

## Québec: the OQLF and its dictionary
