lessons.title: Suivre une conférence: listening and note-taking at C1
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At C1 you follow long talks on unfamiliar subjects: a lecture, a radio interview, a conference
panel. The difficulty is not single words but the length: you have to keep the thread, separate
the main points from the asides, and keep a record you can use afterwards. This lesson teaches
the structure of a lecture and the spoken phrases that reveal it, then note-taking at C1
(abbreviations, symbols, columns, the diagram), and how to infer a speaker's stance. The theme is
*les neurosciences* of learning: memory, attention, multitasking and sleep. The lecture in the
middle of the lesson is also the basis of the listening questions.

## The DALF C1 listening paper in brief

In the current format, FEI's candidate manual describes a paper of about 40 minutes in two
exercises: first one long document (an interview, a lecture, a talk), heard twice, with
questions on the detail; then several short radio documents (news flashes, polls and the like),
heard once, with questions on the gist. A Sorbonne description of the exam gives the long
document as about 8 minutes. The manual describes the questions as a mix of multiple choice and
short written answers: check FEI's current sample papers, because the format of the DELF
comprehension papers changed recently and the DALF's may follow.

Two consequences. You must read the questions before each recording, during the time you are
given. And for the long document, the first hearing is for the structure and the second for the
details: your notes from the first hearing are your map.

## How a lecture is built, and how you hear it

A lecture is a text built to be heard. A good *conférencier* or *conférencière* (lecturer) tells
you where you are all the time, with spoken **[[signposts]]** (*marqueurs de structuration*). Lesson 21 gave the speaker's side; here is
what to listen for:

| what the speaker does | what you hear | what you write |
|---|---|---|
| announces the plan | *Je commencerai par … puis … enfin …* | the parts, numbered, down the margin |
| lists | *premièrement, deuxièmement ; d'une part … d'autre part* | 1, 2, 3 |
| postpones a point | *j'y reviendrai* | a ? or "→ plus tard" next to it |
| digresses | *j'ouvre une parenthèse … je referme la parenthèse* | brackets ( ) around the aside |
| reformulates | *autrement dit, en d'autres termes, c'est-à-dire* | = |
| shortens | *pour faire court, bref, en un mot* | the main point, underlined |
| gives an example | *prenons le cas de, par exemple, ainsi* | ex. |
| contrasts | *or, en revanche, à l'inverse* | ≠ or "mais" |
| concludes | *pour conclure, en définitive, ce qu'il faut retenir* | a box |

*Ouvrir une parenthèse* is to digress briefly; *la parenthèse* is both the bracket sign and the
aside itself. *J'y reviendrai* (I'll come back to that) is a promise: note the point so that you
notice when it returns. *Pour faire court* (to cut a long story short) announces the speaker's
own summary, often the sentence a question will test. Some lecturers open with *le sommaire*
(the contents, an outline of the talk): copy it at once, because it is the plan of your notes.

When there are several speakers, as in a panel, each *intervenant* or *intervenante*
(contributor, speaker at an event) gets a column or an initial.

## Note-taking at C1

B2 taught *la prise de notes* for preparing a talk. Listening notes have to be faster: you can't
stop the speaker. Four techniques:

1. **Keywords, not sentences.** Nouns and verbs carry meaning; leave out articles and
   connectors you can rebuild.
2. **Abbreviations and symbols** (table below).
3. **Layout.** Leave a wide left margin for the parts of the plan, and leave space after each
   point to add details on the second hearing. On a panel, one column per speaker.
4. **The diagram.** For a process or a comparison, a *schéma* (a diagram or outline: also a
   pattern) of boxes and arrows is faster than words.

A **[[note-taking abbreviation]]** is a short form you will recognise later. French note-takers
share many:

| symbol or abbreviation | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| → | leads to, so | *sommeil → mémorisation* |
| ≠ | different from, unlike | *relire ≠ s'interroger* |
| = | is, means, equals | *MdT = mémoire de travail* |
| ↗ / ↘ | increases / decreases | *erreurs ↗* |
| cf. | see, compare | *cf. 1re partie* |
| qqch, qqn | *quelque chose, quelqu'un* | |
| tjrs, svt, bcp | *toujours, souvent, beaucoup* | |
| gvt, pb, ex. | *gouvernement, problème, exemple* | |
| ° at the end of a word | *-tion* (in some note-takers' habits) | *atten°* = *attention* |

Make your own abbreviations for the topic as soon as a term returns (*MdT, CC* for *charge
cognitive*), and write them out in full once at the top, or you will forget them. *Un symbole* (a symbol)
like ↗ is understood in any language, which is why it is quicker than a word.

![A student's lecture notes on a ruled sheet. In the left margin, the three parts of the plan: 1 MdT, 2 attention, 3 sommeil. On the right, notes with symbols: "MdT = qq éléments seulement (≈ 4)", "trop d'infos → surcharge", "multitâche ≠ 2 tâches en même temps", "chaque changement → erreurs ↗", "sommeil → consolidation", and at the bottom "cf. intro" with "relire ≠ s'interroger" in a box. Below the sheet, a key: = is, means; → leads to, so; ≠ unlike; ↗ increases; cf. see, compare; MdT mémoire de travail.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### From notes to answers

After the recording, take one minute to fill gaps while your memory is fresh. In a written
synthesis or *compte rendu* based on a lecture (module 5), your notes then become sentences: *MdT
= qq éléments* becomes *La mémoire de travail ne peut retenir que quelques éléments à la fois.*

## Inferring the speaker's stance

Speakers rarely say "I disagree". They show it:

- **Distancing words** (lesson 08): *ce qu'on appelle, parfois à tort, le multitâche*; *une
  théorie selon laquelle on n'utiliserait que 10 % de son cerveau*. The conditionnel and *à tort*
  report a view the speaker rejects.
- **Evaluative words** (lesson 12): *une idée séduisante mais fausse*; *un résultat robuste*.
- **Intonation**: a stress on *vraiment* or a slower, falling *bien sûr* can turn agreement into
  irony. The app's voice reads every line in a neutral tone, so this part is described here, not
  heard: listen for it on the radio.

Fast, relaxed speech also reduces words (*chais pas* for *je ne sais pas*, lesson 02), and
regional accents change vowels and rhythm (honors 04h1). Lecturers usually speak carefully; radio
guests often don't.

## The lecture: « Apprendre avec son cerveau »

Read the lecture below paragraph by paragraph, with its English summary and glosses; then take
notes as you listen to it in the lesson quiz, where each audio question plays one part. It is
original, and the findings it reports are real and well established.

> **§1.** Bonsoir à toutes et à tous. Ce soir, je voudrais vous parler de ce que les neurosciences nous apprennent sur l'apprentissage. Je commencerai par quelques mots sur le cerveau lui-même ; j'aborderai ensuite trois questions : la mémoire de travail, l'attention, et le sommeil. Je terminerai par des conseils pratiques, mais j'y reviendrai : d'abord, un peu d'anatomie.

*In short:* the lecturer greets the audience and announces the plan: the brain, then working
memory, attention and sleep, then practical advice, promised for the end (*j'y reviendrai*).

> **§2.** Notre cerveau compte des dizaines de milliards de neurones, quelque 86 milliards selon une estimation de 2009 souvent citée. Un neurone communique en moyenne avec des milliers d'autres par l'intermédiaire de synapses. Apprendre, c'est d'abord modifier ces connexions : certaines se renforcent, d'autres s'affaiblissent. C'est ce qu'on appelle la plasticité cérébrale, et elle ne disparaît pas à l'âge adulte. J'ouvre une parenthèse : vous avez sans doute entendu dire qu'on n'utiliserait que 10 % de son cerveau. C'est un mythe ; l'imagerie montre que toutes les régions du cortex, dans les deux hémisphères, ont une activité. Je referme la parenthèse.

*In short:* the brain has tens of billions of neurons (about 86 billion by a widely cited 2009
estimate), linked by synapses; learning changes these connections, which is brain plasticity,
and it lasts into adulthood. An aside dismisses the myth that we use only 10% of our brain.
*Le cortex* = the outer layer of the brain; *l'hémisphère* (masculine) = each half.

> **§3.** Premier point : la mémoire de travail. C'est elle qui retient les informations dont nous avons besoin pendant que nous réfléchissons, par exemple un numéro de téléphone le temps de le composer. Or sa capacité est très limitée : selon une synthèse publiée en 2001 par le psychologue Nelson Cowan, elle ne garde qu'environ quatre éléments à la fois. Quand un cours apporte trop d'informations nouvelles d'un coup, la charge cognitive dépasse cette capacité, et l'élève décroche. Autrement dit, un bon enseignant découpe un contenu difficile en étapes.

*In short:* working memory holds what we need while we think, and it is small: about four items
at once, according to a 2001 review by the psychologist Nelson Cowan. Too much new information at
once exceeds it (*la charge cognitive*, cognitive load) and the learner loses track
(*décrocher*); so difficult content should be split into steps.

> **§4.** Deuxième point : l'attention. Beaucoup d'entre nous pensent pratiquer le multitâche. En réalité, pour des tâches qui demandent de la réflexion, le cerveau ne fait pas deux choses à la fois : il passe très vite de l'une à l'autre, et chaque changement coûte du temps et augmente les erreurs. Une notification, un bruit : tout stimulus nouveau attire notre attention. C'est utile pour survivre, beaucoup moins pour réviser, et chaque distraction se paie. L'attention soutenue, celle qui nous permet de suivre un raisonnement pendant une heure, s'épuise. Pour faire court : une tâche à la fois, et le téléphone dans une autre pièce.

*In short:* for tasks that need thought, what we call multitasking is fast switching, and each
switch costs time and adds errors. Any new stimulus (a notification, a noise) grabs attention,
and every distraction has a cost (*se payer*); sustained attention wears out. Summary: one task at a time, phone in another room. *La
distraction* = lack of focus (also absent-mindedness).

> **§5.** Troisième point : le sommeil. La nuit, le cerveau ne se contente pas de se reposer. De nombreux travaux montrent que, pendant le sommeil, les souvenirs de la journée sont réactivés et consolidés : l'activité neuronale du sommeil contribue à transformer une trace fragile en souvenir durable. C'est pourquoi une période de sommeil après l'apprentissage aide en général à mieux retenir qu'une période équivalente passée éveillé. Réviser toute la nuit avant un examen est donc un mauvais calcul.

*In short:* sleep is active: many studies show that the day's memories are reactivated and
consolidated during it (*neuronal* = neural); a period of sleep after learning generally helps
retention more than the same time awake, so an all-night revision session is a bad bet.

> **§6.** J'en viens, comme promis, aux conseils. Relire son cours, ou l'apprentissage par cœur à force de répétitions, donne une impression de maîtrise, mais cette impression est trompeuse. Dans une expérience publiée en 2006, Henry Roediger et Jeffrey Karpicke ont montré que des étudiants qui, après l'avoir lu, devaient restituer un texte de mémoire s'en souvenaient mieux une semaine plus tard que ceux qui le relisaient, alors même que ces derniers pensaient mieux le retenir. Ajoutez-y l'espacement : mieux vaut trois séances courtes réparties sur une semaine qu'une longue séance la veille. En somme, ce qu'il faut retenir, c'est que la mémorisation dépend moins du temps passé que de la manière.

*In short:* the promised advice. Rereading and rote learning (*l'apprentissage par cœur*) feel
effective but mislead: in a 2006 experiment by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, students who
had to recall a text from memory after reading it remembered it better a week later than
students who reread it, although the rereaders expected to remember more. Add spacing: three short sessions over a week beat
one long one the night before. Conclusion: *la mémorisation* (memorising) depends less on time
spent than on method.

> **§7.** Pour conclure, je voudrais vous mettre en garde contre ce qu'on appelle, parfois à tort, les « méthodes fondées sur le cerveau ». On vous dira par exemple que chacun aurait un style d'apprentissage, visuel ou auditif, et qu'il faudrait enseigner selon ce style. C'est une idée séduisante, mais les études qui l'ont testée ne la confirment pas. Ce que les neurosciences et la psychologie cognitive nous offrent est plus modeste et plus solide : dormir, se concentrer sur une seule chose, s'interroger plutôt que relire, et espacer les révisions. Je vous remercie de votre attention, et je suis prête à répondre à vos questions.

*In short:* a warning against so-called "brain-based methods", such as the claim that each of us
has a visual or auditory learning style to be taught in: an attractive idea that the studies
testing it don't support. What the research offers is more modest and more solid: sleep, focus on
one thing, test yourself, space your revision. Note the stance markers: *ce qu'on appelle,
parfois à tort*, the conditionnel *aurait*, *séduisante, mais*.

Notice the structure: the plan in §1, the parenthesis in §2, *Premier point, Deuxième point,
Troisième point*, *autrement dit* and *pour faire court* before the two summaries, and *j'en
viens, comme promis* keeping the promise of §1. *Cognitif* (cognitive; feminine *cognitive*)
and *la cognition* are the general words of the field: *les sciences cognitives* study how we
perceive, remember and reason.

![A simplified cross-section of the brain: two halves side by side, joined at the bottom and separated by a groove from the top, each with a shaded outer layer. Labels: un hémisphère, on one half, and le cortex (couche externe), on the shaded layer. To the right, an inset shows two nerve cells, each a round body with short branches; a long fibre runs from the first to a small dot near the branches of the second, labelled une synapse, and the first is labelled un neurone.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *Le neurone* [nøʁɔn]; *neuronal* [nøʁɔnal]; *les neurosciences* [nøʁosjɑ̃s].
- *L'hémisphère* [emisfɛʁ]: *ph* = [f], silent *h*.
- *Le stimulus* [stimylys]: the final *s* is pronounced.
- *La synapse* [sinaps]; *le cortex* [kɔʁtɛks].

## Common mistakes

- **Writing everything.** You lose the next sentence. Keywords and symbols only.
- **Missing the plan.** The first minute of a lecture is the most important to note.
- **Treating a parenthèse as a main point.** Bracket it; questions rarely test asides.
- **Forgetting what *j'y reviendrai* promised.** Mark it and tick it when it returns.
- **L'hémisphère as feminine.** It is masculine: *l'hémisphère gauche*.
- **Les neurosciences in the singular.** The plural is usual: *les neurosciences cognitives*.

## Key points

- DALF C1 listening (current format, per FEI's manual): about 40 minutes; a long document heard
  twice, then short radio documents heard once. Read the questions first.
- Listen for the plan and the signposts: *je commencerai par, j'y reviendrai, j'ouvre / je
  referme la parenthèse, autrement dit, pour faire court, j'en viens à*.
- Note in keywords, **[[note-taking abbreviations]]** and symbols (→ ≠ = ↗ ↘ cf.), with the plan in
  the margin, space for the second hearing, and a *schéma* for processes.
- A speaker's stance shows in distancing (*à tort*, the conditionnel), evaluative words and
  intonation.
- From the lecture: working memory is small, multitasking is switching, sleep consolidates, and
  testing yourself beats rereading.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Le DALF C1: the exam and a course review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This last core lesson explains what C1 means, describes the **[[DALF]]** C1 and how it is marked,
gives a strategy for each part, and reviews the course with three charts and pointers to the
lessons. You don't need to sit the exam to use this course, but FEI's sample papers are the best
test of whether you have reached the level, and a diploma can open doors: universities often ask
foreign applicants for proof of a B2 or C1 level, such as a *certification* (check each
institution's own rules).

## What C1 means

The levels A1 to C2 come from the **[[CEFR]]** (Common European Framework of Reference for
Languages), published by the Council of Europe. They describe what a learner can *do* with a
language. A1–A2 are basic users, B1–B2 independent users, and C1–C2 **[[proficient users]]**
(*utilisateurs expérimentés*): C1 is the lower of the two top levels. In practical terms, at C1
you can:

- read a long opinion piece, a report or a novel and say what it hints at as well as what it says;
- follow a lecture or a fast radio discussion on a subject you don't know;
- take part in a meeting or a seminar without planning each sentence, and change your tone for
  the person in front of you;
- write a synthesis, a report or an essay that a French reader finds well organised and easy to
  follow.

The step from B2 is one of control. At B2 you could argue; at C1 you choose: the register for
the reader (module 1), the mood and tense that carry the nuance you mean (module 2), the
connector that says exactly how two ideas relate, and what you leave implicit (module 3), the
idiom or collocation a native would use (module 4), and how to condense and combine long texts
(module 5). In French the qualities are *la précision*: saying exactly what you mean, and *la
fluidité* (fluency) and *la spontanéité* (spontaneity): saying it without visible effort.

## The DALF C1

*DALF* stands for *Diplôme approfondi de langue française*. *Approfondi* means advanced, in
depth: the verb is *approfondir* (B2). The DALF C1 and C2 are the official French diplomas at the
top two levels, awarded by the French Ministry of Education and run by France Éducation
international (FEI); like the DELF, each level is a separate diploma, valid for life, and you
can take the C1 without having taken the B2. The table follows FEI's *Manuel du candidat DALF C1*
(July 2022) and a university description of the exam; FEI's own pages are the final word.

| part | time | points | what it involves (current format) |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Compréhension de l'oral* (listening) | about 40 minutes | 25 | one long recording (interview, lecture) heard twice; several short radio documents heard once |
| *Compréhension des écrits* (reading) | 50 minutes | 25 | one long *texte d'idées*, journalistic or literary, with questions |
| *Production écrite* (writing) | 2 h 30 | 25 | a synthesis of several documents (200 to 240 words in the manual), then an argued essay (at least 250 words) |
| *Production orale* (speaking) | up to about 30 minutes, after 1 hour of preparation | 25 | an exposé of about 8 to 10 minutes from documents, then a discussion with the jury |

The first three parts are **[[collective papers]]**: *épreuves collectives*, sat in a room with other
candidates, about four hours in all. The speaking test is an *épreuve individuelle*, in front of
two examiners, often on another day.

![An overview chart of the DALF C1. A box for the collective papers, about 4 hours in all, holds three parts side by side: compréhension de l'oral, listening, about 40 minutes, one long document heard twice and short documents heard once, 25 points; compréhension des écrits, reading, 50 minutes, one long text of ideas, 25 points; production écrite, writing, 2 hours 30, a synthesis and an essay, 25 points. A separate box for the individual test, production orale: 1 hour of preparation, then about 30 minutes, an exposé and a discussion, 25 points. Below: total 100; pass with 50 and at least 5 out of 25 in every part; check FEI's pages, as details can change.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Passing

Each part is marked out of 25. The **seuil de réussite** (pass mark) is 50 out of 100, and a mark
below 5 out of 25 in any part is a **note éliminatoire** (fail mark): it fails the diploma even
with a total above 50. A *contre-performance* (below-par performance) in one part can be made up
by the others, as long as it stays at 5 or above.

You receive a *relevé de notes* (results slip) with your mark in each part. Centres usually issue
an *attestation de réussite* (certificate of achievement) first, because the diploma itself is
printed and sent later. French school diplomas such as the *baccalauréat* carry a *mention*
(*assez bien, bien, très bien*) for high marks; the DALF manual describes a pass mark, not
*mentions*, so don't expect one.

### Older books and pages

Before March 2020 the DALF C1 writing and speaking papers came in two fields, *lettres et sciences
humaines* or *sciences*, and candidates chose one. FEI announced in October 2019 that the choice
would go, because both versions tested the same skills. Many books and some centre pages still
mention the two fields; they also differ on details such as the split of points between the
synthesis and the essay (an older sample paper gave 13 and 12, the 2022 manual 12.5 each). Train with any
good book, but check the format against FEI's current sample papers:

- [DALF C1: description of the exam (FEI)](https://www.france-education-international.fr/article/dalf-c1)
- [DALF C1 sample papers (exemples de sujets)](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/dalf/niveau-c1/exemples-sujets)

Each exam centre sets its own dates, fees and registration deadlines.

## How the papers are marked

The listening and reading papers are marked by key. The writing and speaking parts are marked by
trained examiners with a marking grid. FEI announced new grids in 2019, so the exact criteria and
point splits may change; in general terms, markers look at:

- **the task** (*la consigne*): did you do what was asked? For the synthesis: no opinion, no
  outside ideas, your own words, the word range. For the essay: a position, argued, in the form
  asked (a letter, an article, a contribution to a debate);
- **coherence and cohesion:** a plan the reader can follow, with links between ideas;
- **range** (*l'étendue* du vocabulaire et des structures) and **accuracy** (*la précision*,
  *la correction*): varied, precise words and complex sentences, with errors rare;
- **register:** right for the reader and kept throughout;
- at the oral, also **pronunciation**, *fluidité*, *spontanéité* and interaction: answering,
  nuancing, defending a view.

## Strategies for each part

### Listening (lesson 23)

Read the questions before each recording. On the long document, note the plan and the
signposts the first time, details the second. The short documents are heard once: be ready.

### Reading

The *texte d'idées* is long (a Sorbonne description gives 1,500 to 2,000 words), so don't read it
three times. Read the questions first, then the text once, writing a three-word summary in the
margin of each paragraph; then answer from your map. When a question asks you to justify an
answer, quote the exact words of the text. Watch the connectors that turn an argument (*or, il
n'en demeure pas moins que, loin s'en faut*: lessons 09–10) and the distancing of lesson 08: a
view the author reports in the conditionnel is often one they reject.

### Writing (lessons 18–20)

*La gestion du temps* (time management) decides this paper: 2 h 30 for two texts. One way to
divide it:

| task | read and plan | write | reread |
|---|---|---|---|
| synthesis | 30 min | 35 min | 10 min |
| essay | 15 min | 50 min | 10 min |

Plan on scrap paper (it isn't marked), but don't write the whole text twice: there is no time
for *la mise au propre* (writing out a clean copy) of a full draft. Write straight onto the
answer sheet from a detailed plan. Write *le décompte des mots* (the word count) at the end of
each text, as the paper asks; how words are counted (*l'homme*, numbers, hyphens) is set by the
instructions, so follow them.

### Speaking (lessons 21–22, honors 24h1)

During the hour of preparation, the manual allows a *dictionnaire unilingue* (monolingual French
dictionary) supplied by the centre, not your own. Use it to check a word, not to read. One way
to use the hour (honors 24h1 details it): about ten minutes on the documents, fifteen on the
problématique and the plan, twenty on the notes, and fifteen on the opening, the conclusion and
two likely objections.

### The day itself

A *compte à rebours* (countdown) is the right way to prepare: a mock exam with a sample paper in
real conditions three or four weeks before, a second one a week before, light revision the last
two days, and sleep the night before (lesson 23). Arrive early with your ID and your
*convocation* (notice to attend).

## Reading: a candidate's story

> J'ai passé le DALF C1 en juin. Les épreuves collectives m'ont paru longues, surtout la production écrite : deux heures et demie, c'est peu pour une synthèse et un essai. J'avais pourtant bien travaillé la gestion du temps. Ma vraie contre-performance a été l'écoute : j'ai pris trop de notes pendant la première écoute et j'ai perdu le fil. Heureusement, j'ai eu 11 sur 25, bien au-dessus de la note éliminatoire. L'oral s'est mieux passé que prévu : le sujet de réflexion portait sur le télétravail, que je connais bien, et le jury m'a laissé défendre mon point de vue. Quand j'ai reçu mon relevé de notes, avec 68 sur 100, j'ai enfin pu valider mon inscription à l'université. Le centre m'a remis une attestation de réussite en attendant le diplôme. Mon conseil : faites plusieurs examens blancs, et ne négligez aucune épreuve.

Translation:

> I took the DALF C1 in June. The collective papers felt long to me, especially the writing paper: two and a half hours isn't much for a synthesis and an essay. And yet I had worked hard on time management. My real below-par performance was the listening: I took too many notes during the first hearing and lost the thread. Fortunately, I got 11 out of 25, well above the fail mark. The oral went better than expected: the topic for discussion was remote working, which I know well, and the jury let me defend my point of view. When I received my results slip, with 68 out of 100, I was finally able to confirm my university registration. The centre gave me a certificate of achievement while I waited for the diploma. My advice: do several mock exams, and don't neglect any paper.

*Valider* is to validate, to confirm, and in education to pass a unit (*valider un module, valider
ses acquis*). *Un sujet de réflexion* is a topic for discussion or for an essay. *Certifier* is to
certify (*une copie certifiée conforme*, a certified copy); *la certification* is the act or the
diploma that certifies a *niveau de compétence* (proficiency level). Don't confuse it with *un
bilan de compétences*: in France that is a formal skills assessment for a career change, which
employees can ask for.

## Review: the course in three charts

### Register (module 1)

| | familier | courant | soutenu |
|---|---|---|---|
| to understand | *piger* | *comprendre* | *saisir* |
| to work | *bosser* | *travailler* | *œuvrer (à)* |
| book | *le bouquin* | *le livre* | *l'ouvrage* |
| negation | *J'sais pas.* | *Je ne sais pas.* | *Je ne saurais dire.* |
| question | *Vous venez ?* | *Est-ce que vous venez ?* | *Venez-vous ?* |

Choose the register for the reader, then keep it (lessons 01–04).

### Grammar map (modules 1, 2, 3 and 5)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The grammar of French C1 at a glance
  accDescr: A top-down map in six boxes. Register and the formal sentence, lessons 01 to 04, with inversion and ne used alone. The subjunctive in independent clauses and the sequence of tenses, lessons 05 and 06. The stylistic values of the tenses, lesson 07, such as the présent historique and the futur historique. Certainty and distance, lesson 08, with the conditionnel of reported claims. Connectors of cause, consequence and concession, cohesion and the implicit, lessons 09 to 12. Participial clauses and the long sentence, lesson 17. A side note: produce the drilled tenses and moods; recognise the passé simple, the passé antérieur and the imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive.
  A["Register, formal sentence (01–04): inversion, ne alone"] --> B["Independent subjunctive, sequence of tenses (05–06)"]
  B --> C["Stylistic tenses (07): présent historique, futur historique"]
  C --> D["Certainty and distance (08): conditionnel of reported claims"]
  D --> E["Connectors, cohesion, the implicit (09–12)"]
  E --> F["Participial clauses, the long sentence (17)"]
  F -.-> N["Produce the drilled forms; recognise the passé simple and literary subjunctives"]
```

### Connectors by function and register (module 3)

| function | courant | soutenu |
|---|---|---|
| cause | *parce que, comme, puisque* | *dans la mesure où, attendu que* (legal) |
| consequence | *donc, alors, du coup* (informal) | *par conséquent, il s'ensuit que* |
| concession | *même si, mais* | *il n'en demeure pas moins que, si … soit-il* |
| opposition | *par contre, alors que* | *en revanche, à l'inverse* |
| adding | *en plus, aussi* | *en outre, de surcroît* |
| concluding | *bref, en gros* (informal) | *en définitive, somme toute* |

*Par contre* is fine in speech; *en revanche* is the safer choice in an exam (lesson 10). The
full tables are in the reference sheets of modules 1, 2 and 3.

## What comes next

Above C1 is C2, the top level of the CEFR, and its diploma, the DALF C2. Before you think about
it, use the language: read French books and the press every week, listen to the radio and
podcasts on the reading list, and write something for a real reader. Language you use is
language you keep.

## Pronunciation

- *Le DALF* [dalf]: said as a word, not letter by letter.
- *La certification* [sɛʁtifikasjɔ̃]; *éliminatoire* [eliminatwaʁ].
- *La spontanéité* [spɔ̃taneite]: five syllables, *-néi-* is two vowels.
- *Le seuil* [sœj], as at B2.

## Common mistakes

- **Neglecting one part.** Every part needs at least 5/25.
- **Training only with old books.** Their two fields and point splits are out of date.
- **Copying the documents in the synthesis.** Your own words, except keywords.
- **Forgetting the word count** at the end of each written text.
- **Writing a full draft and then copying it out.** There is no time: plan in detail, then
  write once.
- **Un bilan de compétences for an exam result.** It is a career assessment; a result is a
  *relevé de notes*.
- **Valider for "to value".** *Valider* is to validate or pass; "to value" is *valoriser* or
  *apprécier*.

## Key points

- C1 is the lower **[[proficient user]]** level of the **[[CEFR]]**: control of register, nuance, long
  texts and synthesis.
- DALF C1 (current format, per FEI's manual): listening about 40 min, reading 50 min, writing
  2 h 30 (synthesis of 200 to 240 words, essay of at least 250), speaking up to about 30 min
  after 1 h of preparation. The three **[[collective papers]]** take about 4 hours.
- Each part out of 25; pass with 50/100 and at least 5/25 in every part.
- The choice of field was removed in 2020: older books still show it.
- Markers look at the task, coherence and cohesion, range, accuracy, register (and, at the oral,
  pronunciation, fluency and interaction). Check FEI's pages before you register.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. Félicitations : vous avez terminé le tronc commun du cours de français C1 !

lessons.title: Honors: L'oral du DALF C1 en pratique
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 gave you the method of the **[[exposé]]** and lesson 22 the language of debate. This honors
lesson applies both to a model test: two original subjects, the hour of preparation, a model plan
and extract, and a model interaction with a hostile question, a request to defend the other side,
and a recovery. The figures follow FEI's *Manuel du candidat DALF C1* (July 2022): 1 hour
of preparation, an exposé of 8 to 10 minutes, then the interaction, about 30 minutes at most in
all. Check the instructions on the day.

## The two subjects

You draw two subjects and choose one. Each comes with one or more short documents, the
*documents déclencheurs* (trigger documents): they raise the question without settling it. The
ones below are original and their sources invented.

> **Sujet A. Accueillir un grand événement sportif : une chance pour une ville ?**
>
> *Document 1 (presse locale).* La ville de Bréval se porte candidate pour accueillir une grande compétition internationale. Le maire promet des emplois, des équipements neufs et une image renouvelée.
>
> *Document 2 (tribune d'un collectif d'habitants).* « On nous parle de rayonnement, mais qui paiera les stades quand les caméras seront parties ? »
>
> **Sujet B. Faut-il obliger les fabricants à rendre leurs appareils réparables ?**
>
> *Document 1 (magazine de consommateurs).* Selon un sondage du magazine *Consommer mieux*, plus d'un lecteur sur deux a déjà remplacé un téléphone qu'il aurait voulu faire réparer, parce que la réparation coûtait presque le prix d'un appareil neuf.
>
> *Document 2 (entretien).* Le porte-parole d'un fabricant, Novatek, répond que des appareils démontables seraient plus épais, plus lourds et plus chers, et que les clients « votent avec leur portefeuille ».

In English: in A, an invented town bids to host a major competition, promising jobs and a new
image; residents ask who will pay for the stadiums afterwards (*le rayonnement* = prestige). In
B, a survey finds that over half of a magazine's readers have replaced a phone they wanted
repaired, because repair cost almost as much as a new one; a manufacturer replies that devices
you can take apart would be thicker and dearer, and that customers "vote with their wallets".

Choose the subject on which you can *se positionner* (take a position) fastest and find two or
three arguments with an example each, not the one you find most interesting. The candidate here
chooses B: she has had a phone battery replaced and can give concrete examples.

## Example 1: the hour of preparation

One way to divide the hour (advice, not an exam rule):

| minutes | what you do |
|---|---|
| 0–10 | read both subjects, choose; reread your documents, underline the tension |
| 10–25 | write the problématique and your position; choose the plan |
| 25–45 | the notes on one sheet: parts, arguments, examples, transitions, in keywords |
| 45–55 | write out the accroche, the first sentences and the conclusion in full |
| 55–60 | list two or three objections and a short answer to each; reread your sheet |

The *temps de préparation* (preparation time) is short: decide the question and your answer
*before* you write any notes.

*S'approprier* les documents (to make them your own) means using them as material for *your*
argument, not repeating them in order. Note that *se* is indirect in this verb: *elle s'est
approprié les documents* (no agreement), but *les idées qu'elle s'est appropriées* (agreement with
the direct object placed before the verb).

*La mise en perspective* (putting into perspective) is what turns a good exposé into a C1 one:
*mettre en perspective* a debate is to place it in a wider frame, historical, international or
ethical (Example 2 shows one).

![A timeline of the DALF C1 speaking test in three bands from left to right. The first and widest band, preparation, about 1 hour, is divided into four steps: read and choose, question and plan, notes, opening and objections. The second band, the exposé, about 8 to 10 minutes. The third band, the interaction with the jury, until the end of the test, about 30 minutes at most for exposé and interaction together. A note below says the times follow the candidate manual and should be checked on the day.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### The candidate's plan

- **Problématique:** *Faut-il imposer la réparabilité aux fabricants, au risque de renchérir les
  appareils ?*
- **Position:** oui, mais progressivement et par des règles simples (pièces détachées, notices,
  prix encadrés), plutôt qu'en interdisant certains modèles.
- **I. Pourquoi la réparabilité est devenue nécessaire:** le coût pour le consommateur (doc. 1);
  les déchets et les ressources; *ex.* sa batterie de téléphone.
- **II. Les objections des fabricants, et leurs limites:** prix et design (doc. 2); mais le
  « vote avec le portefeuille » suppose un vrai choix, qui n'existe pas si aucun modèle n'est
  réparable.
- **III. Une obligation progressive:** des pièces disponibles pendant plusieurs années, des
  outils standard, une information claire au moment de l'achat.
- **Fil rouge:** *On ne choisit librement que ce qu'on peut comparer.*

## Example 2: a model exposé (extract)

A full exposé of 8 to 10 minutes is about 1,000 to 1,300 spoken words. The extract below, just under 500
words (about four minutes at a calm pace), gives the introduction and part I; parts II and III
would follow the plan above.

> Qui, parmi nous, n'a jamais jeté un téléphone qui fonctionnait presque ? D'entrée de jeu, je voudrais souligner que cette question, qui paraît banale, touche à la fois à notre pouvoir d'achat, à l'environnement et à notre liberté de consommateurs.
>
> Les deux documents du sujet le montrent bien. Le premier, un sondage publié par le magazine *Consommer mieux*, révèle que plus d'un lecteur sur deux a déjà remplacé un téléphone qu'il aurait préféré faire réparer, faute d'une réparation abordable. Le second donne la parole au porte-parole d'un fabricant, pour qui des appareils démontables seraient plus épais et plus chers, et pour qui les clients « votent avec leur portefeuille ». Ces deux documents s'opposent moins qu'il n'y paraît : tous deux parlent du prix. D'où la question que je voudrais poser : faut-il imposer la réparabilité aux fabricants, au risque de renchérir les appareils ?
>
> Je défendrai l'idée qu'une telle obligation est nécessaire, à condition d'être progressive et de reposer sur des règles simples. Dans un premier temps, je montrerai pourquoi la réparabilité est devenue un enjeu. J'en viendrai ensuite aux objections des fabricants, que je prends au sérieux, avant de proposer, dans un dernier temps, une obligation par étapes.
>
> Commençons par le constat. Il fut un temps où l'on faisait ressemeler ses chaussures et réparer son téléviseur ; la réparation faisait partie de la vie quotidienne. Si elle a reculé, ce n'est pas que nous soyons devenus plus négligents, c'est que nos appareils sont devenus plus difficiles à ouvrir. On peut y voir le prix du progrès : des appareils plus fins, plus étanches. Mais le résultat est là : une batterie collée, une vis propriétaire, une pièce introuvable, et la réparation coûte presque le prix du neuf. C'est exactement ce que décrit le premier document.
>
> Prenons mon propre exemple. L'an dernier, la batterie de mon téléphone ne tenait plus une journée. Le réparateur m'a d'abord dit qu'il fallait compter trois semaines pour recevoir la pièce, puis m'a annoncé un prix proche de la moitié de celui d'un appareil neuf. J'ai fini par le faire réparer, par principe, mais je comprends ceux qui renoncent.
>
> À ce coût individuel s'ajoute un coût collectif. Chaque appareil remplacé avant l'heure, ce sont des métaux extraits, transportés, puis des déchets qu'il faut traiter. Et je ne parle ici que des téléphones : les mêmes questions se posent pour les ordinateurs, l'électroménager ou les vélos électriques. Autrement dit, ce que le consommateur ne paie pas en réparation, la collectivité le paie en ressources et en pollution. La mise en perspective est utile ici : on parle souvent de la sobriété comme d'un sacrifice ; dans ce cas précis, elle serait plutôt une économie.
>
> Retenons donc de cette première partie que la réparabilité n'est pas un caprice de militants, mais une question de pouvoir d'achat et de ressources. Ce qui m'amène aux objections des fabricants, car elles ne sont pas sans fondement…

**In English, paragraph by paragraph.** (1) The accroche, a question to the audience about
throwing away a phone that almost worked, then the stakes: spending power, the environment,
consumer freedom. (2) The documents in one sentence each, what they share (price), then the problématique with
*D'où*.
(3) The position, with its condition, and the announced plan in three steps. (4) Part I opens
with the *mise en perspective*: repair used to be part of daily life (*ressemeler* = to resole); it
has declined not because we are more careless but because thinner, sealed devices are harder to
open. (5) A
personal example: a phone battery that took three weeks to arrive and cost about half a new
phone. (6) The collective cost: metals, transport, waste, and not only for phones; what the
consumer saves on repair, society pays in resources; *la sobriété* (B2) here is a saving, not a sacrifice. (7) A
summary of the part and the transition to part II.

**Commentary.** The candidate *se positionne* in the third paragraph, not at the end, and every
step has its signpost. Note the C1 grammar used naturally: *ce n'est pas que nous
soyons … c'est que* (a rejected cause in the subjunctive, like *non que*, then the real one in the
indicative: lesson 09), the passé simple *Il fut un temps* in a fixed phrase, the conditionnel of hedging
(*elle serait plutôt*), and *À ce coût s'ajoute* with inversion after a fronted complement.

## Example 3: a model interaction

In the interaction the examiners push back, sometimes harder than they mean. *Défendre son point de vue* (to stand your ground)
does not mean repeating it: it means answering the objection. The extract below is translated
line by line.

```dialogue
# L'interaction (extrait)
Examinatrice: Votre position me paraît un peu naïve. Les gens veulent des téléphones fins et bon marché. Vous voulez leur imposer vos goûts ?
= Your position strikes me as rather naive. People want thin, cheap phones. Do you want to impose your tastes on them?
Candidate: Je comprends l'objection, et je vous accorde que le prix compte. Mais je ne cherche pas à imposer un goût : je demande qu'on puisse choisir. Aujourd'hui, ce choix n'existe presque pas.
= I understand the objection, and I grant you that price matters. But I'm not trying to impose a taste: I'm asking for people to be able to choose. Today that choice hardly exists.
Examinateur: Très bien. Mettez-vous maintenant à la place du fabricant. Défendez sa position.
= Very well. Now put yourself in the manufacturer's place. Defend his position.
Candidate: Si je me fais l'avocat du diable, je dirais qu'une obligation uniforme freinerait l'innovation et favoriserait les grands groupes, les seuls capables d'absorber le coût. C'est un vrai argument.
= If I play devil's advocate, I'd say that a uniform obligation would slow innovation and favour large groups, the only ones able to absorb the cost. It's a real argument.
Examinateur: Alors, vous avez changé d'avis ?
= So you've changed your mind?
Candidate: Non. J'ai joué le jeu, mais cet argument confirme plutôt ma position : c'est justement pour ne pas pénaliser les petits fabricants qu'il faut une obligation progressive.
= No. I played along, but that argument rather confirms my position: it's precisely so as not to penalise small manufacturers that the obligation should be gradual.
Examinatrice: Et si les prix augmentent malgré tout ?
= And if prices go up all the same?
Candidate: C'est une question délicate. Je n'ai pas de chiffres, mais un appareil qui dure deux fois plus longtemps peut coûter deux fois plus cher… pardon, je me reprends : il peut coûter un peu plus cher et revenir moins cher au bout du compte.
= That's a tricky question. I don't have figures, but a device that lasts twice as long can cost twice as much… sorry, let me correct myself: it can cost a little more and still work out cheaper in the end.
```

**Commentary.** To the hostile question, the candidate concedes one point (*je vous accorde que
le prix compte*) and reframes (choice, not taste). Asked to take the other side, she marks it as
an exercise and gives a strong case, which is the *contre-argumentation* (counter-argumentation)
the jury wants to hear: a weak version would be a straw man. When the examiner suggests she has
changed her mind, she turns the manufacturer's argument into a reason for her own position. To the
last question she admits what she doesn't know, says something that undermines her case (*deux
fois plus cher*), notices, and corrects it at once (*pardon, je me reprends*). None of this can be learnt by heart: *l'improvisation* (improvisation) is part of the test;
practise with a partner who plays the examiner.

## Timing

- **Under 8 minutes** usually means a missing example or part: keep a spare example ready.
- **Over 10 minutes**: the jury may stop you before the conclusion. Check the time after each
  part.
- *La prise de parole* (speaking, taking the floor) in the interaction: as a rule of thumb, 30
  seconds to a minute and a half per answer. Too short sounds evasive; too long, like a second
  exposé.

## Common mistakes

- **Choosing the subject you like** rather than the one you can argue.
- **Taking a position only in the conclusion.** Say where you stand in the introduction.
- **A weak defence of the other side.** If asked, make it strong; then say where you stand.
- **Hiding a slip.** *Je me reprends* and a correction cost nothing; a contradiction left in
  place costs a lot.
- **Elle s'est appropriée le projet.** *Se* is indirect: *elle s'est approprié le projet*.

## Key points

- Choose the subject you can *se positionner* on quickly, with two or three arguments and
  examples.
- In the hour: question and position first (by minute 25), then notes on one sheet, then the
  opening, the conclusion and likely objections.
- Make the documents your own (*s'approprier*), and add a *mise en perspective*.
- A full exposé is about 1,000 to 1,300 spoken words for 8 to 10 minutes; signpost every step.
- In the interaction: concede, reframe, defend the other side well when asked, correct slips
  openly, and answer even when unsure.

lessons.title: Honors: Le rapport et la note de synthèse
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 19 taught the DALF *synthèse de documents*: a short, neutral text that compares several
documents for a general reader and never gives an opinion. French administrations use a close
relative every day, the **[[note de synthèse]]**: a document written for a decision-maker from a file
of documents, laid out like an office memo; in some variants it ends with recommendations. Its longer
cousin is the **[[rapport]]** (report). This honors lesson describes both, shows how they differ from
the DALF synthesis, works through a model note on an original file, and ends with a graded
writing task.

## The note and the civil-service exams

In a French town hall, ministry or hospital, *le décideur* (the decision-maker: a mayor, a
director, a minister's office) rarely has time to read a thirty-page file. A junior official reads
it and writes a note of a few pages: what the problem is, what the file says, and, if asked, what
could be done.

The same exercise is a classic of the *concours administratif* (civil-service exam). Many French
civil-service exams, for both senior and middle-grade posts, include a written test in which the
candidate drafts a note from a file of documents; preparation bodies such as the CNED name three
variants: the *note administrative*, the *note avec propositions* and the *note de synthèse*. The
format depends on each exam. As one example, a 2023 framing note for the external exam for
*attaché territorial* (a senior post in local government) describes a four-hour test, a file of
about thirty pages, an expected note of six or seven pages, and no outside knowledge: only the
file counts. Other exams set other lengths, so always read the official framing note
(*note de cadrage*) of the exam you sit.

## The layout of a note

![The first page of an administrative note, drawn as a sheet of paper. At the top left, the issuing service: Mairie de Saint-Varen, Direction générale des services, with the date at the top right. In the centre, in capitals, NOTE, and under it "à l'attention de Madame la Maire". Then a line "Objet : extinction de l'éclairage public la nuit" and a line "Réf. : documents 1 à 3". Below, a block of text for the introduction, then two numbered part titles, I and II, each with two sub-titles, A and B, and grey lines of text. At the bottom, a box titled Propositions with three numbered lines, and a last line "Annexe : …". Red tags in the right margin name the parts: en-tête, destinataire, objet, introduction, titre de partie, annexe.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- **The heading:** the issuing service (*le timbre*) and the date; the word *NOTE*; the
  addressee (*à l'attention de Monsieur le Directeur*); the *objet* (subject) in one line; and the
  *références*, the main documents or texts. In an exam, the instructions often forbid signing
  with your own name or inventing names.
- **The introduction:** the context, the problem, and the announced plan (lesson 20's *annonce du
  plan*), in a short paragraph or two.
- **The body:** two parts, each with two sub-parts, all with titles that say something
  (*I. Une mesure aux effets attendus*, not *I. Avantages*). Titles are a feature of the note that
  the DALF synthesis doesn't have.
- **The recommendations**, when the task asks for them: *les préconisations* (formal
  recommendations) or *pistes d'action* (options for action), numbered and *opérationnelles*
  (operational: who does what, when).
- **The appendices:** an *annexe* is an appendix (a table, a map, a list), mentioned at the end.

The style is neutral, concise and impersonal (*il est proposé de …*, *il conviendrait de …*), in
full sentences, with the documents reformulated, not copied. The note informs; the decision
belongs to the reader.

## The report

**Un rapport** (a report) is longer and usually signed. Its author is *le rapporteur* or *la
rapporteuse*: in Parliament, the member who studies a bill and reports on it to the others; in
an administration or a public inspection body, the official who leads an inquiry. A report
typically starts with *un état des lieux* (an assessment of the current situation; in renting,
*l'état des lieux* is the inventory of a flat at the start and end of a lease), analyses the
causes, compares options and ends with recommendations. Some civil-service exams ask for a
*rapport avec propositions* instead of a note.

Choosing between options is *un arbitrage*: in administrative French, the decision a superior
makes between competing proposals (*rendre un arbitrage*; *l'arbitrage* is also refereeing in
sport, and arbitration in law). A note prepares the *arbitrage*; it doesn't make it.

## How it differs from the DALF synthesis

| | DALF *synthèse de documents* | *note de synthèse* | *note avec propositions*, *rapport* |
|---|---|---|---|
| reader | a general reader, the examiner | a named decision-maker | a named decision-maker |
| layout | paragraphs, no heading | heading, *objet*, titled parts | heading, titled parts, recommendations |
| your view | none | none | only in the recommendations, drawn from the file |
| outside knowledge | none | none in an exam | none in an exam |
| length | 200 to 240 words in the manual | set by the exam, often several pages | set by the exam |

The key difference: the DALF synthesis **never recommends**, while a note with proposals ends
with them. Both share the rules of lesson 19: plan by ideas, not by document; compare the sources;
your own words.

## Example 1: from the file to the plan

The file below is original and the commune invented. It has three short documents, summarised
here; a real exam file is far longer.

> **Document 1 (services techniques, note interne).** L'éclairage public représente près d'un tiers de la facture d'électricité de la commune. Couper les lampadaires de 1 h à 5 h dans les rues résidentielles réduirait cette dépense d'environ 40 % sur ces rues.
>
> **Document 2 (article d'une association naturaliste).** La lumière artificielle nocturne perturbe les insectes, les oiseaux migrateurs et les chauves-souris. Les communes qui éteignent la nuit observent souvent le retour de certaines espèces.
>
> **Document 3 (courrier d'un collectif d'habitants du quartier de la gare).** Les habitants craignent pour leur sécurité en rentrant tard, notamment les personnes qui travaillent en horaires décalés. Ils demandent que les rues proches de la gare restent éclairées.

In English: (1) the council's technical services say street lighting is nearly a third of the
electricity bill and that switching lamps off from 1 to 5 a.m. in residential streets would cut
that cost by about 40% in those streets; (2) a naturalists' association says artificial light at
night disturbs insects, migrating birds and bats, and that species often return where towns
switch off; (3) residents near the station fear for their safety coming home late, especially
shift workers, and want the streets near the station kept lit. *Les horaires décalés* = shift
work, unsocial hours.

A *grille* (lesson 19) gives two ideas in favour (cost, biodiversity) and two reservations
(safety, different needs by area). That suggests the plan: *I. Une mesure aux effets attendus;
II. Des réserves à prendre en compte*; then proposals that answer the reservations.

## Example 2: a model note

The model below (about 260 words) is much shorter than an exam note, because the file is tiny; its
structure is the real one.

> **Mairie de Saint-Varen, Direction générale des services** — le 3 mars
>
> **NOTE à l'attention de Madame la Maire**
>
> **Objet :** extinction de l'éclairage public la nuit
>
> Le poids de l'éclairage public dans la facture d'électricité conduit la commune à envisager son extinction nocturne. Si cette mesure promet des économies et un bénéfice écologique (I), elle suscite des inquiétudes qu'il convient de prendre en compte (II). Des propositions sont formulées en conclusion.
>
> **I. Une mesure aux effets attendus**
>
> *A. Des économies significatives.* L'éclairage public représente près d'un tiers de la facture d'électricité communale. Une extinction de 1 h à 5 h dans les rues résidentielles réduirait d'environ 40 % la dépense correspondante (doc. 1).
>
> *B. Un bénéfice pour la biodiversité.* La lumière nocturne perturbe de nombreuses espèces, des insectes aux chauves-souris ; les communes qui éteignent la nuit constatent souvent le retour de certaines d'entre elles (doc. 2).
>
> **II. Des réserves à prendre en compte**
>
> *A. Un sentiment d'insécurité.* Des habitants, en particulier ceux qui travaillent en horaires décalés, redoutent de rentrer dans des rues sombres (doc. 3).
>
> *B. Des besoins qui varient selon les quartiers.* Les abords de la gare, fréquentés tard, ne sauraient être traités comme les rues résidentielles (doc. 3).
>
> **Propositions**
>
> 1. Expérimenter l'extinction de 1 h à 5 h pendant six mois dans les seules rues résidentielles.
> 2. Maintenir l'éclairage sur les axes principaux et aux abords de la gare.
> 3. Informer les habitants avant la mise en œuvre, puis dresser un bilan avec la police municipale et les associations à l'issue de l'expérimentation, en vue d'un arbitrage du conseil municipal.

In English: the heading names the issuing service, the addressee (the mayor) and the subject.
The introduction gives the context (the share of street lighting in the electricity bill, from document 1), the problem and the plan. Part I sets out
the expected effects, savings and biodiversity; part II the reservations, residents' feeling of
insecurity and the different needs of each area. Three proposals follow: a six-month trial in
residential streets only, lighting kept on main roads and near the station, and information
before, then a review with the municipal police and associations, so that the council can decide.
*Il convient de* = it is appropriate to; *ne sauraient être traités* = cannot be treated (formal:
*savoir* in the conditionnel with *ne* alone means "cannot"); *dresser un bilan* = to draw up a review.

**Commentary.** The introduction states the context, the problem and the plan in three sentences,
with the parts marked (I) and (II). Every title says something. The documents are cited
(*doc. 1*) but reformulated (*redoutent* for *craignent*, *les abords* for *les rues proches*).
There is no *je* and no opinion in parts I and II; the proposals answer the reservations of part
II point by point, and leave the decision, the *arbitrage*, to the council. In a DALF synthesis
the same file would give 200 to 240 words of paragraphs, without heading, titles or proposals.

## Common mistakes

- **One part per document.** Plan by ideas, as in lesson 19.
- **Titles that say nothing** (*I. Avantages*). A title is a short claim.
- **Recommendations that come from nowhere.** Each proposal answers something in the file.
- **Outside knowledge in an exam note.** Only the file counts, whatever you know.
- **Opinion in the body** (*je pense que, malheureusement*). Keep it neutral; proposals go at the
  end, in impersonal form.
- **Recommending in the DALF synthesis.** It never recommends.
- **Une préconisation for any advice.** It is formal and official; in everyday French, *un
  conseil*.

## Key points

- A **[[note de synthèse]]** informs a decision-maker from a file: heading, *objet*, short
  introduction with the plan, two titled parts, and, if asked, numbered *préconisations*.
- A **[[rapport]]** is longer and signed by its *rapporteur*; it often opens with an *état des lieux*
  and ends with recommendations.
- Many French *concours administratifs* include a note written from a file; the format and length
  are set by each exam's framing note.
- Unlike the DALF synthesis, a note has a heading and titles, and may end with proposals; like it,
  it uses only the documents, in your own words.

## Graded writing: a note with proposals

Write a note with proposals from the original file in the task below. Your teacher or parent
grades it with the rubric; you can rate your own draft against it first.

```assignment
writing: fr5-m6-note-cours-oasis
```

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Montaigne et l'invention de l'essai
topics: From Montaigne to the essai argumenté
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 20 taught the **[[essai argumenté]]** of the DALF: a position, a plan, arguments and a
conclusion. The word *essai* itself comes from a book written four centuries earlier by a
Gascon nobleman who shut himself up in a tower to "try out" his own judgement on everything
he read and lived. This lesson gives you a C1 portrait of Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) and
his *Essais*, the book that gave the genre its name. You will read about the self as a subject,
doubt, custom and friendship, see what the French of the sixteenth century looks like (described,
not quoted), and compare Montaigne's way of writing with the essay you write today.

The portrait below is written for this course, in modern French. Nothing in the lesson is a
quotation from Montaigne: his famous lines and his motto are described in English.

## A life in dates

![A vertical timeline from 1533 to 1595 with eight dated events: 1533, birth at the château de Montaigne in Périgord; 1563, death of his friend La Boétie; 1571, retreat to his tower library; 1580, first edition of the Essais, books I and II, in Bordeaux; 1581 to 1585, mayor of Bordeaux (two terms); 1588, edition with book III, in Paris; 1592, death; 1595, posthumous edition prepared by Marie de Gournay.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Michel Eyquem de Montaigne was born on 28 February 1533 at the château de Montaigne, in
Périgord, east of Bordeaux, into a family of merchants recently ennobled. His father had him
taught Latin before French: a tutor and the household spoke only Latin to the child. He studied
at the Collège de Guyenne in Bordeaux, then became a magistrate, first in Périgueux and from 1557
at the Parlement of Bordeaux. There he met Étienne de La Boétie, author of a youthful treatise
against tyranny, the *Discours de la servitude volontaire*. Their friendship lasted only a few
years: La Boétie died on 18 August 1563, and Montaigne sat at his bedside.

In 1570 Montaigne sold his office; in 1571, aged 38, he withdrew to the round tower of his château, where
he had his library, about a thousand books, on the top floor. On the beams of its ceiling he had
sentences painted, in Latin and Greek, taken from ancient authors and the Bible: many of them
about the limits of human knowledge. A Latin inscription on the wall of the next room records his
retreat. The main house was later rebuilt, but the tower still stands and can be visited.

The first edition of the *Essais* (books I and II) came out in Bordeaux in 1580, printed by Simon
Millanges. Montaigne then travelled through Germany, Switzerland and Italy; in Italy, in 1581, he
learned that he had been elected mayor of Bordeaux. He served two terms (1581–1585), the second
ending as plague reached the city. In 1588 a Paris edition added book III and hundreds of
additions to the first two. Montaigne went on writing in the margins of his own copy (now called
the *exemplaire de Bordeaux*) until his death on 13 September 1592. His "adopted daughter" Marie
de Gournay prepared the posthumous edition of 1595.

## Reading: Un homme qui s'essaie

> Lorsque Montaigne se retira dans sa tour, il comptait, dit-on, y goûter le repos et la sagesse des Anciens. Il y trouva tout autre chose : son esprit, livré à lui-même, s'agitait plus que jamais. Pour le discipliner, il entreprit de noter ses pensées, sans plan préconçu, au fil des lectures et des souvenirs. Ces textes, il les appela des « essais », c'est-à-dire des épreuves : il y met son jugement à l'essai sur tous les sujets, la mort, l'éducation, l'amitié, les chevaux ou les pouces.
>
> L'originalité du livre tient à son sujet. Avant lui, on écrivait surtout sur Dieu, sur le monde ou sur les grands hommes ; Montaigne, lui, choisit de s'étudier lui-même, non par vanité mais parce qu'en observant un homme ordinaire on apprend, selon lui, quelque chose sur tous les autres. Cette introspection n'a rien d'une confession : elle observe un homme qui change d'un jour à l'autre et qui l'avoue.
>
> Nourri de Sénèque, il fut, selon bien des critiques, d'abord tenté par le stoïcisme, qui enseigne à se préparer à la mort. Avec l'âge, il se méfia des doctrines trop raides et chercha plutôt une sagesse à hauteur d'homme, faite d'acceptation de la vie et du corps. Il eût été étonné, sans doute, qu'on fît de lui le père d'un genre littéraire.

*When Montaigne withdrew into his tower, he intended, it is said, to enjoy rest and the wisdom of
the Ancients there. He found something quite different: his mind, left to itself, was more
restless than ever. To discipline it, he set about writing down his thoughts, with no plan made in
advance, as his reading and his memories led him. He called these texts "essais", that is to say
trials: in them he puts his judgement to the test on every subject, death, education, friendship,
horses or thumbs.*

*The book's originality lies in its subject. Before him, people wrote mostly about God, the world or great
men; Montaigne chooses to study himself, not out of vanity but because, in his view, observing an
ordinary man teaches you something about all the others. This introspection is nothing like a confession:
it observes a man who changes from one day to the next and admits it.*

*Steeped in Seneca, he was, according to many critics, at first drawn to Stoicism, which teaches you to prepare for death. With
age he grew wary of doctrines that were too rigid and looked instead for a wisdom on a human
scale, made of accepting life and the body. He would no doubt have been astonished that anyone
should make him the father of a literary genre.*

Reading the tenses (lesson 07 and the reference sheet): the narrative is in the *passé
simple* (*se retira, trouva, entreprit, appela, fut, se méfia, chercha*), recognised, not
produced; *met*, *choisit* and *observe* are a présent of commentary, for what is still true of
the book. The last sentence has two recognition-only forms: *Il eût été étonné* is the
conditionnel passé deuxième forme (everyday French: *il aurait été étonné*), and *qu'on fît*
is the imperfect subjunctive (everyday: *qu'on fasse*). *Nourri de Sénèque* is a detached
participle (lesson 17): it refers to the subject, *il*.

## What the *Essais* are

The *Essais* have three books and 107 chapters of very unequal length, from a page to well over a hundred.
Chapter titles promise one subject and often deliver another: *Des cannibales* (I, 31) is as much
about Europe as about Brazil; *Apologie de Raymond Sebond* (II, 12), the longest, starts as a
defence of a theologian and turns into a vast inquiry into what humans can know. The last chapter,
*De l'expérience* (III, 13), ends the book with the body, illness and the art of living well.

Montaigne rarely deleted; he added. Modern editions mark three layers of text: what was printed in
1580, what was added in 1588, and what he wrote in the margins afterwards. You can watch an idea
grow, or contradict itself, over twenty years.

*What his French looks like.* Montaigne wrote the French of the late Renaissance, which linguists
class as late *moyen français* (Middle French) or early *français préclassique*. A modern reader meets spellings such as *-oit* for
today's *-ait* in the imperfect, *u* and *v* used interchangeably, an *s* where we now write a
circumflex, few accents, and Latin quotations left untranslated. The vocabulary looks familiar but
many words have shifted meaning, and the sentences run on through *et*, *car* and semicolons.
Most French readers today use an edition in modernised spelling, or a translation into modern
French.

## Four ideas

*The self as subject.* In his short preface to the reader, Montaigne presents the book as a
portrait of himself, written for his family and friends. Self-observation, *l'introspection*, becomes a method: not to find a fixed
"true self", but to record a self that moves.

*Doubt.* In 1576, according to his biographers, Montaigne had a medal struck showing a pair of scales in
balance; in the *Essais* he links that image to his motto, a short question asking what he really
knows. This is the ancient **[[scepticism]]** of the
Pyrrhonists: suspend your judgement when reasons on both sides weigh the same. Montaigne's
*scepticisme* is not a refusal to think: it is a way of testing every certainty, his own included.
A *sceptique*, in his sense, keeps looking.

*Custom and other peoples.* For Montaigne, *la coutume* (custom, habit) shapes what each society
calls natural or barbaric. In *Des cannibales* he describes the Tupi people of Brazil, from
travellers' accounts and from a meeting with three of them in Rouen (in 1562, according to most
editors), and turns the comparison against Europe: are the wars of religion tearing France apart
less cruel than the customs he is told about? Readers often see here an early form of cultural
relativism, though Montaigne doesn't use the term.

*Friendship.* The chapter *De l'amitié* (I, 28) is a tribute to La Boétie. Montaigne refuses
to explain their bond by any quality or interest: in a famous passage he says it had no cause he
could name outside the two men themselves. He had planned to print La Boétie's treatise at the
heart of book I, then gave it up.

## Humanism

Montaigne is a late figure of **[[humanism]]** (*l'humanisme*), the movement of the Renaissance
(*la Renaissance*, always with a capital) that went back to the Greek and Latin texts, edited and
translated them, and put the study of humankind at the centre of learning. A *humaniste* reads
Plutarch, Seneca and Cicero, cares about education and trusts reason. Montaigne is all this, but
a doubting humanist: he cites the Ancients constantly and still asks whether all that reading
makes anyone wiser.

### Example 1: Essai, essayer, essayiste

Start from the verb. *Essayer* means to try (A1), and also, older, to test or weigh (*essayer
une monnaie*: to assay a coin). Montaigne's *essais* are trials of his judgement. The word then
travelled: Francis Bacon published English *Essays* in 1597, and today an **[[essay]]** (*un essai*) is a
prose work of ideas, *un essayiste* (or *une essayiste*) the person who writes them. Compare:

- *Montaigne s'essaie à penser.* — Montaigne tries himself out in thinking. (the self as a test)
- *Cet essayiste défend une thèse en trois parties.* — This essayist defends a thesis in three
  parts. (the modern genre)
- *Le candidat rédige un essai argumenté.* — The candidate writes an argued essay. (lesson 20)

### Example 2: From a meandering reflection to an argued paragraph

Here is an original reflection in Montaigne's manner (not his words):

> Je voulais parler de l'habitude, et me voilà à parler de mon grand-père, qui buvait son café froid parce qu'on le lui avait toujours servi ainsi. Est-ce goût ou coutume ? Je n'en sais rien. Peut-être ne choisissons-nous presque rien.

In an *essai argumenté*, the same idea needs a topic sentence, a reason, an example and a link
(lessons 11 and 20):

> L'habitude détermine une part de nos choix plus grande que nous ne le croyons. En effet, ce que nous appelons un goût n'est souvent qu'une coutume devenue invisible : on aime ce que l'on a toujours connu. Ainsi, bien des préférences alimentaires se transmettent dans les familles sans avoir jamais été discutées. Encore faut-il distinguer l'habitude subie de celle que l'on a choisie.

*Habit determines a larger share of our choices than we think. Indeed, what we call a taste is
often just a custom that has become invisible: we like what we have always known. Thus many food
preferences are passed down in families without ever having been discussed. Still, we must tell
habits we undergo from those we have chosen.*

The first text follows the mind; the second follows a plan. Note *plus grande que nous ne le
croyons* (expletive *ne* after a comparison, formal) and *Encore faut-il* + infinitive (inversion after a
fronted *encore*: "still, one has to").

## Common mistakes

- *Sceptique* is spelled with *sc* in French (English *sceptic* or *skeptic*); the *c* is silent
  before *e*, and it is pronounced like *septique* (septic): context separates them.
- *Humaniste* is not *humanitaire*. *Un humaniste* is a scholar of the Renaissance or a person who
  puts human beings first; *une organisation humanitaire* gives aid.
- *La coutume* is a custom; customs at the border are *la douane*, and a costume is *le costume*.
- *La Renaissance* takes a capital for the period; *une renaissance* (small *r*) is any revival.
- Don't call the *Essais* a diary or a philosophy treatise. They are neither: say *un livre
  d'essais* or simply *les Essais*.
- Don't quote the motto or the famous lines in an essay unless you have checked them in an
  edition; describe them, as this lesson does.

## Key points

- Montaigne: born 28 February 1533 in Périgord, died 13 September 1592; La Boétie died in 1563;
  retreat to the tower in 1571; mayor of Bordeaux 1581–1585.
- *Essais*: 1580 (books I–II, Bordeaux), 1588 (with book III, Paris), 1595 (posthumous, Marie de
  Gournay). Three books, 107 chapters, three layers of text.
- Key ideas: the self as subject (*l'introspection*), scepticism (the balance, the motto as a
  question), custom (*la coutume*) and other peoples, friendship, a wisdom on a human scale after
  an early Stoicism. Humanism: the return to ancient texts in the Renaissance.
- An essay in Montaigne's sense tries out a judgement; the DALF *essai argumenté* (lesson 20)
  keeps the name and adds a plan.
