lessons.title: Zola, l'affaire Dreyfus et l'intellectuel engagé
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 09 and 10 taught you to present causes, objections and concessions with precision. This
lesson puts those tools to work on the political crisis that divided France at the end of the
nineteenth century: *l'affaire Dreyfus*, the Dreyfus affair. A Jewish army officer was convicted
of treason he hadn't committed; a famous novelist, Émile Zola, risked prison to say so in a
newspaper; and out of the quarrel came a new figure of French public life, the intellectual who
takes a stand. You will read an account of the affair, learn how Zola's open letter worked
(described, not quoted), and present the arguments of both camps as they were made at the time,
without taking them over.

## Zola before the affair

Émile Zola was born in Paris on 2 April 1840 and grew up in Aix-en-Provence. By 1897 he was one of
the most read novelists in Europe. His great cycle, *Les Rougon-Macquart*, twenty novels published
between 1871 and 1893, follows five generations of one family under the Second Empire; its subtitle
calls it a "natural and social history" of that family. Among the best known: *L'Assommoir* (1877),
on alcoholism in a Paris working-class district, and *Germinal* (1885), on a miners' strike in
the north.

Zola was the leader of **[[naturalism]]** (*le naturalisme*), which pushed realism further: the novelist
should observe society as a scientist observes nature, document every milieu (he took notes in
mines, markets and railway depots), and show how heredity and environment shape people. He set
out the theory in *Le Roman expérimental* (1880), drawing on the physiologist Claude Bernard.
Critics accused him of vulgarity; readers bought his books in their hundreds of thousands.

## The affair in dates

![A vertical timeline of the Dreyfus affair from December 1894 to July 1906, with ten events: Dreyfus convicted by a court martial (December 1894); degraded, then deported to Devil's Island (1895); Picquart suspects Major Esterhazy (1896); Esterhazy acquitted by a court martial (11 January 1898); Zola publishes J'accuse in L'Aurore (13 January 1898); Zola convicted of defamation (February 1898); Zola in exile in England (1898 to 1899); the Rennes trial, then a presidential pardon (September 1899); Zola's death (September 1902); rehabilitation by the Cour de cassation (July 1906). A note says the spacing is not proportional to the years.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: Une erreur judiciaire

> En septembre 1894, le service de contre-espionnage de l'armée française obtient une lettre non signée qui proviendrait, selon ce service, de l'ambassade d'Allemagne : un bordereau qui annonce l'envoi de documents militaires. Une affaire d'espionnage, donc. Les soupçons se portent très vite sur le capitaine Alfred Dreyfus, officier d'artillerie alsacien et juif, dont l'écriture ressemblerait à celle du document. Arrêté le 15 octobre, il est jugé à huis clos par un conseil de guerre et condamné, en décembre, à la déportation à vie. Ce que ni lui ni son avocat ne savent, c'est que les juges ont reçu en secret un dossier qui n'a jamais été communiqué à la défense.
>
> Dégradé publiquement en janvier 1895, Dreyfus est envoyé à l'île du Diable, au large de la Guyane. Sa famille, elle, ne renonce pas. En 1896, le lieutenant-colonel Picquart, nouveau chef du renseignement, découvre que l'écriture du bordereau est celle d'un autre officier, le commandant Esterhazy. Loin d'être félicité, il est muté en Tunisie. Jugé à son tour en janvier 1898, Esterhazy est acquitté en quelques minutes.
>
> Il faudra encore huit ans pour que la vérité soit reconnue : en 1906, la Cour de cassation annule le dernier jugement et prononce la réhabilitation de Dreyfus, qui est réintégré dans l'armée.

*In September 1894, the French army's counter-espionage service obtains an unsigned letter that came,
according to that service, from the German embassy: a memorandum announcing the delivery of military documents. A case
of espionage, then. Suspicion very quickly falls on Captain Alfred Dreyfus, an Alsatian Jewish
artillery officer, whose handwriting supposedly resembles that of the document. Arrested on 15
October, he is tried behind closed doors by a court martial and sentenced, in December, to
deportation for life. What neither he nor his lawyer knows is that the judges secretly received a
file that was never shown to the defence.*

*Publicly degraded in January 1895, Dreyfus is sent to Devil's Island, off French Guiana. His
family, for its part, does not give up. In 1896, Lieutenant-Colonel Picquart, the new head of
intelligence, discovers that the handwriting of the memorandum is that of another officer, Major
Esterhazy. Far from being congratulated, he is posted to Tunisia. Tried in his turn in January
1898, Esterhazy is acquitted in a few minutes.*

*It will take another eight years for the truth to be recognised: in 1906 the Cour de cassation
annuls the last judgement and rehabilitates Dreyfus, who is reinstated in the army.*

Notice the **[[présent historique]]** (lesson 07) for the whole story, the reportive conditionals
*proviendrait* and *ressemblerait* (lesson 08: the writer doesn't vouch for the source or the
resemblance), the cleft sentence *Ce
que … c'est que …*, the detached participles *Arrêté*, *Dégradé*, *Jugé à son tour* (lesson 17),
and the futur historique *Il faudra encore huit ans* for an event later than the story's present.
*La réhabilitation* here is the legal clearing of a name; the word also means the renovation of a
building.

## *J'accuse…!*

On 13 January 1898, two days after Esterhazy's acquittal, the daily *L'Aurore* gave its whole front
page to a long open letter (*une lettre ouverte*) from Zola to the President of the Republic, Félix
Faure. The headline, *J'accuse…!*, is usually credited to Georges Clemenceau, then an editorialist
at the paper. Here is what the letter does, in our words:

- it retells the affair as Zola understood it and argues that an innocent man has been convicted
  while the guilty one has been protected;
- it ends with a series of short paragraphs that each begin with the same two words as the
  headline, each naming people Zola held responsible: officers, ministers, handwriting experts,
  and the court martial that acquitted Esterhazy;
- and it closes by saying that he knows he is exposing himself to prosecution, and wants it, so
  that the truth can come out in open court.

The letter is often called a pamphlet: *un pamphlet* in French is a short, violent polemical
text, not a leaflet (*un dépliant*, *un tract*). Zola had already published two shorter appeals
as brochures in December 1897 and January 1898, and the critic Bernard Lazare had denounced the
case as early as 1896, in a pamphlet whose title called it a miscarriage of justice: *une erreur
judiciaire*.

Zola got the trial he wanted. Sued for defamation (*la diffamation*) by the Minister of War, he
was convicted on 23 February 1898 and given the maximum sentence: a year in prison and a 3,000-franc
fine. The verdict was quashed on a point of procedure, but a second trial followed at Versailles in
July; on his lawyers' advice, Zola left for England the same evening and stayed there for almost a
year. Meanwhile, in August 1898, an officer of the intelligence service, Colonel Henry, admitted
that he had forged a document against Dreyfus, and killed himself in prison. A second court
martial, at Rennes in September 1899, convicted Dreyfus again, "with extenuating circumstances";
ten days later the President, Émile Loubet, pardoned him. The full rehabilitation came only on 12
July 1906.

Zola didn't see it. He died in his Paris flat on 29 September 1902, poisoned by the fumes of a
blocked chimney; whether the chimney was blocked on purpose has been suggested but never proved.
His ashes were moved to the Panthéon in 1908.

## Two camps

The affair split families, friends and newspapers into dreyfusards (*les dreyfusards*, *les
dreyfusardes*: supporters of a retrial) and antidreyfusards. Present their arguments as they were
made, with the distance a historian keeps.

*The antidreyfusards* argued that the army, the nation's shield against Germany after the defeat
of 1870, could not be put on trial without weakening the country; that the court martial had
judged, and that a judgement had to be respected; that a review would serve France's enemies.
Part of the camp was openly driven by antisemitism (*l'antisémitisme*), hostility to Jews as
such, spread by newspapers such as Édouard Drumont's *La Libre Parole*; anti-Jewish riots broke out
in several French towns and in Algeria in early 1898.

*The dreyfusards* answered that justice, not the army's prestige, was the foundation of the
Republic; that a man had been convicted on a secret file his defence never saw; and that the
honour of an institution can't rest on a lie. The Ligue des droits de l'homme was founded in June
1898 in this spirit.

### Example 1: Reporting an argument without endorsing it

> Pour les antidreyfusards, réviser le procès aurait affaibli l'armée dans la mesure où celle-ci incarnait la défense nationale. Ils refusaient la révision sous prétexte que la chose avait été jugée.

*For the antidreyfusards, reviewing the trial would have weakened the army insofar as the army
embodied national defence. They refused the review on the grounds that the matter had been judged.*

*Pour les antidreyfusards* and the conditional *aurait affaibli* attribute the claim. *Dans la
mesure où* gives their reason (cause, lesson 09). *Sous prétexte que* signals that the writer
doesn't accept the reason: use it only when you mean to. A neutral version: *au motif que*.

### Example 2: Conceding, then answering

> Certes, l'armée jouissait alors d'un immense prestige. Il n'en demeure pas moins que le procès de 1894 reposait en partie sur un dossier secret : la condamnation n'était pas au-dessus de tout soupçon, tant s'en faut.

*Admittedly, the army then enjoyed immense prestige. The fact remains that the 1894 trial rested partly
on a secret file: the conviction was far from being above all suspicion.*

*Certes … il n'en demeure pas moins que* (+ indicative) concedes, then keeps the argument standing.
*Tant s'en faut* (lesson 10) comes after a negative claim and strengthens it: "far from it". A
common slip is to put it after a positive claim (*la condamnation était au-dessus de tout soupçon,
tant s'en faut*), which turns the sentence against the writer's own point.

## The intellectual

The day after *J'accuse…!*, *L'Aurore* published a petition asking for a review of the trial,
signed by writers, scientists and academics: Anatole France, the young Marcel Proust (lesson 92)
and many others. Clemenceau spoke of a protest of "intellectuals", and the nationalist writer
Maurice Barrès took up the word with scorn. Until then *intellectuel* was mostly an adjective; the
affair made it a noun for a person, *un intellectuel* or *une intellectuelle*, who uses the
authority earned in their field to speak on a public question.

The **[[engaged intellectual]]** (*l'intellectuel engagé*) became a lasting French figure: in the
twentieth century, writers and philosophers such as Jean-Paul Sartre made *l'engagement* a duty.
Its critics have always asked the same question as in 1898: why should a novelist's opinion on a
court case weigh more than anyone else's?

## Common mistakes

- *Un pamphlet* is a polemical text, not a leaflet. *Une brochure* or *un dépliant* informs.
- *L'affaire Dreyfus*: small *a*, no hyphen. *Dreyfusard* takes no capital: *les dreyfusards*.
- *La diffamation* (defamation, libel) is a legal offence; *la calomnie* (slander) is the
  general, older word for a false accusation.
- *L'antisémitisme* and *antisémite* are written as one word in current French.
- Don't write that Zola "was acquitted": he was convicted, then the verdict was quashed and he
  was convicted again in his absence before going into exile; the 1900 amnesty law ended the
  proceedings.
- *Réhabiliter* someone is to clear their name officially; *rééduquer* is to rehabilitate a
  patient.

## Key points

- Zola (1840–1902), leader of naturalism: *Les Rougon-Macquart*, twenty novels (1871–1893).
- The affair: a bordereau, an espionage case, Dreyfus convicted (December 1894) and deported to
  Devil's Island; Esterhazy acquitted (January 1898); *J'accuse…!* in *L'Aurore* (13 January
  1898); Zola convicted of defamation (February 1898) and in exile in England (1898–1899); Rennes
  and the pardon (September 1899); the Cour de cassation's rehabilitation (12 July 1906).
- Two camps: the army's honour and the authority of the judgement against justice and the rights of
  the individual; antisemitism ran through the affair.
- The noun *intellectuel* and the figure of the engaged intellectual date from the affair.
- To present a past argument: attribute it (*pour …, selon …*), use the conditional, and choose
  connectors that show your distance (*dans la mesure où, au motif que, sous prétexte que*).

lessons.title: Proust et la phrase longue
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 17 showed you how a long French sentence holds together: participial clauses, appositions,
a main verb to find. Marcel Proust (1871–1922) is often called the writer who pushed the long sentence furthest,
and his novel *À la recherche du temps perdu* is the book French readers name when they want to
say "difficult". This lesson tells you what the novel is about, explains its central idea,
**[[involuntary memory]]**, and trains you to read a long sentence by taking it apart. The example
sentences are original: no line of Proust's is quoted or imitated. His most famous passages, the
opening sentence and the madeleine, are described in English.

## A life

Marcel Proust was born on 10 July 1871 in Auteuil, then on the edge of Paris, the son of a
professor of medicine, Adrien Proust, and of Jeanne Weil, from a cultivated Jewish family. Asthmatic
from childhood, he spent much of his youth in the salons of the aristocracy and the rich
bourgeoisie, where he was taken for a gifted, rather frivolous *mondain*, a man of society. He
published a collection of stories and poems, *Les Plaisirs et les Jours* (1896), translated the
English critic John Ruskin with his mother's help, and took the side of Dreyfus early: in January
1898 he helped gather signatures for the petition of the intellectuals (lesson 91).

After his parents' deaths (1903 and 1905) he withdrew more and more, wrote at night in a bedroom on
the boulevard Haussmann whose walls he had lined with cork against the noise, and gave the rest of
his life to one book. He died in Paris on 18 November 1922, still correcting the last volumes.

## The novel in seven volumes

| Volume | Published |
|---|---|
| *Du côté de chez Swann* | 1913 (Grasset) |
| *À l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs* | 1919 (prix Goncourt) |
| *Le Côté de Guermantes* | 1920–1921 |
| *Sodome et Gomorrhe* | 1921–1922 |
| *La Prisonnière* | 1923 |
| *Albertine disparue* (also called *La Fugitive*) | 1925 |
| *Le Temps retrouvé* | 1927 |

The first volume had a hard birth. Several publishers turned it down in 1912–1913, among them the
*Nouvelle Revue française*, whose reading committee included André Gide; Bernard Grasset published
it in November 1913, with Proust paying the printing costs. The war interrupted everything. The
second volume came out in 1919 with Gallimard (the NRF publisher, which had changed its mind) and
won the prix Goncourt that December. The last three volumes appeared after Proust's death, prepared
from his manuscripts by his brother Robert and the NRF's editors.

## Reading: De quoi parle la *Recherche* ?

> Un narrateur, qui ressemble beaucoup à l'auteur sans jamais se confondre tout à fait avec lui, se souvient de sa vie. Il y a d'abord l'enfance à Combray, petite ville de province où sa famille passe les vacances chez une tante malade, et où les promenades se partagent entre deux « côtés » : celui de Swann, un ami de la famille, et celui des Guermantes, une illustre famille aristocratique. On découvre ensuite, dans un récit enchâssé, l'amour jaloux de Swann pour Odette, une femme qu'il finira par épouser.
>
> Devenu jeune homme, le narrateur fréquente les salons, où le snobisme règne : la bourgeoise Mme Verdurin méprise en apparence les aristocrates qu'elle rêve d'attirer chez elle. Au bord de la mer, à Balbec, il rencontre Albertine, qu'il aimera d'un amour tourmenté, la gardant presque prisonnière à Paris jusqu'à ce qu'elle s'enfuie. Elle mourra peu après, et l'oubli fera lentement son œuvre.
>
> Dans le dernier volume, alors qu'il se rend à une réception, plusieurs sensations ravivent soudain en lui des pans entiers du passé. Il comprend alors que le temps n'est pas perdu s'il est retrouvé par l'art. Dans les salons, les invités ont tant vieilli qu'il les reconnaît à peine : il décide d'écrire, avant qu'il ne soit trop tard, le livre que nous venons de lire.

*A narrator, who looks a lot like the author without ever quite merging with him, remembers his
life. First there is his childhood in Combray, a small provincial town where his family spends the
holidays at the house of a sick aunt, and where walks divide between two "ways": Swann's way (Swann
is a friend of the family) and the Guermantes way (an illustrious aristocratic family). Then, in a
story within the story, we discover Swann's jealous love for Odette, a woman he will end up
marrying.*

*As a young man, the narrator moves in the salons, where snobbery reigns: the bourgeois Mme Verdurin
seems to despise the aristocrats she dreams of drawing to her house. At the seaside, in Balbec, he
meets Albertine, whom he will love with a tormented love, keeping her almost a prisoner in Paris
until she runs away. She will die soon afterwards, and forgetting will slowly do its work.*

*In the last volume, as he arrives at a party, several sensations suddenly revive whole stretches of
the past in him. He then understands that time is not lost if it is regained through art. In the
reception rooms, the guests have aged so much that he hardly recognises them: he decides to write,
before it is too late, the book we have just read.*

Note *se partagent entre* (are divided between), *un récit enchâssé* (a story set within another),
the futur historique *finira par épouser, aimera, mourra* (lesson 07), and two subjunctives:
*jusqu'à ce qu'elle s'enfuie* and *avant qu'il ne soit trop tard* (the *ne* is expletive and optional). A *snob* in French is mainly someone who admires and imitates people of a
higher social rank; *le snobisme* is that attitude, and Proust is its great analyst.

## Involuntary memory

The famous opening sentence, about going to bed early, is short for once. Then comes the drama of the goodnight kiss his mother sometimes cannot give him. For
years, the adult narrator remembers almost nothing else of Combray: his voluntary memory, the
effort to remember, brings back only a dry outline.

Then, one winter day, his mother offers him tea and a small shell-shaped cake, *une madeleine*. He
dips a piece in the tea, tastes it, and feels an intense happiness he can't explain. After a long
effort, he recognises the taste: the madeleine his aunt used to give him, dipped in her tea or
lime-blossom infusion, on Sunday mornings in Combray. With the taste, his whole childhood there comes back.

This is involuntary memory (*la mémoire involontaire*): a sensation, met by chance, brings back
the past not as an idea but as a lived experience. Proust opposes it to voluntary memory, *la
remémoration*: the deliberate act of recalling. He himself calls the moments
when the past returns in this way *des réminiscences*; in everyday French, *une réminiscence* is
more often a vague memory that comes back half-formed.

In the last volume, other sensations do the same work: the narrator stumbles on uneven paving
stones, hears a spoon knock against a plate, wipes his mouth with a stiff napkin. The idea has
passed into everyday French: *c'est ma madeleine de Proust* means "it brings back memories", often of childhood.

## Reading a long sentence

Proust's sentences are long because they follow a thought, a doubt, a comparison and its
correction without stopping. Grammatically they are made of the pieces you already know: one main
clause (*la proposition principale*) and, attached to it, **[[subordinate clauses]]** (*les
subordonnées*), appositions, participial and infinitive phrases. To read one, find the main verb,
then bracket everything else.

![An original long sentence broken into six boxes, indented to show what depends on what. Box 1, Lorsque, des années plus tard, je revis la maison de mon enfance: adverbial subordinate clause of time. Box 2, vieille bâtisse au toit d'ardoise: apposition to la maison. Box 3, dont les volets avaient pris la couleur du sable: relative clause. Box 4, je compris: main clause. Box 5, avant même d'en franchir le seuil: infinitive phrase. Box 6, que ce n'était pas elle que j'avais aimée, mais l'enfant qui l'habitait: completive clause, object of compris.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: Finding the main clause

> Lorsque, des années plus tard, je revis la maison de mon enfance, vieille bâtisse au toit d'ardoise dont les volets avaient pris la couleur du sable, je compris, avant même d'en franchir le seuil, que ce n'était pas elle que j'avais aimée, mais l'enfant qui l'habitait.

*When, years later, I saw my childhood home again, an old slate-roofed building whose shutters had
taken on the colour of sand, I understood, even before crossing its threshold, that it was not the
house I had loved, but the child who lived in it.*

1. Find the conjugated verbs: *revis, avaient pris, compris, était, avais aimée, habitait*.
2. Take away every verb introduced by a subordinating word: *lorsque* (time), *dont* (relative),
   *que* (completive, then relative), *qui* (relative). One verb is left: *je compris*. That is
   the main clause.
3. Hang the rest on it: *lorsque …* says when; *vieille bâtisse …* is an apposition to *la
   maison*, and *dont …* describes the building; *avant même d'en franchir le seuil* is an
   infinitive phrase; *que ce n'était pas elle …* is what he understood.

*Revis* and *compris* are passé simple (recognition). *Aimée* agrees with *que*, which stands for
*elle*, the house: a direct object placed before *avoir*.

### Example 2: A sentence with literary subjunctives

> Bien qu'il fût tard et que la pluie, qui n'avait cessé de tomber depuis le matin, rendît les routes presque impraticables, ma tante, persuadée qu'un malheur arriverait si elle ne recevait pas de nouvelles avant la nuit, exigea qu'on envoyât quelqu'un à la gare.

*Although it was late and the rain, which had not stopped falling since the morning, made the roads
almost impassable, my aunt, convinced that a disaster would happen if she had no news before
nightfall, demanded that someone be sent to the station.*

- Main clause: *ma tante … exigea* (passé simple of *exiger*).
- *Bien qu'il fût tard et que la pluie … rendît*: a concessive subordinate with two verbs in the
  imperfect subjunctive, recognition only. Today: *bien qu'il soit tard et que la pluie
  rende*.
- *qui n'avait cessé de tomber*: a relative inside the concessive; *ne* alone with *cesser* is
  formal (lesson 03).
- *persuadée qu'un malheur arriverait si …*: a detached participle agreeing with *ma tante*, with
  its own completive and a si-clause.
- *qu'on envoyât quelqu'un*: the object of *exigea*, imperfect subjunctive again (today: *qu'on
  envoie*).

Proust's narrator writes in this classical system: after a past main verb, the imperfect
subjunctive. In your own writing, use the present or perfect subjunctive (lesson 06).

## Sensitivity and society

Two words carry much of the novel. *La sensibilité* is the capacity to feel, perceive and be moved:
the narrator's extreme sensibilité is both his suffering and his gift. *La mondanité*, often plural
(*les mondanités*), is the life of society: dinners, receptions, who is invited where. The adjective
*mondain* (feminine *mondaine*) describes that world (*une soirée mondaine*) or a person who
belongs to it. Proust's humour is sharpest there: his snobs, from Mme Verdurin to the aristocrats
who despise her, all want to be recognised by the circle just above their own.

## Common mistakes

- *Un snob* is a social climber or someone who admires what is fashionable, not just an arrogant
  person. The noun and adjective are the same: *il est un peu snob*.
- *Mondain* doesn't mean "mundane" (banal: *banal, ordinaire*). It means "of high society".
- *Sensibilité* is sensitivity; "sensibility" in English is a slightly different, more literary
  word, and "sense" (good judgement) is *le bon sens*.
- Don't read a long sentence word by word from the start: find the main verb first.
- Don't write imperfect subjunctives in an essay: *bien qu'il fût* is recognised, *bien qu'il
  soit* is what you write.
- *La madeleine* takes a small *m*; *la Madeleine* is a Paris church.

## Key points

- Proust: born 10 July 1871, died 18 November 1922. *À la recherche du temps perdu*: seven volumes,
  1913–1927; *Du côté de chez Swann* published by Grasset in 1913 at the author's expense; prix
  Goncourt 1919 for *À l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs*.
- Involuntary memory: a chance sensation (the madeleine, the paving stones) brings back the
  past as lived experience; *la remémoration* is deliberate recall.
- The novel's worlds: Combray, Swann and Odette, the salons and their *snobisme*, Albertine and
  jealousy, the final party and the decision to write.
- A long sentence = one main clause + subordinate clauses and phrases. Find the main verb,
  bracket the rest, then read the parts in order.

lessons.title: Dossier : faut-il simplifier l'orthographe ?
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the course's capstone. You get a short dossier in the DALF C1 manner on a debate the
French take very seriously: should spelling be simplified, and how should written French include
women and men? Then you use it three ways: a model **[[synthèse de documents]]** (lesson 19) to study,
an **[[essai argumenté]]** (lesson 20) to write and hand in, and the plan of an exposé (lesson 21). All
five documents were written for this lesson; their authors are invented and the survey figures are
invented, but every fact about laws, circulars and institutions is real and dated. The dossier's
four texts total under 500 words of French, half a real DALF corpus (about 1,000 words): read
it twice, once for the positions, once
for the language.

## The facts in brief

- *1990.* The *rectifications orthographiques*, prepared by the Conseil supérieur de la langue
  française with the Académie française's approval, were published in the *Journal officiel* on
  6 December 1990. They are recommendations: in France, traditional and rectified spellings are
  both correct. In January 1991 the Académie added that current spelling remained in use and that the new
  spellings should not be imposed.
- *School.* Ministry of Education texts named the rectified spelling as the reference for
  teaching in 2008 and again in the programmes published on 26 November 2015. The cycle 4
  (collège) French programme published in the *Bulletin officiel* of 5 March 2026 (in force for
  *5e* from September 2026) again refers to the 1990 rectifications and states that the old and the
  rectified spellings are accepted equally.
- *2016.* In early February 2016, a television report that textbook publishers would apply the
  1990 rules from September set off an outcry, much of it about the circumflex. The education
  minister wrote to the Académie on 15 February that the reference was the same as in 2008. The
  Académie's permanent secretary said the Académie had approved only general principles in 1990,
  and on 16 February it published its position: no reform, though a few simplifications could be
  accepted if they were not imposed and were tested by use.
- *Inclusive writing.* On 26 October 2017 the Académie declared itself firmly against
  *l'écriture inclusive*. A circular from the Prime Minister of 21 November 2017 asks ministries
  not to use it in texts published in the *Journal officiel*, while feminising the titles of women
  in office; the Conseil d'État upheld it on 28 February 2019. An education ministry circular of
  5 May 2021 rules out the *point médian* (*les enseignant·es*) in teaching; the Conseil d'État upheld it
  on 20 December 2024. A Senate bill to ban inclusive writing in many documents was adopted by the
  Senate on 30 October 2023 and sent to the Assemblée nationale, which had not voted on it as of
  late 2025.

Rules and programmes change: check the *Bulletin officiel* and the Académie's site before quoting
the current situation.

*What the 1990 rules change*, in brief: the circumflex (*l'accent circonflexe*) is no longer
required on *i* and *u* (*connaitre, il parait, cout, maitre*) except where it tells two words or
forms apart (*mûr, sûr, dû, jeûne, qu'il fût*); numbers take hyphens throughout (*vingt-et-un,
deux-cent-trois*; *le trait d'union* is the hyphen); some compounds are joined (*portemonnaie,
weekend*); some accents follow pronunciation (*évènement, je cèderai*); a few irregular forms are
regularised (*ognon, nénufar*). Some two thousand words (counts vary) gain a second *graphie* (written form),
and both are correct: the *réforme orthographique* adds options rather than removing any.

## Document 1: la brève

> **Orthographe : le ministère répond à l'Académie** (16 février 2016)
>
> La ministre de l'Éducation nationale a répondu aux critiques de l'Académie française sur l'application des rectifications orthographiques de 1990 dans les programmes et les manuels scolaires. Selon elle, les programmes ne font que reprendre une référence déjà présente en 2008. L'annonce de ces manuels avait provoqué, début février, une vive polémique, en particulier autour de l'accent circonflexe.

A news item: dated facts, attribution (*Selon elle*), plus-que-parfait for an earlier event
(*avait provoqué*), *ne font que* (do nothing but).

## Document 2: tribune pour

> **Une orthographe pour tous**, par Hélène Marchal, linguiste (texte inventé)
>
> Chaque année, des milliers d'heures de classe sont consacrées à des règles dont les élèves comprennent mal la logique, quand elles en ont une : pourquoi *chariot* mais *charrette*, *imbécillité* mais *imbécile* ? Une règle que même les adultes instruits doivent vérifier dans le dictionnaire n'est plus une règle : c'est un piège. L'orthographe française est devenue un outil de tri social bien plus qu'un outil de communication. Les enfants des familles cultivées s'en sortent ; les autres accumulent les fautes et finissent par croire qu'ils ne savent pas écrire.
>
> Les rectifications de 1990 n'ont rien d'une révolution : quelques accents, des traits d'union, des pluriels réguliers. Il est temps de les appliquer pleinement, et même d'aller plus loin dans la simplification. Rappelons que l'orthographe n'a jamais cessé d'évoluer : le *Dictionnaire de l'Académie* lui-même a modifié des milliers de graphies au fil de ses éditions. Simplifier, ce n'est pas appauvrir la langue ; c'est rendre à chacun le droit de l'écrire sans honte.

In short: the linguist sees French spelling as a tool of social selection, calls the 1990 changes
modest, wants them applied in full and further simplification, and argues that spelling has always
changed. Note *quand elles en ont une* (if they have one at all), the imperative *Rappelons que*,
and the closing antithesis *Simplifier, ce n'est pas …; c'est …*.

## Document 3: tribune contre

> **Ne touchez pas à la mémoire des mots**, par Marc Delorme, écrivain (texte inventé)
>
> On présente l'orthographe comme un caprice. C'est oublier qu'elle porte l'histoire de la langue. L'accent circonflexe d'*île* ou de *maître* rappelle un *s* disparu, que l'on retrouve dans *insulaire* et *magistral* ; supprimer ces signes, c'est couper les mots de leur famille. La graphie distingue aussi ce que l'oreille confond : *il a*, *à*, *mûr*, *mur*.
>
> Que la maîtrise de l'écrit recule, nul ne le conteste. Mais est-ce la faute des règles ou du temps qu'on cesse d'y consacrer ? Moins de dictées, moins de lecture : la simplification soignerait le symptôme sans toucher à la cause. Et une langue dont on modifierait l'écriture à chaque génération finirait par rendre ses propres livres étrangers à ses lecteurs. Quant à l'écriture inclusive, son point médian rend les textes plus difficiles à lire, ce qui pénalise d'abord les lecteurs fragiles qu'on prétend défendre.

In short: the writer defends spelling as the memory of the language (the circumflex marks a lost
*s*, homophones are told apart), blames the decline on less teaching time, not on the rules, and
argues that the *point médian* makes texts harder to read. Note the fronted clause with the
subjunctive *Que la maîtrise de l'écrit recule, nul ne le conteste* (lesson 05), the conditional
*soignerait* for a hypothesis, and *qu'on prétend défendre*, which casts doubt on the other side's
claim (lesson 08).

## Document 4: l'entretien

```dialogue
# « Dans ma classe, les deux graphies sont justes »
Journaliste: Vous enseignez le français au collège. Appliquez-vous l'orthographe rectifiée ?
Sophie Arnaud: Je l'enseigne comme référence, mais j'accepte les deux graphies, comme le prévoient les textes. En dictée, un élève qui écrit « paraître » avec l'accent ne fait pas de faute.
Journaliste: Les élèves s'y retrouvent-ils ?
Sophie Arnaud: Mieux qu'on ne le croit. Ce qui les gêne, ce ne sont pas les accents, ce sont les accords. Là-dessus, aucune réforme ne dispense de travailler.
Journaliste: Et l'écriture inclusive ?
Sophie Arnaud: La circulaire de 2021 l'exclut de l'enseignement, et je m'y conforme. Cela dit, on peut écrire de façon inclusive sans point médian : « les élèves », « le corps enseignant », « les candidates et les candidats ».
```

In short: an invented teacher teaches the rectified spelling as the reference but accepts both,
says pupils struggle more with agreement than with accents, follows the 2021 circular and points
to inclusive wording without the *point médian* (epicene nouns, collective nouns, doublets). Note
*Mieux qu'on ne le croit* (expletive *ne*), the cleft *Ce qui les gêne, ce ne sont pas … ce sont
…*, and *Cela dit* (lesson 10).

## Document 5: le sondage (chiffres inventés)

| Mesure (part des personnes favorables) | Enseignants | Parents d'élèves |
|---|---|---|
| Accepter les deux graphies à l'examen | 71 % | 58 % |
| Supprimer l'accent circonflexe sur *i* et *u* | 34 % | 22 % |
| Le point médian dans les documents scolaires | 18 % | 15 % |

![A grouped bar chart titled "Enquête inventée pour l'exercice". For three measures it shows the percentage in favour among teachers and parents. Accepting both spellings in exams: teachers 71 percent, parents 58 percent. Dropping the circumflex on i and u: teachers 34 percent, parents 22 percent. The point médian in school documents: teachers 18 percent, parents 15 percent.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

These figures are invented for practice. To describe them: *Une large majorité d'enseignants
(71 %) accepterait les deux graphies, contre 58 % des parents* ; *le point médian ne recueille
qu'un faible soutien dans les deux groupes*. In a synthesis, figures from the corpus may be used;
figures from outside may not.

## Task 1: a model synthesis

*Vous ferez une synthèse des documents proposés, en 200 à 240 mots environ.* (Lesson 19: no
opinion, no outside facts, a plan by ideas, not by document.)

> Faut-il simplifier l'orthographe ? Le dossier, composé d'une brève, de deux tribunes, d'un entretien avec une enseignante et d'un sondage, oppose ceux qui voient dans l'orthographe un obstacle à ceux qui y voient un patrimoine.
>
> Pour les partisans de la simplification, celle-ci serait une mesure de justice. L'orthographe, jugée arbitraire, servirait à trier les élèves selon leur milieu ; les rectifications de 1990, modestes, devraient être pleinement appliquées. Les textes officiels vont d'ailleurs dans ce sens, puisqu'ils font de l'orthographe rectifiée la référence, ce qui a pourtant suscité en 2016 une vive polémique.
>
> Les défenseurs de l'orthographe actuelle estiment au contraire que la graphie conserve l'histoire des mots et distingue les homophones. À leurs yeux, le recul de la maîtrise de l'écrit tient moins aux règles qu'au temps qu'on y consacre, ce que l'enseignante interrogée confirme en partie : ce sont les accords, non les accents, qui gênent ses élèves.
>
> Le débat s'étend à l'écriture inclusive. Si l'écrivain rejette le point médian, jugé difficile à lire, l'enseignante, qui s'en tient à la circulaire de 2021, montre qu'il existe d'autres manières d'écrire de façon inclusive. Le sondage, enfin, révèle une acceptation large de la coexistence des deux graphies, mais un soutien limité aux changements plus visibles.
>
> En somme, les documents divergent moins sur le constat que sur le remède : simplifier la règle ou renforcer son enseignement.

The model has 222 words, not counting punctuation marks that stand alone (follow the paper's own
counting rule on the day). Because this dossier is short, the model condenses far less than you
will on the exam, where 200 to 240 words sum up about 1,000.
Check it against lesson 19: a title-free introduction naming the documents and the problématique;
three parts by idea; the reportive conditional (*serait, servirait*) to keep the writer's distance;
confrontation (*au contraire, à leurs yeux, Si … , …*); a conclusion without opinion.

## Task 2: your essay (graded)

*Le journal de votre université ouvre ses pages à un débat : « Faut-il simplifier l'orthographe
du français ? » Vous lui adressez un article argumenté d'au moins 250 mots, dans lequel vous
prenez position.*

A possible plan (one of many; a dialectical plan works too):

1. Introduction: hook (the 2016 outcry), problématique (*simplifier la règle ou mieux l'enseigner ?*),
   announcement of the plan.
2. What simplification would bring: fairness, time for reading and writing, a language that has
   always changed. One example from the dossier, one of your own.
3. Its limits: etymology and homophones, the risk of two generations writing differently, the real
   cause of the decline.
4. Your position, qualified: for example, accept both spellings everywhere and spend the time
   saved on agreement and reading.
5. Conclusion: an answer and an opening (the debate on inclusive writing, or another language's
   reform).

Before you hand it in, go through the checklist below and count your words.

```assignment
writing: fr5-h1-essai-orthographe
```

## Task 3: an exposé plan

For the oral (lesson 21), the same dossier gives an exposé of about 8 to 10 minutes. Announce the
theme in a sentence, state the problématique as a question, then a two-part plan (*D'un côté … De
l'autre …*) and a clear, personal conclusion. Speak from keywords, give one figure with its source
(*selon un sondage, d'ailleurs inventé pour l'exercice …*), and prepare one objection the jury may
raise.

## Checklist for the whole course

| Check | Lessons |
|---|---|
| Register: consistent, suited to the reader | 01–04 |
| Moods: subjunctive after concession, fronted *que*, independent uses | 05, 08 |
| Sequence of tenses, stylistic tenses | 06, 07 |
| Distance and hedging: conditional, *selon*, epistemic adverbs | 08 |
| Cause, consequence, concession connectors | 09, 10 |
| Cohesion: anaphora, paragraphs, topic sentences | 11 |
| The implicit: what your wording presupposes | 12 |
| Idioms, collocations, academic phrasing, word formation | 13–16 |
| Participial clauses, long sentences, agreement of participles | 17 |
| Summary, synthesis, essay: format, length, plan | 18–20 |
| Exposé, debate, note-taking | 21–23 |
| The exam's instructions and timing | 24 |

## Common mistakes

- Treating the 1990 spellings as errors. In France both are correct; don't "correct" *évènement*.
- Writing *l'orthographe rectifiée est obligatoire*. It is recommended, and the reference at school.
- Copying sentences from the documents into the synthesis. Use keywords, rephrase the rest.
- Adding your opinion to the synthesis. It belongs in the essay.
- Reducing *l'écriture inclusive* to the *point médian*. It also covers doublets (*les candidates
  et les candidats*), epicene words (*les élèves*) and collective nouns (*le corps enseignant*).
- Quoting the Académie's statements from memory. Describe them, and give the date.

## Key points

- 1990 rectifications: *Journal officiel*, 6 December 1990; recommended, both spellings correct;
  the reference in school programmes (2008, 2015, 2026).
- 2016: a textbook announcement turned the circumflex into a national debate.
- Inclusive writing: the Académie against it (2017); kept out of the *Journal officiel* (circular of
  21 November 2017) and out of teaching (circular of 5 May 2021), both upheld by the Conseil d'État.
- The dossier method: positions, problématique, plan by ideas, distance in the synthesis, a
  qualified position in the essay.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

sections.name: Moods and tenses: the fine points
Long texts: summary, synthesis and essay
Speaking at C1 and the DALF C1
Honors: Littérature et pensée (literature and thought)

questions.stem: When was the first edition of the Essais published, and what did it contain?
choices: In 1580, in Bordeaux: books I and II
In 1588, in Paris: books I, II and III
In 1595, after Montaigne's death: all three books
In 1571, in Bordeaux: book I only
questions.explanation: The first edition (Bordeaux, 1580, printed by Simon Millanges) had books I and II. The 1588 Paris edition added book III and hundreds of additions; the 1595 edition, prepared by Marie de Gournay, is posthumous. 1571 is the year Montaigne withdrew to his tower and began writing.

questions.stem: Name the numbered events on this timeline of Montaigne's life.

image.alt: A vertical timeline from 1533 to 1595 with eight dated rows and empty boxes; five rows are numbered.

choices: Première édition des Essais (livres I et II)
questions.explanation: Rows in date order: 1533 birth at the château de Montaigne; 1563 death of La Boétie; 1571 retreat to the tower; 1580 first edition (books I and II); 1588 edition with book III. Montaigne never went to America (he knew Brazil from travellers' accounts and a meeting in Rouen) and was never in the Académie française, which was founded in 1635, after his death.

questions.stem: What does the word "essai" mean in the title of Montaigne's book?
choices: A school exercise on a set subject
A trial or test of his own judgement on a subject
A first draft of a future philosophical treatise
An attempt at writing a novel
questions.explanation: Essayer meant to try and also to test or weigh. Montaigne's essais put his judgement to the test on every subject, without a fixed plan. The school sense (une dissertation, un essai argumenté) came much later and took the name from him.

questions.stem: Montaigne's medal of 1576 shows a pair of scales in balance, an image he links in the Essais to his motto. What does the motto express?
choices: Confidence that reason can know everything
Doubt: it asks what he really knows
questions.explanation: The motto is a short question about what he really knows, and the balanced scales show judgement suspended between equal reasons: the ancient scepticism of the Pyrrhonists, used as a method. Montaigne quotes the Ancients constantly, so contempt for them is the opposite of his attitude.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about Montaigne are true? Select all that apply.
choices: He served two terms as mayor of Bordeaux.
He was taught Latin before French.
He was a close friend of Étienne de La Boétie.
He wrote articles for the Encyclopédie.
He first published book III in 1580.
questions.explanation: He was mayor of Bordeaux from 1581 to 1585 (two terms), learned Latin as a small child from a tutor and a household that spoke only Latin to him, and was La Boétie's friend until La Boétie's death in 1563. The Encyclopédie began in 1751, long after his death; book III first appeared in the 1588 edition.

questions.topic: From Montaigne to the essai argumenté
questions.stem: Complete the sentence: Montaigne est souvent présenté comme le premier ___ français : il a donné son nom au genre de l'essai.
questions.explanation: Un essayiste (une essayiste) writes essays, works of ideas; auteur d'essais is also accepted. Montaigne's Essais gave the genre its name. Un écrivain or un auteur would fit grammatically but don't say what the second half of the sentence explains.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: An ancient philosophy that teaches you to accept what you can't control
A practice that a society takes for natural
Observing your own mind and feelings
The Renaissance return to Greek and Latin texts and the study of humankind
Aid given to the victims of a disaster
questions.explanation: Le stoïcisme is the ancient philosophy of Seneca, which Montaigne admired early on; la coutume is a society's custom; l'introspection is self-observation, the method of the Essais; l'humanisme is the Renaissance movement back to ancient texts. Aid to disaster victims is humanitaire, not humaniste.

questions.topic: From Montaigne to the essai argumenté
questions.stem: Which sentence uses "humaniste" correctly?
choices: Après le séisme, l'aide humaniste est arrivée en trois jours.
La crise humaniste s'aggrave dans la région.
Une catastrophe humaniste a frappé la région.
Érasme fut l'un des grands humanistes de la Renaissance.
questions.explanation: Un humaniste is a Renaissance scholar (or someone who puts human beings first). Aid after a disaster, a crisis affecting civilians, and a disaster that strikes civilians are humanitaire: l'aide humanitaire, la crise humanitaire, une catastrophe humanitaire.

questions.stem: The reading ends: "Il eût été étonné, sans doute, qu'on fît de lui le père d'un genre littéraire." What is "Il eût été étonné" in everyday French?
questions.explanation: Eût été is the conditionnel passé deuxième forme, a literary form you recognise but don't write: today, il aurait été étonné (he would have been astonished). Il avait été étonné is the plus-que-parfait (a fact, not a hypothesis), and il serait étonné is a present conditional.

questions.stem: In the chapter "Des cannibales", what does Montaigne do with the customs of the Tupi people of Brazil?
choices: He condemns them as savage and calls for their conversion
He turns the comparison against Europe and asks which side is really barbaric
He describes them from his own journey to Brazil
He argues that customs are fixed by nature and the same everywhere
questions.explanation: Montaigne knew the Tupi from travellers' accounts and a meeting in Rouen; he never went to Brazil. His point is that each people calls barbaric what is not its own custom, and he sets the cruelty of Europe's wars of religion against what he is told about them. Readers see in it an early cultural relativism, the opposite of "fixed by nature".

questions.stem: Listen. Where was Montaigne when he learned that he had been elected mayor of Bordeaux?

audio.text: Montaigne voyage en Italie lorsqu'il apprend qu'il a été élu maire de Bordeaux. Il ne rentre chez lui qu'à la fin de l'année 1581, et il exercera deux mandats.

choices: In Paris, at the king's court
In Rouen, with the Tupi visitors
questions.explanation: The audio says that Montaigne learned in Italy that he had been elected (in 1581, during his journey through Germany, Switzerland and Italy) and only came home at the end of the year. He then served two terms, until 1585.

questions.stem: Why do modern editions of the Essais mark three layers of text?
choices: Three different authors wrote the book over twenty years
The book was translated into modern French in three stages
The censors cut the text on three occasions
Montaigne kept adding to his book: the 1580 text, the 1588 additions and the notes in the margins of his own copy
questions.explanation: Montaigne rarely deleted; he added. The layers are the text of 1580, what he added in 1588, and what he wrote afterwards in the margins of his own copy (the exemplaire de Bordeaux). Marking them lets you watch an idea grow or contradict itself.

questions.stem: Put these events in chronological order.
choices: The first edition of the Essais appears.
Montaigne is elected mayor of Bordeaux.
Marie de Gournay publishes a posthumous edition.
questions.explanation: La Boétie died in 1563; Montaigne withdrew to his tower in 1571; the first edition came out in 1580; he was elected mayor of Bordeaux in 1581; the edition with book III appeared in 1588; Marie de Gournay's posthumous edition in 1595.

questions.topic: From Montaigne to the essai argumenté
questions.stem: Which sentence would work best as the topic sentence of a paragraph in an essai argumenté on habit?
choices: L'habitude détermine une part de nos choix plus grande que nous ne le croyons.
Je voulais parler de l'habitude, et me voilà à parler de mon grand-père.
Mon grand-père buvait son café froid parce qu'on le lui avait toujours servi ainsi.
Est-ce goût ou coutume ? Je n'en sais rien.
questions.explanation: A topic sentence states the paragraph's idea as a claim the rest will support. The sentence about the grandfather is an example, the digression about "me voilà" follows the mind as Montaigne does, and the question that ends in "je n'en sais rien" leaves the point open: all three belong to the meandering essay, not to the argued one.

questions.stem: A traveller wants to say she went through customs at the airport without any trouble. Which sentence says it?
choices: J'ai passé la coutume sans problème.
J'ai passé la douane sans problème.
J'ai passé le costume sans problème.
questions.explanation: Customs at a border is la douane. La coutume is a custom in the sense of a social practice, le costume is a costume or suit, and l'habitude is a habit.

questions.stem: When and where did Zola's open letter "J'accuse…!" appear?
choices: On 13 January 1898, in La Libre Parole
questions.explanation: The letter filled the front page of L'Aurore on 13 January 1898, two days after Esterhazy's acquittal. December 1894 is Dreyfus's conviction and July 1906 his rehabilitation. La Libre Parole, Drumont's antisemitic paper, was on the other side.

questions.stem: Name the numbered events on this timeline of the Dreyfus affair.

image.alt: A vertical timeline of the Dreyfus affair from December 1894 to July 1906 with ten dated rows and empty boxes; five rows are numbered.

choices: Élection de Zola à l'Académie française
questions.explanation: In date order: Dreyfus convicted by a court martial (December 1894); Esterhazy acquitted (11 January 1898); J'accuse in L'Aurore (13 January 1898); Zola convicted of defamation (February 1898); Dreyfus rehabilitated by the Cour de cassation (July 1906). Dreyfus was never executed (he was deported, then pardoned), and Zola was never elected to the Académie française.

questions.stem: What was the bordereau in the Dreyfus affair?
choices: Zola's letter to the President of the Republic
The secret file shown to the judges in 1894
A confession signed by Dreyfus before his trial
An unsigned memorandum announcing military documents, blamed on Dreyfus but written by Esterhazy
questions.explanation: Le bordereau was an unsigned handwritten memorandum that, according to the army's intelligence service, came from the German embassy and announced the delivery of military documents. Its handwriting was said to resemble Dreyfus's; in 1896 Picquart found it was Esterhazy's. The secret file was a separate set of papers; Dreyfus never confessed.

questions.stem: Which of these arguments were made by the antidreyfusards? Select all that apply.
choices: Reviewing the trial would weaken the army.
A judgement that has been delivered must be respected.
A man had been convicted on a secret file his defence never saw.
A review would serve France's enemies.
Justice, not the army's prestige, is the foundation of the Republic.
questions.explanation: The antidreyfusards put the army, the authority of the judgement and national security first. The secret file and the primacy of justice were the dreyfusards' arguments.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: Après « J'accuse… ! », Zola a été poursuivi pour ___ par le ministre de la Guerre.
questions.explanation: Zola was prosecuted for la diffamation (defamation, libel) of the court martial that had acquitted Esterhazy, and convicted on 23 February 1898. After pour, the noun takes no article here: poursuivi pour diffamation.

questions.stem: Which description fits naturalism, Zola's movement?
choices: The novelist observes society like a scientist and shows how heredity and environment shape people
The novelist celebrates feeling and nature against reason
The writer takes his own changing self as the subject of his book
The poet uses sound and symbol to suggest hidden meanings
questions.explanation: Naturalism (about 1870–1890) pushed realism further: documentation of each milieu, heredity and environment, a scientific model (Le Roman expérimental, 1880). Feeling against reason is Romanticism; the changing self is Montaigne (lesson 90); sound and symbol are Symbolism.

questions.stem: "Ils refusaient la révision sous prétexte que la chose avait été jugée." What does "sous prétexte que" tell the reader?
choices: That the reason given is certain
That the writer doesn't accept the reason given
That the judgement is a consequence of the refusal
That the two events happened at the same time
questions.explanation: Sous prétexte que gives a cause the writer disputes (lesson 09). To report the same reason neutrally, write au motif que or parce que, attributed to the speakers: Ils refusaient la révision au motif que la chose avait été jugée.

questions.stem: "La condamnation n'était pas au-dessus de tout soupçon, tant s'en faut." What does "tant s'en faut" add?
choices: It concedes that the conviction was fair
It introduces the cause of the conviction
It strengthens the negative claim: far from it
questions.explanation: Tant s'en faut (formal, lesson 10) follows a negative claim and reinforces it: the conviction was far from being above suspicion. It neither concedes nor gives a cause or a consequence.

questions.stem: Who was Picquart in the Dreyfus affair?
choices: Dreyfus's lawyer at the 1894 court martial
The editorialist of L'Aurore who chose the headline J'accuse
The officer who forged a document and killed himself in prison
The head of intelligence who found that the bordereau was in Esterhazy's handwriting
questions.explanation: Lieutenant-Colonel Picquart, the new head of intelligence, found the truth in 1896 and was posted to Tunisia for it. The headline is usually credited to Clemenceau; the forger who killed himself in August 1898 was Colonel Henry.

questions.stem: Listen. What happened in September 1899?

audio.text: En septembre 1899, à Rennes, un second conseil de guerre condamne de nouveau Dreyfus, avec des circonstances atténuantes. Dix jours plus tard, le président Loubet lui accorde sa grâce.

choices: Dreyfus was convicted again at Rennes, then pardoned by the President
Dreyfus was acquitted at Rennes and rejoined the army
The Cour de cassation cleared Dreyfus's name
Zola returned from England and was sent to prison
questions.explanation: The audio says that a second court martial at Rennes convicted Dreyfus again, with extenuating circumstances, and that ten days later President Loubet pardoned him. His full rehabilitation by the Cour de cassation came only in July 1906.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: A letter addressed to one person but published for all
The conviction of an innocent person
The official clearing of a convicted person's name
Passing secrets to a foreign power
A leaflet handed out in the street
questions.explanation: Une lettre ouverte is addressed to one person but published for everyone; un pamphlet is a short polemical text (a leaflet is un tract or un dépliant); une erreur judiciaire is the conviction of an innocent; la réhabilitation clears a name; l'espionnage is spying.

questions.stem: What does the Dreyfus affair have to do with the word "intellectuel"?
choices: Jean-Paul Sartre coined the word after the Second World War
It made the word a noun for a person who uses their standing to take a public stand
Zola invented the word in J'accuse
The Académie française created the word in 1906
questions.explanation: In January 1898 writers and academics signed a petition for a retrial; Clemenceau spoke of a protest of intellectuals, and Barrès took up the word with scorn. Until then intellectuel was mostly an adjective. Sartre later made engagement a duty, but the noun predates him.

questions.stem: Put these events of the affair in order.
choices: Dreyfus is convicted by a court martial.
Dreyfus is convicted again at Rennes, then pardoned.
The Cour de cassation rehabilitates Dreyfus.
questions.explanation: Dreyfus was convicted in December 1894; Picquart suspected Esterhazy in 1896; Esterhazy was acquitted on 11 January 1898; J'accuse appeared on 13 January 1898; the Rennes trial was in 1899; the rehabilitation came in July 1906.

questions.stem: In the reading, "dont l'écriture ressemblerait à celle du document": why the conditional?
choices: It is the result of an unstated si-clause
It makes a request more polite
The writer reports what was claimed without vouching for it
It describes a future event seen from the past
questions.explanation: This is the reportive conditional (lesson 08): the resemblance was what the accusers claimed, and the writer keeps a distance, since the bordereau turned out to be Esterhazy's. Nothing here is polite, hypothetical or later in time.

questions.stem: How did Zola die?
choices: In prison in 1898, after his conviction for defamation
In 1908, during the ceremony at the Panthéon
In 1902, poisoned by the fumes of a blocked chimney, before Dreyfus was rehabilitated
questions.explanation: Zola died in his Paris flat on 29 September 1902; a deliberate blocking of the chimney has been suggested but never proved. He never served his prison sentence (he left for England in July 1898 and returned in 1899), and 1908 is the year his ashes were moved to the Panthéon.

questions.stem: How was Du côté de chez Swann first published?
choices: By Grasset in 1913, with Proust paying the printing costs
By Gallimard in 1913, after André Gide's enthusiastic report
By Grasset in 1919, after the prix Goncourt
By Gallimard in 1927, after Proust's death
questions.explanation: Several publishers turned the book down, including the Nouvelle Revue française, whose committee included Gide; Grasset published it in November 1913 at the author's expense. Gallimard took over the novel after the war; the Goncourt (1919) went to the second volume, and 1927 is the last, posthumous volume.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this long sentence.

image.alt: The long sentence about the childhood house broken into six indented boxes, without the names of their grammatical roles; five boxes are numbered.

questions.explanation: Lorsque … je revis la maison de mon enfance: subordinate of time; vieille bâtisse au toit d'ardoise: apposition to la maison; dont les volets …: relative; je compris: the main clause (no subordinating word); que ce n'était pas elle …: completive, the object of compris. There is no participial clause (no participle with its own subject) and no indirect question in the sentence.

questions.stem: What is involuntary memory in Proust?
choices: The deliberate effort to recall a past event
A chance sensation that brings back the past as a lived experience
The loss of memory after an illness
A memory invented to fill a gap
questions.explanation: Involuntary memory comes unbidden, through a taste, a sound or a step, and restores the past in full. The deliberate effort is voluntary memory, la remémoration, which in the novel brings back only a dry outline.

questions.stem: A friend says of a song: "C'est ma madeleine de Proust." What does she mean?
choices: It makes her want to write a novel
It brings back a memory of her past
It is a song she has forgotten
questions.explanation: Une madeleine de Proust is a sensation (taste, smell, song) that brings back a memory, after the madeleine dipped in tea in Du côté de chez Swann.

questions.stem: Which statements about À la recherche du temps perdu are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Its last three volumes appeared after Proust's death.
Its second volume won the prix Goncourt in 1919.
At the end, the narrator decides to write the book.
Proust finished correcting all seven volumes before he died.
Its first volume was accepted at once by the NRF on Gide's advice.
questions.explanation: Seven volumes, 1913–1927; La Prisonnière (1923), Albertine disparue (1925) and Le Temps retrouvé (1927) are posthumous; À l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs won the Goncourt; the novel ends with the decision to write. Proust died still correcting the last volumes, and the NRF turned down the first volume before Grasset published it.

questions.stem: Example 2 begins "Bien qu'il fût tard …". In an essay you would write the modern form: Bien qu'il ___ tard.
questions.explanation: Fût is the imperfect subjunctive of être, which you recognise but don't write. After bien que, modern French uses the present subjunctive: bien qu'il soit tard. Bien qu'il fasse tard (from the idiom il fait tard) is also correct French and is accepted.

questions.stem: "Bien qu'il fût tard et que la pluie, qui n'avait cessé de tomber depuis le matin, rendît les routes presque impraticables, ma tante, persuadée qu'un malheur arriverait si elle ne recevait pas de nouvelles avant la nuit, exigea qu'on envoyât quelqu'un à la gare." What is the main clause?
choices: qui n'avait cessé de tomber depuis le matin
qu'on envoyât quelqu'un à la gare
questions.explanation: Remove every verb introduced by a subordinating word (bien que, que, qui, si) and one is left: ma tante exigea. Bien qu'il fût tard is concessive, qui n'avait cessé is a relative, and qu'on envoyât quelqu'un is the object of exigea.

questions.stem: In "ce n'était pas elle que j'avais aimée", why is the participle "aimée" feminine?
choices: Its direct object, que (standing for elle, the house), comes before avoir
It agrees with the subject, je
The cleft c'est … que always makes the participle feminine
questions.explanation: With avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object placed before it: here que, whose antecedent is elle (la maison). It never agrees with the subject of avoir, aimer takes avoir, and agreement in a cleft depends on what que stands for.

questions.stem: What is "une soirée mondaine"?
choices: An evening spent alone at home
questions.explanation: Mondain means "of high society" (feminine mondaine), not English "mundane", which is banal or ordinaire. A worldwide event is mondial.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: A vague memory that comes back half-formed
The past revived by a chance sensation
The capacity to feel and be moved
The social events of high society
questions.explanation: La remémoration is the act of recalling; une réminiscence is a vague memory that comes back; la mémoire involontaire is Proust's chance revival of the past; la sensibilité is the capacity to feel. Social events are les mondanités.

questions.stem: Listen. What was Proust doing at the time of his death?

audio.text: Né à Auteuil en 1871, Marcel Proust meurt à Paris en novembre 1922, alors qu'il corrige encore les derniers volumes de son roman.

choices: Writing the first pages of his novel
Still correcting the last volumes of his novel
questions.explanation: The audio says Proust died in Paris in November 1922 while he was still correcting the last volumes. The Goncourt was in 1919, and the Ruskin translations date from the early 1900s.

questions.stem: In French, who is "un snob"?
choices: Someone who avoids high society on principle
A shy person who dislikes parties
A person who refuses to spend money
Someone who admires and imitates a higher social circle or what is fashionable
questions.explanation: Un snob looks up to the circle just above his own and copies its tastes; le snobisme is that attitude, which Proust analyses through Mme Verdurin and the Guermantes. The word is also an adjective: elle est un peu snob.

questions.stem: Put the seven volumes of À la recherche du temps perdu in order of publication.
choices: À l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs
questions.explanation: 1913 Swann; 1919 Jeunes filles (Goncourt); 1920–1921 Guermantes; 1921–1922 Sodome et Gomorrhe; 1923 La Prisonnière; 1925 Albertine disparue; 1927 Le Temps retrouvé.

questions.stem: What is the best first step in reading a very long French sentence?
choices: Find the conjugated verbs, then the one not introduced by a subordinating word
Translate it word by word from the beginning
Read only the last clause, where the meaning is
Look up every word you don't know before reading on
questions.explanation: Find the verbs, set aside those introduced by qui, que, dont, lorsque, bien que and so on, and the one left is the main verb. Then hang the subordinates on it. Word-by-word reading gets lost in the subordinates.

questions.stem: Proust's narrator writes "exigea qu'on envoyât quelqu'un". Which form would you use in your own essay?
questions.explanation: Exiger que takes the subjunctive. Modern French uses the present subjunctive even after a past main verb (lesson 06): qu'on envoie. Envoyait, enverrait and a envoyé are indicative or conditional forms, wrong after exiger que.

questions.stem: When were the rectifications orthographiques published in the Journal officiel?
questions.explanation: They appeared in the Journal officiel on 6 December 1990. In May 1990 the Académie gave its approval, in January 1991 it said the new spellings should not be imposed, and 26 November 2015 is the date of school programmes that took them as the reference.

questions.stem: In France today, is "connaitre" (without a circumflex) a spelling mistake?
choices: Yes: the rectified spelling is refused in exams
Yes: since 2016 only the traditional spelling is allowed
No, and "connaître" with a circumflex is now a mistake
No: both spellings are correct, and the rectified one is the reference at school
questions.explanation: The 1990 rectifications are recommendations: traditional and rectified spellings are both correct, and school programmes name the rectified spelling as the reference while accepting both. Neither spelling may be counted as a mistake.

questions.stem: Under the 1990 rules, which words keep their circumflex? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The circumflex on i and u stays where it tells words apart: mûr (≠ mur), dû (≠ du), jeûne (≠ jeune). Elsewhere it becomes optional: maitre, cout.

questions.stem: Write "il paraît" in the rectified spelling: il ___
questions.explanation: Since 1990 the circumflex is no longer required on i and u when it doesn't distinguish two words: il parait, connaitre, s'il vous plait. The traditional il paraît is still correct.

questions.stem: According to the invented survey in the dossier, which measure has the most support among parents?

image.alt: The invented survey as a grouped bar chart: accepting both spellings, teachers 71 percent, parents 58 percent; dropping the circumflex on i and u, teachers 34, parents 22; the point médian in school documents, teachers 18, parents 15.

choices: Dropping the circumflex on i and u
Using the point médian in school documents
All three measures have the same support
questions.explanation: In the invented figures, 58 % of parents favour accepting both spellings, 22 % dropping the circumflex and 15 % the point médian. The figures were made up for practice: never quote them as a real survey.

questions.stem: Document 3 says: "Que la maîtrise de l'écrit recule, nul ne le conteste." In careful written French, which mood does a fronted que-clause like this take?
choices: The indicative, because the decline is a fact
The subjunctive (here recule has the same form in both moods)
The conditional, because it is a hypothesis
questions.explanation: A que-clause placed at the head of the sentence takes the subjunctive in careful writing, even for a fact (lesson 05): Que les prix aient augmenté, personne ne le nie. With recule, the subjunctive and the indicative look the same; try another verb to see it. Casual speech sometimes uses the indicative here.

questions.stem: Which sentence would be out of place in the synthesis of this dossier?
choices: Pour les partisans de la simplification, celle-ci serait une mesure de justice.
Les défenseurs de l'orthographe actuelle estiment au contraire que la graphie conserve l'histoire des mots.
Personnellement, je trouve que l'accent circonflexe ne sert à rien.
Le sondage révèle un soutien limité aux changements les plus visibles.
questions.explanation: A synthesis reports the documents without the writer's opinion (lesson 19). Personnellement, je trouve … is an opinion: it belongs in the essay. The other three report positions or figures from the dossier.

questions.stem: What does the Prime Minister's circular of 21 November 2017 do?
choices: It bans inclusive writing in all French publications
It makes the point médian compulsory in schools
It orders all textbooks to apply the 1990 rectifications
It asks ministries not to use inclusive writing in texts published in the Journal officiel, while feminising women's titles
questions.explanation: The circular concerns official texts published in the Journal officiel: no abbreviated inclusive forms, but the titles of women in office are feminised. It doesn't govern the press or private writing. The Conseil d'État upheld it on 28 February 2019.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the audio say about the circular of 5 May 2021?

audio.text: Le 5 mai 2021, une circulaire du ministère de l'Éducation nationale écarte le point médian de l'enseignement. Le Conseil d'État l'a validée en décembre 2024.

choices: It excludes the point médian from teaching, and the Conseil d'État upheld it in 2024
It makes the point médian compulsory, and the Conseil d'État annulled it
It concerns spelling reform, not inclusive writing
It was rejected by the Senate in 2023
questions.explanation: The education ministry's circular of 5 May 2021 rules out the point médian in teaching; the Conseil d'État upheld it in December 2024. The Senate bill of 2023 is a separate text, which the Senate adopted.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: Raised dot used in inclusive writing
questions.explanation: Le trait d'union is the hyphen (vingt-et-un); l'accent circonflexe the circumflex; le point médian the raised dot of abbreviated inclusive forms (les enseignant·es); la graphie the written form of a word; la dictée dictation. An apostrophe is une apostrophe.

questions.stem: Put the steps of writing a synthesis in order.
choices: Read the documents and note each position.
Group the ideas in a reading grid.
Write the synthesis, starting with the introduction.
questions.explanation: Read and note who says what; group the ideas in a reading grid, which shows the problématique and the plan by ideas; write, introduction first; then count the words and reread. You can't build a grid before reading, or count before writing.

questions.stem: What does the linguist argue in document 2?
choices: Spelling preserves the history of words and should not change
The point médian makes texts harder to read
Spelling sorts pupils by social background, so the 1990 changes should be applied in full and taken further
Pupils struggle more with agreement than with accents
questions.explanation: Document 2 sees spelling as a tool of social selection and wants more simplification. The history of words and the point médian are document 3's arguments; agreement versus accents is the teacher's view in document 4.

questions.stem: According to the teacher in document 4, what gives her pupils most trouble?
questions.explanation: She says what troubles pupils is not the accents but the agreements, and that no reform spares anyone that work. She doesn't use the point médian, since the 2021 circular excludes it from teaching.

questions.stem: What set off the spelling controversy of February 2016?
choices: A report that textbook publishers would apply the 1990 rules from September
A new law making the 1990 rules compulsory
The Académie's decision to drop the circumflex
A decree banning dictation in primary schools
questions.explanation: A television report in early February 2016 said publishers would apply the rectifications in new textbooks; the circumflex became the symbol of the outcry. No law or decree changed: the reference in the programmes was the same as in 2008.

questions.stem: Which sentence reports the invented survey accurately in a synthesis?
choices: Le point médian recueille la majorité des suffrages des parents.
Selon le sondage, une large majorité d'enseignants accepterait les deux graphies.
Les parents sont plus favorables que les enseignants à la suppression du circonflexe.
Personne ne soutient l'usage du point médian.
questions.explanation: 71 % of teachers favour accepting both spellings: a large majority. Only 15 % of parents support the point médian, parents (22 %) are less favourable than teachers (34 %) to dropping the circumflex, and 15–18 % is not "nobody". The conditional accepterait keeps the reporting distance.

questions.stem: Which request suits a formal email to an administration best?
choices: Je vous serais reconnaissant de bien vouloir me transmettre l'attestation mentionnée dans votre courrier du 3 mars.
questions.explanation: The formula je vous serais reconnaissant de bien vouloir + infinitive, the precise verb transmettre and the reference to the letter of 3 March fit an administration. A question by intonation with vous is polite but conversational, tu is for a colleague or friend, and the bare order with svp is curt.

questions.stem: Which of these words is informal?
questions.explanation: Le bouquin is the informal word for a book. Le livre is neutral, l'ouvrage formal (a substantial or technical book), and le manuscrit is the neutral word for an author's text.

questions.stem: In which sentence is "exercer" used naturally?
choices: J'ai exercé toute la journée au bureau.
Nous exerçons la réunion demain matin.
Il a exercé un bouquin sur la mer.
Elle exerce le métier d'avocate depuis dix ans.
questions.explanation: Exercer goes with a profession or a job: exercer le métier d'avocate. A day at the office is travailler (or, informally, bosser); a meeting is tenir or organiser; and a book is lu or écrit.

questions.stem: Which word clashes with the register of this email? "Madame, je vous remercie de votre réponse, mais je n'ai pas pigé la deuxième partie de votre message."
questions.explanation: Piger is informal (to get it). The rest of the sentence is formal, so the repair is je n'ai pas bien saisi (or compris) la deuxième partie.

questions.stem: Mme Roche, a senior partner at the law firm where you have just started, says: "On peut se tutoyer, si vous voulez." What is she doing?
choices: Asking you to keep using vous
Proposing that you both use tu
Telling you off for being overfamiliar
Asking whether you want to leave the firm
questions.explanation: Se tutoyer = to call each other tu. As the senior person, she is the one who usually proposes it; si vous voulez leaves you free, and you can accept.

questions.stem: In a French workplace, who usually proposes switching from vous to tu?
choices: Whoever speaks first in the morning
The older or more senior person
The younger person, to be friendly
questions.explanation: The older or more senior person usually proposes the switch. A junior who proposes tu to a manager can come across as overfamiliar; some companies use tu with everyone from the first day, in which case there is nothing to propose.

questions.stem: Where are you most likely to be called tu by a shop assistant of your own age?
questions.explanation: Tu is far more widespread in Québec, including with strangers and in shops. In France, Switzerland and Belgium a shop assistant normally says vous to a customer.

questions.stem: Which question is in the formal register?
questions.explanation: Inversion (Venez-vous ?) marks the formal register. A question by intonation (Tu viens ? Vous venez ?) is conversational, and est-ce que is neutral; tu also rules out a formal context with a stranger.

questions.stem: Which sentence suits a written report?
questions.explanation: A report uses nous and no dislocation. On for "we" is everyday speech, and moving le projet to the front or the end with a pronoun (dislocation) is the order of conversation.

questions.stem: At 7 p.m. a colleague sighs: "Je suis crevé." What does he mean?
questions.explanation: Crevé is informal for exhausted. Un pneu crevé is a punctured tyre, but about a person who sighs at the end of the day it means worn out.

questions.stem: The HR director "s'est enquise de votre santé". What did she do?
questions.explanation: S'enquérir de = to inquire about, formal: she asked after your health. Se renseigner sur is the neutral verb; s'inquiéter is to worry.

questions.stem: Which list goes from informal to neutral to formal?
questions.explanation: Piger is informal, comprendre neutral, saisir formal (to grasp). The same pattern: bouquin, livre, ouvrage; crevé, fatigué, exténué.

questions.stem: You drop your coffee in front of your manager. Which exclamation is safe?
questions.explanation: Mince (like zut and punaise) is a mild substitute that nobody minds. The other three are vulgar and hard to use well in a foreign language.

questions.stem: Listen to the voicemail. What does HR ask Mme Durand to bring?

audio.text: Bonjour madame Durand, ici le service des ressources humaines. Nous avons bien reçu votre courriel concernant l'incident de jeudi soir. Pourriez-vous passer à mon bureau demain à dix heures, munie de la liste des personnes présentes ? Je vous remercie.

choices: the list of the people who were present
questions.explanation: Munie de la liste des personnes présentes = bringing the list of the people present. (Munie agrees with madame Durand.)

questions.stem: Listen to two colleagues disagreeing. What does the second speaker prefer with her boss?

audio.text: Moi, je trouve que le tutoiement, ça rapproche les gens. – Pas forcément. Avec mon chef, je préfère garder le vouvoiement : ça me laisse une certaine distance.

choices: tu, because it brings people closer
not speaking to him at all
vous, because it keeps some distance
questions.explanation: Je préfère garder le vouvoiement : ça me laisse une certaine distance. The first speaker is the one who thinks tu brings people closer.

questions.stem: Give the neutral word for the informal "le toubib", with its article.
questions.explanation: Le toubib is informal for le médecin (A1). Le docteur is also common and neutral in speech, as a title and as a noun.

questions.stem: Match each informal word to its neutral equivalent.
