questions.explanation: Two hearings and short documents: listening. One long text of ideas: reading. A synthesis and an essay: writing. The exposé and interaction: speaking. The synthesis is one task inside the writing paper, and an examen blanc is a mock exam.

questions.stem: According to the lesson, which of the two subjects should you choose?
choices: the one you can take a position on fastest, with two or three arguments and examples
the one whose theme you find most interesting
the one with the longest documents
the one the examiners seem to prefer
questions.explanation: Choose on practical grounds: where you can se positionner quickly and find arguments with examples. Interest alone, the length of the documents or guessing the jury's taste don't help you build a talk in an hour.

questions.stem: In the lesson's plan for the hour of preparation, when should the problématique and your position be decided?
choices: before you have read the documents
questions.explanation: Decide the question and your answer by about minute 25, then write the notes. Leaving it to the end, or until after the notes, means notes without a direction; deciding before reading is impossible.

questions.stem: What does "s'approprier les documents" mean for an exposé?
choices: to copy them onto your sheet
to use them as material for your own argument
to read them aloud to the jury
to leave them out of the talk
questions.explanation: S'approprier = to make something your own: the documents feed your argument instead of being summarised in order. They are mentioned, briefly, not read aloud or ignored.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: In s'approprier the se is indirect (approprier quelque chose à soi), and the direct object, le projet, comes after the verb, so the participle doesn't agree: elle s'est approprié le projet. The verb is pronominal in this sense, so avoir is wrong.

questions.stem: Complete: "Les idées qu'elle s'est ___ viennent du deuxième document."
questions.explanation: The direct object, que (= les idées, feminine plural), comes before the verb, so the participle agrees with it: appropriées. The subject elle plays no part in the agreement.

questions.stem: Which sentence of the model exposé puts the debate into perspective (une mise en perspective)?
choices: Il fut un temps où l'on faisait réparer son téléviseur.
Retenons donc de cette première partie que …
Je vous remercie de votre attention.
questions.explanation: Placing the question in a historical frame (repair used to be normal) is a mise en perspective. The others introduce an example, sum up a part and close the talk.

questions.stem: Why is "soyons" in the subjunctive in "Ce n'est pas que nous soyons devenus plus négligents, c'est que nos appareils sont plus difficiles à ouvrir"?
choices: Ce n'est pas que introduces a rejected cause, which takes the subjunctive.
It is a passé simple used for a past event.
questions.explanation: Ce n'est pas que (like non que) presents a cause the speaker rejects, in the subjunctive; the real cause follows with c'est que and the indicative. Soyons is not a passé simple, there is no wish, and devenir has no effect on the mood.

questions.stem: When the examiner asks the candidate to defend the manufacturer's position, what does the lesson recommend?
choices: refuse politely, since it isn't her view
pretend she has changed her mind
mark it as an exercise, give a strong case, then say where you stand
questions.explanation: "Si je me fais l'avocat du diable …": a strong contre-argumentation shows C1 control, and she then returns to her own view. A weak version would be a straw man.

questions.stem: About how many spoken words does a full exposé of 8 to 10 minutes contain, according to the lesson?
questions.explanation: At a calm pace of about 130 words a minute, 8 to 10 minutes is roughly 1,000 to 1,300 words. The model extract of just under 500 words lasts about four minutes.

questions.stem: What does "je me reprends" mean in the model interaction?
questions.explanation: Se reprendre = to correct oneself after a slip. Taking the floor back is reprendre la parole; repeating oneself is se répéter.

questions.stem: Complete the phrase used to defend the other side as an exercise: "Si je me fais l'avocat du ___, je dirais que …"
questions.explanation: Se faire l'avocat du diable = to play devil's advocate: it marks clearly that you are defending a view that isn't yours.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the hour of preparation in the order the lesson suggests.
choices: read both subjects and choose one
write the problématique and your position, choose the plan
write the notes on one sheet, in keywords
write out the accroche, the first sentences and the conclusion
list two or three likely objections and a short answer to each
questions.explanation: Choose, then decide the question and your answer, then the notes, then the sentences you write out in full, and finally the objections, which depend on your position and plan.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: a short document that raises the question
the whole case against a view
the time you get to prepare
a summary of all the documents
questions.explanation: Déclencher = to trigger; la contre-argumentation is the set of counter-arguments (le contre-argument, B2, is one of them); la prise de parole is each time you speak. Nothing here is a summary.

questions.stem: In the model interaction, what does the candidate do well? Select all that apply.
choices: She concedes one point, then reframes the debate.
She corrects a slip as soon as she notices it.
She admits she has no figures but still answers.
She refuses to defend the other side.
questions.explanation: She concedes the price point and reframes (choice, not taste); she corrects "deux fois plus cher" with "je me reprends"; she answers the last question honestly without figures. She doesn't dodge, and she does defend the manufacturer's case when asked.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between the DALF synthèse de documents and a note avec propositions?
choices: The note may end with recommendations; the DALF synthesis never does.
The DALF synthesis has titled parts and a heading.
The note gives the writer's opinion throughout.
The DALF synthesis is addressed to a named decision-maker.
questions.explanation: Both use only the documents, reformulated, and keep the body neutral, but only the note has a heading and titles and may end with proposals. The DALF synthesis is paragraphs for a general reader.

questions.stem: Who is "le décideur" in a note?
choices: the official who writes the note
the person the note is written for, who will decide
the author of one of the documents
questions.explanation: Le décideur (la décideuse) is the reader: a mayor, a director, a minister's office. The note prepares the decision; it doesn't make it.

questions.stem: Which is the best title for a part of a note, according to the lesson?
choices: I. Une mesure aux effets attendus
questions.explanation: A title says something: a short claim about the content. "Avantages" is vague, a part per document is a summary, and the introduction comes before the parts, untitled.

questions.stem: In an exam note, what may you add from your own knowledge?
choices: examples, to show your general culture
outside facts, but only in the proposals
outside facts, but only in the introduction
questions.explanation: Framing notes for civil-service exams (such as the 2023 one for attaché territorial) say only the file counts; outside information is penalised. The DALF synthesis has the same rule.

questions.stem: What is "une préconisation"?
questions.explanation: Préconiser = to recommend; une préconisation is formal and administrative. A precondition is une condition préalable, a prediction une prévision, a precaution une précaution.

questions.stem: In a report, what is "l'état des lieux"?
choices: an assessment of the current situation
the place where the report was written
questions.explanation: A report often opens with un état des lieux, an assessment of where things stand, before analysing causes and comparing options. (In renting, the same phrase is the inventory of a flat.)

questions.stem: In administrative French, what does "rendre un arbitrage" mean?
choices: to take the minutes of a meeting
questions.explanation: L'arbitrage here is the decision a superior makes between options; a note prepares it. In sport, refereeing is also l'arbitrage, but rendre un arbitrage in an administration is a decision.

questions.stem: What makes a proposal "opérationnelle"?
choices: It is about a surgical operation.
It says who does what, and when or where.
It repeats a document word for word.
questions.explanation: Operational proposals can be carried out as written: "Expérimenter l'extinction de 1 h à 5 h pendant six mois dans les rues résidentielles." A general wish ("améliorer la sécurité") is not operational.

questions.stem: In the French Parliament, what does "le rapporteur" or "la rapporteuse" do?
choices: studies a bill and reports on it to the other members
takes the minutes of every sitting
speaks for the government in the press
questions.explanation: The rapporteur studies a bill or a question and presents a report. Taking minutes and counting votes are other jobs, and the government's spokesperson is le porte-parole.

questions.stem: In the model note, what does "Les abords de la gare ne sauraient être traités comme les rues résidentielles" mean?
choices: The area around the station doesn't know how to be treated.
The area around the station will be treated like residential streets.
The area around the station cannot be treated like residential streets.
Nobody knows how the area around the station is treated.
questions.explanation: Ne + savoir in the conditionnel, without pas, is a formal way to say "cannot": ne sauraient être = cannot be. It has nothing to do with knowing.

questions.stem: Complete the heading of a note: "NOTE à l'___ de Madame la Maire"
questions.explanation: À l'attention de = for the attention of: the line that names the addressee in a note or a formal letter.

questions.stem: Put the parts of a note in order.
choices: the heading: service, date, addressee, objet
I. Une mesure aux effets attendus
II. Des réserves à prendre en compte
questions.explanation: Heading, introduction with the announced plan, the two titled parts, then the proposals, which answer the reservations of part II. An appendix, if any, is mentioned at the very end.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: an appendix (a table, a map, a list)
a briefing note for a decision-maker
a signed report by a member of Parliament
questions.explanation: L'annexe is attached at the end; une piste d'action is an option; un concours administratif is a civil-service exam; la note de synthèse informs a decision-maker. A signed report is un rapport, by a rapporteur.

questions.stem: Which of these belong in the heading of a note? Select all that apply.
choices: the issuing service and the date
questions.explanation: The heading gives who writes, when, to whom and about what. Proposals come at the end, and the writer's opinion has no place in the heading (or in the body).

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this note.

image.alt: The first page of an administrative note with seven numbered markers: 1 on the issuing service at the top left; 2 on the line under NOTE; 3 on the line that starts the subject; 4 on a block of grey lines under it; 5 on the title of part I; 6 on the heading of a box with three numbered lines at the bottom; 7 on the last line of the page.

questions.explanation: Top left, the issuing service (and the date at the right); under NOTE, à l'attention de …; the Objet line; the introduction; a titled part; the numbered proposals; an Annexe line at the end. A note has no letter-style closing formula, and in an exam it usually isn't signed.

cards.back: Born 28 February 1533 at the château de Montaigne (Périgord); died there on 13 September 1592.
Friends at the Parlement of Bordeaux; La Boétie (author of the Discours de la servitude volontaire) died on 18 August 1563. Montaigne's chapter De l'amitié (I, 28) is his tribute.
Montaigne withdrew there at 38; about a thousand books, and Latin and Greek sentences painted on the ceiling beams, many on the limits of human knowledge.
Magistrate at the Parlement of Bordeaux; elected mayor of Bordeaux while in Italy in 1581; two terms, 1581–1585.
1580: books I–II (Bordeaux, Millanges). 1588: with book III (Paris). 1595: posthumous edition prepared by Marie de Gournay.
Three books, 107 chapters of unequal length; the self as subject; three layers of text (1580, 1588, later margin notes). Essai = a trial of one's judgement.
Suspend judgement when reasons weigh the same: the balanced scales of his 1576 medal, an image he links to his motto, a question asking what he really knows. A method of testing every certainty.
Custom shapes what each society calls natural or barbaric. Des cannibales (I, 31) turns the comparison with the Tupi of Brazil against Europe.
Renaissance movement back to Greek and Latin texts, centred on the study of humankind and education. Un humaniste ≠ humanitaire (aid).
Montaigne's essai follows the mind and tries out a judgement; the essai argumenté (lesson 20) takes a position and follows a plan: introduction, arguments, objection, conclusion.
cards.topic: From Montaigne to the essai argumenté

cards.back: Born in Paris on 2 April 1840, died 29 September 1902. Les Rougon-Macquart: twenty novels (1871–1893), including L'Assommoir (1877) and Germinal (1885).
Zola's movement (about 1870–1890): observe society like a scientist, document each milieu, show heredity and environment at work. Theory: Le Roman expérimental (1880).
1894: a bordereau offering military documents reaches army counter-espionage; Captain Alfred Dreyfus, Jewish and Alsatian, is convicted by a court martial in December and deported to Devil's Island.

cards.front: The real author of the bordereau
cards.back: Major Esterhazy. Picquart, head of intelligence, found it in 1896 and was posted to Tunisia; Esterhazy was acquitted on 11 January 1898.
Zola's open letter (une lettre ouverte) to President Félix Faure in L'Aurore; headline usually credited to Clemenceau. Describe it, don't quote it.
Prosecuted for defamation (la diffamation); convicted 23 February 1898 (one year, 3,000 francs); verdict quashed, retried at Versailles; exile in England July 1898 – June 1899.
September 1899: convicted again at Rennes, then pardoned by President Loubet. 12 July 1906: rehabilitated by the Cour de cassation and reinstated in the army.
Antidreyfusards: the army's honour, the authority of the judgement, national security (and, for many, antisemitism). Dreyfusards: justice, truth, the rights of the individual.
Attribute it (pour les antidreyfusards…), use the conditional (aurait affaibli), and pick connectors carefully: au motif que (neutral) vs sous prétexte que (you dispute the reason).
The noun for a writer or scholar who takes a public stand dates from the affair: the petition published the day after J'accuse. Later: l'intellectuel engagé (Sartre).
Born 10 July 1871 in Auteuil; died in Paris on 18 November 1922, still correcting his last volumes.

cards.front: À la recherche du temps perdu
cards.back: Seven volumes, 1913–1927: Swann (1913), Jeunes filles (1919), Guermantes, Sodome et Gomorrhe, La Prisonnière (1923), Albertine disparue (1925), Le Temps retrouvé (1927).
Turned down by several publishers, including the NRF; published by Grasset in November 1913 at Proust's expense.
Awarded to À l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs, the second volume, published by Gallimard (NRF).
A chance sensation brings the past back as lived experience: the madeleine dipped in tea brings back Combray. Voluntary recall (la remémoration) gives only an outline.
A taste, smell or song that brings back a memory: Cette chanson, c'est ma madeleine de Proust.
Un snob admires and imitates the circle above his own; le snobisme is the attitude. Mondain = of high society, not "mundane" (banal).
Find the conjugated verbs; set aside those introduced by qui, que, dont, lorsque, bien que…; the one left is the main clause. Then hang the subordinates on it.
Relative (qui, que, dont, où), completive (que after a verb: je compris que…), adverbial or circonstancielle (lorsque, bien que, parce que…).
Bien qu'il fût tard → bien qu'il soit tard; exigea qu'on envoyât → qu'on envoie; il eût été → il aurait été.
Published in the Journal officiel on 6 December 1990; recommendations: traditional and rectified spellings are both correct.
No circumflex required on i and u (connaitre, cout) unless it distinguishes (mûr, sûr, dû, jeûne); hyphens in all compound numbers (vingt-et-un); évènement; ognon; portemonnaie.
The reference in the programmes of 2008 and 2015 and in the cycle 4 programme of March 2026; both spellings accepted.
February 2016: news that textbooks would apply the 1990 rules caused an outcry over the circumflex; the minister and the Académie exchanged statements (15–16 February).
The Académie against it (26 October 2017). Prime Minister's circular of 21 November 2017: not in texts for the Journal officiel; women's titles feminised. Upheld by the Conseil d'État (2019).
Education circular of 5 May 2021: no point médian in teaching. Upheld by the Conseil d'État on 20 December 2024.
Doublets (les candidates et les candidats), epicene words (les élèves), collective nouns (le corps enseignant).
Synthesis: 200–240 words, no opinion, no outside facts, a plan by ideas. Essay: at least 250 words, your position, an objection answered, your own examples.
Use the dossier's figures in a synthesis with their source; never quote invented exercise figures as a real survey.
Que la maîtrise de l'écrit recule, nul ne le conteste: in careful writing the fronted que-clause takes the subjunctive.
familier (friends, chat), courant (neutral: most speech and writing), soutenu (formal letters, speeches, literature). A neutral word fits almost everywhere.
book: informal / neutral / formal (a substantial or technical book). Not perfect synonyms: un ouvrage de référence, but not un ouvrage de plage.
to understand: informal / neutral / formal (to grasp)
tired: informal / neutral / formal and stronger (drained). Un pneu crevé = a punctured tyre.
to steal: informal (small things) / neutral / formal (des documents dérobés)
to get dressed: neutral / formal (il se vêt, elle s'est vêtue). La robe is a dress.
to find out, inquire: neutral / formal (elle s'est enquise de votre santé)

cards.front: Informal → neutral: le flic, les fringues, le gosse, le toubib, la clope
cards.back: le policier, les vêtements, l'enfant, le médecin, la cigarette. In Québec les gosses is vulgar: say les enfants.
on / nous; dropped ne (je sais pas); questions (Tu viens ? / Est-ce que tu viens ? / Viens-tu ?); ça / cela; sentence length; le truc vs the precise noun
A word or structure out of line with the text (je n'ai pas pigé in a formal email). Repair the whole sentence, not one word.
Usually the older or more senior person: On peut se tutoyer, si vous voulez. Vous by default with clients, strangers and most managers; follow the house custom. Québec uses tu far more.
Mince ! Zut ! Punaise ! (merde, putain: vulgar, recognise only)
no ne (j'ai pas faim); ça and on; questions by intonation with the question word at the end (Tu pars quand ?); c'est qui qui … (informal); presentatives (y a, c'est, voilà)
The ordinary way to name the topic first: Moi, mon frère, sa voiture, elle est en panne. To write it, put the noun back where the pronoun is.

cards.front: chuis, t'as, y a, faut que, p't-être
cards.back: je suis, tu as, il y a, il faut que, peut-être: reduced forms to hear, not to write
hesitation (well) / opening or closing a topic / at the end: you know, sums up / right? (asks for agreement)
approximation or quoting (genre vingt personnes; et lui, genre, il s'en fiche) / in a mood or manner (en mode vacances): informal, younger speakers
strong informal agreement: absolutely!
it's really good (trop = very, younger speakers), not "too good"
really (informal, all ages): vachement bien. Neutral: très, vraiment.
to struggle / a hassle, a nightmare (informal): c'est la galère pour se garer
at a guess, at random (le pif = the nose, informal)
to turn up, to hand over (or rush off), to pinch: all informal
meh / no worries / all good, OK (informal)

cards.front: Aussi at the head of a clause
cards.back: = therefore, with inversion in careful writing: Aussi la délégation a-t-elle quitté la salle. Without inversion it reads as "also".
He's probably right. Sans doute = probably; without a doubt = sans aucun doute.
Noun subject + verb + repeating pronoun: Sans doute le ministre a-t-il raison.

cards.front: Du moins le croit-on / Encore faut-il que …
cards.back: or at least that's what people think / still, … has to (+ subjunctive)
Adjective or verb before the noun subject: Rares sont les traités ratifiés si vite. Telle est notre position. Reste à savoir si …
Simple inversion after que, où, comme with a noun subject (optional; never with a pronoun subject).
With cesser, oser, pouvoir, savoir: Il ne cesse de pleuvoir. Je n'ose y croire. Fixed: si je ne m'abuse.
I could not possibly accept: firm, polite refusal (conditional of savoir + ne alone)
in no way, not at all (formal). Never with pas. Ne … point: literary.
so-la-nel, so-la-ni-té: the first e sounds like a

cards.front: la préséance, le protocole, la délégation
cards.back: order of precedence; official etiquette; the group sent to negotiate
to deign (often ironic: il n'a pas daigné répondre); to abstain, to refrain (elle s'est abstenue)
faire un virement → effectuer; faire une liste → dresser; faire un plan → élaborer; avoir trois parties → comporter; avoir un record → détenir; faire un métier → exercer; dire une règle → énoncer
to carry out (formal): procéder à une vérification
to embark on (like prendre: ils entreprennent, entrepris) / to accomplish (like finir)
to make an inventory of / to flesh out / to lighten (j'allège, nous allégeons)

cards.front: Four ways to avoid repeating a noun

cards.front: se plaindre de ce que / s'étonner de ce que
cards.back: Formal. Both moods occur: indicative for a fact, subjunctive as after a feeling. Les familles se plaignent de ce que personne ne les consulte.

cards.front: Concordance: main verb in the past (indicative)
cards.back: Same time: imparfait (était). Earlier: plus-que-parfait (avait pillé). Later: conditionnel (fouillerait). Done before a later point: conditionnel passé (aurait fini).
The conditionnel présent after a past main verb: Il croyait qu'elle viendrait = he thought she would come.
Present subjunctive for the same time or later, past subjunctive for earlier, whatever the main tense: Il exigeait qu'on suspende les travaux.
Imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive after a past main verb: classical concordance, for recognition. Modern: qu'on suspende, qu'il ait suspendu.
Present for the same time or later (Elle espérait trouver …); past for earlier (Il affirme avoir vu les pilleurs).

cards.front: General truth after a past verb
cards.back: Can stay in the present: Le guide a rappelé que la céramique se conserve mieux que le bois. A fact still true: present (speaker vouches for it) or imparfait (reported).

cards.front: Mixed hypothetical: past condition, present result
cards.back: si + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel présent: Si on avait fouillé plus tôt, on saurait aujourd'hui …

cards.front: Mixed hypothetical: permanent condition, past result
cards.back: si + imparfait → conditionnel passé: S'il était prudent, il n'aurait pas creusé là.

cards.front: Time words in a past narrative
cards.back: hier → la veille; demain → le lendemain; la semaine prochaine → la semaine suivante; aujourd'hui → ce jour-là.

cards.back: mettre au jour = to unearth, bring to light (une amphore); mettre à jour = to update (un fichier).

A softened request: Je voulais vous demander un renseignement. Even softer, the plus-que-parfait: J'étais venu vous parler de …
What nearly happened: Un pas de plus, et il tombait = one more step and he would have fallen.
A jump forward inside a past story: Elle quitte l'école à quinze ans ; vingt ans plus tard, elle exposera à Paris. English: would.
Je vous demanderai de patienter (polite). On sonne : ce sera le facteur (supposition). Tu rangeras ta chambre (firm instruction).

What turned out to be true after checking: L'information s'est avérée fausse. Le traitement s'est révélé efficace.

cards.back: Elle s'est mis le doigt dans l'œil: se is indirect and the direct object (le doigt) follows, so no agreement, as in elle s'est lavé les mains.

Participle: invariable, can take an object (convainquant le jury). Adjective: agrees (des preuves convaincantes).

glossary.definition: A prose work of moderate length in which a writer tests an idea or a judgement rather than setting out a complete doctrine. The genre takes its name from Montaigne's Essais (1580–1595), where essai means a trial of one's own judgement on a subject. The modern French essai is any book of ideas; the DALF essai argumenté keeps the name but adds a fixed plan and a clear position.

The intellectual movement of the Renaissance (in France, chiefly the 16th century) that went back to Greek and Latin texts, edited and translated them, and put the study of humankind, education and moral life at the centre of learning. Its scholars are called humanists (les humanistes). By extension, any outlook that puts human beings first.

In philosophy, the position that we cannot be certain of what we claim to know, so judgement should be suspended when the reasons on each side weigh the same (the ancient Pyrrhonists). Montaigne used it as a method: test every certainty, his own included. In everyday use, a doubting attitude.

A French literary movement of about 1870–1890, led by Émile Zola, that pushed realism further: the novelist observes society as a scientist observes nature, documents each milieu in detail and shows how heredity and environment shape people. Key works: Zola's Rougon-Macquart cycle (twenty novels, 1871–1893); theory in Le Roman expérimental (1880).

A writer, scholar or artist who uses the authority earned in their field to take a public stand on a political or moral question. The noun intellectuel for such a person dates from the Dreyfus affair (1898), when writers and academics signed a petition for a retrial; the idea of engagement as a duty was later developed by Jean-Paul Sartre and others.

Proust's term for a memory brought back unbidden by a chance sensation (a taste, a sound, an uneven paving stone), which restores the past as a lived experience; he contrasts it with voluntary memory, the deliberate effort to recall, which gives only a dry outline. The madeleine episode in Du côté de chez Swann (1913) is the best-known example.

A clause that cannot stand alone and depends on another clause, introduced by a relative pronoun (qui, que, dont, où…), by que (completive) or by a conjunction of time, cause, concession and so on (lorsque, parce que, bien que…). Its verb is conjugated, unlike an infinitive or participial phrase. The clause it depends on is the main clause (la proposition principale).

The level of formality a speaker or writer chooses for a reader and a situation. French is usually described with three registers: familier (informal: friends, chat messages), courant (neutral: most speech and writing) and soutenu (formal: official letters, speeches, literature). A register shows in the words (bouquin / livre / ouvrage) and in the grammar (on or nous, with or without ne, the form of a question).

The ability to adjust what you say and how you say it to the person, the relationship and the situation: the same request worded differently for a colleague, a manager, a stranger and an administration. The CEFR lists it among the skills of a C1 user.

A word or structure out of line with the register of the rest of a text: an informal word in a formal email (je n'ai pas pigé), or a very formal one in a chat message (je m'enquiers de ta santé). Repair it by rewording the whole sentence in the text's register.

Addressing someone as tu (verb tutoyer). Usual in France among friends, family, students and colleagues of the same level who know each other, and in many start-ups and sports clubs; far more widespread in Québec. The older or more senior person usually proposes it.
Addressing one person as vous (verb vouvoyer). The default in France with strangers, clients, older people and most managers. Going back to vous after tu signals distance or conflict.

A small word that organises speech rather than adding content: it hesitates (ben, bon), agrees (carrément, c'est clair), approximates or quotes (genre, en mode) or closes a turn (quoi, hein, bref). Mostly spoken and informal.

Moving a noun or a stressed pronoun to the front or the end of a sentence and repeating it with a pronoun inside: Ce film, je l'ai adoré; Il est sympa, ton coloc. In writing it gives emphasis; in conversation it is the ordinary way of naming the topic first.

A word or group pronounced with sounds dropped or fused in rapid speech: chuis (je suis), t'as (tu as), y a (il y a), faut que (il faut que), p't-être (peut-être). For listening; written only to quote speech or in a chat message.

Placing the subject after the verb in a statement, in formal French: after aussi (therefore), peut-être, sans doute, à peine, du moins, encore (Sans doute a-t-il raison); after rares sont, tel est, reste (Reste la question du budget); and, optionally, after que, où, comme with a noun subject (comme le rappelait l'ambassadrice). With a noun subject at the head of the clause, complex inversion repeats it with a pronoun: Sans doute le ministre a-t-il raison.

Negation with ne and no pas, in formal French: with cesser, oser, pouvoir and savoir followed by an infinitive or (savoir) a clause (Il ne cesse de pleuvoir; Je ne saurais accepter), and in fixed phrases (si je ne m'abuse). Pas is still correct with these verbs; with other verbs, apart from fixed phrases and older literary texts, use ne … pas. Not to be confused with the expletive ne after avant que or de peur que, which has no negative meaning.
Negative words of careful writing and speech that replace pas: ne … nullement and ne … aucunement (in no way), ne … guère (hardly), and the literary ne … point. Never combined with pas.

A verb so general that it fits almost any sentence and says little: faire, dire, mettre, avoir, être, il y a, donner. Careful writing replaces it with a precise verb where one exists (effectuer un virement, dresser une liste, comporter trois parties), without banning set phrases such as faire attention.

Redundancy inside one phrase: two words that say the same thing, such as monter en haut, prévoir à l'avance, voire même (common, but criticised). Usually a fault in writing; a few are accepted for emphasis (je l'ai vu de mes propres yeux).

Saying again what a text has already said: a sentence that repeats the previous one in other words, two connectors for the same link (car en effet), a conclusion that only repeats. A pleonasm is redundancy inside a single phrase.

A more general word whose meaning covers a more specific one: l'ouvrage or le livre for le roman, la fleur for la tulipe. Used to avoid repeating a noun, usually after the specific word has been named.

A word, sense or construction used in one French-speaking area and not in the others: la panosse (Switzerland), la tirette (Belgium), la tuque (Québec). Regionalisms belong to the standard of their area and are not informal in themselves.
A regionalism of the French of Belgium: le bourgmestre (mayor), la tirette (zip), le GSM (mobile phone), à tantôt, savoir for pouvoir (je ne sais pas venir).
A regionalism of the French of Switzerland (from Helvetia, its Latin name): la votation (popular vote), la panosse (floorcloth), le natel (mobile phone), huitante in some cantons.
A regionalism of the French of Québec: la tuque (woolly hat), le char (car, informal), magasiner (to go shopping), bienvenue as "you're welcome", the question particle -tu (Tu viens-tu ?).

An email written at work: an informative subject line (l'objet), a greeting fitted to the reader (la formule d'appel), the purpose in the first sentence, one subject, short paragraphs, a short closing (Cordialement, Bien cordialement, Bien à vous) and a signature. The long letter formula is kept for formal letters sent by email.

The written record of a meeting: date, place, people present and excused, the agenda, the decisions under each item and the actions (who, what, by when). Le procès-verbal is the official version (boards, councils, associations); le compte rendu is less formal. Written in one tense (present or passé composé), impersonally.

Slang. Originally the secret language of thieves and beggars (old Paris argot gave le fric, le flic, la thune); today the informal vocabulary of any group, especially young people, which changes fast. For recognition at C1.
Reversing a verlan word again once it has become too common: meuf (from femme) → feumeu; beur (from arabe) → rebeu.

A subjunctive in a clause with no main verb in front of it, as if je veux que or je souhaite que had been left out. It gives an order or a wish for a third person (Qu'il patiente !), a formal hypothesis (Qu'un seul donneur se retire, et l'essai s'arrête), or a set phrase (Advienne que pourra, Qu'à cela ne tienne, que je sache). Literary wishes such as Puisse-t-il guérir ! are for recognition.

A clause that sets two possibilities side by side and says the main clause holds either way: Qu'on l'approuve ou qu'on le rejette, ce texte fera date; Qu'il le veuille ou non, … Both halves take the subjunctive. Formal soit que … soit que + subjunctive gives two possible causes.

The que that replaces a repeated conjunction in a second clause: Comme il pleuvait et qu'il faisait froid … It keeps the mood of the conjunction it replaces (indicative after quand, comme, puisque, parce que; subjunctive after bien que, pour que). After si, the second clause takes the subjunctive in careful style or the indicative in common use; both are correct.

The rules that match the tense of a subordinate clause to the tense of the main verb and to the time relation (earlier, same time, later). After a past main verb the indicative shifts back: imparfait, plus-que-parfait, conditionnel (the future of the past). Everyday modern French uses only the present and past subjunctive whatever the main tense; classical prose used the imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive after a past verb.

A si-sentence whose condition and result belong to different times: si + plus-que-parfait with a conditionnel présent (Si on avait fouillé plus tôt, on saurait aujourd'hui …: past condition, present result), or si + imparfait with a conditionnel passé (S'il était prudent, il n'aurait pas creusé là: permanent condition, past result).

A statement true at all times, which keeps the present even after a past main verb: Le guide a rappelé que la céramique se conserve mieux que le bois. A fact that is still true may also keep the present (Il a rappelé que le site date du Néolithique), which adds the speaker's own commitment; the shifted tense (datait) is also correct.

The present tense used to tell past events, common in biographies, history books and the press: En 1895, les frères Lumière projettent leurs premiers films. It makes the story vivid; translate it with the English past.

An imparfait that presents one completed event, usually after a time phrase at the start of the sentence, in written narrative and the press: Deux ans plus tard, elle remportait le prix. It slows the event down and gives it weight; it does not describe a background.
An imparfait that softens a request or a wish by placing it in the past: Je voulais vous demander un renseignement. The plus-que-parfait can do the same (J'étais venu vous parler de …).

A future that jumps forward from a point in a past story, usually one told in the présent historique: Elle quitte l'école à quinze ans; vingt ans plus tard, elle exposera à Paris. English uses 'would'.

A compound tense with two auxiliaries (il a eu fini, quand elle a été partie) marking an action completed before another in the passé composé. Spoken and regional, avoided in careful writing (quand il a fini, après avoir fini); for recognition only.

Everything a speaker adds to a statement to show how far they stand behind it: certainty, probability, doubt or distance. Adverbs (assurément, manifestement, sans doute = probably, peut-être), verbs (s'avérer, sembler), impersonal phrases with their moods (il est probable que + indicative, il n'est pas exclu que + subjunctive) and distancing devices.

Softening a claim so that it says no more than the evidence allows, as science and academic writing require: Tout porte à croire que …, Il n'est pas exclu que …, Ces résultats suggèrent que … Its opposite is overstatement (un discours catégorique).

The devices that show a claim belongs to someone else and that the writer doesn't vouch for it: the reportive conditional (Le produit protégerait …), prétendu, soi-disant, présumé, quotation marks of distance, à en croire, sous toute réserve.

An adverb that tells the reader how certain the speaker is that a statement is true: assurément, indéniablement, incontestablement (certain), manifestement (evident), probablement, sans doute (probable), peut-être (possible).

A novel told entirely through letters exchanged between characters, with no narrator: Montesquieu's Lettres persanes (1721), Rousseau's Julie ou la Nouvelle Héloïse (1761), Laclos's Les Liaisons dangereuses (1782). The reader builds the story from several points of view.
A work or passage that mocks the faults of a society, a group or a person in order to criticise them. The Lettres persanes satirise French customs through the eyes of two Persian visitors.

The European fashion for the East and the way Europe imagined it, popular in France after Galland's translation of the Mille et Une Nuits (from 1704). Since Edward Said's Orientalism (1978), also a criticism of Western clichés about the East; critics disagree about how far it applies to the Lettres persanes.

A word or phrase that introduces a cause. Each presents the cause differently: parce que as new information (it alone answers 'pourquoi ?'), puisque as already known or accepted, comme first, as background, car as a justification added afterwards, sous prétexte que as someone's claim the writer doubts, à force de as repetition. C1 adds dans la mesure où (cause or extent), en ce sens que (in that) and legal attendu que (recognition).

C'est que + indicative goes from an observed fact to its explanation: S'il hésite, c'est qu'il doute (if he hesitates, it's because he has doubts). Si … c'est parce que puts a known cause in focus: Si l'usine ferme, c'est parce que les commandes ont chuté.

Granting a fact or an argument that seems to go against your conclusion, without giving up the conclusion. A C1 paragraph often grants (certes, il est vrai que), counters (il n'en demeure pas moins que, il reste que, cela dit) and supports the counter. Tant s'en faut and loin s'en faut reinforce a denial; si + adjective + soit-il concedes by inversion.

The formal concession si + adjective + soit + subject pronoun, without que: Si ambitieux soit-il, ce plan reste flou (however ambitious it may be). The adjective agrees with the noun the pronoun announces: Si coûteuse soit-elle, la transition … It is the formal equivalent of si ambitieux qu'il soit (B2).

A clause that limits what a statement claims. Pour autant que + subjunctive means 'as far as' or 'provided that': pour autant que je sache (as far as I know); la taxe sera acceptée, pour autant que les recettes soient redistribuées. Not to be confused with pour autant (for all that), which takes no clause.
The visible links that hold a text together: pronouns and other words that refer back (anaphora), connectors, repeated or related words, punctuation. Compare coherence, the logic underneath.
The logic of a text: the ideas follow each other, nothing contradicts, and the reader can see the plan. A text can be cohesive (every sentence linked) and still incoherent (going nowhere).

In grammar, a word that points back to something already named, so it isn't repeated: pronouns, ce dernier (the last-named noun of its gender and number), le premier … le second (the former … the latter), lexical anaphora (a hyperonym or a nominalisation: le conseil a voté … cette décision), and legal ledit. Not the figure of speech of the same name (a repeated opening word).

How the themes (what each sentence is about) follow each other through a paragraph: constant (the same theme each time), linear (the new element of one sentence becomes the theme of the next) or split (a general theme divided into parts taken in turn).
The sentence, usually the first of a paragraph, that states the paragraph's one idea; the rest explains, illustrates and limits it. In a synthesis, the topic sentences alone should show the plan.

What a sentence takes for granted. It survives when the sentence is negated or turned into a question: Il a cessé de mentir / Il n'a pas cessé de mentir both presuppose that he lied. Triggers: cesser de, encore, ne … plus, aussi, même, enfin, factive verbs (regretter que, savoir que), definite descriptions (le nouveau scandale).

What a speaker leaves the listener to infer from the words and the situation (le sous-entendu). Unlike a presupposition, it depends on context and can be denied: Il est déjà minuit … (said by a host) implies 'time to go'. An insinuation is a hostile implication.

Saying one thing while meaning something else, usually the opposite, and letting the listener see the gap. Signs in writing: praise that clashes with the facts, exaggeration, a register that doesn't fit, quotation marks of distance, false surprise. Antiphrasis is its simplest form.

What a word suggests beyond what it names: le gouvernement and le régime can name the same thing, but régime connotes a hostile judgment; so do individu (vs personne) and attroupement (vs rassemblement).
Saying the exact opposite of what one means, as a form of irony: Bravo, quelle organisation ! after a fiasco. Par antiphrase = ironically.

A play on words that sound alike (homophones) or on a word with two meanings. French has many homophones (ver, verre, vert, vers), so the calembour is common in jokes and press headlines. Le jeu de mots is the wider term.

A swap of sounds between two words that makes a new phrase: le bout du pain → le pou du bain. In French, la contrepèterie is an old game in which the reader must find the hidden phrase; classic ones are often bawdy.
In Aristotle's rhetoric, the proof that comes from the speaker's character as the audience perceives it: competence, honesty, goodwill. One of the three proofs, with pathos and logos.

In Aristotle's rhetoric, the proof that comes from the emotions the speaker stirs in the audience (pity, indignation, pride). It is usually strongest in the peroration. In everyday French, le pathos can also mean overdone emotion.
In Aristotle's rhetoric, the proof that comes from the reasoning itself: facts, figures, arguments and refutation.

L'exorde (masculine): the opening of a classical speech, which wins attention and goodwill and often builds the speaker's ethos. The five parts are exorde, narration, confirmation, réfutation, péroraison.
La péroraison: the closing of a classical speech, which sums up and appeals to the audience, usually with the strongest pathos.

A group of words whose meaning isn't the sum of its parts: tourner autour du pot means to beat about the bush, not to walk round a pot. Its words are fixed, but its verb is conjugated normally (il lui a passé un savon). Most idioms are neutral or informal.

The meaning speakers actually use, as opposed to the literal picture the words make. Jeter l'éponge literally throws a sponge; figuratively it means to give up. Headlines sometimes revive the literal meaning for a pun.

An expression whose words and determiners can't be changed: jeter l'éponge, not jeter une éponge; prendre la mouche, not prendre une mouche. Tense, person, pronouns, negation and adverbs still move: Il s'est complètement mis le doigt dans l'œil.

A habitual combination of words that a native speaker chooses without thinking: prendre une décision, poser une question, un vif intérêt, une pluie battante, hautement improbable. The alternatives may be grammatical, but they sound foreign.

A verb with little meaning of its own that carries the tense and person while the noun carries the meaning: faire preuve de patience (to be patient), porter atteinte à (to harm), mettre en œuvre (to implement). Learn verb, noun and preposition together; the verb can't be swapped.
A word that strengthens another, chosen by habit: un vif intérêt, un profond désaccord, une hausse sensible, un refus catégorique, hautement improbable, vivement recommandé.

A word-for-word copy of a foreign expression. Some English calques are mistakes in French (faire une décision for prendre une décision, prendre place for avoir lieu); others, such as faire sens, are common but disputed in careful writing.

The formal, impersonal and carefully sourced French of theses, articles and conference papers: nous of modesty or on instead of je, impersonal formulas (il convient de, il importe de), sources introduced and cited, defined terms, hedged claims.

In French, la citation is a quotation: someone's exact words, in « guillemets », with […] for a cut and [sic] after an error in the original, and a reference in a footnote or in brackets. English citation (a reference) is a false friend.
Restating a source's idea in your own words and your own sentence structure while still naming the source: Comme le montre Martin (2018), … Changing a few words of the original is not a paraphrase.
Presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, whether by copying them or by reworking them lightly without naming the source. Le plagiat; the verb is plagier.

The nous a single author uses instead of je in academic writing. The verb is plural, but adjectives and participles agree with the real author: nous sommes convaincu (a man), nous sommes convaincue (a woman).
Making a new word by adding a prefix or a suffix to a stem: lire → lisible → illisible; connecter → déconnecter. Compare compounding.
Making a new word by joining two elements that each carry meaning: chrono + phage → chronophage; porte + monnaie → porte-monnaie. Compare derivation.

A word borrowed almost unchanged from written Latin or Greek (fragile, hôpital, potion), as opposed to a popular word that came down through centuries of sound change (frêle, hôtel, poison). Learned words are long, transparent and often close to English.
Le radical: the part of a word that carries its meaning, to which prefixes and suffixes are added: lis- in illisible. La racine (the root) is the older, historical form behind a word family.

A piece added before a stem: in- (im-, il-, ir-) and a- for not, dé- for undoing, sur- and sous- for over and under. In- usually changes form before b, m, p (im-), l (il-) and r (ir-), with a few exceptions (inlassable).
A piece added after a stem, often changing the word class: -able and -ible make adjectives of possibility (lisible), -ique and -el adjectives of relation (numérique, virtuel), -tion and -ment nouns.

A word made of two or more words, usually hyphenated: le porte-monnaie, l'arc-en-ciel, le chef-d'œuvre. Plurals: traditional (des porte-monnaie, des après-midi) or 1990 (des porte-monnaies, des après-midis) for verb + noun and preposition + noun compounds; both are correct.

Initials or syllables read as a word: l'ONU, l'Unesco, le Smic. A sigle is read letter by letter: la SNCF. The gender is usually that of the first noun of the full name; sigles don't take s in the plural (des ONG).

A French equivalent of a foreign (usually English) term, proposed by expert groups, examined by the Commission d'enrichissement de la langue française and the Académie française, and published in the Journal officiel: courriel, mot-dièse, infox. It binds the State's services; for everyone else it is a recommendation. In Québec the OQLF recommends its own terms.

A word that packs two words into one, keeping a piece of each: courriel (courrier + électronique), infox (information + intoxication), divulgâcher (divulguer + gâcher), franglais (français + anglais).

A short, anonymous sentence of popular wisdom quoted as it stands: Qui ne dit mot consent. Proverbs keep old grammar: the generic present, no article (Chat échaudé craint l'eau froide), qui = whoever, inversion and ellipsis.
A short rule of conduct or general truth, often by a named author: La Rochefoucauld's Maximes (first edition 1665). Unlike a proverb, a maxim has an author and a point of view, so you cite it.

A participle with its own subject, different from the subject of the main verb, set off by a comma: La réunion terminée, chacun est rentré; Le contrat signé, les travaux commenceront. It gives the time or the cause of the main action, and the participle agrees with its own subject. Written and formal; fixed phrases such as cela dit and tout compte fait are everyday examples.

A noun phrase, without a verb, set beside a noun or pronoun to describe it: Fille d'ouvriers, elle est devenue ministre. At the head of a sentence it describes the subject of the main verb; otherwise it dangles.

An adjective made from a present participle. Unlike the participe présent, which is invariable and can take an object, it agrees and describes a quality: des arguments convaincants (but convainquant le jury). Some pairs are spelled differently: fatigant / fatiguant, précédent / précédant, négligent / négligeant.

A participle, gérondif or apposition at the head of a sentence that does not describe the subject of the main verb: Étant malade, le médecin m'a prescrit du repos says the doctor was ill. Treated as a mistake in careful writing; fix it by changing the subject (Étant malade, j'ai consulté) or using a clause (Comme j'étais malade, …).

A text that argues ideas rather than tells a story: an essay, an opinion piece, a long article. The DALF C1 reading paper is built on one, of 1,500 to 2,000 words in university descriptions of the exam. Read it in three passes: skim for the thesis, map the plan, then read for detail and the author's stance.

A condensed version of one text, written as if by its author: the author's order and proportions, no l'auteur dit, no opinion, usually about a quarter of the length. The strict school version is called a contraction de texte.

A report on a text written from outside it, in the third person: the source named first, each step introduced by a reporting verb (L'auteure montre que …, Elle souligne ensuite …), no opinion. Also the word for the minutes of a meeting and for a review.
The one idea a whole text defends. Look for it in the title, the end of the introduction and the conclusion; check that every paragraph serves it. Finding it is the first step of any summary.
Saying the same with fewer words: a hyperonym for a list, cutting examples and anecdotes, nominalising, turning a paragraph into one sentence. Connectors stay, so the logic survives.

One short, neutral text that combines several documents around a common question: introduction, two or three parts organised by ideas that confront the documents, and a conclusion, with no opinion and nothing from outside. In FEI's 2022 candidate manual, the DALF C1 synthesis is 200 to 240 words.

A table for reading a corpus: one column per document, one row per idea, a short note in each cell or an empty cell. Reading across a row shows common ground, divergence and the document that stands apart; rows that answer the same question become one part of the plan.

The precise question a text answers. In a synthesis, the question the documents answer together; in an essay, the question you build from the subject. It is a real question, not a topic, and not un problème.

Setting documents side by side so the reader sees how they relate: agreement (s'accorder à dire, rejoindre), following (à l'instar de), turning to another (quant à, de son côté, pour sa part), contrast (à l'inverse, tandis que). The heart of a synthesis, as opposed to a list of summaries.

A text that takes and defends a personal, nuanced position on a subject, in a set form (a contribution to a debate, a formal letter, a critical article, a report). In FEI's 2022 candidate manual, the DALF C1 essay is at least 250 words, on the theme of the synthesis documents.
An essay plan for a problem to explain and solve: constat (what is happening), causes, conséquences, solutions. The solutions carry the writer's position.

The move in an introduction that turns the subject into a real question and shows why it is one: Mais travailler quatre jours, est-ce travailler mieux, ou seulement plus vite ? It comes after the opening and before the annonce du plan.

The last sentence of an introduction, which announces the parts in one flowing sentence rather than as a list: Après en avoir rappelé les atouts, j'en examinerai les limites, avant de proposer des conditions de réussite.

The French school and university essay: an argued answer to a question or quotation (the libellé), in two or three parts with sub-parts, often dialectical with a final part that goes beyond the opposition, each argument proved by examples from works. Not a doctoral thesis (la thèse).
An analysis of one passage, organised by two or three reading axes, showing how the form of the text makes its meaning. Its oral twin, the explication de texte, follows the passage line by line.

One line of interpretation in a commentaire de texte, such as un village transformé or la mémoire plus forte que le réel, proved by precise observations of tenses, images, rhythm and vocabulary. Each axis becomes a part of the commentaire.

A prepared talk that starts from documents, asks a real question (the problématique), and defends the speaker's own answer in an announced plan of two or three parts, each argument with an example. In the DALF C1 speaking test it lasts about 8 to 10 minutes in the current format and is followed by a discussion with the jury. Not a summary of the documents.

The opening line of a talk, an article or an advert, meant to catch the listener's attention before the subject is introduced: a fact from the documents, a question to the audience, a short scene, a paradox. One or two sentences, linked straight away to the problématique. L'amorce is the usual word for the opening of a written introduction.

The phrases a speaker uses to show the listener where they are in a talk: announcing the plan (Je commencerai par … avant d'en venir à …), moving on (J'en viens à …, Ce qui m'amène à …), giving an example, summing up a part, concluding (Pour conclure …). A talk needs more of it than a text, because a listener can't look back.

Disagreeing firmly without sounding rude, a C1 skill: present the disagreement as your difficulty (Je ne suis pas certain de vous suivre), soften it with the conditionnel or a verb of opinion (Je dirais plutôt que …, il me semble que …), concede a point before turning it (Je vous accorde que …, il n'en reste pas moins que …).

An argument that looks valid but isn't (un sophisme). Common ones in debate: the appeal to authority (l'argument d'autorité), the attack on motives (le procès d'intention), the straw man, the false dilemma (le faux dilemme), the personal attack and the hasty generalisation. Name one politely: Ce n'est pas parce que … que …

A fallacy that attributes to the other side a weaker or more extreme view than they hold, in order to refute it easily (l'homme de paille, l'argument de l'épouvantail). The answer: Ce n'est pas ce que j'ai dit, then restate your real position.

A word or phrase that shows the structure of a talk or text (un marqueur de structuration): premièrement, j'y reviendrai, j'ouvre une parenthèse, autrement dit, pour faire court, j'en viens à. When listening, signposts tell you where the main points are and what to write down.

A short form or symbol used to take notes quickly: → (leads to), ≠ (unlike), = (means), ↗ / ↘ (increases / decreases), cf. (see), qqch, qqn, tjrs, gvt, pb. Make your own for the terms of a topic, and write them out in full once so you can read your notes later.

aliases: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages
glossary.definition: The Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (in French le CECR or CECRL), published by the Council of Europe. It describes six levels, A1 to C2, by what a learner can do with a language: A1–A2 basic users, B1–B2 independent users, C1–C2 proficient users.

Diplôme approfondi de langue française: the official French diplomas at levels C1 and C2, awarded by the French Ministry of Education and run by France Éducation international (FEI). Each level is a separate diploma, valid for life. The DELF covers A1 to B2.

The CEFR's name for levels C1 and C2 (utilisateur expérimenté). C1 is the lower of the two: you understand long, demanding texts and what they imply, speak fluently without visible searching, and write well-organised texts for social, academic and professional purposes.

In DELF and DALF exams, a paper sat in a room with other candidates (une épreuve collective): listening, reading and writing. At the DALF C1 they take about four hours in all. The speaking test is an épreuve individuelle, in front of two examiners.

In French administrations and civil-service exams, a document written for a decision-maker from a file of documents: a heading (issuing service, date, addressee, objet), a short introduction with the plan, two parts with informative titles, and, when the task asks for them, numbered recommendations (a note avec propositions). Unlike the DALF synthèse de documents, it has a heading and titles and may recommend; like it, it uses only the file, reformulated.

A report: a longer, usually signed document by a rapporteur or rapporteuse that analyses a question, often opening with an état des lieux (assessment of the situation), compares options and ends with recommendations (préconisations). Some civil-service exams ask for a rapport avec propositions.

references.title: Connectors and cohesion at C1
references.body:
B1 and B2's connectors still apply (*parce que, puisque, car, comme, étant donné que, vu que,
d'autant que, non que, si bien que, au point que, de sorte que, bien que, même si, alors que,
tandis que, en revanche, pour autant, quel que soit, quand bien même, il n'empêche que, toujours
est-il que, il n'en reste pas moins que* …). These are the C1 distinctions and additions.

## Cause: what each connector presents

| connector | the cause is … | mood / register | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *parce que* | new information, the answer to "why?" | indicative, all | *Il a démissionné parce qu'on l'a muté.* |
| *puisque* | already known or obvious to the reader (can sound polemical) | indicative, all | *Puisque tu sais tout, réponds.* |
| *comme* | given first, as background | indicative, all | *Comme la ligne était coupée, …* |
| *car* | a justification added after the statement | indicative, mostly written | *Il faut agir, car le temps presse.* |
| *sous prétexte que* | claimed by someone, doubted by the writer | indicative, all | *Il refuse, sous prétexte qu'il est trop tard.* |
| *à force de* | repetition or effort | + noun or infinitive | *À force de patience, il a réussi.* |
| *dans la mesure où* | a cause, or an extent (say which) | indicative, formal | *Le projet est rentable dans la mesure où les coûts baissent.* |
| *en ce sens que* | an explanation of a claim | indicative, formal | *Ce texte est novateur en ce sens qu'il …* |
| *attendu que* | a legal ground (recognition) | indicative, legal | *Attendu que le contrat n'a pas été signé, …* |
| *c'est que* | the explanation of an observed fact | indicative, all | *S'il hésite, c'est qu'il doute.* |

## Consequence

| connector | register | example |
|---|---|---|
| *il s'ensuit que* | formal | *Les recettes ont baissé ; il s'ensuit que le déficit se creuse.* |
| *tant et si bien que* | neutral, a bit literary | *Il a insisté, tant et si bien qu'on a cédé.* |
| *partant* | literary (recognition) | *Il n'y a plus d'industrie, partant plus d'emplois.* |
| verbs | formal | *imputer à, induire, aboutir à, se traduire par, se solder par* (B2: *entraîner, susciter, découler de, résulter de*) |

## Concession and opposition

| connector | grammar | example |
|---|---|---|
| *il reste que, il n'en demeure pas moins que* | + indicative | *Certes, le coût est élevé ; il n'en demeure pas moins que la mesure est nécessaire.* |
| *tant s'en faut, loin s'en faut* | after a negative claim | *Le problème n'est pas résolu, tant s'en faut.* |
| *au demeurant* | adverb (for that matter) | *Une mesure modeste, au demeurant peu coûteuse.* |
| *cela dit, ceci dit* | adverb, spoken and written | *Cela dit, je comprends vos réserves.* |
| *si* + adjective + *soit-il* | inversion, formal | *Si ambitieux soit-il, ce plan reste flou.* |
| *pour autant que* | + subjunctive (restriction) | *pour autant que je sache* |
| *tout en* + gérondif | concession or simultaneity | *Tout en reconnaissant ses mérites, je reste sceptique.* |
| *en revanche / par contre* | adverb | both are current; the Académie long criticised *par contre* in writing; *en revanche* is safer in an exam |

## Cohesion: referring back

| device | example | watch out |
|---|---|---|
| *ce dernier, cette dernière* | *Le maire a reçu l'urbaniste. Ce dernier a présenté son plan.* | refers to the last-named noun: check it can't be read two ways |
| *le premier … le second* | *Deux options : le tram et le bus. Le premier coûte plus, le second pollue plus.* | for exactly two |
| *celui-ci / celle-là* | *celui-ci* = the nearer (last named), *celui-là* = the farther | formal in writing |
| lexical anaphora | *Le conseil a voté la piétonnisation. Cette décision …* | use a hyperonym or a nominalisation |
| *lequel* (B1) | *la sœur de l'architecte, laquelle …* | removes an ambiguity of *qui* |
| *ledit, ladite* | legal and administrative (recognition) | not in an essay |

## Organising a long text

| function | connectors |
|---|---|
| opening a list | *en premier lieu, d'abord, d'une part* |
| adding | *de plus, en outre, par ailleurs, de surcroît, qui plus est* |
| reformulating | *autrement dit, en d'autres termes, c'est-à-dire, à savoir* (namely) |
| illustrating | *ainsi, par exemple, notamment, à titre d'exemple* |
| concluding | *en définitive, somme toute, au bout du compte, en fin de compte, bref* (spoken) |
| moving on | *quant à, pour ce qui est de, en ce qui concerne* |

## Comparing sources (synthesis)

*Les deux auteurs s'accordent à dire que … ; X rejoint Y sur … ; À l'instar de X, Y … ; X se
démarque de Y en … ; De son côté, Y … ; Quant à Z, il … ; à l'inverse, … ; tandis que X …, Y …*
No *je*, no opinion, no outside ideas.

references.title: Certainty, distance and the implicit
references.body:
## How sure is the writer? (modalisation)

| degree | adverbs and phrases | verbs and impersonal phrases | mood |
|---|---|---|---|
| certain | *assurément, indéniablement, incontestablement, sans aucun doute, à l'évidence* | *il est certain / évident que, force est de constater que* | indicative |
| very likely | *manifestement, vraisemblablement, selon toute vraisemblance* | *tout porte à croire que, il est probable que* | indicative |
| likely | *probablement, sans doute* (= probably, not "without doubt") | *il semble que* (usually subjunctive), *il semblerait que* | subjunctive or indicative |
| possible | *peut-être, éventuellement* (= possibly, not "eventually") | *il se peut que, il n'est pas exclu que, il est possible que* | subjunctive |
| doubtful | *guère probable, douteux* | *il est peu probable que, il est douteux que* | subjunctive |

- *S'avérer, se révéler* + adjective state what turned out to be true: *L'hypothèse s'est
  avérée fausse.*
- Degrees of commitment in verbs: *affirmer* > *soutenir* > *estimer* > *penser* > *supposer* >
  *se demander si*.
- Over- and understatement: *un véritable désastre* vs *un résultat mitigé*; a *nuancé* view vs a
  *catégorique* one.

## Distancing: "this is what others say"

| device | example |
|---|---|
| reportive conditional (B2) | *Le virus aurait été détecté dès mars.* |
| *selon, d'après, à en croire* | *À en croire ses partisans, la réforme serait un succès.* |
| *prétendu, soi-disant, présumé* | *ce prétendu remède ; le présumé coupable* (*présumé* is the legal word; *soi-disant* is informal and ironic) |
| quotation marks of distance | *ce qu'il appelle sa « méthode »* |
| *sous toute réserve* | unconfirmed information |
| *il semblerait que* | a cautious report |

## Hedging in academic and scientific writing

*On peut penser que … ; Il est permis de supposer que … ; Ces résultats suggèrent que … ;
Dans l'état actuel des connaissances, … ; Il y a lieu de nuancer …* Avoid *je pense que* in a
synthesis (no opinion) and in a research paper (use *nous* or impersonal forms).

## The implicit

| notion | what it is | example | what is implied |
|---|---|---|---|
| **presupposition** (présupposé) | what a sentence takes for granted, even if negated | *Il a cessé de mentir.* / *Il n'a pas cessé de mentir.* | he lied before |
| triggers | *encore, de nouveau, ne … plus, aussi, même*, *regretter que, savoir que*, *enfin* | *Même Paul a compris.* | Paul is slow to understand |
| **implication** (sous-entendu, B2) | what the speaker leaves the listener to infer; deniable | *Il est minuit…* (said to guests) | it's time to leave |
| **irony / antiphrasis** | saying the opposite of what one means | *Bravo, quelle organisation !* (after a fiasco) | the organisation was bad |
| **litotes** (B2) | saying less to mean more | *Ce n'est pas faux.* | that's right (a reserved agreement) |
| **connotation** | the associations of a word | *un régime* vs *un gouvernement* | a hostile view |
| **rhetorical question** | a question that is a statement | *Qui pourrait s'y opposer ?* | nobody can |
| **second degré** | not to be taken literally | *au second degré* | humour, irony |

## Reporting the implicit neutrally (synthesis, compte rendu)

*L'auteur laisse entendre que … ; Le document suggère que … ; Sans le dire explicitement, X
présente … comme … ; Le ton ironique de Y montre qu'il désapprouve …*

## Politeness through indirectness

*Vous auriez l'heure ?* (= what time is it?) ; *Je me demandais si vous pourriez …* ; *Il serait
peut-être bon de …* ; *Je ne suis pas certain de vous suivre* (= I disagree / I don't understand);
*Je me permettrai de nuancer …* (= I disagree).

references.title: The subjunctive and mood choice at C1
references.body:
B1 and B2 taught the subjunctive after verbs of will, feeling, doubt and necessity, after
conjunctions (*bien que, pour que, avant que, à condition que* …), in relatives (*Je cherche
quelqu'un qui sache …*), after superlatives, and in concession (*quel que soit, si … que*). C1
adds the subjunctive without a main verb, alternatives, and the fine cases below.

## The subjunctive in independent clauses

| use | examples | register |
|---|---|---|
| order or wish for a third person | *Qu'il patiente ! Que personne ne sorte !* | all |
| set phrases (B1) | *Vive la République ! Soit ! Ainsi soit-il. Sauve qui peut !* | all |
| set phrases (C1) | *Advienne que pourra. Qu'à cela ne tienne. Que je sache, … Grand bien vous fasse. Dieu vous entende !* | neutral to formal |
| hypothesis + consequence | *Qu'un seul donneur se retire, et l'essai s'arrête.* | formal |
| hypothesis in reasoning | *Soit un triangle ABC.* (let ABC be a triangle) | maths, logic |
| literary wish (recognition) | *Puisse-t-il réussir ! Plût au ciel qu'il fût là !* | literary |

## Alternatives

| construction | mood | example |
|---|---|---|
| *que … ou que …* | subjunctive | *Qu'on l'approuve ou qu'on le rejette, ce texte fera date.* |
| *que … ou non* | subjunctive | *Qu'il le veuille ou non, il devra signer.* |
| *soit que … soit que …* (formal) | subjunctive | *Il s'est tu, soit qu'il eût peur, soit qu'il ne sût rien.* (literary tenses: recognition) / *soit qu'il ait eu peur, soit qu'il n'ait rien su* |

## *Que* replacing a conjunction

A second clause can repeat a conjunction with plain *que*. *Que* keeps the mood of the
conjunction it replaces, except after *si*:

| first conjunction | second clause | example |
|---|---|---|
| *quand, lorsque, comme, puisque, parce que* (indicative) | *que* + indicative | *Comme il pleuvait et qu'il faisait froid, on est restés.* |
| *bien que, pour que, avant que* (subjunctive) | *que* + subjunctive | *Bien qu'il soit tard et que tu sois fatigué, …* |
| *si* (indicative) | *que* + subjunctive in careful writing; + indicative in common use | *Si le comité accepte et qu'il obtienne / qu'il obtient les fonds, …* (both correct: don't test one) |

## After verbs and adjectives of feeling

| construction | mood | note |
|---|---|---|
| *être content, navré, ravi, surpris que* | subjunctive | *Je suis navré que vous ayez attendu.* |
| *se plaindre, se réjouir, s'étonner de ce que* | indicative or subjunctive | more formal than *que*; both moods occur: label |
| *au grand soulagement de, à mon grand regret* | — (noun phrase) | *À mon grand regret, je ne pourrai venir.* |
| *il est regrettable, étonnant, normal que* | subjunctive | value judgement |
| *il est certain, évident, probable que* | indicative | certainty (B2's reviewer fixed an overgeneralisation here) |

## Restriction and concession with the subjunctive (C1)

- *pour autant que* + subjunctive: *pour autant que je sache* (as far as I know).
- *si* + adjective + *soit-il* (formal inversion, concession): *Si grand soit-il, ce musée ne
  peut tout exposer.* Also *Si grand qu'il soit* (B2) and *Tout grand qu'il est / qu'il soit*.
- *quand bien même* + conditionnel (B2): *Quand bien même il le voudrait, …*

## Mood after *il semble que*, *il semblerait que*

| expression | usual mood |
|---|---|
| *il semble que* | subjunctive (the indicative is also found, for a firmer impression) |
| *il me semble que* | indicative |
| *il semblerait que* | subjunctive or indicative (softer; journalistic) |
| *il paraît que* | indicative (hearsay) |

## One chart: which mood?

| the clause expresses … | mood |
|---|---|
| a fact, a certainty, a statement, hearsay | indicative |
| a wish, an order, a necessity, a feeling, a judgement, a doubt, a possibility | subjunctive |
| a hypothesis seen as unreal or a softened statement | conditionnel |
| a concession with *quel que soit, si … que, bien que, encore que* | subjunctive |
| a concession with *même si, alors que, tandis que* | indicative |
| a concession with *quand bien même* | conditionnel |

When natives and grammars accept two moods (superlative + relative, *le fait que, après que, si
… et que, ne pas nier que*), choose by meaning and register: the subjunctive presents the idea, the
indicative presents a fact.

references.title: Registers, spoken French and the formal sentence
references.body:
Three registers (*niveaux de langue*): **familier** (friends, family, texting), **courant**
(neutral: most speech and writing), **soutenu** (formal writing, speeches, literature). A neutral
word fits almost everywhere; an informal word in a formal text, or a very formal word in a chat,
is a **register clash**.

## Words in three registers

| familier | courant | soutenu |
|---|---|---|
| *un bouquin* | *un livre* | *un ouvrage* |
| *la bagnole* | *la voiture* | *le véhicule, l'automobile* |
| *le fric* | *l'argent* | *les fonds, les deniers* |
| *bosser* | *travailler* | *exercer (un métier), œuvrer* |
| *piger* | *comprendre* | *saisir, concevoir* |
| *crevé* | *fatigué, épuisé* | *exténué* |
| *se grouiller* | *se dépêcher* | *se hâter* |
| *chiper* | *voler* | *dérober* |
| *la bouffe* | *la nourriture, le repas* | *les mets* (dishes) |
| *se fringuer* | *s'habiller* | *se vêtir* |
| *rigoler, se marrer* | *rire* | *s'esclaffer* (burst out laughing) |
| *chez moi* | *chez moi, à la maison* | *à mon domicile* |
| *demander* | *se renseigner* | *s'enquérir de* |

## Grammar markers

| feature | familier | courant | soutenu |
|---|---|---|---|
| negation | *J'sais pas.* (no *ne*) | *Je ne sais pas.* | *Je ne sais.* (*ne* alone with *savoir, pouvoir, oser, cesser*) |
| question | *Tu viens ?* *Tu pars quand ?* | *Est-ce que tu viens ?* | *Viens-tu ? Quand partez-vous ?* |
| "we" | *on* | *on / nous* | *nous* |
| demonstrative | *ça* | *ça / cela* | *cela* |
| word order | dislocation: *Moi, ce film, je l'ai adoré.* | *J'ai adoré ce film.* | fronted adverbials, inversion: *Sans doute a-t-il raison.* |
| "there is" | *y a* | *il y a* | *il existe, on compte* |

## Spoken French (recognise; use only in informal speech)

- **Reduced forms:** *chuis* (je suis), *t'as* (tu as), *y a* (il y a), *faut* (il faut), *p't-être*
  (peut-être), *ch'ais pas* (je ne sais pas). Never write them, except to quote speech.
- **Discourse markers:** *ben, bah* (hesitation), *bon* (starting or closing a topic), *hein* (tag:
  right?), *quoi* (end of a statement: you know), *genre* (like, approximation), *du coup* (so),
  *en fait* (actually), *carrément, grave* (totally), *bof* (meh).
- **Intensifiers:** *vachement, trop* (= very: *c'est trop bien*), *super, hyper, grave*.

## The formal sentence

| device | example |
|---|---|
| inversion after *ainsi, aussi* (consequence) | *Le budget manquait ; aussi le projet a-t-il été reporté.* |
| inversion after *peut-être, sans doute, à peine, du moins, tout au plus, encore* | *Du moins le croit-on. Encore faut-il le prouver.* |
| *rares sont, tel est, reste* + subject | *Rares sont les traités ratifiés si vite. Reste à savoir si …* |
| simple inversion in relative and comparative clauses | *la ville où naquit le poète ; comme le rappelait l'ambassadrice* |
| *ne* alone | *Il ne cesse de pleuvoir. Je n'ose y croire. Je ne saurais vous dire.* |
| fixed *ne* alone | *si je ne m'abuse ; il y a longtemps que je ne l'ai vu* |
| formal negation | *nullement, aucunement* (in no way); *ne … point, ne … guère* (literary) |
| conditional of *savoir* (polite refusal) | *Je ne saurais accepter.* |

## Tu and vous

*Vous* is the default with strangers, clients, older people and most managers in France; *tu* is
usual among friends, students, young colleagues and in many start-ups and sports clubs. The person
of higher status or the older person usually proposes *tu* (*On peut se tutoyer ?*). In Québec
*tu* is far more widespread, including at work; in Belgium and Switzerland usage is close to
France's.

## Regional words (see honors 04h1)

| Belgium | Switzerland | Québec | France |
|---|---|---|---|
| *septante, nonante* | *septante, huitante, nonante* | *soixante-dix, quatre-vingt-dix* | *soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix* |
| *le GSM* | *le natel* | *le cellulaire* | *le portable* |
| *le bourgmestre* | *le syndic* (some cantons) | *le maire* | *le maire* |
| *à tantôt* | *à tout à l'heure* | *à tantôt* | *à tout à l'heure* |

Check every regional word in Usito, the *Dictionnaire suisse romand* or a Belgian source before
using it.

references.title: Sequence of tenses, stylistic values and participles at C1
references.body:
## Concordance des temps (sequence of tenses)

The tense of the subordinate clause depends on the main verb and on the time relation (before,
same time, after).

**Indicative and conditional**

| main verb | earlier | same time | later |
|---|---|---|---|
| present: *Elle pense que …* | *il est parti* | *il part* | *il partira* |
| past: *Elle pensait / a pensé que …* | *il était parti* | *il partait* | *il partirait* (later than then) / *il serait parti* (done before a later point) |
| future: *Elle dira que …* | *il est parti* | *il part* | *il partira* |

A general truth or a fact still true can keep the present after a past main verb: *Le guide a
rappelé que le site date du Néolithique* (*datait* is also correct: the present insists that it
is still true).

**Subjunctive (modern French)**

| main verb (any tense) | same time or later | earlier |
|---|---|---|
| *Je veux / Je voulais / Je voudrai que …* | *qu'il vienne* | *qu'il soit venu* |

Classical prose (until the early 20th century) used the imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive after
a past main verb: *Je voulais qu'il vînt; Je doutais qu'il fût venu.* Recognise them; don't write
them.

**Infinitive:** present infinitive for the same time or later, past infinitive for earlier: *Il
espère réussir / Il pense avoir réussi.*

**Hypotheses (si-clauses), including mixed ones**

| si + | main clause | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| present | present, future, imperative | real condition |
| imparfait | conditionnel présent | unreal now |
| plus-que-parfait | conditionnel passé | unreal past |
| plus-que-parfait | conditionnel présent | past condition, present result: *Si on avait fouillé plus tôt, on saurait aujourd'hui …* |
| imparfait | conditionnel passé | permanent condition, past result: *S'il était prudent, il n'aurait pas creusé là.* |

## Stylistic values of the tenses

| tense | value | example |
|---|---|---|
| présent | historique / de narration | *En 1940, quatre adolescents découvrent la grotte.* |
| présent | general truth | *L'eau bout à 100 °C.* |
| présent | near future or past | *J'arrive dans cinq minutes. Il sort d'ici.* |
| imparfait | narratif (de rupture): a single completed event, in writing | *Deux ans plus tard, elle remportait le prix.* |
| imparfait | d'atténuation (politeness) | *Je voulais vous demander un service.* |
| imparfait | hypothétique (what almost happened) | *Un pas de plus, et il tombait.* |
| imparfait | hypocoristique (to a child or pet; recognition) | *Il avait faim, mon bébé ?* |
| plus-que-parfait | d'atténuation | *J'étais venu vous parler de mon projet.* |
| futur | historique / prospectif (a later event in a past story) | *Elle ne le sait pas encore : dix ans plus tard, elle dirigera le musée.* |
| futur | de politesse | *Je vous demanderai de patienter.* |
| futur | de supposition | *On sonne : ce sera le facteur.* |
| futur | injonctif (a firm instruction) | *Tu rangeras ta chambre avant de sortir.* |
| futur antérieur | supposition about the past (B2) | *Il aura oublié.* |
| conditionnel | reportive (B2) | *Le séisme aurait fait vingt victimes.* |
| passé surcomposé | completed before a passé composé (spoken, regional; recognition) | *Quand il a eu fini, il est parti.* |

## Recognition-only forms

| form | example | everyday equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| passé simple | *il fut, elle prit, ils vinrent* | passé composé |
| passé antérieur | *quand il eut fini* | passé composé / *après avoir fini* |
| imparfait du subjonctif | *qu'il fût, qu'elle prît, qu'ils vinssent* | subjonctif présent |
| plus-que-parfait du subjonctif | *qu'il eût fini, qu'elle fût partie* | subjonctif passé |
| conditionnel passé deuxième forme | *il eût fallu, j'eusse aimé* | conditionnel passé |

## Participles in long sentences

| construction | example | note |
|---|---|---|
| proposition participiale (own subject) | *La réunion terminée, chacun rentra. Une fois la décision prise, …* | the participle agrees with its own noun |
