levels.description: Answers the question in the right form, with small lapses of register or a slightly short or overlong text.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Drifts from the question, ignores the form or the readers, or is well under 250 words.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Does not answer the question set.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: States a clear, qualified position; develops each argument with a reason and an example; presents an objection fairly and answers it.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Takes a position and supports it, but one argument is thin or the objection is only mentioned.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: The position is unclear or arguments are listed without reasons or examples; no objection is considered.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No identifiable position or argument.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Draws on the documents accurately and in its own words, gives dates and sources, and adds examples of its own.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Uses the documents accurately but leans on them, or adds no example of its own.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Copies sentences from the documents, or misstates a fact or a position.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Ignores the dossier or misrepresents it throughout.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Introduction with hook, problématique and plan; one idea per paragraph with a topic sentence; precise connectors and clear reference; a conclusion that answers and opens.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: A visible plan and paragraphs, with some repetitive or imprecise connectors.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Paragraphs are missing or mix ideas; links between ideas are often unclear.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No discernible organisation.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Varied, precise vocabulary and sentence structures; moods, tenses and agreement are controlled; errors are rare and do not hinder reading.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Good range with some repetition; occasional errors of mood, agreement or spelling that do not obscure meaning.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Limited range or frequent errors that sometimes obscure meaning.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Errors make much of the text hard to understand.

rubrics.title: Register shift into a professional email (C1)

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Reports every relevant fact accurately (the crash, the time, the lost files, the two-day delay, the client, the proposal), in a clear order, and leaves out the jokes, feelings and requests meant for colleagues.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Reports the main facts accurately, but one is missing or something irrelevant to the director stays in.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Several facts are missing, changed or out of order, so the director would need to ask questions.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The email does not report the incident.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Every informal word is replaced by a neutral or formal one that fits its context (tomber en panne or cesser de fonctionner, comprendre, se plaindre or être mécontent), with no new clash from an overformal or misused word.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: The register is formal throughout except for one informal word or one word that does not quite fit its context.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Several informal words remain, or formal words are used with the wrong meaning or combination.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The vocabulary stays mostly informal.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Uses nous, the full negation, cela and complete sentences throughout; the proposal is in the conditional or a polite formula; no dislocation or spoken question form remains.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: The grammar is formal with one slip (an on, a missing ne, a ça).

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Several spoken features remain (on, missing ne, dislocation, question by intonation).

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The grammar is that of the chat message.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: An informative subject line, a greeting suited to a director the writer calls vous, the purpose in the first sentence, short paragraphs, and a short professional closing with a signature.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: The conventions are there, with one weak element (a vague subject line, a greeting that is too warm, a long letter formula).

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Two or more conventions are missing or wrong.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The text does not look like a professional email.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Agreement, moods, tenses, accents and spelling are controlled; errors are rare and do not distract.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: A few errors of agreement, accents or mood that do not obscure the meaning.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Frequent errors that sometimes obscure the meaning.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Errors make the email hard to understand.

rubrics.title: Compte rendu of an opinion piece (C1)

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: States the author's main idea and reports every step of the argument in the author's order and proportions, without distorting any point; illustrations are left out or reduced to the idea they support.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: The main idea and most steps are there and accurate; one step is missing, over-weighted or slightly bent.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Several steps are missing or out of proportion, or the text follows the examples rather than the argument.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The main idea is missing or misread.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Names the source at the start, stays in the third person, uses varied and precise reporting verbs that match what the author does (sets out, maintains, stresses, regrets), and keeps the author's caution; no opinion of the writer's own.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: The stance is right, but the reporting verbs repeat (dit, dit que) or one verb misstates what the author does.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: The source is missing, or the text slips into the author's voice or into a judgement of the writer's own.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The text is a summary in the author's voice or a personal reaction, not a report.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Every sentence is the writer's own: keywords kept, structures changed (nominalisation, regrouping, generalisation).

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Mostly reformulated; one or two phrases stay close to the original.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Several sentences are copied or changed by one word.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The text is largely copied.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: The author's plan is visible through well-chosen links (d'abord, ensuite, enfin; or, pourtant, en effet); sentences flow without repetition.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: The order is clear, with one weak or wrong link.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Sentences follow each other as a list; the logic of the original is hard to see.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No recognisable order.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Precise vocabulary and controlled grammar (agreement, moods, accents), errors rare; the length is within the set range and the count is given.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: A few errors that do not obscure meaning, or the length is slightly outside the range.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Frequent errors, or the length is far outside the range.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Errors make the text hard to follow.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Neutral throughout: no opinion, no je, no outside fact or example, no quoted sentence; length within 200 to 240 words, with the count given.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: One small breach: a judging word (heureusement, à juste titre), one outside detail, or a length just outside the range.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Several breaches, or a paragraph of opinion, or a length far outside the range.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The text is a personal essay or a copy of the documents.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Keeps the key ideas of every document, with their weight and their nuances (the authors' caution, their concessions), and attributes each to its source.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: The key ideas are there; one is missing, misattributed or slightly bent.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: One document is neglected, or several ideas are wrong or unattributed.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The documents are misread.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: The introduction presents the theme, the documents and a problématique they share; the body is organised by ideas, each paragraph confronting at least two documents; the conclusion answers the problématique without opinion.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Organised by ideas, but the problématique is vague or one paragraph rests on a single document.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Mostly document by document, or no problématique, or no conclusion.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: A string of summaries of each document.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Agreement, difference and nuance between the documents are stated explicitly with varied tools (s'accorder à dire, rejoindre, quant à, à l'inverse, tandis que); references and connectors keep the text easy to follow.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: The relations are shown, with a narrow or repetitive set of links.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Documents are placed side by side without saying how they relate.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No relation between documents is shown.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Condensed in the writer's own words throughout; only keywords come from the documents.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Mostly reformulated; one or two phrases are close to the originals.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Several sentences are copied or lightly changed.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Largely copied.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: A wide, precise vocabulary and varied structures (nominal style, relatives, participial clauses); only a few minor slips.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Good range with a few errors that do not obscure meaning.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Limited range or frequent errors that sometimes obscure meaning.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Errors make the synthesis hard to follow.

rubrics.title: Essai argumenté in a set form (C1)

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Answers the exact question asked, in the set form (here a formal letter, with its layout) and for its reader; the register is consistent from greeting to closing; at least 250 words, with the count given.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Answers the question in the right form, with one lapse (a missing element of layout, one word out of register).

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Drifts from the question, ignores the form or the reader, or is clearly under length.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Off the subject or not an argued text.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Takes a clear, qualified position; each argument is explained and supported by a relevant example of the writer's own; the strongest objection is stated fairly and answered.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: A clear position with developed arguments, but examples are thin or the objection is weak or not answered.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: The position is unclear or one-sided; arguments are listed rather than developed.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No identifiable position.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: An introduction that opens, frames the question and announces the plan; two or three parts that each serve the answer, linked by transitions; a conclusion that answers and may open the question.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: A sound plan with one weak element (a flat opening, a missing transition, a conclusion that only repeats).

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Paragraphs exist but the plan is hard to see, or the introduction or conclusion is missing.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No visible structure.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Varied, accurate connectors of cause, concession and consequence; the writer's commitment is graded (certes, à condition que, du moins, il me semble); references are clear.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Good links with some repetition or one misused connector.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Few or misused connectors; claims are all-or-nothing.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Sentences are not linked.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: A wide, precise vocabulary (collocations, the theme's terms) and complex structures used with control; moods, agreement and accents are accurate, errors rare.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Good range with a few errors that do not obscure meaning.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Limited range or frequent errors that sometimes obscure meaning.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Errors make the text hard to follow.

rubrics.title: Note with proposals for a decision-maker (C1)

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: A complete heading (issuing service, date, NOTE à l'attention de …, an Objet line, references to the documents), titled parts I and II with sub-parts A and B, and a separate numbered list of proposals.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: The layout of a note is there, with one element missing or weak (no Objet line, untitled sub-parts, proposals mixed into the body).

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Some features of a note, but it reads mostly like an essay or a letter.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No heading, no parts and no proposals: the text is not laid out as a note.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Every important point of the three documents is there, accurately, with the documents cited (doc. 1, doc. 2, doc. 3), reformulated rather than copied, and nothing is added from outside the file.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: The main points are there and accurate, but one important point is missing, or a sentence is copied, or one idea comes from outside the file.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Several points are missing or distorted, or the note relies on long copied passages or outside knowledge.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The note does not use the file.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: A short introduction gives the context, the problem and the announced plan; the parts are organised by ideas, not by document, and every title says something (a short claim, not just Avantages).

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: A clear plan by ideas, but the introduction lacks one element or one title is vague.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: The note follows the documents one by one, or the plan is announced but not kept.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No recognisable introduction or plan.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Two to four numbered proposals, each operational (who does what, when or where), each drawn from the file and together answering the reservations of part II; the decision is left to the mayor.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Sound proposals drawn from the file, but one is vague or does not answer anything raised in the body.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Proposals that are general wishes, or that do not follow from the file.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: No proposals.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Neutral and impersonal throughout (no je, no opinion in parts I and II; il est proposé de, il conviendrait de), in concise full sentences, within the word range.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: Mostly neutral and concise, with one personal or emotional slip, or slightly outside the word range.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Several personal comments or informal phrases, or wordy and well outside the range.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: The register is that of a personal opinion piece or a chat message.

levels.label: Strong
levels.description: Agreement, moods, tenses, accents and spelling are controlled; vocabulary is precise and varied (nominal style, connectors, the conditionnel of hedging); errors are rare.

levels.label: Clear
levels.description: A few errors of agreement, accents or mood that do not obscure the meaning; vocabulary mostly precise.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Frequent errors or a narrow vocabulary that sometimes obscure the meaning.

levels.label: Not yet
levels.description: Errors make the note hard to understand.

writing.title: Essai argumenté : faut-il simplifier l'orthographe ?
writing.prompt:
Write an argued essay in French, using the dossier in lesson 93 (the news item, the two opinion pieces, the interview and the invented survey).

*Le journal de votre université ouvre ses pages à un débat : « Faut-il simplifier l'orthographe du français ? » Vous lui adressez un article argumenté d'au moins 250 mots, dans lequel vous prenez position.*

- Give your article a title and write for students and teachers who read the paper.
- Take a clear position, and present at least one objection fairly before you answer it.
- Use the documents in your own words, with their facts and dates, and add at least one example of your own. Don't present the survey's invented figures as real.
- Write the word count at the end, as in the exam, then reread with the lesson's checklist.

writing.title: Changer de registre : du message d'équipe au courriel à la direction
writing.prompt:
Lucas, an engineer in your team, posted this message in the team chat this morning. You are his colleague, and your manager, Mme Claire Vasseur, the technical director, has asked you to report the incident to her by email.

> Salut la team ! Bon, grosse galère ce matin : le serveur a planté vers 9 h et on a perdu tous les fichiers du projet Delta qu'on avait pas sauvegardés. J'ai rien pigé, le prestataire dit que c'est pas sa faute. Du coup, on a deux jours de retard, et le client va râler, c'est sûr. Faudrait qu'on ait une vraie sauvegarde automatique, franchement, et que quelqu'un vérifie ça chaque semaine. Je peux m'en occuper si la direction est OK. Vous pouvez me filer vos fichiers perso avant jeudi ? Merci !

Write the email in French to Mme Vasseur, whom you call *vous*.

- Give it a subject line (*Objet : …*), a greeting and a closing suited to a professional email.
- Keep every fact she needs (what happened, when, the consequences, Lucas's proposal) and leave out what doesn't belong in a message to her.
- Use the formal register throughout: words (*planter, piger, râler, filer, la galère* …), grammar (*nous*, not *on*; the full negation; *cela*), and complete sentences.
- Turn Lucas's suggestion into a polite proposal (the conditional, or *il me semblerait utile que* + subjunctive).
- Reread in passes, as lesson 04 suggests: facts, register, then accents and agreement.

writing.title: Compte rendu : « Le mal assis »
writing.prompt:
Write a **compte rendu** in French of the opinion piece below (document 2 of lesson 18, 357 words; the author and the newspaper are invented).

> **Le mal assis**, par le Dr Karim Benali, médecin du sport, *La Gazette du Val*, avril 2026 > > Nous n'avons jamais autant parlé de sport, et jamais aussi peu bougé. Entre le bureau, la voiture et le canapé, il n'est pas rare qu'un adulte passe plus de sept heures par jour assis. Cette sédentarité est trop souvent confondue avec le manque d'activité physique. Ce sont pourtant deux choses distinctes : on peut courir trois fois par semaine et rester, le reste du temps, parfaitement sédentaire. > > Or la position assise prolongée est néfaste en elle-même. Les études convergent : de longues heures quotidiennes passées assis sans interruption augmentent le risque de maladies cardiovasculaires, de diabète et d'obésité, y compris chez des personnes qui font du sport de temps en temps. L'heure de jogging du dimanche ne compense pas cinq jours passés vissé à une chaise. Je le constate chaque semaine en consultation : des patients sportifs, persuadés d'être à l'abri, découvrent un surpoids abdominal ou des douleurs lombaires qu'ils ne s'expliquent pas. > > Les enfants n'échappent pas à la règle. Entre les heures de classe, les trajets en voiture et les écrans du soir, beaucoup passent l'essentiel de leur journée assis. On s'inquiète, à juste titre, des heures qu'ils passent devant les écrans ; on s'inquiète beaucoup moins de leur immobilité, qui en est pourtant le corollaire. > > Le mal ne s'arrête pas au corps. Le travail sédentaire s'accompagne souvent de surmenage : longues journées, visioconférences enchaînées, courriels du soir. Fatigués, nous renonçons à bouger ; moins actifs, nous dormons plus mal. Le cercle est vicieux. > > La bonne nouvelle, c'est que les bienfaits du mouvement se font sentir très vite. Se lever quelques minutes toutes les heures, marcher pendant un appel téléphonique, prendre l'escalier plutôt que l'ascenseur : ces gestes simples suffisent à réduire une partie des effets nocifs de la position assise. Les recommandations de santé publique invitent d'ailleurs à limiter le temps passé assis et à l'interrompre régulièrement. > > Encore faut-il que les entreprises et les écoles s'en donnent les moyens. Je déplore qu'on investisse dans des salles de sport d'entreprise fréquentées par une minorité, quand des bureaux réglables en hauteur et des pauses actives profiteraient à tous. Bouger ne devrait pas être une performance réservée au week-end, mais une habitude de chaque heure.

What to do:

- Name the source (author, genre, newspaper, date) in your first sentence.
- Write in the third person and report each step of the author's argument with a precise reporting verb (*exposer, avancer, soutenir, mettre en avant, souligner, déplorer* …).
- Follow the author's plan and keep its proportions; leave out the illustrations that only decorate an idea.
- Reformulate: keep the keywords, change the structures. Give no opinion of your own.
- Write **90 to 130 words**, about a quarter to a third of the text. The DALF C1 has no compte rendu task, so this is not an exam figure: it follows lesson 18's rule of thumb (a summary keeps about a quarter of the text, and a compte rendu runs a little longer because the reporting verbs take room). The editor counts *l'homme* as one word; an exam paper may count differently, so follow its instructions there.
- Write the word count at the end, then reread for agreement, moods and accents.

writing.title: Synthèse de documents : le téléphone portable à l'école
writing.prompt:
Write a **synthèse de documents** in French from the short dossier below: three original documents of about 650 words in all. The school, the authors, the association and its survey are invented; the 2018 law in document 1 is real.

**Document 1.** *Article in a regional daily, December 2026.*

> **Au collège des Tilleuls, les téléphones restent au casier** > > Depuis la rentrée, au collège des Tilleuls, les téléphones ne quittent plus le casier où les élèves les déposent en arrivant. La loi interdit déjà depuis 2018 aux élèves des écoles et des collèges d'utiliser leur téléphone dans l'établissement, sauf pour un usage pédagogique ou dans les lieux prévus par le règlement intérieur ; mais, reconnaît la principale, « l'interdiction était devenue théorique : les appareils restaient dans les poches, et l'on jouait au chat et à la souris dans les couloirs ». > > Trois mois plus tard, le bilan dressé par l'équipe est encourageant. Les cours de récréation, autrefois silencieuses, ont retrouvé leurs ballons et leurs bavardages. Les surveillants constatent moins de bagarres déclenchées par une photo ou un message, et les conseillers d'éducation traitent moins de cas de harcèlement en ligne pendant les heures de cours. Plusieurs professeurs affirment que leurs élèves sont plus attentifs, même s'ils reconnaissent qu'il est trop tôt pour mesurer un effet sur les résultats. > > Tout n'est pas réglé pour autant. Certains parents s'inquiètent de ne plus pouvoir joindre leur enfant en cas d'urgence ; le collège leur rappelle que l'accueil reste joignable à toute heure. Surtout, l'équipe sait que l'essentiel se joue ailleurs : « Nous pouvons protéger sept heures par jour, explique un professeur principal. Mais si le téléphone reste allumé jusqu'à minuit dans la chambre, nous ne faisons que déplacer le problème. »

**Document 2.** *Opinion piece by Thomas Leroy, a teacher of French in a lycée, in an education magazine, 2026.*

> **Interdire n'est pas éduquer**
>
> Chaque année, le même débat revient, et chaque année la même réponse s'impose : interdire. Je comprends la tentation. Mais à force de traiter le téléphone comme un objet dangereux, nous renonçons à apprendre à nos élèves à s'en servir. > > Dans ma classe, le smartphone est un outil parmi d'autres. Mes élèves de seconde l'utilisent pour s'enregistrer avant un oral et s'écouter ensuite, pour consulter un dictionnaire en ligne, pour répondre à un questionnaire dont je vois les résultats en direct. Ces usages ne remplacent ni le livre ni le cahier ; ils les complètent, à des moments choisis, et l'appareil retourne ensuite au fond du sac. > > Surtout, l'école est le seul lieu où l'on puisse apprendre, avec un adulte, à vérifier une information, à protéger ses données, à repérer une manipulation. Ces compétences ne s'acquièrent pas dans un casier fermé à clé. Les adolescents passeront leur vie avec un téléphone en poche : mieux vaut qu'ils apprennent à le maîtriser en classe que seuls, le soir, devant des contenus conçus pour les captiver. > > Je ne plaide pas pour le téléphone libre en cours : un usage pédagogique suppose des règles claires et un enseignant qui les fasse respecter. Mais la frontière que nous devons tracer ne passe pas entre l'école et l'écran ; elle passe entre l'usage subi et l'usage choisi.

**Document 3.** *Extract from the 2026 report of a parents' association,* Ensemble pour l'école.

> **Des parents partagés**
>
> Notre questionnaire, auquel ont répondu 1 200 parents d'élèves de collège et de lycée, révèle des familles plus partagées qu'on ne le croit. Une large majorité, près de sept parents sur dix, approuve les règles qui limitent l'usage du téléphone en classe. Mais lorsqu'on leur demande s'ils accepteraient que leur enfant parte le matin sans téléphone, la proportion s'inverse : la plupart y voient un moyen de rassurer et d'être rassurés, en particulier sur les longs trajets. > > Les inquiétudes les plus fréquentes portent sur le harcèlement en ligne, cité par un parent sur deux, puis sur le temps passé sur les réseaux sociaux et sur le sommeil. Beaucoup reconnaissent leur propre difficulté à fixer des limites : « Comment interdire à mon fils ce que je fais moi-même à table ? » écrit une mère. > > Les familles attendent surtout de la cohérence. Elles souhaitent que les règles soient les mêmes d'une classe à l'autre et d'un établissement à l'autre, et que l'école les associe aux décisions plutôt que de les leur annoncer. Plusieurs proposent des réunions consacrées aux usages numériques, où parents et enseignants pourraient s'accorder sur quelques principes communs. Une demande revient enfin avec insistance : que l'on parle moins d'interdire et davantage d'accompagner.

What to do, as lesson 19 teaches:

- Fill a *grille de lecture* (documents in columns, ideas in rows), then find the question the three documents answer together.
- Write an introduction (theme, the documents in a phrase, the problématique, the plan), two or three paragraphs organised **by ideas**, each confronting at least two documents, and a short conclusion that answers the problématique.
- Report only what the documents say: no opinion, no *je*, no outside facts or examples, no quoted sentences (keywords may stay). Name the source of each idea.
- A title is optional here; if you give one, it isn't counted.
- Write **200 to 240 words**, the length FEI's candidate manual (July 2022) gives for the DALF C1 synthesis; an exam corpus is usually longer (about 1,000 words in all, in a university description), and the paper's own instructions always win. The editor counts *l'homme* as one word.
- Write the word count at the end, then reread for agreement, moods, connectors and the source of every idea.

writing.title: Essai argumenté : joignable jusqu'à 21 heures ?
writing.prompt:
Write an **essai argumenté** in French, in the form of a formal letter.

*La direction de l'entreprise où vous travaillez prépare une charte sur le droit à la déconnexion. Dans un courriel adressé à tout le personnel, la directrice des ressources humaines, Mme Hélène Robin, propose que les salariés restent « joignables jusqu'à 21 heures en cas d'urgence » et invite chacun à lui donner son avis par écrit. Vous lui adressez une lettre dans laquelle vous prenez position sur cette proposition.*

(Mme Robin and the company are invented.)

What to do, as lesson 20 teaches:

- Read the subject with the four questions: form (a formal letter), addressee (a director you call *vous*), register (formal throughout), and the question behind it (should employees be reachable until 9 p.m., and on what terms?).
- Lay it out as a letter: place and date, *Objet :* line, *Madame,* and a formal closing formula.
- Take a clear position and qualify it: grant what is reasonable in the proposal, refute the strongest objection to your view, and, if you wish, make a counter-proposal (what counts as an urgency? who decides? what in return?).
- Use your own examples (your job, your country, what you have read); the lesson's background facts may help, but don't present any figure you aren't sure of.
- Plan in two or three parts, with an introduction that frames the question and a conclusion that answers it.
- Write **at least 250 words**, the minimum FEI's candidate manual (July 2022) gives for the DALF C1 essay (an older sample paper said "about 250"); there is no maximum, but 300 to 400 words is a sensible target. In the exam the essay is on the theme of the synthesis documents; here it follows lesson 20's theme.
- Write the word count at the end, then run the lesson's self-check (task, plan, moods, agreement, connectors, register, length).

writing.title: Note avec propositions : végétaliser les cours d'école
writing.prompt:
You work in the education department (*Direction de l'éducation*) of the town hall of Montrevel, an invented town. The mayor, Monsieur le Maire, is considering turning the tarmac playgrounds of the town's three primary schools into greener *cours* (trees, soil, shade and ground that lets rain soak in). He asks you for a note with proposals, based only on the file below. The file is original and its figures are invented.

> **Document 1 (services techniques, note interne).** Les cours des trois écoles élémentaires sont entièrement goudronnées. En juillet dernier, les agents ont relevé au sol plus de 50 °C en milieu d'après-midi. Remplacer une partie du bitume par de la terre, des arbres et des revêtements perméables coûterait entre 150 000 et 250 000 euros par cour. Une partie de la dépense pourrait être couverte par des subventions, à condition de déposer un dossier avant le 30 juin. Ouvertes au public le samedi, ces cours pourraient aussi servir d'îlots de fraîcheur pendant les canicules. > > **Document 2 (presse locale).** À Saint-Aubert, commune voisine, la cour de l'école Jules-Ferry a été végétalisée il y a deux ans. Les enseignants décrivent des récréations plus calmes et des jeux moins centrés sur le football. Certains parents regrettent toutefois la boue en hiver et les vêtements salis, et l'entretien des plantations demande du temps aux agents municipaux. > > **Document 3 (courrier de l'association des parents d'élèves).** Les parents soutiennent le projet, mais demandent à être consultés sur l'aménagement des cours, souhaitent que les travaux aient lieu pendant les vacances d'été et rappellent que les cours doivent rester accessibles aux enfants à mobilité réduite.

Write the note in French.

- Lay it out as a note: the issuing service and the date, *NOTE à l'attention de Monsieur le Maire*, an *Objet* line and the references (documents 1 to 3). Don't sign it with a name.
- Write a short introduction with the context, the problem and the announced plan.
- Write two parts (I and II), each with two sub-parts (A and B), all with titles that say something. Plan by ideas, not by document, and cite the documents (*doc. 1*).
- End with two to four numbered, operational proposals (*préconisations*) drawn from the file, which answer the reservations of your second part. Leave the decision to the mayor.
- Use only the file, in your own words; stay neutral and impersonal (*il est proposé de …*, *il conviendrait de …*); no *je* and no opinion in the body.
- Aim for 250 to 350 words. A real exam note condenses a long file; this file is short, so the note is about as long as the file once you add the heading, titles and proposals. Count your words and write the total at the end, as you would in an exam.
